## 1. Daḷhavagga
## 1. Rājovāda Jātaka

Story of the Present: The Fully Enlightened Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, spoke this Rājovāda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Daḷhaṃ daḷhassa khipati," concerning the instruction of King Kosala.

The instruction of King Kosala will become clear in the Tesakuṇa Jātaka. Specifically, one day, King Kosala, having righteously decided a difficult case that had been influenced by prejudice, finished his morning meal and, with hands still moist, mounted his decorated chariot. He went to the presence of the Blessed One, prostrated at the feet that were as beautiful as blooming lotuses, and sat in a suitable place. Then the Blessed One said to him: "Great King, from where have you come at this time of day?" "Venerable Sir, today, because I was righteously deciding a difficult case that had been influenced by prejudice, I only now found the opportunity. Having finished that case and eaten my morning meal, I have come to attend upon you with hands still moist," he replied.

The Blessed One said: "Great King, deciding a case in accordance with the Dhamma and justice is indeed good; this practice of justice is the path to heaven. It is not surprising that you, receiving instruction from a Fully Enlightened Buddha like me, should decide cases in accordance with the Dhamma and justice. What is truly surprising is that in the past, kings, even though they did not know all things, listened to the words of the wise and decided cases in accordance with the Dhamma..."
2:
...and justice, avoiding the four wrong paths of prejudice such as favoritism, not violating the ten royal virtues, ruling righteously, and filling the heavenly realm. That which happened in the past is indeed wonderful." Having said this, he remained silent. Then, being requested by King Kosala, he brought forth the past.

Story of the Past: Great King, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the Chief Queen. Having received the protection for the fetus, he was safely born from his mother's womb. On the day of his naming, they named him Prince Brahmadatta. In due course, when he reached the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā, attained proficiency in all arts, and upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingship and ruled righteously. He did not follow the wrong paths of prejudice such as favoritism and administered justice.

While the Bodhisatta was ruling righteously in this way, the ministers also decided legal cases with truth. When cases were decided truthfully, there were no more fraudulent litigants. Because of the absence of such fraudulent litigants, the noise of disputes in the palace courtyard ceased. Even if the ministers sat in the place of judgment all day, they saw no one coming for a decision, so they would rise and depart. It is true that the place of judgment reached a state of being abandoned.

The Bodhisatta thought: "While I, King Brahmadatta, am ruling righteously, there are no people coming to the place of judgment, the noise of disputes has ceased, and the place of judgment has reached a state of being abandoned. Now, it is proper for me to search for my own faults. If I hear that 'this is my fault,' I will abandon it and conduct myself only in virtues." From that time on, while investigating whether there was anyone who spoke of his faults, he found no one among those who served inside the palace who spoke of his faults, hearing only praise of his virtues. Thinking, "These people might not speak of my faults out of fear of me and might speak only of my virtues," he investigated among the group of people serving outside the palace. Finding no one there either, he investigated within the city.

He investigated outside the city, at the four gates, and in the villages at the four quarters. In those places too, he found no one who spoke of his faults, hearing only praise of his virtues. Thinking, "I will investigate the countryside," he handed over the kingdom to his ministers, mounted his chariot, took only his charioteer, and left the city in disguise. Investigating the countryside, he went as far as the border regions. Finding no one who spoke of his faults and hearing only praise of his virtues, he turned back from the border toward the city along the main road.
3:
1. He meets the harsh with harshness, Ballika meets the mild with mildness.
He conquers the good with goodness, and the bad with badness.
Such is this king; move out of the way, O charioteer.

He spoke this first verse.

"O charioteer! Our King Ballika imposes harsh punishment upon the harsh. He conquers the mild with mildness. He conquers the good with goodness. He conquers the bad with badness. O charioteer, this king of ours is of such a nature. You, move out of the way."

At that time, King Ballika of Kosala, ruling righteously, was searching for someone who would speak of his faults. Finding no one among his inner circle who spoke ill of him, but hearing only praise of his virtues, he went to the countryside to investigate and reached that place.

Those two kings met face-to-face on a narrow cart track in a low-lying area. There was no place for a chariot to turn aside. Then, King Ballika's charioteer said to the King of Bārāṇasī's charioteer, "O charioteer, move your chariot aside." The King of Bārāṇasī's charioteer also said to King Ballika's charioteer, "O charioteer, move your chariot aside; in this chariot sits the Great King Brahmadatta, the lord of the kingdom of Bārāṇasī." The other also said to him, "O charioteer, in this chariot sits the Great King Ballika, the lord of the kingdom of Kosala. Move your chariot aside and give way to our king's chariot."

The King of Bārāṇasī's charioteer thought, "This one is also a king; what should be done?" Thinking, "There is this way," he decided, "I will ask their ages and make the younger one's chariot move aside to give way to the elder." Upon inquiring and investigating the age of the King of Kosala from his charioteer, he found they were of equal age. He then asked about the extent of the kingdom, army, wealth, fame, birth, lineage, and family background. He learned that both were lords of kingdoms three hundred leagues in extent and were equal in army, wealth, fame, birth, lineage, and family background.
4:
2. Conquer anger with non-anger; conquer the bad with goodness.
Conquer the stingy with giving; conquer the liar with truth.
Such is this king; move out of the way, O charioteer.

He spoke this verse, which completes the two.

"O charioteer! Our king, the lord of Bārāṇasī, conquers the angry with loving-kindness. He conquers the bad with goodness. He conquers the stingy with giving. He conquers the one who speaks falsehood with truth. O charioteer, this king of ours is of such a nature. You, move out of the way."

Knowing that they were equal in army, wealth, attendants, birth, lineage, and family, he thought, "I will give way to the one who possesses virtue," and asked, "O charioteer, what is the nature of your king's virtue and conduct?" Then King Ballika's charioteer, wishing to present even his king's faults as virtues, said, "This is our king's virtue and conduct"—

Then the King of Bārāṇasī's charioteer said to King Ballika's charioteer, "O charioteer, did you speak of your king's virtues?" When King Ballika's charioteer said "Yes," the King of Bārāṇasī's charioteer replied, "If you call those virtues, then what would faults be like?" and added, "Let those be faults for now; what then is your king's virtue?" When King Ballika's charioteer asked this, he said, "In that case, listen"—

When this was said, both King Ballika and his charioteer descended from the chariot, unyoked the horses, moved the chariot aside, and gave way to the King of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī gave advice to King Ballika, saying, "Friend, a king should do such and such things," and then went to Bārāṇasī. Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he filled the heavenly city at the end of his life. King Ballika also took the advice of the King of Bārāṇasī, investigated the countryside, and finding no one who spoke of his faults, went to his own city. Having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, he also filled the heavenly city at the end of his life.
5:
Identifying the Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha, for the purpose of instructing the King of Kosala, brought this Dhamma teaching and said: "O noble King of Kosala, at that time, Moggallāna was the charioteer of King Ballika, Ānanda was King Ballika, Sāriputta was the charioteer of the King of Bārāṇasī, and I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī." Thus He identified the Jātaka.

## Truly Righteous, Precious, and Noble
The Rājovāda Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Siṅgāla Jātaka
## The Jackal and the Lion

The Present Story: While the Omniscient Buddha, who is capable of instructing the world including the devas, was residing at the Kūṭāgārasālā, He told this Siṅgāla Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Asamekkhitakammantaṃ", concerning a certain barber's son living in Vesālī.

The father of that young man performed all the duties for the kings, the royal concubines, the princes, and the princesses, such as trimming beards and dressing hair. He was endowed with faith, had confidence in the Triple Gem, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and observed the Five Precepts. From time to time, he spent his time listening to the Dhamma of the Blessed One.

One day, when that barber went to the royal palace to perform his work, he took his son with him. There, the barber's son saw a Licchavī princess, who was like a celestial nymph and was beautifully adorned. His mind became infatuated through defilement. After leaving the palace with his father, he thought, "I will live only if I get this princess; if I do not get her, let death come to me right here." He stopped eating and lay down, embracing the frame of his bed.

Then his father approached the youth and said, "Dear son, do not have such intense desire for what is unattainable. You are a barber's son of low birth, while the Licchavī maiden is a princess of noble birth. That Licchavī princess is not suitable for you. I will bring you another maiden of similar birth and lineage."
6:
The young man did not take his father's words. Then his mother, brother, sister, uncles, aunts, and all his relatives and close friends gathered and tried to advise him, but they were unable to make him understand. That young man, wasting away on that very bed, reached the end of his life.

Then the father, having performed the funeral rites for the deceased, and with his grief diminished, thought, "I will pay homage to the Blessed One." Taking many perfumes and flowers, he went to the Mahāvana forest, made offerings to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. When the Blessed One asked, "Lay disciple, why have you not been seen for many days?", he reported the matter. The Blessed One said, "Lay disciple, it is not only now that your son has met with destruction by giving rise to intense desire for what is unattainable; in the past also, he met with it." Being requested by the barber, He brought forth the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a lion's family in the Himalayan region. He had six younger brothers and one sister. All the lions lived in a Golden Cave. Near that Golden Cave, there was a Crystal Cave on a Silver Mountain. In that Crystal Cave lived a jackal.

Later, the parents of the lions died. Those lions, leaving their younger sister, the lioness, in the Golden Cave, went out to search for food and brought back meat to give to her.

The jackal, seeing the young lioness, fell in love with her. While the parents of the lioness were alive, he did not get an opportunity. When those seven lions went out to search for food, the jackal descended from the Crystal Cave, went to the door of the Golden Cave, and spoke these secret words related to sensual pleasures, known as worldly bait, in front of the lioness:
7:
3. "One who performs deeds without reflection, rushing headlong into action, their own deeds burn them, like hot food placed in the mouth."

He spoke this first verse. 

"Mukhe," into the mouth. "Ajjhohitaṃ," that which is put in. "Uṇhaṃ," hot food. Just as it burns the mouth and so on, "tathā," likewise, "yāni asamekkhitakammāni," those deeds which are done without reflection, "tāni kammāni," those unreflective deeds, "tappenti," burn the "asamekkhitakammantaṃ," the unreflective doer who is "turitābhinipātinaṃ," accustomed to acting with undue haste.

What does this mean? The young lioness thought: "I am a four-footed beast, and you are also a four-footed beast. Be my wife, and I shall be your husband. Let us live together in harmony and joy. From this day forth, please support and cherish me through the power of passion."

Hearing the jackal's words, the young lioness thought: "This jackal is low among four-footed beasts, loathsome, and like one of the outcaste (caṇḍāla) class. We, however, are of the noble royal lineage of lions. This jackal speaks words to me that are improper and unworthy. Why should I live after hearing such words? I will hold my breath and die." Then, another thought occurred to her: "It is not yet proper for me to die like this. Let my brothers come; I will tell them and then die."

The jackal, receiving no reply from the young lioness, became dejected, thinking, "Now this young lioness is angry with me," and he entered the crystal cave and lay down.

At that time, a young lion, having killed a buffalo or an elephant and eaten its meat, brought some for his sister and said, "Dear sister, eat this meat." She replied, "Dear brother, I will not eat; I am going to die." When asked why she would die, she told him what the jackal had said. When he asked, "Dear sister, where is that jackal now?" she, mistakenly thinking the jackal lying in the crystal cave was in the sky, said, "Dear brother, why do you not see him? That jackal is lying in the sky at the peak of the Silver Mountain."

The young lion, not knowing that the jackal was lying inside a crystal cave and believing him to be in the sky, rushed with the speed of a lion to kill the jackal and struck the crystal cave with his chest. His heart burst, and he died right there, falling at the foot of the mountain.

Then another lion came. The young lioness told him the same thing. That lion also did the same, met his end, and fell at the foot of the mountain. In this manner, six brother lions died. After all six had perished, the Bodhisatta arrived. The lioness told the Bodhisatta the same story. When he asked where the jackal was, she said, "Elder brother, that jackal is lying in the sky at the peak of the Silver Mountain."

The Bodhisatta thought, "There is no such thing as a jackal standing in the sky; he must be lying in a crystal cave." Having thought thus, the Bodhisatta went down to the foot of the mountain and, seeing his six younger brothers dead, thought, "These lions, due to their own foolishness and lack of investigative wisdom, did not realize it was a crystal cave. They must have died from striking it with their chests. The deeds of those who act too hastily without reflection are indeed like this." Thus he said:
8:
4. "The lion, with a lion's roar, made the Daddara mountain echo. Hearing the sound of the lion, the jackal living in Daddara, filled with fear and terror, his heart burst asunder."

The Teacher spoke this verse which completes the two. 

Upāsaka (lay follower), "Sīho ca," the lion king who has mastery over the beasts. "Sīhanādena," with a lion's roar like the sound of thunder. "Daddaraṃ," the Silver Mountain. "Abhinādayi," made it echo continuously. "Daddare," on the peak of the Silver Mountain mixed with crystal. "Vasaṃ (vasanto)," living there. "Siṅgālo," the jackal. "Sīhassa," of the lion king. "Nigghosaṃ," the powerful sound. "Sutvā," having heard. "Bhīto," he was afraid. "Santāsaṃ," into terror. "Āpādi," he fell. "Bhītena," because of extreme fear, "assa," that jackal's "hadayañca," heart also "apphali," burst.

Lay follower, that lion spoke this verse: "My brothers, being unskilled in discerning causes, rushed too quickly to kill the jackal and died themselves. I, however, will not act like my brothers, but will cause the jackal's heart to burst while he lies in the crystal cave." Having noted the jackal's path of ascent and descent, he faced that direction and roared the lion's roar three times. The earth and the sky echoed as one. While the jackal was lying in the crystal cave, his heart burst due to extreme terror. That jackal met his end right there inside the crystal cave.

Thus, the All-Knowing Buddha, having preached that the jackal met his end upon hearing the lion's roar, and having attained Enlightenment, said:

In the manner described, the lion king caused the jackal to meet his end, covered his six brothers in one place, informed his sister of their death, comforted her, and lived in the Golden Cave for the rest of his life, eventually passing away according to his kamma.

Concluding the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the proclamation of the Truths, the lay follower (the barber) was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, the barber's son was the jackal, the young Licchavi princess was the young lioness, the obscure elders were the six younger brother lions, and I myself was the eldest brother lion."

## Obsession with the Unworthy Leads to Destruction

The Siṅgāla Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Sūkara Jātaka
## The Boar and the Lion

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sūkara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Catuppado ahaṃ samma," while staying at Jetavana Monastery, concerning "an old monk."

To elaborate: One day, while a Dhamma talk was being held at night, the All-Knowing Buddha stood on the beautiful staircase at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), gave the Sugata's advice to the assembly of monks, and entered the Fragrant Chamber. Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma and foremost in wisdom, paid homage to the Buddha and went to his own dwelling (pariveṇa). The Venerable Moggallāna also went to his dwelling, rested, and then came to the Venerable Sāriputta to ask questions. The Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, answered every question asked, making the meaning clear as if making the moon appear in the sky. The fourfold assembly sat listening to the Dhamma.

Among that fourfold assembly, an old monk thought: "If I challenge Sāriputta in the midst of this Dhamma assembly and ask him a question, the assembly will recognize me as a very learned monk and will then provide me with requisites and show me great respect." Having thought thus—
9:
He rose from among the assembly, approached the Elder, stood in a suitable place, and spoke. How did he speak? 'Friend Sāriputta, we also wish to ask you a question; grant us the opportunity. Give me a decision in direct explanation, or in complete explanation, or in refutation, or in commendation, or in distinction, or in further distinction.' The Elder Sāriputta looked at the old monk and thought, 'This old monk lives under the influence of greed; he is empty and knows nothing.' Without speaking to him, feeling embarrassed, he laid down his fan, rose from his seat, and entered the precinct (parivena). The Elder Moggallāna also went to his own precinct.

The people rose and said, 'Seize this empty old monk; he did not allow us to listen to the sweet Dhamma.' They pursued him. As the old monk fled, he fell into a latrine with broken planks at the edge of the monastery and stood there smeared with excrement. Seeing the old monk covered in filth, the people became displeased and went to the presence of the Buddha.

Seeing the lay devotees, the Buddha asked, 'Lay devotees, why have you come at an unseasonable time?' The people reported the matter. The Buddha said, 'Lay devotees, it is not only now that this old monk, being frivolous and not knowing his own strength, competed with those of great power and became smeared with excrement. In the past also, being frivolous and not knowing his own strength, he competed with those of great power and was smeared with excrement.' Having said this, he remained silent. Being requested by the lay devotees, he brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Lay devotees, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a lion and lived in a mountain cave in the Himālaya region. Near that cave, many boars lived by a certain lake. Ascetics also lived in leaf-huts by that same lake. One day, the lion killed one of the buffaloes, elephants, or other animals, ate as much meat as he desired, went down to the lake, drank water, and came up. At that moment, a frivolous boar was taking food near that lake. Seeing the boar, the lion thought, 'On another day, other than today, I shall eat this boar.'
10:
5. "I am a four-footed animal, friend; you too, friend, are four-footed.
Come, friend, turn back! Why do you run away in fear?"

This was the first verse he spoke.

"Friend Lion, I am a four-footed beast. Friend Lion, you too are a four-footed beast. Friend Lion, are you running away because you are afraid of me? Turn back! Come here!"

Indeed, the lion, seeing him, thought, "This pig might not come again," and fearing his non-arrival, he came up from the lake and began to go by one side.

The pig looked and thought, "This lion, seeing me and being afraid of me, does not dare to come near and is fleeing. Today, it is proper for me to engage in battle with this lion." Lifting his head and wishing to challenge him to battle—

The lion, hearing the pig's words, said, "Friend Pig, today there is no battle between us. From today, on the seventh day, let there be a battle in this very place," and he departed.

The pig, overjoyed thinking, "I shall fight with a lion," reported the news to his relatives. Hearing the pig's words, they were greatly terrified and said, "Now you will destroy all of us! Without knowing your own strength, you wish to fight with a lion. When the lion comes, he will bring us all to the end of our lives. Do not perform such a reckless act." The pig, also becoming very afraid, asked, "What shall I do now?"

The pigs said, "Friend, go to the place where the ascetics void their excrement, roll your body in the foul filth for seven days, let it dry, and on the seventh day, moisten your body with dewdrops. Go before the lion arrives, find the direction of the wind, and stand upwind. The lion, being of a clean nature, will smell the stench of your body permeated with foul filth, and giving you the victory, he will depart." He did exactly as instructed and stood in that place on the seventh day.

The lion, smelling the stench of the pig's body and knowing he was smeared with excrement, thought, "Friend Pig, you have thought of a good trick. If you were not smeared with excrement, I would have brought you to the end of your life right here. But now, it is not possible to bite your body with my mouth, nor to strike you with my paw. I give you the victory." Wishing to say this, he spoke this verse which completes the two:

6. "You are impure, with foul-smelling fur; you emit a stench, O pig.
If you wish to fight, I give you the victory, friend."

"Friend Pig, you have foul fur because of being smeared with excrement. You emit a stench that is undesirable and loathsome. If you wish to fight, I give you the victory."
11:
Having said this, the lion turned back from that very place, took his food, drank water at the pond, and went to his mountain cave. The pig also told his relatives, "I have defeated the lion." Those relatives, fearing that the lion would return one day and cause the death of them all, fled and went elsewhere.

Identifying the birth: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the old monk was the pig, and I myself was the lion."

## Greedy for honor, honor does not rise; behold the pig and the lion.

The Sūkara Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Uraga Jātaka
## The Ascetic, the Nāga, and the Garuḍa

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Uraga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Idhūragānaṃ pavaro paviṭṭho," concerning the "quarrel between two generals."

It is said that two high ministers, who were generals serving at the feet of King Kosala, used to argue whenever they met. The enmity between these two high ministers became well-known throughout the city. Neither King Kosala nor their relatives and friends were able to reconcile them.

Then one day, at dawn, as the All-Knowing Buddha was surveying those who were ready to be enlightened, He saw the merit that was the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga) in both those generals. On the following day, He entered Sāvatthī alone for alms and stood at the door of one of the two generals. That general came out, took the bowl, invited the Buddha inside, prepared a seat, and requested Him to sit. The Buddha sat and preached the benefits of the meditation on loving-kindness (metta-bhāvanā) to that general. Knowing that his mind was ready, He revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, that general was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

The Buddha, knowing that the general had become a Stream-enterer, had that same general carry His bowl, rose, and went to the door of the other general's house. That general also came out, paid homage to the Buddha, and said, "Venerable Sir, please enter," inviting Him into the house to sit. The first general also entered along with the Buddha, carrying the bowl. The Buddha preached the eleven benefits of loving-kindness to that general. Knowing that his mind was ready, He revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, that general also was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry.
12:
Thus, both those generals became Stream-enterers, confessed their faults to each other, asked for forgiveness, and became united, joyful, and of one mind. On that very day, they ate together in the presence of the Buddha. The All-Knowing Buddha, having finished His meal, returned to the monastery. Those two generals took many flowers, perfumes, and ointments, as well as ghee, honey, molasses, and so on, and departed along with the Buddha. When the assembly of monks performed their duties for the Buddha, the Sugata gave them an exhortation and entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī).

In the evening, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall about the virtues of the Buddha: "Friends, the Buddha is indeed the tamer of the untamed. Even though King Kosala tried for a long time, he could not reconcile the two high ministers; neither could their relatives and friends. Yet, in a single day, the Tathāgata has tamed those two generals."

The Buddha came and asked, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, for such and such a conversation," He said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have reconciled these two people; in the past also, I reconciled them," and He brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a festival was proclaimed in the city of Bārāṇasī, and a great assembly took place. Many humans, as well as devas, nāgas, garuḍas, and others, gathered to see the festival. At one place in that festival, a nāga and a garuḍa stood together, watching the assembly. The nāga, not knowing the other was a garuḍa, placed his hand on the garuḍa's shoulder. When the garuḍa turned and looked, wondering, "Who has placed a hand on my shoulder?" he recognized the nāga.
13:
7. "The best of those who prey on snakes has entered here,
In the form of a stone, seeking release.
Respecting the Brahma-appearance,
Though hungry, I do not venture to eat."
He spoke this first verse.

O monk! The king of Nagas, the most excellent of snakes, desiring release from me, has entered your bark-cloth robe in the form of a gem. I, respecting your noble Brahma-appearance, the form of your bark-cloth robe, though very hungry, do not venture to eat that Naga.

8. "May you, protected by the Brahma-power, live for a long time,
And may divine foods appear for you;
Who, respecting the Brahma-appearance,
Though hungry, did not venture to eat."
He spoke this verse to complete the two.

O King of Supaṇṇas! You who, respecting the noble form of the bark-cloth robe, though very hungry, did not venture to eat that Naga—may you, by protecting the noble bark-cloth robe, live for a long time. May foods that are fit for deities appear for you.

When the Naga looked and realized it was a Garuda, he was terrified of death and fled from the city to the riverbank. The Garuda followed to catch the Naga.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic living in a leaf-hut on the bank of that river. To cool himself from the heat, he wore a water-cloth, left his bark-cloth robe, and went down into the river to bathe. The Naga, thinking he would save his life by depending on this monk, gave up his natural form, transformed into the shape of a gem, and entered the folds of the bark-cloth robe.

The Garuda followed, and seeing the Naga enter the folds of the bark-cloth robe, out of respect for the robe, he did not take him. He called to the Bodhisatta, saying, "Venerable sir, I am hungry. Please take your robe so that I may eat this Naga." To show this meaning—

When he said this, the Bodhisatta, while still standing in the water, wishing to praise the King of Garudas—

Thus the Bodhisatta, having expressed his appreciation while still in the water, came up, put on his bark-cloth robe, called both the Naga and the Garuda, went to the monastery, preached on the benefits of the meditation on loving-kindness (metta-bhāvanā), and reconciled the two. From then on, the Naga and the Garuda were united and lived happily in harmony.

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Naga and the Garuda were these two high ministers. The ascetic, however, was I myself."

## With loving-kindness, free from faults, maintain a friendly bond.

The Uraga Jātaka is finished.
14:
## 5. Bhagga Jātaka
## The Sneeze-Blessing Mantra

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Rājikārāma built by King Pasenadi of Kosala near the Jetavana monastery, told this Bhagga Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Jīva vassa-sataṃ bhagga," concerning his own sneezing.

To elaborate: One day, while the Blessed One was sitting in the midst of the fourfold assembly at Rājikārāma preaching the Dhamma, he sneezed. The monks made a loud, tumultuous noise, saying, "May the Blessed One live long! May the Sugata live long!" Because of that noise, the preaching of the Dhamma was interrupted.

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, if someone says 'Live!' when one sneezes, would he live or die because of that?" "No, venerable sir," the monks replied. "Monks, if that is so, one should not say 'Live!' when someone sneezes. Whoever should say it, let there be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

At that time, when the monks sneezed, people would say, "May you live long, venerable sirs!" The monks, being scrupulous, did not respond. The people complained: "How is it that these Sakyan monks do not speak when we say 'May you live long, venerable sirs'?"

They informed the Blessed One of this matter. "Monks, laypeople appreciate auspicious words. Monks, I allow you to respond to laypeople so that they may be told 'Live long.' Monks, when laypeople say 'Venerable sir, may you live long,' it is proper to respond 'May you live for a long time.'"

The monks asked the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, when did the practice of saying 'Live' and responding 'Live' first arise?" The Teacher said, "Monks, the practice of saying 'Live' and responding 'Live' arose in ancient times," and he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. The Bodhisatta's father earned his living through trade. When the Bodhisatta was sixteen years old, the Brahmin had him carry a bundle of goods for sale and traveled through villages and market towns. Reaching Vārāṇasī, they had a meal cooked at a gatekeeper's house. Having eaten, and finding no place to stay, he asked, "Where do travelers who arrive at an unseasonable hour stay?" Then the people told him, "There is a rest-house outside the city, but it is possessed by a non-human (ogre). If you wish, stay there." The Bodhisatta said, "Father, come, let us go. Do not be afraid of the ogre. I will subdue that ogre and make him lie at your feet." Taking his father, he went to that rest-house.
15:
9. "Live for a hundred years, O Bhagga, and for twenty more. May the spirits not eat me; live you for a hundred autumns."

This was the first verse he spoke.

Bhagga: O father Bhagga. For a hundred years: for the duration of a hundred years. And another twenty: and for another twenty years. Live: may you live long. Me: myself. Spirits: the ogres (yakkhas). May they not eat: may they not devour. You: you as well. For a hundred autumns: for a hundred years with an additional twenty. Live: may you live long.

At that time, the Bodhisatta's father was lying on a bench. The Bodhisatta himself sat massaging his father's feet. The ogre who guarded that rest house had served King Vessavaṇa for twelve years and, upon receiving that rest house, obtained a boon: "Among the people who enter this rest house, if someone sneezes and another says 'Live long', or if someone says 'Live long' and the other replies 'Live long in return', you must spare them. Except for those who say 'Live long' and those who reply 'Live long', you may eat the rest."

That ogre lived in the rafters of the roof. Thinking, "I will make the Bodhisatta's father sneeze," he released a fine powder by his power. The powder came and entered the brahmin's nostrils. That brahmin sneezed while still lying on the bench. The Bodhisatta said "Live long" to his father. The ogre descended from the rafters to eat the brahmin.

The Bodhisatta saw the ogre descending and thought, "This ogre must have made my father sneeze. This must be the ogre who eats those who do not say 'Live long' when one sneezes." Thinking of his father, he spoke the first verse.

The ogre heard the Bodhisatta's words and thought, "I cannot eat this youth because he said 'Live long' to his father. I will, however, eat his father." He went towards the father. The brahmin saw the ogre approaching and thought, "This must be the ogre who eats those who do not reply 'Live long in return'. I shall make the reply." Having thought so, the brahmin, referring to his son, spoke this second verse which completes the pair:

10. "You too live for a hundred years, and for twenty more. May the spirits eat poison; live you for a hundred autumns."

Dear son: O beloved son. You too: you as well. For a hundred years: for the duration of a hundred years. And another twenty: and for another twenty years. Live: may you live long. Spirits: the ogres. Poison: let them eat only the deadly halāhala poison. You: you. For a hundred autumns: for a hundred years with an additional twenty. Live: may you live long.

Hearing the brahmin's words, the ogre thought, "I should not eat either of these two, father or son," and he turned back. Then the Bodhisatta asked him, "O ogre, why do you eat the people who enter this rest house?" "Because I received this right after serving King Vessavaṇa for twelve years." "Do you have the right to eat everyone?" When asked, the ogre replied, "Except for those who say 'Live long' and those who reply 'Live long', I may eat the rest."
16:
"O ogre, in the past you committed unwholesome deeds and were reborn as a cruel, harsh ogre who harms others. If you commit such evil again now, you will surely go from darkness to greater darkness. Therefore, from this day forward, refrain from killing and other sins." Thus, the Bodhisatta admonished the ogre, threatened him with the fear of hell, established him in the Five Precepts, and made the ogre like a servant.

The next morning, people wandering about saw the ogre and, learning that the Bodhisatta had tamed him, informed the King. They reported, "Great King, a youth has tamed that ogre and keeps him like a servant." The King summoned the Bodhisatta and appointed him to the position of Commander-in-Chief (Senāpati). He also gave the Bodhisatta's father great wealth. The King made the ogre a recipient of sacrificial offerings (bali). Following the Bodhisatta's advice, the King performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and eventually filled the city of heaven.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, "The custom of saying 'Live long' and replying 'Live long' originated at that time." He then identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the ogre was Aṅgulimāla, the King was Ānanda, the father was Kassapa, and the son was I myself."

## The ancient tradition of saying "Live long" when one sneezes.

End of the Bhaggajātaka.

## 6. Alīnacittajātaka
## The Power of the White Elephant

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who admonishes the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Alīnacittajātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Alīnacittaṃ nissāya," concerning a monk who had given up his effort.

The story will become clear in the Saṃvarajātaka of the Eleventh Division (Ekādasakanipāta). When the Teacher asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you have given up your effort?" the monk replied, "It is true, Blessed One." Then the Teacher said, "Monk, in the past, you did not give up your effort and won the kingship of the twelve-league-wide city of Bārāṇasī for a young child who was like a mere lump of flesh. Why do you now give up your effort after ordaining in such a Dispensation (Sāsana)?" Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a carpenters' village not far from Bārāṇasī. Five hundred carpenters lived there.
17:
The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a village of carpenters not far from the city of Bārāṇasī. Five hundred carpenters lived in that village. These carpenters would go upstream by boat and enter the forest. They would hew timber for house-building and, in that very forest, prepare house components such as those for one-story or two-story houses. Starting from the pillars, they would mark all the timbers, bring them to the riverbank, load them onto boats, and come downriver to the city. To those who desired such houses, they would build them, take the money (kahāpaṇas), and go back to that same place to bring more house components.

While the carpenters, who made their living in this way, were once camping in the forest and hewing wood, an elephant nearby stepped on a khadirā (acacia) stump. That stump pierced the elephant's foot. Severe pains arose. The foot swelled and became filled with pus. Afflicted by pain and hearing the sound of the carpenters hewing wood, the elephant thought, 'Depending on these carpenters, I shall find relief.' He went to the carpenters on three legs and lay down nearby.

The carpenters, seeing the elephant with the swollen foot, approached him. Seeing the acacia stump in his foot, they made a cut around the stump with a sharp adze, tied it with a rope, pulled it out, drained the pus, washed it with warm water, and smeared it with suitable medicines. Before long, they made the wound heal.

The elephant, having recovered, thought, 'I have received my life depending on these carpenters; now it is proper for me to do them a favor.' Having thought so, from that day on, the elephant extracted timber along with the carpenters. He would turn the wood over for the carpenters who were hewing it. He would bring tools like the adze. He would wrap his trunk around the end of the blackened measuring line and hold it. The carpenters also, at mealtime, would each give him a lump of rice, providing five hundred lumps of rice. Now, that elephant had a son, a young noble elephant who was entirely white. Therefore, the elephant thought, 'I am now old. It is proper that I should give my son to work for these carpenters and then depart.' Such was his thought.
18: From that day on, the young elephant followed the words of the carpenters and, being amenable to instruction, performed all their tasks. The carpenters also fed him with five hundred lumps of rice. After finishing his work, the elephant would go down to the river, bathe, play, and then return. The carpenters' children would also play with him in the water and on land, holding onto his trunk and other parts. Indeed, noble elephants, noble horses, and noble men do not void excrement or urine in the water. Therefore, that young elephant also did not void excrement or urine in the water but did so only on the riverbank. Then, one day, it rained upstream. Because of the rain, dried elephant dung fell into the river and floated down until it got caught in a bush at the bathing ghat of Bārāṇasī. At that time, the King's elephant keepers brought five hundred elephants to bathe. Having caught the scent of the noble elephant's dung, not even a single elephant dared to enter the river. All of them raised their tails and began to flee. The elephant keepers informed the elephant trainers. The trainers, thinking, 'There must be some danger in the water,' had the water cleared. Seeing the noble elephant's dung in that bush, they realized, 'This is the reason why the elephants do not dare to descend into the water.' They had a jar brought, filled it with water, dissolved the dung in it, and had it sprinkled over the bodies of the royal elephants. Their bodies became fragrant. At that time, those elephants entered the river and bathed. The elephant trainers reported the matter to the King, saying, 'Your Majesty, it is proper to search for and bring that noble elephant.' The King set out on the river and, traveling upstream with boat-rafts, reached the dwelling place of the carpenters. While the young elephant was playing in the river, he heard the sound of drums, went to the carpenters, and stood near them. The carpenters went out to welcome the King and said, 'Your Majesty, if you have need of timber, for what reason have you come? It would have been proper to send for it and have it brought.'
19:
When the King said, "Friends, I have not come for the sake of the wood, but only for the sake of this elephant," they replied, "Great King, please take him and proceed." The young elephant did not wish to follow. "Friends, what does the young elephant want?" the King asked. "Great King, the elephant wishes to repay its debt of gratitude to the carpenters," they replied. The King then ordered one hundred thousand pieces of money to be placed near each of the elephant's four legs, its trunk, and its tail. Even with this much wealth provided, the elephant still would not follow until bundles of cloth were given to all the carpenters, garments were given to the carpenters' wives, and gifts and honors were bestowed upon the children who were its playmates. Only after looking back at the carpenters, the women, and the children did the elephant follow the King.

The King took the white elephant and went to the city. He ordered the city and the elephant stable to be decorated. Having the elephant circumambulate the city clockwise, he led it into the stable, adorned it with all kinds of ornaments, and performed the consecration ceremony. He made it his state elephant, treated it as his friend, gave it half the kingdom, and accorded it the same honors as himself. From the time of the elephant's arrival, the sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa came into the hands of the King of Bārāṇasī.

As time passed, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. While the Queen was pregnant, the King passed away. If the auspicious white elephant were to know of the King's death, its heart would surely break right there in the stable. Therefore, they served the auspicious elephant without letting it know that the King had died.
20:
The Queen said to the elephant, "Lord, your friend is dead. We did not tell you for fear your heart would break. This child is your friend's son. The King of Kosala has come, besieged the city, and is fighting against your son. Our forces are retreating. Either kill your son yourself, or take the kingdom and give it to him."

At that time, the elephant stroked the Bodhisatta with its trunk, lifted him up, and placed him on its frontal globes. After weeping, it lowered the Bodhisatta and placed him in the Queen's hands, saying, "I will capture the King of Kosala," and then emerged from the elephant stable. Then the ministers put on their armor, and having decorated the elephant, they opened the city gate and went out surrounding it. The elephant emerged from the city, let out a trumpeting roar (koñcanāda), terrified the multitude and put them to flight. It broke through the enemy's stockade, seized the King of Kosala by his topknot, and brought him to be laid at the Bodhisatta's feet. When the elephant rose to kill him, the Bodhisatta restrained it, and the elephant admonished the King, saying, "From now on, be heedful; do not think, 'The prince is young,'" and then sent him away. From that time on, the sovereignty over the entire Jambudīpa came into the hands of the Bodhisatta; no other rival was able to rise against him. At the age of seven, the Bodhisatta was consecrated and became known as King Alīnacitta. He ruled the kingdom with righteousness and, at the end of his life, filled the city of heaven.

The Teacher, having brought this past story and becoming fully enlightened, uttered these two verses:

11. "Relying on Alīnacitta, the great army was joyful;
It captured the King of Kosala alive, who was dissatisfied with his own forces."

12. "Thus, a monk endowed with support, with energy aroused,
Developing wholesome states for the sake of attaining security from bonds,
Should reach by degrees the destruction of all fetters."

(Commentary): Bhikkhu: monk. Mahatī camū: the great army of Bārāṇasī. Alīnacittaṃ nissāya: relying on Prince Alīnacitta. Pahaṭṭhā: being joyful and delighted, thinking, "We have obtained our ancestral kingdom." Asantuṭṭhaṃ senaṃ Kosalaṃ: the King of Kosala who, dissatisfied with his own kingdom, came out of greed for another's kingdom. Jīvaggāhaṃ agāhayi yathā: just as that army, by means of the elephant, caused the King to be captured alive without killing him.

Evaṃ-tathā: In the same way. Yogakkhemassa pattiyā: for the sake of reaching Nibbāna, which is the security from the four bonds (yogas). Kusalaṃ dhammaṃ: the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) which are blameless and characterized by bringing about welfare and happiness. Bhāvayaṃ-bhāvayanto: developing. Nissayasampanno: endowed with the good support of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇa-mitta). Āraddhavīriyo: endowed with the four types of blameless energy that have been exerted. Bhikkhu: a person of pure virtue. Anupubbena: gradually, starting from the practice of insight (vipassanā). Sabbasaṃyojanakkhayaṃ: the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) which occurs at the end of the destruction of all ten fetters. Pāpuṇe: should reach.

Upon hearing of the King's death and thinking, "The kingdom of Bārāṇasī is empty," the King of Kosala, who lived near the adjacent city, came with a large army and besieged Bārāṇasī. The citizens closed the city gates and sent a message to the King of Kosala. They sent word: "Our King's Chief Queen is fully pregnant. The brahmins who can predict the future by observing the limbs and body parts say that on the seventh day from now, she will give birth to a son. If she gives birth to a son, we will fight on the seventh day; we will not give up the kingdom. Wait for this much time." The King of Kosala agreed, saying, "Very well."

The Queen gave birth to a son on the seventh day. On the day of the prince's naming, because he was born taking a courageous heart, free from the shrinking or retreating of the people, they named him Prince Alīnacitta. From the very day of the Bodhisatta's birth, the citizens of Bārāṇasī fought with the King of Kosala. Because the army had no leader, even though the forces were large, they retreated little by little while fighting.

The ministers informed the Queen of this matter, saying, "We fear that if the forces retreat like this, we will be defeated. The state elephant, who is the Great King's friend, does not yet know of our King's death, the birth of the son, or the King of Kosala's arrival and the ongoing battle. Let us inform the state elephant."

The Queen agreed, had her son adorned, and laid him on a spread of white cloth. Descending from the palace and surrounded by a group of ministers, she went to the elephant stable. She laid the Bodhisatta at the elephant's feet and said, "Lord, your friend is dead. We did not tell you for fear your heart would break. This child is your friend's son. The King of Kosala has come, besieged the city, and is fighting against your son. Our forces are retreating. You alone must protect your son."
21:
"Take the kingship for your son and give it to him," she said.
At that time, the elephant stroked the Bodhisatta with its trunk, lifted him up, and placed him on its frontal globes. After weeping, it set the Bodhisatta down into the Queen's hands to sleep and left the elephant stable, intending to capture King Kosala. Then the ministers donned their armor, decorated the elephant, opened the city gates, and went out surrounding the elephant. The elephant left the city, let out a trumpeting cry like a crane, terrified the people and made them flee, broke through the army, seized King Kosala by his topknot, and brought him back to be placed at the Bodhisatta's feet. It forbade those who came to kill the king and admonished him, saying, "From this day forth, do not be negligent. Do not think that the prince is small," and then released him.
From that day on, the kingship of the entire Jambudīpa came into the hands of the Bodhisatta. There was no other opponent capable of rising against him. In his seventh year, the Bodhisatta received the royal consecration and became King Alīnacitta. He ruled righteously and, at the end of his life, filled the heavenly realms.
The Buddha, having brought this past story after becoming the Buddha, concluded the Jātaka:
Thus the Blessed One, having reached the summit of the Dhamma teaching with the Great Deathless Nibbāna and having further declared the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the backsliding monk was established in the Fruit of Arahatship. As for how the Jātaka was identified: Mahāmāyā was then the mother; King Suddhodana was then the father; the backsliding monk was then the white elephant who took and gave the kingship; Sāriputta was then the white elephant who was the father of the noble elephant; Moggallāna was then the neighboring King of Kosala; and I myself was then Prince Alīnacitta. Thus he identified the Jātaka.
## Great is the benefit of power and effort, ruling the whole country
Alīnacitta Jātaka ends.
## 7. Guna Jātaka
## The Jackal and the Lion
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Buddha, the Teacher who admonishes the world including the devas, told this Guna Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yena kāmaṃ paṇāmeti," concerning the Elder Ānanda's receipt of a thousand robes.
The story of the Elder Ānanda teaching the Dhamma in the palace of King Kosala has already appeared below in the Mahāsāra Jātaka of the Ekanipāta. In the manner mentioned in the Mahāsāra Jātaka, while the Elder Ānanda was teaching the Dhamma in the palace of King Kosala, a thousand robes, each worth a thousand, were brought to the King. King Kosala gave five hundred of those robes to his five hundred queens. All those queens set aside those robes and, on the following day, offered them to the Elder Ānanda. They themselves wore only their old robes and went to the place where King Kosala was having his breakfast.
King Kosala asked, "Queens, I gave you robes worth a thousand each. Why have you come without wearing those new robes?" They replied, "Great King, we have offered those robes to the Elder Ānanda." King Kosala asked, "Did the Elder Ānanda accept all the robes?" The queens replied, "Yes, Great King."
22:
King Kosala thought: "The Blessed One has allowed only three robes. I think the Elder Ānanda will engage in the trade of cloth. Because he will engage in such trade, he has accepted so many robes." Being angry with the Elder Ānanda, after finishing his breakfast, he went to the monastery, entered the Elder Ānanda's residence, paid homage to the Elder, and while sitting, asked: "Venerable sir, do the women in our palace learn or listen to the Dhamma in your presence?" "Yes, Great King, they learn what is fit to be learned and listen to what is fit to be heard," the Elder Ānanda replied.
King Kosala asked, "Do they only listen to the Dhamma, or do they also give you garments or robes?" "Great King, today those women offered me five hundred robes, each worth a thousand," the Elder Ānanda replied. King Kosala asked, "Venerable sir, did you accept them?" "Yes, Great King," the Elder Ānanda replied.
King Kosala asked, "Venerable sir, did not the Teacher allow only three robes?" "Yes, Great King, the Blessed One allowed only three robes for each monk for the purpose of personal use. However, he did not forbid the acceptance of robes. Therefore, I accepted those robes to give to other monks whose robes are worn out," the Elder Ānanda replied. King Kosala asked, "Venerable sir, what will those monks do with their old robes after receiving the robes from you?"
"Great King, they will make the old outer robes (saṅghāṭi) into upper robes (uttarāsaṅga)," the Elder Ānanda replied. "Venerable sir, what will they do with the old upper robes?" "Great King, they will make them into under-robes (antaravāsaka)," the Elder Ānanda replied. "Venerable sir, what will they do with the old under-robes?" "Great King, they will make them into bedspreads (paccattharaṇa)," the Elder Ānanda replied. "Venerable sir, what will they do with the old bedspreads?" "Great King, they will make them into floor coverings (bhūmattharaṇa)," the Elder Ānanda replied. "Venerable sir, what will they do with the old floor coverings?" King Kosala asked.
23:
“Great King, we shall use them as foot-wipers,” Venerable Ānanda replied. “Venerable Sir, what will you do with the old foot-wipers?” King Kosala asked.

“Great King, it is not proper for things offered out of faith to be wasted. Therefore, we shall chop the old foot-wipers with a hatchet, mix them with clay, and use them to plaster the walls of the monasteries,” Venerable Ānanda said. “Venerable Sir, even when the robes offered to you become foot-wipers, they are not wasted,” King Kosala remarked. “Great King, it is true; the robes offered to us are not wasted, they are simply used for various purposes,” Venerable Ānanda replied.

King Kosala, being filled with joy and satisfaction, sent another five hundred cloths from the palace and offered them to Venerable Ānanda. After giving a talk on appreciation (anumodanā), Ānanda circumambulated the King and departed. Venerable Ānanda gave the first five hundred cloths he received to monks whose robes were worn out. Venerable Ānanda had five hundred resident pupils (saddhivihārika).

Among those five hundred resident pupils, one young monk was very helpful to Venerable Ānanda. He swept the precinct, prepared drinking and washing water, provided tooth-sticks, water for washing the face, and water for bathing. He cleaned the toilet, the fire-room, and the living quarters. He performed massages on the hands, feet, and back. Venerable Ānanda, thinking, “This young monk is very helpful,” gave all five hundred cloths he received later to that young monk alone, according to what was appropriate. That young monk divided all the cloths and gave them to his fellow students who shared the same preceptor.

Thus, all those monks who received the cloths cut and dyed them, and wearing and draping the robes which were the color of Kaṇikāra flowers, approached the Buddha. After paying homage and sitting in a suitable place, they asked: “Venerable Sir, is there such a thing as ‘looking at faces’ (favoritism) in giving for a Noble Disciple who is a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna)?” “Monks, there is no such thing as ‘looking at faces’ in giving for Noble Disciples,” the Buddha replied. “Venerable Sir, our preceptor, Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, gave five hundred cloths worth a thousand each to only one young monk. That monk then divided the cloths he received and gave them to us,” the monks reported.

“Monks, Ānanda did not give to that monk by looking at his face. That young monk was very helpful to Ānanda. Therefore, thinking ‘One should return a favor to one who has helped,’ he gave out of gratitude and recognition of service (kataññū-katavedī), according to what was appropriate and based on merit. Indeed, wise men of old also returned favors to those who helped them.” Having said this, at their request, he told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a lion and lived in a mountain cave. One day, leaving the cave, he stood on the mountain peak and looked down at the foot of the mountain. Around the foot of the mountain was a large lake. In one elevated place, on top of the hard mud, soft green grass grew. Hares, deer, and other light animals roamed there eating the grass. On that day, a deer was roaming and eating that green grass.

The lion, thinking “I will catch that deer,” leapt from the mountain top and pounced with the speed of a lion. The deer, terrified of death, fled crying out. The lion, unable to check his speed, fell into the mud and sank. Unable to get out, he stood there for seven days without food, his four legs stuck like pillars.

Then, a jackal searching for food saw the lion and fled in fear. The lion called out to the jackal, “O jackal, do not run! I am stuck in the mud. Save my life!” The jackal went near the lion and said, “O lion, I would like to pull you out, but I am afraid that once out, you would eat me.” When he said this, the lion replied, “O jackal, do not fear. I will not eat you. Instead, I will do you a great favor. Please pull me out by some means.”
24:
The jackal, taking the lion's promise, cleared the mud from around the four legs, dug four channels from where the legs were towards the water, and let the water in to soften the mud. At that moment, the jackal went under the lion's belly and said, “Master, make an effort!” while making a loud noise and pushing the belly with his head. The lion, exerting force, rose from the mud, leapt out, and stood on dry land.

After resting for a moment, the lion went down to the lake, washed off the mud, bathed, and relieved his distress. Then he killed a buffalo, pierced it with his fangs, and turned over the meat, saying, “Eat, good jackal,” placing it before the jackal. After the jackal had eaten, the lion ate himself. Then the jackal bit into a piece of meat and took it. When asked, “Good jackal, what is this meat for?” he replied, “Master, I have a mate; it is for her share.” The lion said, “Take it,” and he himself took meat for the lioness. He said, “Come, good jackal, let us go to the mountain top and go to the dwelling place of your friend (mate).” Going there, he let them eat the meat, comforted the male and female jackals, and said, “From now on, I will look after you.” He took them to his own dwelling and had them live in another cave near the entrance of his cave.

From that day on, when the lion and jackal went to search for food, they left the lioness and female jackal behind. They went together, killed various animals, both ate meat there, and brought back meat for the lioness and female jackal. As time passed, the lioness gave birth to two cubs, and the female jackal also gave birth to two cubs. They all lived together in harmony.

Then one day, a thought occurred to the lioness: “This lion is extremely fond of the male jackal, the female jackal, and the jackal cubs. Surely he must have an intimacy with the female jackal; that is why he shows such affection. What if I harass and threaten this female jackal to make her flee from here?” When the lion and the male jackal went out to search for food, the lioness oppressed and harassed the female jackal, threatening and scolding her.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a minister who accomplished all affairs and advised on what is beneficial and righteous. That King Brahmadatta was somewhat greedy for wealth. He had a rogue horse named Mahāsoṇa. At that time, horse traders from the northern region (Uttarāpatha) brought five hundred horses. They informed the King of the arrival of the horses. Previously, the Bodhisatta used to value the horses and have the price paid without reducing the principal amount.

The King, wishing to reduce the principal price, summoned another minister and said, 'Friend, you value the horses. The horse traders were displeased and reported the King's actions to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Is there no rogue horse in your city?' They replied, 'Lord, there is a fierce and harsh rogue horse named Suhanu.' 'In that case,' said the Bodhisatta, 'bring that horse when you come again.' The horse traders agreed and, upon their return, brought the rogue horse named Suhanu.

King Brahmadatta, hearing that the horse traders had arrived, opened the lion-window (sīhapañjara), looked at the horses, and ordered Mahāsoṇa to be released. King Brahmadatta asked the Bodhisatta, 'Do you see these two rogue horses? These two rogue horses are fierce, harsh, and violent only toward other horses; they bite other horses and cause them to fall ill. "Great King, these two horses do not have unequal habits, nor do they have unequal natures. These two horses have equal habits and equal natures."

Having said this, the Bodhisatta advised the King: "Great King, one who is called a King should not be overly greedy. It is not proper to destroy the property of others." He then had the horses valued and made the King pay the true price. The horse traders, receiving the price according to the true nature of the horses, went away joyful and satisfied. The King also remained in the advice of the Bodhisatta and went according to his karma.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, these two bad monks were the two bad horses, Ānanda was the King, and I myself was the wise minister."

## 9. Mora Jātaka

## The Golden Peacock and the Snare

The Blessed One, the Teacher who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mora Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Udetayaṃ cakkhumā ekarājā," concerning a monk who was dissatisfied with the holy life.

Indeed, that dissatisfied monk was brought by his fellow monks to the presence of the Teacher. When asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?" he replied, "It is true, Bhante." When asked, "Having seen what?" he said, "Having seen a woman dressed and adorned." Then the Teacher said to him, "Monk, why would a woman not be able to agitate the mind of one like you? She certainly can. Indeed, it is true; even for the wise of old, defilements that had not arisen for seven hundred years found an opportunity and arose in an instant upon hearing the voice of a woman. Even pure beings become defiled; even those endowed with great fame reach a state of ill-repute; what then to say of one who is not pure?" Having said this, he brought the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of a peacock. Even in the egg stage, he was in an eggshell the color of a Kaṇikāra bud. When he hatched from the egg, he was golden-colored, beautiful, and pleasing to look at.

## 2. Dutiyacetovimuttiphala-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'perception of impermanence' (anicca-saññā) is the perception that arises as 'impermanent' in the sense of non-existence after having been, regarding the five aggregates of clinging. 'Perception of suffering in the impermanent' (anicce dukkha-saññā) is the perception that arises as 'suffering' in the sense of being oppressed, regarding those five aggregates which are impermanent. 'Perception of non-self in suffering' (dukkhe anatta-saññā) is the perception that arises as 'non-self' in the sense of not being under control, regarding those five aggregates which are suffering. The rest is as explained below. In these two suttas, the benefit of insight (vipassanā) is taught.

The hunter captured the Bodhisatta and presented him to the King. Seeing the perfection of the golden peacock's appearance, the King was delighted and had a seat prepared for him. The Bodhisatta sat on the prepared seat and asked, "Great King, why did you have me captured?" The King replied, "I have heard that those who eat your flesh become ageless and immortal. Desiring to be ageless and immortal by eating your flesh, I had you captured."

The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, let it be that those who eat my flesh become ageless and immortal, but I myself shall die. Since I am mortal, how can those who eat my flesh not die?" The King replied, "Noble peacock, you have a golden complexion; therefore, it is said those who eat your flesh will become ageless and immortal."

"Great King," said the Bodhisatta, "I do not have this golden complexion without a cause. In the past, I was a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) in this very city. I myself observed the Five Precepts and made all the inhabitants of the world observe them as well. When I passed away, I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having stayed there for the full lifespan and then passing away, I was reborn in the womb of a peacock due to the result of some other unwholesome deed. However, due to the power of my former virtue (sīla), I have a golden complexion."

The King asked, "Noble peacock, you say you were a Universal Monarch, observed virtue, and became golden-colored as a result of that virtue. How can we believe this? Is there any witness?" "There is, Great King," he replied. "Who is it?" "Great King, during my time as a Universal Monarch, I used to travel through the air in a jeweled chariot. That chariot of mine was buried within the earth at the bottom of the royal pond. Have it raised from the royal pond; it will be my witness."

The King agreed, saying "Very well," and had the water drained from the pond and the chariot brought out. Then the King believed the Bodhisatta.

The Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma to the King, saying, "Great King, setting aside the Great Nibbāna which is the Deathless (Amata), all other conditioned things (saṅkhata-dhamma) arise and are of a nature to pass away; they are impermanent, subject to decay and destruction." ## 10. Vinīla Jātaka

## The Swan Brothers and the Hybrid Crow-Swan

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Vinīla Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Evameva nūna rājānaṃ," concerning Devadatta's imitation of the Buddha.

This is the story: When Devadatta, at Gayāsīsa, lay down imitating the posture of the Buddha before the two Chief Disciples who had arrived there, the two Elders preached the Dhamma and, taking their followers, returned to the Veḷuvana Monastery. Then the Blessed One asked, "Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do when he saw you?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, by imitating the posture of the Buddha, he met with great destruction." The Blessed One said, "Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has met with destruction by imitating me; he did so in the past as well." Having said this, at the request of the Elder Sāriputta, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when the King of Videha was reigning in Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the King's Chief Queen. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and, upon his father's passing, was established in the kingship.

At that time, in the feeding ground of a certain Golden Swan King, there was a union with a female crow. She gave birth to a son. That young bird resembled neither the mother nor the father. Because of his dark blue (vinīla) color, they named him "Vinīlaka." The Golden Swan King would come frequently to see his son.
