“Where do they live?” “In the kingdom of Videha, not far from Mithilā, at a certain place, on the top of a palm tree.” “Father, the path of men is full of suspicion and fear. Do not go; we will go and bring him.” The two young geese, following the directions given by their father, went there, made Vinīla sit on a stick, gripped the ends of the stick with their beaks, and flew over the city of Mithilā.

At that moment, the King of Videha, seated in a magnificent chariot drawn by four all-white Sindh horses, was circumambulating the city. Vinīla saw him and thought: “What is the difference between me and the King of Videha? He travels around the city seated in a chariot drawn by four Sindh horses, while I travel seated in a chariot drawn by geese.” Flying through the air, he spoke this first verse:

19. “Just so, indeed, the King of Videha, who dwells in Mithilā, is carried by thoroughbred horses; just as these geese carry me, Vinīla.”

(In this verse: *Evameva* means just so. *Nūna* is a particle used in reflection, or it can mean ‘certainly’. *Vedehaṃ* means the lord of the kingdom of Videha. *Mithilaggahaṃ* means one who has taken up residence in a house in Mithilā. *Ājanyā* means those who know what is a cause and what is not. *Yathā haṃsā vinīlakaṃ* means just as these geese carry me, Vinīla, so do they carry him.)

The young geese, hearing his words, became angry and thought, “We shall drop him right here and go.” But fearing their father’s reproach, they brought him to their father and told him of Vinīla’s conduct.

Then the father, becoming angry, said: “Are you superior to my sons, that you treat them like Sindh horses yoked to a chariot? You do not know your own measure. This place is not your range; go to your mother’s dwelling place.” Having threatened him thus, he spoke the second verse:

20. “Vinīla, you frequent a difficult place; you resort to a ground that is not yours, dear. Frequent the outskirts of villages; that is your mother’s home.”

(In this verse: *Vinīla* is an address by name. *Duggaṃ bhajasi* means you frequent the mountain fastnesses by means of these geese. *Abhūmiṃ, tāta, sevasi* means, dear, you have come to the rugged mountains which are not your proper ground.)

That Golden Goose King had two other sons who were young geese. These young geese, seeing their father, the Golden Goose King, constantly flying to the world of men, asked him: “Father, why do you constantly go to the path of the world of men?” He replied: “My sons, I have a son born of a union with a crow. That son is named Vinīla. I go to see that Vinīla.”

“Father, where does that Vinīla live?” “My sons, he lives on the top of a palm tree at a certain place not far from Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha.” “Father, the place where men frequent is loathsome and full of danger. Do not go; we will go and bring that Vinīla.” Saying this, the two geese went to that place according to the sign given by their father, made Vinīla sit on a stick, gripped the ends of the stick with their beaks, and carried him through the air over the city of Mithilā.

At that moment, the King of Videha was circumambulating the city to the right, seated in a noble chariot drawn by four Sindh horses. Vinīla saw the King of Videha and thought: “How am I different from the King of Videha? This King of Videha circumambulates the city in a chariot drawn by four Sindh horses, while I travel in a chariot drawn by geese.” Thinking thus, while traveling through the air—

The young geese brothers, hearing Vinīla’s words, became angry and intended to drop him right there and leave. However, fearing their father’s reproach, they brought him to their father and reported Vinīla’s behavior.

Then the father became angry with Vinīla and said: “Are you more noble than my sons?”
36:
“You oppress my sons and treat them like Sindh horses yoked to a chariot; you do not know your own measure. This place is not your range; go only to your mother’s dwelling place.” Having threatened him thus—

After threatening Vinīla in this way, the Golden Goose said to his sons: “Go, drop that Vinīla at the rubbish heap of Mithilā and return.” The young geese did exactly as their father said.

At the conclusion of the teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, Vinīla was Devadatta. The two young geese were the two Chief Disciples. The father was Ānanda. The King of Videha was I myself.”

## One who wrongs a helper meets great destruction.
The Vinīla Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Santhava Vagga
## 1. Indasamānagotta Jātaka
## The Ascetic and the Elephant

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One who admonishes the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana, told this Indasamānagotta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Na santhavaṃ kāpurisena kayirā,” concerning a difficult-to-admonish monk.

The story of that monk will appear clearly in the Gijjha Jātaka of the Navaka Nipāta. Specifically, the Teacher said, “Monk, in the past too, because of your stubbornness, you did not listen to the words of the wise and were crushed to pieces by the feet of a rutting elephant,” and he brought the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he came of age, he renounced the household life, became an ascetic, and became the leader of a group of five hundred ascetics, living in the Himalayan region. At that time, among those ascetics, there was one named Indasamānagotta who was difficult to admonish and would not take advice.

This ascetic Indasamānagotta reared a young elephant. The Bodhisatta, hearing of this, sent for Indasamānagotta and asked, “Is it true, ascetic, that you are rearing a young elephant?” When he replied, “Yes, teacher, I am rearing a young elephant whose mother died,” the Bodhisatta said, “Ascetic, when elephants reach maturity...”
37:
1. One should not make an acquaintance with a base man,
A noble one who knows the benefit [should not associate] with a non-noble one.
Even if lived with for a long time, he does evil,
Just as the elephant did to Indasamānagotta.

2. But if one knows a person to be like oneself,
In virtue, in wisdom, and in learning,
With such a one should one make friendship;
Truly, association with a good man is pleasant.

Thus he spoke these verses.

O ascetics! A noble one (Ariya), who is established in good conduct and who knows the benefit (atthaṃ pajānaṃ), should not make an acquaintance (santhavaṃ) with a non-noble (anariya), base person (kāpurisa). For what reason should one not do so? Just as the elephant (gaja) raised by the ascetic Indasamānagotta did a wicked deed (pāpaṃ) by killing Indasamānagotta, so too, because a non-noble person, even after living together for a long time (cirānuvuṭṭho), is prone to doing evil deeds, one should not make an acquaintance.

If one knows a person (yaṃ tveva puggalaṃ) to be equal to oneself (sadiso mamaṃ) in virtue (sīla), in wisdom (paññā), and in learning (suta), with such a person alone should one make friendship (mettiṃ kayirātha). For what reason should one make friendship only with such a person? Because association (saṅgamo) with a good man (sappurisa) is truly (have) pleasant (sukho). Therefore, with such a person alone should one make friendship.

"They kill their own fosterers. Do not raise that young elephant," he said. When the teacher said this, [the ascetic] replied, "Teacher, I cannot live without this young elephant." [The Bodhisatta] said, "In that case, it will become clear [to you]." That young elephant, being raised by Indasamānagotta, later became large in body. When he had grown large, at one time, those ascetics went far away for the sake of forest roots and fruits and stayed there for a few days.

The elephant, when the first south wind blew, became intoxicated with musth. He destroyed Indasamānagotta’s leaf-hut, broke the water jar, threw away the stone slab, pulled out the bench, and thinking, "I will go only after killing that ascetic," he entered a thicket and stood watching the path of his arrival. The ascetic Indasamānagotta, taking food for the elephant, arrived ahead of all the other ascetics. Seeing the elephant, he approached him with his usual perception [of him being friendly]. Then the elephant came out of the thicket, seized him firmly with his trunk, dashed him to the ground, stepped on his head with his foot, and brought him to the end of his life. Then, making a sound like a crane, he entered the forest.

The remaining ascetics reported that matter to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta said, "One should not associate with base men," and—
38:
With these two verses, the Bodhisatta taught the assembly of ascetics, saying, "One should not be stubborn (difficult to admonish); one should practice well according to the advice of the wise." After performing the funeral rites for Indasamānagotta, he developed the Divine Abidings (Brahma-vihāras) and passed away to the Brahma world.

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, this stubborn monk was the ascetic Indasamānagotta, and I myself was the leader of the group of ascetics."

## Stubbornness leads to ruin, meeting death at the end.
The Indasamānagotta Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Santhava Jātaka
## The Ascetic and the Fire
The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, who admonishes the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Santhava Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na santhavasmā paramatthi pāpiyo," concerning "fire-worship."

This story is just like the one told in the Nanguṭṭha Jātaka of the Ekanipāta below. The monks, seeing those ascetics of wrong view sacrificing to fire, asked the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, the ascetics perform various kinds of false austerities; is there any benefit in these false practices?" The Blessed One replied: "Monks, there is no such thing as benefit in false practices."
39:
3. There is no worse evil than intimacy,
When that intimacy is with a wicked man.
Though satiated with ghee and milk-rice,
It burnt the leaf-hut built with great effort.

"The wise of old, seeing only the disadvantage in fire-worship—though they had worshipped it for a long time thinking there was benefit in it—extinguished the fire with water, beat it with branches and the like, and did not even look back at it," the Master said, and then he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. On the day of his birth, his parents took the birth-fire, and when he reached the age of sixteen, they said to him: "Dear son, will you take your birth-fire and tend it in the forest? Or will you study the three Vedas, acquire wealth, and lead the life of a householder?"

The Bodhisatta replied, "I have no need for the householder's life. I shall take my birth-fire, tend it in the forest, and make the Brahma world my destination." Having said this, he took his birth-fire, paid respects to his parents, entered the forest, and lived in a leaf-hut tending the fire.

One day, having gone to a place where he was invited for a meal, he received milk-rice (pāyāsa) mixed with ghee. Thinking, "I shall offer this milk-rice to the Great Brahmā," he brought the milk-rice back, lit the fire, and saying, "O Lord Fire, first I shall let you drink this milk-rice mixed with ghee," he cast the milk-rice into the fire. As soon as the milk-rice, which contained much oily ghee, was cast into the fire, the flames flared up and rose high, burning down the leaf-hut.

The ascetic, being greatly terrified, ran away and stood outside, saying, "One should not form an intimacy with wicked persons. Now this fire has burnt my leaf-hut which I built with great effort." He then uttered this first stanza:

It burnt the leaf-hut built with great effort.

[Word-by-word commentary:]
Kāpurisena: with a wicked man. Yo santhavo: whatever intimacy there is. Pāpiyo: is very evil. Hoti: it is. Asmā santhavā: than that intimacy with a wicked man. Paraṃ: any other greater evil. Natthi: there is not. Sappinā ca: with ghee. Pāyasena ca: and with milk-rice. Santappito api: although being satiated. Ayaṃ aggi: this fire. Mayā: by me. Kicchākataṃ: built with great effort. Paṇṇakuṭiṃ: the leaf-hut roofed with leaves. Adayhi: has burnt.

Having said this, the Bodhisatta thought, "I have no need for you who betrays a friend," and he extinguished the fire with water and beat it with branches. Entering the depths of the Himavanta, he saw a doe named Sāmā—so called because of her golden complexion—licking the faces of a lion, a tiger, and a leopard. He thought, "There is nothing better than intimacy with the virtuous," and uttered the second stanza:

Of the lion, the tiger, and the leopard,
40:
4. There is no higher good than intimacy,
When that intimacy is with a virtuous man.
Sāmā licks their faces through intimacy.

He uttered this stanza which completes the pair.

[Word-by-word commentary:]
Sappurisena: with a virtuous man. Yo santhavo: whatever intimacy there is. Seyyo: is noble. Hoti: it is. Asmā santavā: than that intimacy with the virtuous. Paraṃ: any other higher good. Natthi: there is not. Sāmā: the doe with a complexion like gold. Santhavena: because of love/intimacy. Sīhassa ca: of the lion. Vyagghassa ca: of the tiger. Dīpino ca: of the leopard. Mukhaṃ: the face. Lehati: licks.

Having said this, the Bodhisatta entered the depths of the Himavanta, became an ascetic, developed the super-knowledges (abhiññā) and the eight attainments (samāpatti), and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

[The Connection:] The Master, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the ascetic."

## When the Dhamma of the virtuous is not followed and one practices wrongly, the benefit is destroyed and the result is very bitter.

The Santhava Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Susīma Jātaka
## The Brahmin and the Elephant Ceremony

[Present Story:] While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the All-Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Susīma Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Kāḷā migā setadantā tavīme," concerning "giving by subscription" (chandaka-dāna).

To expand on this: In the city of Sāvatthī, sometimes a single family alone would give alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Sometimes they would give to those of other sects (titthiyas). Sometimes many people would form a group and give together. Sometimes they would give by way of their respective streets. Sometimes the residents of the entire city would collect subscriptions and give alms.

On this occasion, the residents of the entire city collected subscriptions and prepared a gift of all the requisites. They were divided into two groups. Some said, "We shall give this gift of all requisites to the teachers of other sects." Others said, "We shall give it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha." As the discussion continued, the followers of other sects spoke for their own teachers, while the followers of the Buddha said, "We shall make it for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha." As the discussion grew, those who said, "We shall give to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha" became the majority.
41:
When such words were spoken repeatedly, the disciples of those with other views said, “We will give only to the teachers of other views,” while the disciples of the Buddha said, “We will give only to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha.”

Among these two statements, many people spoke the latter. When the majority of the people said, “We will follow this word because it is spoken by many,” those who said, “We will give to the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha,” became the majority. Their word prevailed. The disciples of those with other views were unable to obstruct the offering intended for the Buddha. The townspeople invited the Saṅgha of monks led by the Buddha, performed a great offering for seven days, and on the seventh day, they offered all the requisites.

The Teacher, having given the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), awakened the multitude from the sleep of delusion with the paths and fruits. He then returned to the Jetavana Monastery. When the Saṅgha of monks performed their duties, he stood at the entrance of the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), gave the advice of the Sugata, and entered the Perfumed Chamber.

In the evening, the monks assembled in the Dhamma Hall and raised a discussion: “Friends, although the disciples of those with other views strove to obstruct the offering intended for the Buddha, they were unable to do so. That offering of all requisites came to the feet of the Buddha himself. Oh, how great is the power of the Buddha!”

The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you sitting here now?” When they replied, “For such a discussion,” he said, “Monks, it is not only now that these disciples of other views strive to obstruct the offering intended for me; they strove in the past as well. However, those requisites always come to my feet in all times.” Having said this, he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, a king named Susīma reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the wife of King Susīma's chaplain. When the Bodhisatta was sixteen years old, his father died. That Brahmin chaplain, while he was alive, was the one who performed the auspicious elephant ceremony for the king.

In the place where the auspicious ceremony for elephants was performed, that Brahmin alone received all the materials and goods brought there, as well as the elephant ornaments. Thus, for each ceremony, wealth amounting to a crore accrued to that chaplain. At that time, after the Brahmin had died, the time for the elephant festival arrived. The remaining Brahmins approached the king and said, “Great King, the time for the elephant festival has arrived; it is proper to perform the ceremony. However, the son of the chaplain is very young. He does not yet know the three Vedas, nor does he know the treatise on elephants. We will perform the auspicious elephant ceremony.” The king agreed, saying, “Very well.” The Brahmins, not giving the elephant ceremony to the chaplain's son, went about joyfully, thinking, “We will perform the elephant ceremony and take the wealth.”

Then, when it was said that the elephant festival would take place on the fourth day, the Bodhisatta's mother, the Brahmin lady, heard the news and wept in sorrow, thinking, “The performance of the elephant ceremony has been our lineage for seven generations. Our lineage will now perish, and we will also decline in wealth.”
42:
The Bodhisatta asked, "Mother, why are you crying?" and having heard the reason, he said, "Mother, shall I not perform the ceremony?" She said, "Dear son, you do not know the three Vedas, nor do you know the Elephant Lore. How will you perform the ceremony?" He asked, "Mother, when will the elephant-consecration be held?" She replied, "On the fourth day from now, dear son." He asked, "Mother, where does the teacher live who is proficient in the three Vedas and knows the Elephant Lore?"

She said, "Dear son, such a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) lives in Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra, a hundred and twenty leagues (yojana) from here." He said, "Mother, I will not let our lineage perish. Tomorrow, I will go to Takkasilā in a single day, learn the three Vedas and the Elephant Lore in a single night, return the following day, and perform the elephant-consecration on the fourth day. Mother, do not cry." Having consoled his mother, the Bodhisatta ate early the next morning and set out alone. By the power of the Bodhisatta, because the deities contracted the earth, he reached Takkasilā in a single day, paid respects to the teacher, and sat in a suitable place.

Then the teacher asked him, "Young man, where have you come from?" "From Bārāṇasī, teacher." "For what purpose have you come?" "I have come to learn the three Vedas and the Elephant Lore from you." The teacher said, "Very well, young man, learn."

The Bodhisatta said, "Teacher, my business is very urgent," and having told the whole story, he said, "I have traveled a distance of a hundred and twenty leagues in a single day. Grant me the opportunity for this very night. The elephant-consecration will take place on the third day from now. I will learn everything in a single course of recitation." Having obtained the teacher's permission, he ate while the teacher was eating, washed the teacher's feet, placed a bag of a thousand pieces of money before him, paid respects, and sitting in a suitable place, began his studies. By dawn, through the power of his wisdom, he completed the three Vedas and the Elephant Lore. He asked, "Teacher, is there anything else besides this?" When the teacher said, "No, young man, everything is finished," the Bodhisatta said, "Teacher, in this text, this many words are corrupted; this many places are confusing in terms of recitation. From today onwards, when you teach your disciples, do not teach them in this way." Having thus corrected the teacher's art, he ate early, paid respects to the teacher, and returned to Bārāṇasī in a single day. When his mother asked, "Dear son, have you learned the art?" he replied, "Yes, mother," and gladdened her heart.

The next day, the elephant-consecration festival was prepared. They made and placed trunk-ornaments for a hundred elephants, gold banners, and coverings of golden nets.
43:
On the following day, the Elephant Festival was prepared. They decorated over a hundred elephant trunks and placed gold banners covered with golden nets, and they adorned the royal courtyard. The Brahmins, dressed and decorated, stood saying, "We shall perform the Elephant Festival, we shall perform it." King Susīma, also adorned with all ornaments, had the ceremonial equipment brought and went to the place of the festival.

The Bodhisatta, adorned with the grace of a youth and surrounded by his own retinue, went to the King and said: "Is it true, O Great King, that you, destroying our lineage and your own, have said, 'I will have other Brahmins perform the Elephant Festival and give them the elephant ornaments and equipment'?" and he spoke this first verse:

5. These dark elephants with white tusks are yours,
Over a hundred covered in gold nets.
You say, "I give them," O Susīma,
Remembering your fathers and grandfathers?

"O Susīma, Great King Susīma. In your presence, these elephants, dark in color, of noble breed, with white tusks, numbering over a hundred, and covered with golden nets, are present. O Susīma, Great King Susīma, while you are able to remember the practices of the fathers and grandfathers in our lineage and your own, is it true that I hear you have said, 'I shall give those elephants to other Brahmins for the purpose of performing the ceremony, after destroying our lineage and your own'?"

6. These dark elephants with white tusks are mine,
Over a hundred covered in gold nets.

They adorned the royal courtyard. Again, the Brahmins stood decorated with ornaments, saying, "We shall perform the Elephant Festival." King Susīma, also adorned with all ornaments, had the buildings and equipment suitable for the elephants brought and went to the place of the festival.

The Bodhisatta, adorned with a retinue of youths and accompanied by his own followers, went to the King and said: "O Great King, is it true that I hear you have said you will destroy our lineage and your own, and have other Brahmins perform the Elephant Festival, and give the ornaments and equipment of the elephants to those other Brahmins?"

King Susīma, hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, spoke this verse which completes the two:

"I say I give them, O young man,
Remembering my fathers and grandfathers."
44:
"O young man, these elephants, dark in color, of noble breed, with white tusks, numbering over a hundred, and covered with golden nets, are mine. I say it is indeed true that I give these elephants to other Brahmins for the purpose of the ceremony, while remembering the deeds of the fathers and grandfathers."

Then the Bodhisatta said to King Susīma: "O Great King, while remembering our lineage and your own, why do you exclude me and have other Brahmins perform the Elephant Festival?"

"Dear young man, the Brahmins told me that you do not yet know the Three Vedas and the Elephant Lore (Hatthisutta). Therefore, I am having other Brahmins perform it."

When this was said, [the Bodhisatta] spoke: "O Great King, if that be so, if there is even one Brahmin among all these who is able to debate with me even a portion of the Three Vedas or the Elephant Lore, let him stand up! O Great King, excluding me, there is no one in the entire Jambudīpa who knows the Three Vedas and the Elephant Lore along with the performance of the Elephant Festival." Thus he roared a lion's roar, a fearless and bold speech.

Not a single Brahmin was able to stand up as his opponent. The Bodhisatta, having established his family lineage and performed the ceremony, took much wealth and went to his home.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jataka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some monks became Stream-enterers, some Once-returners, some Non-returners, and some attained Arahatship. 

How did he identify the Jataka? "Monks, at that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā, the father was King Suddhodana, King Susīma was Ānanda, the world-renowned teacher was Sāriputta, and the young man was I myself."

## If one contemplates when needed, finds the way, and is aided by effort, one will succeed.

The Susīma Jataka is finished.
45:
## 4. Gijjha Jātaka
## The Vulture who Supported his Parents
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who is capable of disciplining the world including the devas, told this Gijjha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yaṃ nu gijjho yojanasataṃ," concerning a certain monk who supported his parents.

The story will be clearly manifested in the Suvaṇṇasāma Jātaka. Specifically, the Fully Enlightened Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that I have heard you are supporting laypeople?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Blessed One," the Buddha asked, "Who are they that you support?" Upon the monk's reply, "I support my parents, Bhante," the Buddha praised him, saying, "Excellent, excellent!" and gave him his approval. He then said, "Monks, do not disparage this monk. Wise men of old, by the power of knowing gratitude, also performed acts of gratitude even to those who were not their relatives. For this monk, supporting his parents is indeed his duty," and he then related the past story.

In the past, monks, when a king named Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the vulture species on Gijjhakūṭa Mountain and supported his parents. At one time, there was a heavy storm of wind and rain.

The vultures, being unable to endure the wind and rain, went to Bārāṇasī out of fear of the cold. They sat shivering from the cold near the city gate posts and near the moat.

At that time, the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī, while leaving the city to go bathe in the river, saw those distressed vultures. He gathered them in a place where the rain did not reach, had a fire lit, sent his attendants to the cemetery to fetch beef, fed the vultures, and set a guard over them. When the wind and rain subsided, the vultures, having healthy bodies, flew back to Gijjhakūṭa Mountain.

Those vultures gathered on that very mountain and consulted together: "Friends, the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī has done us a favor. It is proper to return the favor to one who has previously done a favor. Therefore, from this day forward, whichever vulture among you obtains any cloth or ornament, let that vulture drop it in the open courtyard of the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī's house."

From then on, the vultures watched for the negligence of people drying their clothes and ornaments in the sun. Just as hawks snatch a piece of meat, they quickly seized them and dropped them in the open courtyard of the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī's house. That Treasurer of Bārāṇasī, knowing that they were brought by the vultures, kept all those clothes and ornaments separately.
46:
7. "A vulture, it is said, from a hundred leagues,
Can look down and see carcasses.
Why then, having come upon a net and a snare,
Do you not perceive them?"
This was the first verse spoken.

"O vulture! It is said that a vulture can see carcasses lying as far as a hundred leagues away. Why then, having come upon a net and a snare set for your capture, do you not perceive them?"

8. "When a person is destined for ruin,
At the end of his life,
Then, even having come upon a net and a snare,
He does not perceive them."
This was the second verse, completing the pair.

"Great King, when a being is destined for destruction and his life is at an end, then that being, even having come upon a net and a snare set for his capture, does not perceive them."

The townspeople reported to the King, "Great King, the vultures are destroying the city." The King said, "Catch just one vulture first, and I will have all the clothes and ornaments brought back." He then had snares and nets set in various places. The vulture who supported his mother was caught. They took that vulture who supported his mother and went to present him to the King.

The Treasurer of Bārāṇasī, while on his way to serve the King, saw those men taking the vulture and said, "Friends, do not kill this vulture." He then followed the men who were taking the vulture.

The men presented the vulture to the King. Then the King asked the vulture, "O vulture, did you all destroy the city and take clothes and such?" "Yes, Great King," he replied. "O vulture, to whom did you give those clothes and ornaments?" "Great King, we gave them to the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī." "Why did you give them to the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī?" "Great King, that Treasurer of Bārāṇasī gave us our lives. It is proper to return a favor to one who is kind. Therefore, we gave them to him."

Then the King, wanting to say to the Bodhisatta, "O vulture, vultures can see carcasses from a hundred leagues away; why did you not see the snare set for your capture?"—

The vulture, hearing the King's words—

The King, hearing the vulture's words, asked the Treasurer, "Is it true, Great Treasurer, that the vultures brought clothes and such to your house?" "It is true, Sire," he replied. "Great Treasurer, where have you kept those clothes and ornaments?" "Sire, thinking that I would return them to their owners, I have kept all those clothes and ornaments separately," he replied. The King ordered, "Release this vulture," and had the Treasurer return all the goods to their respective owners.

The Teacher, having related this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who supported his parents was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How was the Jātaka identified? "Monks, Ānanda was the King of Bārāṇasī at that time, Sāriputta was the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī, and I myself was the vulture who supported his mother." Thus he identified the Jātaka.
47:
## One must especially repay the gratitude of parents
The Gijjha Jātaka is finished.

9. Having made a truce with the enemy, O womb-born one, with the egg-born one.
Opening your fangs, you sleep; from where has fear come to you?

This first verse was spoken. 
[Gloss]: Jalābuja: O mongoose. Tvaṃ: you. Amittena: with the enemy. Aṇḍajena: with the snake. Sandhiṃ katvā: having made a truce of friendship. Dāṭhaṃ: the fangs. Vivariya: revealing. Sesi: you sleep. Te: to you. Kuto: from where. Bhayaṃ: fear. Āgataṃ: has come?

## 5. Nakula Jātaka
## Two Rival Generals
The Present Story: While the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Nakula Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sandhiṃ katvā amittena," concerning the "quarreling of two ministers."

This story is similar to what was told in the Uraga Jātaka below. In this Nakula Jātaka as well, the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have reconciled these two great ministers; in the past, I also reconciled them," and he brought forth the past story.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a small village. When he reached the age of maturity, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, renounced the household life, and became an ascetic. Having attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), he lived in the Himalayan region, sustaining himself on forest roots and fruits. In an anthill at the end of his walking path lived a mongoose. Near that same anthill, in a tree hollow, lived a snake. Those two, the snake and the mongoose, were constantly quarreling.

The Bodhisatta taught them the danger of quarreling and the benefits of developing loving-kindness (mettā). He advised them, "It is proper to live in harmony without quarreling," and he reconciled the two, the snake and the mongoose.
48:
10. One should suspect an enemy, and even a friend one should not trust.
Fear arising from the fearless even cuts off the roots.

This verse, which completes the two, was spoken.
[Gloss]: Ayya: O Venerable Ascetic. Amittasmiṃ pi: even in an enemy. Mittasmiṃ pi: even in a friend. Saṅketheva: one should indeed be suspicious. Na vissase: one should not trust. Abhayā: from the friend (the fearless). Uppannaṃ: arisen. Bhayaṃ api: fear also. Mūlāni: the roots. Kantati: cuts off.

At that time, when the snake went out, the mongoose put its head out of the anthill hole at the end of the walking path, opened its mouth, and lay there breathing in and out, falling asleep.

The Bodhisatta, seeing the mongoose lying and sleeping in that manner, wishing to ask, "Mongoose, based on what has fear arisen in you?"

The mongoose, being thus questioned by the Bodhisatta, wishing to say, "Venerable sir, one should not despise a so-called enemy; one must indeed be suspicious."

Then the Bodhisatta advised the mongoose, "Do not be afraid. I will act in such a way that the snake does not harm you. From this day forward, do not be suspicious of that snake." Having developed the four Brahma-vihāras, he was destined for the Brahma realm. Those two also went according to their kamma.

The Identification: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the snake and the mongoose were these two great ministers. The ascetic, however, was I myself."

## By letting go of grudges and keeping loving-kindness, one will prosper and be happy
The Nakula Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Upasāḷaka Jātaka
## The Brahmin Seeking a Pure Cemetery
The Present Story: While the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, he told this Upasāḷaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Upasāḷaka nāmāni," concerning "a Brahmin named Upasāḷaka who sought a pure cemetery where no corpse had ever been discarded."

That Brahmin was said to be wealthy and of great possessions. Because of his holding wrong views (micchā-diṭṭhi), he had never offered support to the Buddhas who resided in the nearby monastery. The son of that Brahmin Upasāḷaka, however, was wise and endowed with wisdom. When the Brahmin Upasāḷaka was old, he said to his son, "Dear son, do not cremate me in a cemetery where other low-born people are cremated. Especially, cremate me only in a cemetery where not even a single person has been cremated before."
49:
"Father, I do not know of a place suitable for your cremation. Please, take me and show me yourself, saying, 'Cremate me in this spot.'" The Brahmin replied, "Very well, dear son," and taking him, he left the city, climbed to the top of Gijjhakūṭa mountain, and said, "This is a place where no other low-born person has ever been cremated. Cremate me here." Then he began to descend the mountain with his son.

On that day, at dawn, the Teacher, surveying those who were ready to be awakened to the Truth, saw the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path of Stream-entry in that father and son. Therefore, like a hunter waiting on a path where deer are expected to pass, he went to the foot of Gijjhakūṭa mountain and sat waiting for the father and son descending from the mountain top. 

As they descended from the mountain top, the father and son saw the Teacher. The Teacher, wishing to engage them in conversation, asked, "Where are you going, Brahmins?" The young Brahmin explained the matter. The Teacher said, "If that is so, come, let us go to the place shown by your father." Taking both father and son, he climbed to the mountain top and asked, "Which spot is it?"

The young Brahmin replied, "Venerable sir, my father pointed out the space between these three mountains."

The Teacher said, "Young man, it is not only now that your father seeks a pure cemetery where no corpse has been laid; in the past too, he sought a pure cemetery. It is not only now that he tells you, 'Cremate me in this spot'; in the past too, he pointed out this very spot as the place for his own cremation." Being requested by the young man, he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Young man, in the past, in this very city of Rājagaha, this very Brahmin was a Brahmin named Upasāḷaka. This very son was his son. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Magadha. Having mastered all the arts, he became an ascetic, attained the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lived for a long time in the Himālaya region, sporting in jhāna. He then resided in a leaf-hut on Gijjhakūṭa mountain to make use of salt and vinegar.
50:
11. Fourteen thousand men named Upasāḷaka
Have been burned in this very spot;
There is no place in the world where no one has died.

12. Where truth, Dhamma, non-violence, restraint, and self-control exist—
The Noble Ones frequent such a person;
This is the deathless state in the world.

Thus he spoke these verses.

Young man, in this very spot, fourteen thousand people named Upasāḷaka have been cremated. In this world, there is no such thing as a place where no one has died (anāmata-ṭṭhāna).

Young man, in whichever person there exists the knowledge of the Truths (sacca-ñāṇa) which precedes the supramundane Dhamma, the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) itself, non-violence (ahiṃsā) toward others, restraint (saṃyama) in virtue, and self-control (dama) of the senses—this collection of qualities exists. The Noble Ones (ariyas)—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddhas—frequent such a person who is the locus of these five qualities. This collection of qualities is called the "deathless" (anāmata) in the world because it achieves the state of the Deathless.

At that time, the Brahmin had spoken to his son with that intention, and when the son said, "Father, you yourself show me such a place," he pointed out this very spot between the three mountains. As they descended from the mountain top, they saw the Bodhisatta and approached him. The Bodhisatta questioned them in the same manner, and having heard the young man's words, he said, "Come, young man, let us investigate whether the place shown by your father has been used for cremating corpses or not." He climbed to the mountain top with the father and son. When the young man said, "Venerable ascetic, this space between these three mountains is a place where not even a single corpse has been cremated," the Bodhisatta replied, "Young man, there is no limit to those who have been cremated in this very spot. Your father himself, having been born in this very city of Rājagaha, in this very Brahmin family, with the very name Upasāḷaka, has been cremated in this very mountain cleft fourteen thousand times. That is true. It is impossible to find a spot on earth where no one has been cremated, which is not a cemetery, or where no one has died." Having discerned this with his knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa):

In this way, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to the father and son, developed the four Sublime Abodes (brahma-vihāra), and became destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, both father and son were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Jātaka? "The father and son then were the same as the father and son now. The ascetic, however, was I myself."

## No place on earth is free from being a cemetery.

The Upasāḷaka Jātaka is finished.

13. O monk, you beg without having enjoyed; indeed, you do not beg after having enjoyed.
Having enjoyed, O monk, then beg; let not the time pass you by.

This is the first verse spoken [by the goddess].

Bhikkhasi, you beg (become a monk). Kilesakāmavasena, by the power of the defilement of sensuality. Vatthukāme, the objects of sensuality. Bhutvāna, having enjoyed.
