Pacchā, afterwards. Mahallakakāle, in the time of old age. Bhikkhassu, do beg (become a monk). Taṃ, for you. Kālo, the time of youth which is for enjoying sensual pleasures. Mā upaccagā, let it not pass by.

## 7. Samiddhi Jātaka
## The Ascetic and the Goddess

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Tapodārāma monastery near the city of Rājagaha, told this Samiddhi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Abhutvā bhikkhasi bhikkhu," concerning the Elder Samiddhi.

This is the account: The Venerable Elder Samiddhi, having exerted effort throughout the night, bathed at the time of dawn and stood drying his golden-hued body, wearing his inner robe and holding his upper robe in his hand. He stood like a well-crafted golden statue. Because of the perfection (samiddhi) of his physical body, he was named "Samiddhi."

Then, seeing the beauty of the Elder Samiddhi's body, a certain goddess, her heart filled with lust, said to the Elder: "Monk, you are young, youthful, a mere lad with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, handsome, beautiful, and pleasing to look at. For one such as you, what is the use of the monkhood without having enjoyed the objects of sensuality and the pleasures of the senses? Enjoy the objects of sensuality and the pleasures of the senses first. Later, you can become a monk and practice the Dhamma."

Then the Elder said to her: "Goddess, I do not know the time of my death, thinking 'I shall die at such and such an age.' This time of death is hidden from me. Therefore, I will practice the Dhamma while I am still young and make an end of suffering."

That goddess, failing to receive a favorable response from the Elder, vanished right there.

The Elder approached the Teacher and reported the matter. The Teacher said, "Samiddhi, it is not only now that you have been tempted by a goddess; in the past also, goddesses tempted those who had gone forth," and being requested by the Elder, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi. When he came of age, he attained proficiency in all the arts, went forth as an ascetic, and having developed the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti), he lived near a natural lake in the Himalayan region. That Bodhisatta, having exerted effort throughout the night, bathed at the time of dawn, wore one bark garment and held another bark garment in his hand, and stood drying the water from his body.

At that time, a certain goddess, seeing the Bodhisatta's body which had reached the height of beauty and having a heart filled with lust, desiring to tempt the Bodhisatta, spoke the first verse:
52:
14. I do not know the time; the time is hidden and not seen.
Therefore, I beg without having enjoyed; let not the time pass me by.

He spoke this verse which completes the two [verses].

Devadhīte, O goddess. Ahaṃ, I. Kālaṃ, the time of death. Na jānāmi, do not know. Mayhaṃ, for me. Channo, being hidden. Kālaṃ, the time of death. Na dissati, is not seen. Tasmā, therefore. Pañcakāmaguṇe, the five strands of sensual pleasure. Abhutvā, without having enjoyed. Maṃ, for me. Kālo, the time for practicing the Dhamma of a monk. Mā upaccagā, let it not pass by. Bhikkhāmi, I beg (become a monk).

**The Past Story of Samiddhi**
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a certain village of Kāsi. When he came of age, he attained proficiency in all the arts, went forth as an ascetic, and having developed the higher knowledges and attainments, he lived near a natural lake in the Himalayan region. That Bodhisatta, having exerted effort throughout the night, bathed at the time of dawn, wore one bark garment and held another bark garment in his hand, and stood drying the water from his body.

At that time, a certain goddess, seeing the Bodhisatta's body which had reached the height of beauty and having a heart filled with lust, desiring to tempt the Bodhisatta—

The Bodhisatta, hearing the words of the goddess and wishing to reveal his own intention—

The goddess, hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, vanished right there.

**The Identification of the Jātaka**
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka. How did He identify the Jātaka? "Samiddhi, the goddess who tempted you now was the goddess who tempted me then. I myself was the ascetic at that time." Thus He identified the Jātaka.

## Physical beauty, the realm of sensuality, many are the temptations.

The Samiddhi Jātaka is finished.
53:
## 8. Sakunagghi Jātaka
## The Quail and the Falcon

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sakunagghi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Seno balasa patamāno," based on the Sakunovāda Sutta which he preached of his own accord.

That is true. One day, the Buddha addressed the monks, saying, "Monks, wander only in your own feeding ground, your ancestral domain," and while preaching this sutta from the Mahāvagga Saṃyutta, he said, "Monks, let alone you, in the past, even animals who left their ancestral domain and wandered in an improper range fell into the hands of their enemies; yet, having fallen, they escaped from the hands of their enemies through their perfection of wisdom and skill in means." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a quail and lived in a place of earth-clods turned up by a plowshare attached to a plow.

One day, that quail left his own domain to find food and went to the edge of a forest, thinking, "I will take food in the domain of others." At that time, a falcon, seeing the quail taking food at the edge of the forest, swooped down swiftly and seized him.

While being carried away by the falcon, the quail lamented: "We are indeed unlucky; we are indeed meritless, for we wandered in an improper range, the domain of others. If today we had wandered in our own feeding ground, our ancestral domain, this falcon would not have been able to strike us in such a way."

When he lamented thus, the falcon asked, "Quail, what is your own feeding ground, your ancestral domain?" The quail replied, "Falcon, it is the place of earth-clods turned up by a plowshare attached to a plow; that is my feeding ground." Then the falcon, being confident in his own strength, released him, saying, "Go then, quail; even if you go there, you shall not escape me."

The quail went to his feeding ground, climbed onto a large earth-clod, and stood there calling the falcon, "Come now, falcon!"

The falcon, confident in his own strength, spread both wings and swooped down swiftly toward the quail. When the quail knew, "This falcon is coming toward me very fast," he turned around and entered right into the gap of that earth-clod.
54:
He preached this first verse:

15. A falcon, swooping down with force,
Upon a quail in his feeding ground,
Swiftly reached him, but through that act,
He met his own death.

Monks, when the falcon swooped down with force to seize the quail who was staying at the edge of the forest to find food, he reached him swiftly. Because of that reason, that falcon met his death.

16. I, endowed with the means,
Delighting in my ancestral domain,
Free from the enemy, I rejoice,
Seeing my own well-being.

He spoke this verse which completes the two. I, who am endowed with the wisdom that is the means of escaping danger, delighting in my ancestral domain, being free from the enemy, rejoice because I clearly see my own well-being, which is the state of being free from harm.

The falcon, unable to check his speed, struck his breast right against that earth-clod. Thus, his breast was broken, his eyes popped out, and he reached the end of his life.

The All-Knowing Buddha, having shown this past story, said: "Monks, in this way, even animals fall into the hands of enemies when they wander in an improper range. But when they wander in their own feeding ground, their ancestral domain, they can suppress their enemies. Therefore, you too, do not wander in an improper range, the domain of others. Monks, if you wander in the domain of others, an improper range, Māra will get an opportunity. Māra will find an object of attachment."

"Monks, what is the improper range, the domain of others for a monk? It is the five cords of sensual pleasure. What are the five? They are forms cognizable by the eye... and so on. Monks, these five cords of sensual pleasure are the improper range, the domain of others for a monk." Having preached thus, after attaining Buddhahood—

When that falcon had met his death, the quail came out from between the earth-clods and, thinking "Indeed, I have seen the destruction of my enemy," he kept it in his heart and uttered a joyful cry—

Conclusion of the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching and illustrated the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, many monks reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and so on. How did he identify the Jātaka? "Monks, Devadatta was the falcon at that time. I, the Buddha, was the quail at that time." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Live and act only in what is suitable for oneself.

The Sakunagghi Jātaka is finished.
55:
## 9. Araka Jātaka

## The Benefits of Loving-kindness

**The Present Story**
While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Araka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Yo ve mettena cittena,' concerning the Metta Sutta.

Indeed, on one occasion, the Buddha addressed the monks: 'Monks, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (metta-cetovimutti) is cultivated, developed, practiced frequently, made into a vehicle, made into a foundation, well-established, consolidated, and properly undertaken, eleven benefits are to be expected.'

What are the eleven? 'One sleeps happily, wakes happily, and does not see evil dreams. One is dear to humans and dear to non-humans. Deities protect one. Neither fire, poison, nor weapons can harm one. The mind concentrates quickly. The complexion is clear. One dies unconfused. If one does not penetrate the higher Path and Fruit, one goes to the Brahma realm.' These are the eleven.

'Monks, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is cultivated... properly undertaken, these eleven benefits are to be expected.' Having praised the meditation on loving-kindness based on these eleven benefits, the Buddha said: 'Monks, a monk should develop loving-kindness towards all beings by way of specified and unspecified pervasion. One should pervade with a mind of welfare those who desire one's welfare, those who do not desire one's welfare, and those who are neutral. Thus, loving-kindness should be developed towards all beings by way of specified and unspecified pervasion.'

'Compassion (karuṇā), empathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā) should also be developed. One should indeed perform the work in the four Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāras). Indeed, a monk who does so, even if he does not attain the Path or Fruit, will be bound for the Brahma realm. Wise men of old also developed loving-kindness for seven years and lived in the Brahma realm for seven aeons of contraction and expansion.' Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

**The Past Story**
Monks, in the past, during a certain aeon, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he reached maturity, he renounced sensual pleasures, became an ascetic, and attained the four Divine Abodes. He became a teacher named Araka and lived in the Himalayan region. This teacher Araka had a large following.

While instructing the group of ascetics, he said: 'One who has gone forth should develop loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy, and equanimity. Indeed, this mind of loving-kindness, when it reaches absorption (appanā), ensures one is bound for the Brahma realm.' To show the benefits of loving-kindness, he spoke these verses:
56:
17. Whoever, with a mind of loving-kindness,
Has compassion for the whole world,
Above, below, and across,
Everywhere without limit.

18. With an immeasurable, beneficial mind,
Fully complete and well-cultivated,
Whatever limited action was done,
It does not remain there.

He spoke these two verses.

'O group of ascetics! Whoever among kings and so forth, or among recluses and Brahmins, has compassion for the entire world of beings with an immeasurable mind of loving-kindness. "Above" (uddhaṃ) means the region from the surface of the earth up to the Brahma realm of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. "Below" (adho) means the region from the surface of the earth down to the Ussada great hells. "Across" (tiriyaṃ) means the horizontal directions in the human world, as many universes as there are. In all these places, for all beings born there, may they be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from suffering, and may they keep themselves happy. This is the meaning of having compassion with a mind of loving-kindness thus developed. "Without limit" (appamāṇena) means because it has immeasurable beings as its object. "Everywhere" (sabbaso) means in every way, by way of above, below, and across, and by way of all happy and unhappy destinations.'

'"An immeasurable, beneficial mind" means a mind wishing for the welfare of all beings, developed immeasurably. "Fully complete" (paripuṇṇaṃ) means without deficiency. "Well-cultivated" (subhāvitaṃ) means well-developed; this is a name for the mind of absorption (appanā-citta). "Whatever limited action was done" (yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ) means any small sensual-sphere action (kāmāvacara-kamma) that was done without being expanded by way of the triad of objects as "immeasurable, having an immeasurable object" and by way of mastery. "It does not remain there" (na taṃ tatrāvasissati) means that small action does not remain in that fine-material sphere action (rūpāvacara-kamma) which is reckoned as the "immeasurable, beneficial mind."

Just as a small amount of water overwhelmed by a great flood does not remain or stay within the flood without being swept away—rather, the great flood stays there, having overwhelmed it—even so, that limited action does not remain or stay within that lofty action (mahaggata-kamma), as its opportunity for result is cut off and not taken up by that lofty action; it is unable to give its own result. Instead, the lofty action itself stays there, having overwhelmed it, and gives its result.'

Thus, the Bodhisatta taught the benefits of the meditation on loving-kindness to his disciples. Having maintained his meditative absorptions (jhāna) without decline, he was reborn in the Brahma realm and did not return to this world for seven aeons of contraction and expansion.
57:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, the Fully Enlightened One identified the birth-story: "O monks, the group of ascetics at that time have now become the Buddha's followers. At that time, I myself was the teacher named Araka." Thus He identified the birth-story.

## Strive to obtain the eleven benefits of loving-kindness

The Araka Jātaka is finished.

## 10. Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka

This Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Nāyaṃ pure unnamati," will be clearly explained in the Mahā-Ummagga Jātaka.

The Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Kalyāṇa Vagga

## 1. Kalyāṇa-dhamma Jātaka

## The Wealthy Man and the King

The Story of the Present: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kalyāṇa-dhamma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kalyāṇadhammo," concerning a certain deaf mother-in-law.

Indeed, in the city of Sāvatthī, there was a certain householder who was endowed with faith. He had devotion, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and was endowed with the five precepts. One day, taking many medicines such as ghee and the like, as well as flowers, perfumes, and clothes, he went to the Jetavana Monastery to listen to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.

At the time of the householder's departure, his mother-in-law, bringing some food and wishing to see her daughter, came to that house. That woman, the mother-in-law, was also somewhat deaf.
58:
After eating with her daughter and dispelling her post-meal drowsiness, she asked, "Dear daughter, does your husband live with you happily, without quarreling, and in a loving manner?" The daughter replied, "Mother, what are you saying? Such is the nature of your son-in-law in terms of virtue and perfection of conduct. Even among those who have gone forth as monks, such a person is rare." The laywoman, unable to hear her daughter's words clearly, caught only the word "monk" and shouted loudly, "Dear daughter, why has your husband become a monk?"

Hearing that sound, all the residents of the house lamented, "It is said that our householder has become a monk." Hearing the voices of the household, people passing by the gate asked, "For what reason are you crying?" They were told, "It is said that in this house, the householder has become a monk."

That householder, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, left the monastery and was entering the city. Then, a man saw the householder on the way and said, "Friend, it is said that you have become a monk; your wife, children, and attendants are weeping and lamenting in your house."

Then, this thought occurred to the householder: "He says I have become a monk, though I have not. A good reputation has indeed arisen. This good reputation should not be allowed to vanish. It is proper for me to ordain this very day." Having had this thought, he turned back and went to the presence of the Blessed One. When the Buddha asked, "Lay follower, you have just finished attending to the Buddha and left; why have you returned so soon?", he explained the matter and said, "Venerable Sir, it is not proper to let a so-called good reputation vanish. Therefore, wishing to ordain, I have come."

That lay follower received the lower and higher ordinations, and by practicing well, he attained Arahatship before long. This matter became well-known among the community of monks.

Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks raised a discussion: "Friends, a householder of such a name, saying 'a good reputation that has arisen should not be allowed to vanish,' ordained and has now attained Arahatship."
59: 1. When a man, O leader of men, attains the reputation in the world of being 'one of good character,' a wise man should not fall away from that; for the virtuous, out of shame, take up the burden. 2. That reputation has come to me here today, O leader of men, as 'one of good character.' Considering that, I shall go forth into the homeless life; for I have no desire for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures here. He spoke these verses. O Janinda, the lord of men. In the world. Kalyāṇadhammo, one who has a good nature. Yadā, when. Samaññaṃ, the designation or name of being a virtuous person, one of good character, or a monk. Anupāpuṇāti, attains. Sapañño, the wise. Naro, noble man. Tasmā, from that designation of being a virtuous person, one of good character, or a monk. Na hiyyetha, should not fall away. Mahārāja, O great king. Santo, those who are virtuous. Hiriyāpi, through moral shame. Ottappenapi, through moral dread. Dhuraṃ, the burden of being a monk. Ādiyanti, they take up. O Janinda, the lord of men. Idha loke, in this world. Pavattā, which has occurred. Sāyaṃ samaññā, that designation or name of being a monk. Ajja, today. Mayā, by me. Pattā, is attained. Kalyāṇadhammo, one who has good conduct. Ahaṃ, I. Taṃ, that designation or name attained by the power of virtue. Samekkhaṃ, considering well. Idha, in this world. Pabbajissaṃ, I shall go forth as a monk. Idha, in this world. Kāmabhoge, in the enjoyment of the objects of desire through sensual passion. Me, for me. Chando, desire. Na hi atthi, does not exist at all. The Master, having arrived, asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here now?" When they replied, "We are gathered with such and such a conversation," he said, "Monks, in the past, wise men also, thinking it improper to let a good reputation that had arisen be lost, went forth as monks," and he brought forward the past story. The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant's family, and upon reaching maturity, he attained the position of a merchant after his father passed away. One day, the Bodhisatta left his house and went to a place near the King. At that time, the Bodhisatta's mother-in-law went to her daughter's house to see her. That laywoman was somewhat hard of hearing. All the words are just like the present story. As for the Bodhisatta, a man saw him coming home after going to the place near the King and said, "It is said that the merchant has become a monk; there is great lamentation in your house." The Bodhisatta thought, "It is not proper to let a good reputation that has arisen vanish," and returning from that place, he went to the King. When the King asked, "Great Merchant, you just left; why have you come back again?" he replied, "O King, it is said that my household members are lamenting, saying 'He has become a monk' even though I have not. Indeed, a good reputation that has arisen should not be allowed to vanish. Therefore, I shall go forth as a monk. Please grant me permission for the monkhood." To explain this matter, the Bodhisatta spoke these verses, and having spoken thus and obtained the King's permission for the monkhood, he went to the Himālaya region, became an ascetic, developed the higher knowledges and attainments, and became destined for the Brahma realm.
60:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "Monks, at that time Ānanda was the King of Bārāṇasī, and I myself was the Merchant of Bārāṇasī." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Good omens are true; they should be followed; it is very appropriate.

The Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Daddara Jātaka

## The Jackal who imitated the Lion

The Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Daddara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ko nu saddena mahatā", concerning Kokālika.

This is the account: At that time, many learned monks were preaching the Dhamma with melodious voices (sarabhañña) in the midst of the Saṅgha, like young lions roaring on a vermilion plain, or as if bringing down the celestial Ganges.

When those learned monks were preaching with melodious voices, Kokālika, unaware of his own emptiness, thought, "I too will preach with a melodious voice." Entering among the monks, he went about saying in various places, without mentioning the name of the Saṅgha, "The monks do not let us preach with a melodious voice. If they were to let us, we too would preach."

That talk of Kokālika became well-known among the Saṅgha of monks. Those monks, with the intention of testing him, said: "Friend Kokālika, today preach the Dhamma with a melodious voice to the Saṅgha." Kokālika, without knowing his own strength, accepted, saying, "Very well," and thinking, "Today I will preach with a melodious voice," he drank the gruel that came to him, ate snacks, and had a meal with suitable curry.

When the sun set and the time for hearing the Dhamma was announced, the assembly of monks gathered.
61: 3. Who is this that makes the Daddara mountain echo with a great sound? The lions do not roar back. Who is this lord of beasts? Thus he spoke this first verse. Migādhibhū: Lord of beasts, the lion king. Yo: Whichever creature. Mahatā saddena: With a great sound. Daddaraṃ: The silver mountain. Abhinādeti: Makes it echo. So: That creature. Ko nu: Who is it? Yassa: Of which creature. Taṃ saddaṃ: That sound. Sīhā: The lions. Nappaṭinadanti: Do not roar in response. Eso: This creature. Ko nāma: What is its name? That Kokālika, wearing an inner robe the color of a liphayway flower and an outer robe the color of a mahāhlekar flower, entered the midst of the Saṅgha. Having paid homage to the senior monks, he ascended the seat of the Dhamma-preachers in the decorated jeweled pavilion. Holding an ornate fan, he intended to preach the Dhamma. At that very moment, sweat poured from Kokālika's body. He was overcome by loathing. At the start of the sermon, having recited the first word, he could not see anything beyond it. Trembling, Kokālika descended from the seat and, feeling ashamed, left the midst of the Saṅgha and went to his own dwelling. Another learned monk preached the Dhamma. From then on, the monks knew of Kokālika's emptiness. Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: 'Friends, previously Kokālika's emptiness was hard to know. Now, by his own speech, his emptiness has become clear.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?' When they replied, 'It is such and such,' the Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has made his emptiness known by his own speech; in the past also, he made it known by his speech.' He then brought forth the past. The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a lion's womb in the Himalayan region and became the king of many lions. That lion king, surrounded by a large pride of lions, lived in a cave. Near that cave, a jackal also lived. One day, after the rain had ceased, all the lions gathered at the entrance of the lion king's cave, roaring their lion's roar and playing their lion games. While the lions were roaring and playing in this way, that jackal also howled. Hearing the jackal's voice, the lions felt ashamed, thinking, 'This jackal is howling along with us,' and they became silent. While the lions were silent, the Bodhisatta's son, a young lion, seeing that the lions had become silent out of shame upon hearing that creature's voice while they were roaring and playing, wished to ask his father, the lion king who rules over his kind, 'Who is this creature that makes itself known by its own voice?' Hearing his words, the father spoke this second verse: 4. The lowest of beasts, the jackal, is howling, my son. The lions, loathing his kind, remain silent. Tāta: Dear son. Migajātānaṃ: Among the species of beasts. Adhamo: The base one. Siṅgālo: The jackal. Vassati: Howls. Assa: Of that jackal. Jātiṃ: The birth/kind. Jigucchanto: Being loathsome. Sīhā: The lions. Tuṇhī: Silent. Samaccare: They remain.
62:
The Teacher said, "Monks, not only now has Kokālika revealed himself by his own cry; he did so in the past as well." Having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Kokālika, the young lion was Rāhula, and the lion king was I myself."

## Imitating the incomparable, boasting, loathed by the people.

The Daddara Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Makkaṭa Jātaka
## The Ascetic and the Monkey

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Makkaṭa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Tāta māṇavako eso," concerning a certain hypocritical monk.

The full story will be revealed in the Uddālaka Jātaka of the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta. At that time, the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now is this monk a hypocrite; in the past also, as a monkey, he practiced hypocrisy for the sake of fire." And he told a story of the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a village of Kāsī. When he came of age, he studied the arts at Takkasilā and established a household. Later, his wife gave birth to a son, and when the child was old enough to run about, she passed away. The Bodhisatta performed her funeral rites and thought, "What use is the household life to me? I will take my son and become an ascetic." Leaving his weeping kinsmen and friends, he took his son to the Himalayas, became an ascetic, and lived there, subsisting on wild roots and fruits.

One day during the rainy season, while it was raining, he lit a fire with some heartwood and lay down on a wooden pallet to warm himself. His son, the young ascetic, sat massaging his father's feet.
63:
5. Tata māṇavako eso, tālamūlaṃ apassito.
Agārakañcidaṃ atthi, handa demassagārakaṃ.
He spoke this first verse:
Father (tata), this young ascetic (eso māṇavako) is leaning (apassito) against the base of a palm tree (tālamūlaṃ). We have (amhākaṃ... atthi) this little hut (idañca agārakaṃ). Come now (handa), let us give (dema) the hut (agārakaṃ) to him (assa).

6. Ma kho tvaṃ tata pakkosi, dūseyya no agārakaṃ.
Netādisaṃ mukhaṃ hoti, brāhmaṇassa susīlino.
He spoke this second verse to complete the pair:
Dear son (tata), the face (mukhaṃ) of a virtuous (susīlino) Brahmin (brāhmaṇassa) is not (na hoti) like that (etādisaṃ). This creature (eso) is a monkey (makkaṭo). If this monkey (ayaṃ) enters (paviṭṭho) here (idha) into the hut, he would foul (dūseyya) our (no) hut (agārakaṃ). Do not call him (tvaṃ mā kho pakkosi).

At that time, a certain forest monkey, afflicted by the cold, saw the fire in the Bodhisatta's leaf-hut and thought, 'If I enter that hut as a monkey, they will beat me, crying "Monkey! Monkey!" and drive me out. I will not be able to warm myself. Now I have a plan: I will go in the guise of an ascetic, adopting their appearance.' Having found the robes of a deceased ascetic and taking a basket and a goad-stick, he stood leaning against a palm tree at the door of the leaf-hut, crouching down.

The young ascetic, seeing the monkey and not realizing its true nature, thought, 'An old ascetic, oppressed by the cold, must have come to warm himself by the fire.' He told his father, the ascetic, intending to let the old ascetic into the leaf-hut to warm himself.

When the Bodhisatta heard his son's words, he stood at the door of the leaf-hut and looked. Recognizing the creature as a monkey, he meant to say, 'My son, a human face is not like this. This creature is a monkey; he must not be invited inside.'

Saying 'This creature is a monkey,' the Bodhisatta took a firebrand and threw it, saying, 'Do not stay here!' and made the monkey flee. The monkey cast off the robes, climbed a tree, and entered the forest. The Bodhisatta developed the four Sublime States (Brahma-vihāra) and was reborn in the Brahma realm.
64:
Identifying the Birth: The Fully Enlightened Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, identified the Birth as follows: "At that time, the deceitful monk was the monkey. Rāhula was the young ascetic. I myself was the elder ascetic."

## Disguised as an ascetic, the monkey shows wonders.

The Makkata Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Dubbhiya-makkata Jātaka

## The Brahmin and the Monkey

The Present Story: The Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Veluvana Monastery, told this Dubbhiya-makkata Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Adamma te vāri pahūtarūpaṃ,' concerning Devadatta.

This is the truth: One day in the Dhamma Hall, the monks were discussing Devadatta's ingratitude and his treachery toward friends. The Buddha arrived and said, "Monks, not only now is Devadatta ungrateful and treacherous; in the past, he was the same," and he then related the story of the past.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a village of Kāsī. When he came of age, he established a household. At that time, there was a deep well near a main road in the Kāsī kingdom, which was so deep that animals could not descend to drink. Meritorious travelers would draw water using a bucket tied to a long rope, fill a trough, and give water to the animals.

Around that well was a great forest where many monkeys lived. For two or three days, the flow of travelers ceased, and the animals could not get water. A certain monkey, overcome by thirst, wandered near the well searching for water.

The Bodhisatta, traveling that way on some business, arrived at the well, drew water, drank, and washed his hands and feet. While standing there, he saw the monkey. Realizing the monkey's thirst, he drew water, poured it into the trough, and gave it to him.
65:
7. We gave you plenty of water,
To you who were oppressed by heat and thirsty.
Now, having drunk, you make the "kiri" sound;
Non-association with a wicked person is better.

He spoke this first verse.

O wicked monkey! We gave you plenty of water, you who were thirsty and oppressed by heat. Now, having drunk, you make the sound "kiri kiri." It is better not to associate with a wicked person.

After giving the water, he lay down at the foot of a tree to rest. The monkey, having drunk the water, stayed nearby and made a distorted, ugly face with its snout to frighten the Bodhisatta.

The Bodhisatta, seeing the monkey's behavior, said: "O wicked monkey, I gave plenty of water to you when you were exhausted from thirst. Now you make a distorted face at me. Doing a favor for a wicked person is indeed fruitless."

The treacherous monkey, hearing those words, thought: "You think that this much is the end of my mischief? Now I will drop dung on your head and go."

8. Who have you ever heard of or seen, a monkey that is virtuous?
Now I shall drop dung on you; this is our nature.

He spoke this verse to complete the two.

O Brahmin, where have you heard or seen a monkey called virtuous? Now I will drop dung on your head. This act of dropping dung is the nature of us monkeys; this is our birth-nature, to drop dung on the head of a benefactor.

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta made an effort to get up and leave. At that very moment, the monkey jumped up, sat on a branch, and as if descending while hanging, dropped dung on the Bodhisatta's head, shrieked, and entered the forest. The Bodhisatta bathed and went on his way.

The Master said: "Monks, not only now, but in the past too, Devadatta did not know the favor I did." Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monkey was Devadatta, and I was the Brahmin."

## When favors are done, they are met with ingratitude; such is the nature of fools.

The Dubbiyamakkaṭa Jātaka is finished.
66:
9. Among all beings, it is said, there are those endowed with virtue.
Look at this wretched monkey; he stands worshipping the sun.

They spoke this first verse.

Among all beings, there are indeed those endowed with virtue. Look at this wretched monkey. This monkey stands worshipping the sun.

## 5. Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka
## The Hermit and the Monkey

The Master, the All-Knowing Buddha, who teaches the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sabbesu kira bhūtesu," concerning a certain hypocritical monk. The story is the same as the one told below.

The Past Story: Long ago, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he studied all the arts in Takkasilā, became an ascetic, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti), and became the teacher of a large group of ascetics living in the Himalayas.

The Bodhisatta lived in the Himalayas for a long time. To seek salt and vinegar, he came down from the mountains and stayed in a leaf-hut near a border village. At that time, a mischievous monkey would come to the hermitage when the ascetics went for alms, jump and play on the roof of the leaf-hut, spill water from the jars, break the water-pots, and defecate in the fire-hall.

The ascetics, having stayed through the rainy season, said to the lay supporters in the border village, "Now the Himalayas are pleasant and full of flowers and fruits; we shall return there." The people said, "Venerable sirs, tomorrow we will bring food to your hermitage. Please eat and then depart." On the second day, they brought plenty of food and snacks to the monastery.

The monkey saw the food and thought, "I will perform a miracle to please the people so they will give me food and snacks too." Having thought so, the monkey acted as if he were practicing the ascetic way and stood worshipping the sun not far from the hermits.

The people, seeing the monkey, said, "By living in the presence of the virtuous, he has become virtuous."
67:
10. You do not know his virtue, yet you praise him without knowing.
The fire-hut is defiled, and two water jars are broken.

He spoke this verse to complete the two points:

"O laypeople! You do not know the virtue of this wicked monkey. Without knowing, you praise him. This wicked monkey has defiled our fire-hut with excrement and has broken two water jars."

Seeing the people thus praising the monkey's supposed merits, the Bodhisatta said, "You do not know the conduct and virtue of this frivolous monkey, and you are inspired by what is unworthy."

In this way, the Bodhisatta spoke of the monkey's lack of merit. Realizing the monkey's trickery, the people took clods of earth and sticks, struck him, and drove him away. They then offered alms-food to the group of ascetics. The ascetics returned to the Himalayas and, having maintained their meditative absorptions (jhāna), became destined for the Brahma-realm.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the trickster monk was the monkey. The Buddha's followers were the group of ascetics. I myself was the teacher of the group."

## Do not act like a monkey, using trickery for a single meal.
The Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka
## Losing a Handful for a Single Pea

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Bālo vatāyaṃ dumasākhagocaro," concerning the King of Kosala.

Indeed, at one time during the rainy season, there was a rebellion in the borderlands of the King of Kosala. The soldiers stationed there engaged in two or three battles but were unable to overcome the enemies, so they sent word to the King. Even though it was the rainy season and not the time for war, the King set out and established a camp near Jetavana Monastery, where he reflected:

"I have set out for war at an improper time. The ravines and lakes are full of water, and the roads are difficult to travel. I shall visit the Teacher. He will ask me, 'Great King, where are you going?' Then I will inform him of this matter. The Teacher does not only benefit me with regards to the future life; he also benefits me in the present life. Therefore, if my going to war will be without profit, he will say, 'Great King, it is not the right time.' If it will be profitable, he will remain silent."

Having so reflected, the King of Kosala entered Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place.
68: 11. "Foolish indeed is this branch-dweller; he has no wisdom, O Lord of Men. Having scattered a whole handful of peas, he searches for the one pea that fell." He spoke this first verse. "O Lord of Men, ruler of people! This monkey that roams among the branches of trees is truly foolish. Because he lacks wisdom, this branch-dweller has scattered the entire handful of peas and searches for the one pea that fell." The Master asked, "Now, Great King, from where have you come at midday?" "Venerable Sir, I have set out to suppress the border revolt. I have come to pay homage to you before I go," he replied. The Master said, "Great King, in the past also, when kings were setting out with their armies to fight, they listened to the words of the wise and did not go at an improper time." At the King's request, he told a story of the past. Story of the Past: Great King, long ago, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister, an advisor on temporal and spiritual matters, attending to all affairs. When the border region revolted, the soldiers there sent a letter to King Brahmadatta. The King set out during the rainy season and pitched an encampment in a park. The Bodhisatta stood near the King. At that moment, they boiled peas for the horses and put them in a trough. One of the monkeys in the park came down from a tree, took the peas from the trough, filled his mouth, and also took some in his hands. He jumped up, sat on a tree, and prepared to eat. While he was eating, one pea fell from his hand to the ground. The monkey dropped all the peas he held in his mouth and hands, climbed down, and looked for that one pea. Not finding it, he climbed back up the tree and sat on a branch, looking dejected and sorrowful, like someone who had lost a thousand pieces of wealth in a lawsuit.
69:
12. "Even so, O King, we and others who are excessively greedy, lose much for the sake of a little, just like the monkey with the peas."

He spoke this verse to complete the two points:

"Mahārāja, Great King. Just as a monkey, while searching for a single pea, loses all the peas because of that one pea; even so, other people who are excessively greedy, as well as ourselves, will destroy a great benefit for the sake of a small one."

The King, seeing the monkey's behavior, called the Bodhisatta and asked, "O Minister, did you see that action performed by the monkey? What kind of act is it?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, foolish people who do not look at the great benefit but only at the small, are prone to act in such a manner." Having said this—

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta again used the monkey as an example to make the King understand.

Hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, the King returned from that garden and entered the city of Bārāṇasī. The thieves also, hearing that the King had come out of the city saying, "I will suppress the thieves," fled from the border regions.

In the present time as well, the thieves fled upon hearing that the King of Kosala had set out. The King of Kosala, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage, performed a circumambulation, and entered the city of Sāvatthī.

Concluding the Jātaka: The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda. I myself was the wise minister."

## Greed for a little, loss of much; a painful mistake of the foolish.

The Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Tinduka Jātaka

## The Wise Monkey

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Tinduka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dhanuhatthakalāpehi," concerning his own Perfection of Wisdom (Paññāpāramī).

That statement is true. The Blessed One, hearing his own wisdom being praised as in the Mahābodhi Jātaka and the Ummaṅga Jātaka, said, "Monks, not only now is the Tathāgata wise; in the past also, I was wise and skilled in means." He then brought forth the past story. (The Mahābodhi Jātaka is in the Paṇṇāsa Nipāta; the Ummaṅga Jātaka is in the Mahā Nipāta.)
70:
The Past Story: Monks, in the long past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the monkey womb and lived in the Himalayan region surrounded by eighty thousand monkeys. Near that Himalayan region, there was a certain border village that was sometimes inhabited and sometimes deserted. In the middle of that village, there was a Tinduka tree with many branches and sweet, excellent fruit. When the village was deserted, the troop of monkeys would come and eat the fruit of that Tinduka tree.

Later, during another fruiting season, that village was again inhabited by people. It was strongly and securely fenced and had a gate. That Tinduka tree stood with its branches bending low under the weight of the fruit. The troop of monkeys thought:

"In the past, we used to eat Tinduka fruits in such-and-such a village. Is that tree fruiting now or not? Is that village inhabited or not?" Having thought thus, they sent a monkey, saying, "Go and find out the news."

That monkey went and, having learned that the tree was fruiting and that the village was densely inhabited, returned and informed the monkeys.

Hearing that the tree was fruiting, the monkeys became eager, saying, "We shall eat the sweet Tinduka fruits," and informed the Monkey King of the matter. The Monkey King asked, "Is the village inhabited or uninhabited?" When they said, "Lord, it is inhabited," he replied, "In that case, you should not go. It is true that humans are full of guile."

"Lord, we will eat at the time of midnight when humans are asleep," said many monkeys. They persuaded the Monkey King to agree and, descending from the Himalayas, waited near that village for the time when humans would be asleep. They lay on a large flat rock, and during the middle watch when humans fell into a deep sleep, they climbed the tree and ate the Tinduka fruits.

Then, a certain man came out of his house to attend to a call of nature and, going into the middle of the village, saw the monkeys and told the villagers. Many people, equipped with bows and quivers and holding various weapons, took up stones, sticks, and the like. They surrounded the tree and waited, saying, "When the night turns to dawn, we will catch the monkeys."

The eighty thousand monkeys, seeing the people, were terrified of the fear of death. Realizing, "We have no other refuge except for the Monkey King," they went to the Monkey King and spoke the first verse:

13. "Surrounded on all sides by men with bows in hand and quivers, and those bearing excellent swords, how shall our escape be?"
71:
14. Perhaps for those with many duties, some other matter may arise.
There are still fruits on the tree; eat the Tinduka as you wish.

He spoke this verse to complete the two points:

"O monkeys! For humans who have many duties, some other business might arise. There are still many fruits on this Tinduka tree that have not been plucked. You may eat the Tinduka fruits as much as you desire."

They spoke this first verse:

"O Monkey King! Men holding bows and quivers, and carrying excellent swords, have surrounded us on all sides. How—by what means—shall we escape from the fear of death?"

Hearing the words of those monkeys, the Monkey King comforted them, saying, "Do not be afraid. Humans have many tasks. It is now the middle watch of the night. For these people who have surrounded us intending to kill us, some other business might arise that interferes with this task of surrounding us."

In this way, the Bodhisatta gave relief to the troop of monkeys. Indeed, if they had not received such comfort, all those monkeys would have died of broken hearts. The Bodhisatta, having comforted the troop of monkeys, said, "Gather all the monkeys together." When they were gathered, they did not see his nephew, a monkey named Senaka, and reported to the Monkey King, "Senaka has not come."

"If Senaka is not here, do not be afraid. Now Senaka will bring about your safety," he said.

As for Senaka, he had been asleep when the troop of monkeys left. When he woke up later and saw no other monkeys, he followed their tracks. Upon arriving, he saw the humans and realized that danger had befallen the troop of monkeys. He went to an old woman's house at the edge of the village where a fire was burning and she was spinning thread. Like a village boy going to the field, he took a torch, stood upwind, and set fire to the village. The people abandoned the monkeys and ran to extinguish the fire.

As the monkeys fled, they each took one Tinduka fruit for the sake of Senaka and escaped.
72:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jataka: "At that time, the nephew Senaka was Mahānāma the Sakyan, the monkey troop was the Buddha's assembly, and I myself was the Monkey King."

## When danger is imminent, with good wisdom, the group attains happiness.

The Tinduka Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Kacchapa Jātaka
## The Potter and the Tortoise

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, who is the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Kacchapa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Janittaṃ me bhavittaṃ me," concerning a certain man who escaped from the pestilence.

In Sāvatthī, it is said that the pestilence occurred in a certain family. The parents said to their son, "Dear son, do not stay in this house. Break through the wall, flee, go to any place, and save your life. Later, return; in such and such a place, there is much buried treasure. Dig up that treasure, establish your wealth, and live happily."

The son, accepting the words of his parents, broke through the wall and fled. When his illness was cured, he returned, dug up the buried treasure, established his wealth, and lived as a householder. One day, he had ghee, oil, and other offerings, as well as robes and clothing, brought and went to the Jetavana monastery, where he worshipped the Teacher and sat down.

The Fully Enlightened One engaged in friendly conversation with that man and asked, "Lay follower, we heard that the pestilence occurred in your house. How did you escape?" The man reported that matter.

The Teacher said, "Lay follower, indeed in the past too, when danger arose, those beings who were attached to their dwelling places and did not go elsewhere met their end."

Na siyā, would not be. "Creatures who, without attachment, go to another place, have preserved their lives," he said, and being requested by that lay follower, he brought forth the past. The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a potter's family in a small Kāsika village, and he supported his wife and children by doing the work of a potter. At that time, there was a large natural lake in Bārāṇasī connected to a great river. During the rainy season, the lake and the river were one body of water. When the water receded, they became separate. The fish and tortoises, knowing that "this year the rain will be good" or "this year there will be a drought," would leave the lake and go to the river only while the lake was still connected to the river. One tortoise, however, thought, "This is my birthplace, my place of growth, the place where my parents lived; I cannot leave this place," and did not go to the river. Then, in the summer, the water in the lake dried up. That tortoise dug into the earth and lay there at the spot where the Bodhisatta used to take clay. The Bodhisatta went there to take clay, and while digging the earth with a large spade, he struck the tortoise's shell. He lifted the tortoise with the spade as if it were a lump of clay and threw it onto the dry land. The tortoise, being in great pain and unable to give up its attachment to its dwelling, reached such destruction, and wishing to lament, said: Thus, while speaking with the Bodhisatta, that tortoise died. The Bodhisatta took the tortoise, gathered all the villagers, and wishing to admonish them, said:
74:
"Friends, look at this tortoise. When other fish and tortoises went to the great river, this tortoise, being unable to give up attachment to its dwelling place, did not go with them but entered the place where I dig clay and stayed there. Then, while I was taking clay, I struck its back with a large hoe and cast it onto the dry ground like a lump of clay. This tortoise, remembering its own deed, lamented with two verses and died. Thus, this tortoise met its death because of its attachment to its dwelling place.

Do not be like this tortoise. From this day forward, do not grasp with craving or for the sake of enjoyment, thinking 'my form, my sound, my smell, my taste, my touch, my son, my daughter, my male and female servants, my gold and silver.' A being wanders alone through the three realms of existence."

In this manner, with the grace of a Buddha, he gave advice to the multitude. That advice spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa and lasted for sixty thousand years. The people, established in the Bodhisatta's advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and, at the end of their lives, filled the heavenly city. The Bodhisatta also performed meritorious deeds in the same way and filled the heavenly city.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, that clansman was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Birth? "At that time, the tortoise was Ānanda, and the potter was I myself."

## Abandoning the Home Village When Death Approaches Brings Happiness
The Kacchapa Jātaka is finished.

## 9. Satadhamma Jātaka
## The Outcaste and the Brahmin
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Satadhamma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Tañca appañca ucchiṭṭhaṃ," concerning twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood (anesana).

At one time, many monks made their living through twenty-one kinds of wrong livelihood, such as practicing medicine, acting as messengers, performing various tasks for employers, running errands, and giving food in exchange for food. This wrong livelihood will be explained in the Sāketa Jātaka.

The Omniscient Buddha, knowing that those monks were making their living in such a manner, thought: "Now many monks make their living through wrong livelihood. By living in this way, they will not be released from the state of yakkhas or petas. They will be reborn like oxen yoked to a cart. They will take rebirth in hell."
75:
## 

"I should preach another Dhamma discourse that is according to my own inclination and apparent to my own intuition for the benefit and happiness of these monks," he thought. Having gathered the assembly of monks, he said: "Monks, requisites should not be obtained through the twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood (anesanā). This is true: almsfood obtained through improper livelihood is like a glowing, red-hot iron ball; it is like a lethal poison (halāhala). This is true: what is called improper livelihood is censured and rejected by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.

For a monk who eats almsfood obtained through improper livelihood, there is no joy or gladness. This is true: such almsfood in my Dispensation is like the leftover food of an outcast (caṇḍāla). Partaking of such almsfood obtained through improper livelihood is like the youth Satadhamma partaking of the leftover rice of an outcast." Having said this, he related the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in an outcast (caṇḍāla) family. When he came of age, he set out on a journey for some business, taking provisions of rice and a bundle of cooked rice.

At that time, there was a youth in Bārāṇasī named Satadhamma, born into a high-class Northern Brahmin (udicca-brāhmaṇa) family of great wealth. That youth also set out on a journey for some business, but without taking any rice or a food bundle. The two of them met on the high road.

The youth Satadhamma asked the Bodhisatta, "Friend, of what caste are you?" The Bodhisatta replied, "I am an outcast," and asked the youth, "Of what caste are you?" The youth Satadhamma said, "I am of the Northern Brahmin caste." Saying, "Very well, let us go," the two of them traveled together.

At breakfast time, the Bodhisatta sat in a pleasant place near water, washed his hands, opened his food bundle, and said, "Youth, please eat." The youth replied, "Hey, you outcast, I have no need for your food." The Bodhisatta said, "Very well," and without making the food in the bundle leftovers, he put enough for his own meal on a leaf, tied up the bundle, placed it in a suitable spot, ate, drank water, washed his hands and feet, and then taking the rice and the remaining food, said, "Youth, let us go," and continued the journey.

The two of them traveled all day, and in the evening, they both bathed at a pleasant place near water and came up.
76:
17. "That which was little and leftovers, and which he gave me with difficulty;
I, who am a Brahmin by birth—what was eaten, that too has been vomited."
He uttered this first verse.

(Word-for-word explanation): "The rice I ate was little and it was leftovers. That outcast did not give it to me of his own will; he gave it because of my pressuring him with difficulty. I am one born of the pure Brahmin caste. Therefore, the rice I ate has been vomited along with blood."

The Bodhisatta sat in a pleasant place near water, opened his food bundle, and began to eat without inviting the youth. The youth, exhausted from traveling all day, became famished and stood watching, thinking, "If he gives me food, I will eat."

The outcast ate without saying a word. The youth Satadhamma thought: "This outcast is eating everything without even calling me to eat. It is proper for me to pressure this outcast, take the food, make him discard the top part which is being eaten, and eat the rest." Having thought so, the youth Satadhamma did exactly as he had planned and ate the leftover food.

Then, even as he was eating, a powerful remorse arose in the youth Satadhamma: "I have eaten the leftover food of an outcast, which is unbecoming of my birth, lineage, family, and region." At that very moment, the food mixed with blood was vomited from his mouth.

The youth Satadhamma, thinking, "Indeed, for the sake of a trifle of food, I have committed an unbecoming deed," and being filled with intense grief, desired to lament:

Having lamented thus, the youth Satadhamma thought, "What is the use of my living now after doing such an unbecoming deed?" He entered the forest and, without letting anyone see him, met a helpless death.

The All-Enlightened Buddha, having shown this past story, said: "Monks, just as the youth Satadhamma felt no joy or gladness after eating the outcast's leftover food because he had eaten food unsuitable for him, even so, a monk in this Dispensation who makes his living through improper livelihood (anesanā) and partakes of requisites obtained in such a manner, feels no joy or gladness because his life is censured and rejected by the Buddhas." Having said this, and having become the Buddha, he preached this second verse which completes the pair:

18. "Thus, having cast aside the Dhamma, he who lives by unrighteousness,
Like Satadhamma, does not rejoice even in the gain he has obtained."

(Word-for-word explanation): Monks, just as the youth Satadhamma did not rejoice in the gain of the outcast's leftover food obtained through pressure, even so, in this Dispensation, whatever monk casts aside the Dhamma called the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla) and lives by unrighteousness called the twenty-one kinds of improper livelihood (anesanā), that monk cannot rejoice.
77:
Conclusion of the Jātaka: Thus the Omniscient Buddha, having taught this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the revelation of the Truths, many monks attained the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. How did he identify the Jātaka? "Monks, at that time Ānanda was the youth Satadhamma, and I myself was the son of the Cāṇḍāla." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Eating what should not be eaten leads to great suffering
The Satadhamma Jātaka is finished.

## 10. Duddada Jātaka
## The Ascetic and the Donor
The Present Story: While the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Duddada Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Duddadaṃ dadamānānaṃ," concerning a group alms-giving (gaṇadāna).

In Sāvatthī, two friends who were sons of householders, having collected contributions and prepared all the requisites for alms, invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. They conducted a great alms-giving for seven days, and on the seventh day, they offered all the requisites.

Among those donors, the leader of the group paid homage to the Blessed One, sat in a suitable place, and said: "Venerable Sir, in this alms-giving, there are those who gave much and those who gave little. May this alms-giving be of great fruit for all of them." Thus he dedicated the alms.

The Omniscient Buddha said: "Lay followers, by giving alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and dedicating the alms in this way, you have performed a noble deed. Wise men of old, having given alms, also dedicated them in this very same way." Being requested by the donor, he told the story of the past.

The Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he went to Takkasilā and learned all the arts. Renouncing the household life, he became an ascetic and the leader of a group. After living in the Himālaya region for a long time, he traveled through the countryside to seek salt and vinegar. Reaching Bārāṇasī, he stayed in the royal park, and the next day, he went for alms in a gate village with his followers.

## 4. Asadisa Vagga
## 1. Asadisa Jātaka
## The Prince Skilled in Archery

**The Story of the Present**
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Asadisa Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Dhanuggaho asadiso," concerning his Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana).

The Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have renounced the world through the Great Renunciation; in the past also, I renounced the world after abandoning the white parasol (the throne)," and He brought forth the story of the past.

**The Story of the Past**
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of the king's chief queen. On the day he was safely born and named, they gave him the name Prince Asadisa. Later, when the Bodhisatta was at the age where he could run here and there, another meritorious being took conception in the queen's womb. On the day that prince was safely born and named, they gave him the name Prince Brahmadatta.

Among those two princes, when the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen, he went to Takkasilā and studied the three Vedas and the eighteen sciences under a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha). Having become peerless in the art of archery among all archers, he returned to Bārāṇasī.

When the King was about to pass away, he said, "Give the kingship to Prince Asadisa and the position of Viceroy (Uparāja) to Prince Brahmadatta," and then he died. After his death, when the kingship was offered to the Bodhisatta, he rejected it, saying, "I have no need for the kingship." They then consecrated Prince Brahmadatta as king. Although the Bodhisatta did not desire the kingship, while his younger brother ruled, he lived in the manner of a royal official as was natural.
80:
The courtiers who served at the king's feet slandered the Bodhisatta to the king, saying, "Prince Asadisa covets the kingship." King Brahmadatta, believing their words, became estranged in heart and ordered his men, "Seize my elder brother."

Then, a man who looked after the Bodhisatta's interests informed him of the situation. The Bodhisatta, being angry with his younger brother, left the city and went to another kingdom, where he sent word to the king, "An archer has arrived and is standing at the palace gate." The king asked, "What amount of wealth do you desire?" When he replied, "I desire one hundred thousand per year," the king said, "Very well, let him come."

When he arrived and stood nearby, the king asked, "Are you an archer?" When he replied, "Yes, Great King," the king said, "Very well, serve me." From then on, Prince Asadisa served the king. Seeing the allowance given to him, the old archers grumbled, saying, "He receives far too much."

Then one day, the king went to the park and had a curtain enclosure set up near the auspicious stone slab. While lying on a magnificent couch at the foot of a mango tree, he looked up and saw a cluster of mangoes at the top of the tree. Thinking, "It is not possible to climb up and take this," he summoned the archers and asked, "Will you be able to shoot this mango cluster with an arrow so that it falls?"

The old archers replied, "Great King, making that mango cluster fall is not a heavy burden for us. However, Your Majesty has seen our work many times. The newly arrived archer receives much more allowance than we do. Let Your Majesty have this new archer shoot it down."

The king summoned the Bodhisatta and asked, "Dear son, will you be able to make that mango cluster fall?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, if I may have a certain space, I shall be able to." The king asked, "What space do you require?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, if I may have the space within Your Majesty's seating area, I shall be able to." The king had the couch moved and prepared the space for shooting.

The Bodhisatta did not have a bow in his hand; he went about with the bow fastened inside his lower garment. Therefore, he said, "It is necessary to have a curtain." The king said, "Very well," and had a curtain brought and set up as an enclosure.
81:
The Bodhisatta entered within the curtain, removed the white outer garment he usually wore, and put on a red lower garment. He tucked it in firmly, tied another red cloth around his waist, and drew a sword sharp as a house-edge, slinging it on his left side. He donned a golden tunic, slung a quiver full of arrows on his back, and took up a great bow made of goat-horn with its joints well-fitted. He fixed the bowstring, which was the color of coral, placed a headband on his head, and while rubbing the sharp arrow-head with his nails, he parted the curtain in two and emerged like a young Naga splitting the earth. He went to the place for shooting arrows, fitted the arrow-head to the shaft, and addressed the King:

"Great King, shall I bring down that cluster of mangoes with an upward-flying arrow? Or shall I bring it down with a downward-descending arrow?"

"My dear, I have often seen it brought down with an upward-flying arrow, but I have never seen it brought down with a downward-descending arrow. Bring it down with a downward-descending arrow," the King replied.

"Great King, this arrow will ascend to a great distance, as far as the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika), and will descend by itself. You must wait until its descent," he said. The King agreed, saying, "Very well."

Then he spoke to the King again: "Great King, as this arrow ascends, it will cut through the middle of the mango cluster's stem. As it descends, it will not deviate even a hair's breadth to this side or that, but will fall straight down, taking the mango cluster with it. Look, Great King!" Having said this, he generated great force and shot the arrow. That arrow ascended, cutting through the middle of the mango cluster's stem.

Knowing that the arrow would now have reached the realm of the Four Great Kings, the Bodhisatta generated a speed even greater than the first arrow and shot another arrow. This subsequent arrow went and struck the nock of the first arrow, causing it to turn back, while it itself ascended to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. There, the deities caught that arrow. The sound of the returning arrow cutting through the air was like a clap of thunder.

When the people asked, "What is this sound?" the Bodhisatta replied, "It is the sound of the returning arrow." Seeing the people greatly terrified by the danger of the arrow falling on them, he comforted them, saying, "Do not be afraid," and added, "I will not allow the arrow to fall to the ground."
82: 1. The peerless archer, the prince of great strength, a far-shooter, a marksman who hits the target, a piercer of great masses. 2. Having fought all enemies, he harmed no one. Having made his brother safe, he entered into self-restraint. The Teacher preached these verses: Monks, Mahabbalo: Having great physical and intellectual strength. Dūrepātī: Able to make an arrow reach as far as the realms of the Four Great Kings and Tāvatiṃsa. Akkhaṇavedhī: Able to shoot without missing. Alternatively, Akkhaṇavedhī: Able to shoot seven or eight arrows in a flash of lightning. Mahākāyappadālano: Able to shoot through great masses or groups. Rājaputto: Being a king's son. Asadiso: Named Asadisa. Dhanuggaho: The famous archer. Sabbāmitte: All enemies. Raṇaṃ katvā: Having waged war. Palāpesi: He made them flee. Kañci ca: Even a single person. Na viheṭhayi: He did not harm. Bhātaraṃ: His younger brother. Sotthiṃ katvāna: Having made him safe. Saṃyamaṃ: To the state of a hermit who guards virtue. Ajjhupāgami: He approached. When the arrow descended, it did not move even a hair's breadth this way or that, but fell exactly on the mark and severed the cluster of mangoes. The Bodhisatta did not let either the mango cluster or the arrow fall to the ground; catching them in mid-air, he took the arrow in one hand and the mango cluster in the other. The people, seeing that wonder, praised the Bodhisatta, saying, 'We have never seen such skill before.' They shouted with great joy, made the place echo, clapped their arms, snapped their fingers, and tossed many garments. The wealth given to the Bodhisatta by the king's assembly out of joy was of an immense amount. The king also gave him much wealth and a large retinue, as if a great rain were falling. While the Bodhisatta lived in that city because of the king's respect and honor, seven kings came and surrounded Bārāṇasī, hearing that Prince Asadisa was not there. They sent a message to King Brahmadatta: 'Will you give up the kingdom or give battle?' King Brahmadatta, fearing death, asked, 'Where is my elder brother living?' Hearing that he was serving another neighboring king, he said, 'If my brother does not come, I shall not live. Go, pay homage to Prince Asadisa's feet in my name, ask for his forgiveness, and bring him back.' He sent messengers. Those messengers went and informed the Bodhisatta of the matter. The Bodhisatta took leave of the king and returned to Bārāṇasī. He comforted the king, saying, 'Do not fear.' 'I, Prince Asadisa, have come. By shooting one more arrow, I will take the lives of all the kings. Let those who desire life flee!'
83:
In this way, he wrote letters on the arrows and, standing on the watchtower, caused the seven arrows to fall exactly on the lid of the golden dish while the seven kings were eating. Those kings, seeing the letters and fearing death, fled.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, without causing even as much blood to flow as a small fly could drink, made the kings of the seven kingdoms flee. Having asked permission from his younger brother, he renounced sensual pleasures, became an ascetic, developed the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti), and at the end of his life, was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, the Omniscient One, wishing to show that "Monks, this Prince Asadisa, having put to flight the kings of seven kingdoms and being victorious in battle, entered the state of an ascetic," spoke after attaining Buddhahood:

[Identification of the Jātaka] Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the younger brother, and I myself was Prince Asadisa."

## Not clinging to wealth, entering the forest, difficult for men to practice.

The Asadisa Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka

## The Scene of the King's Renunciation and the Easily Admonished Elephant

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who admonishes the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Saṅgāmāvacaro sūro," concerning Elder Nanda.

To elaborate: When the Teacher first went to Kapilavatthu, he ordained his younger brother, Prince Nanda. Leaving Kapilavatthu and eventually reaching Sāvatthī, while he was staying there, Venerable Nanda—who had taken the Buddha's bowl and left the palace with the Tathāgata—recalled the words of Janapadakalyāṇī. When she heard that Prince Nanda was going with the Teacher, she looked out through the window with her hair half-combed and said, "My lord, please return quickly." Remembering these words, he longed for the lay life, and due to his dissatisfaction, he became extremely pale like a withered leaf, with his veins standing out on his body.
84:
The Teacher, knowing this, thought, "It would be good if I could establish Nanda in the fruit of Arahantship." He went to the Elder Nanda's quarters and, sitting on the prepared seat, asked, "Nanda, are you finding delight in this Dispensation?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, my mind is attached to Janapadakalyāṇī, and I do not find delight."

The Teacher asked, "Nanda, have you ever wandered in the Himavanta?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I have never been there." "Then let us go." When this was said, he replied, "Venerable Sir, I have no psychic power; how shall I go?" The Teacher said, "Nanda, I will take you by my psychic power." Taking the Elder by the hand and flying through the air, he showed him a female monkey in a burnt-out field, sitting on a burnt stump, with her ears, nose, and tail cut off, her hair singed, her skin shriveled, and her body covered in blood. "Nanda, do you see that monkey?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "Look at her well."

Then, taking Nanda, he showed him the Manosilā plateau of sixty leagues, the seven great lakes such as Lake Anotatta, the five great rivers, and the Himavanta mountains adorned with mountains of gold, silver, and gems, and many hundreds of delightful spots. He then asked, "Nanda, have you ever seen the Tāvatiṃsa heaven?" When he replied, "No, Venerable Sir," the Teacher said, "Come, Nanda, I will show you the Tāvatiṃsa heaven." Taking him there, the Teacher sat on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat.

Sakka, the king of devas, came with a host of devas from the two deva realms, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Five hundred celestial nymphs, who were attended by a retinue of twenty-five million and had feet like those of a dove, also came, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher made Venerable Nanda look at those five hundred nymphs again and again with desire.

"Nanda, do you see these nymphs with dove-like feet?" "Yes, Venerable Sir." "Are they more beautiful, or is Janapadakalyāṇī?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, just as that burnt and shriveled monkey is compared to Janapadakalyāṇī, so is Janapadakalyāṇī compared to these nymphs." When he replied thus, the Teacher asked, "Nanda, what will you do now?"
85:
“Venerable Sir, what meritorious deed should I perform to obtain these celestial nymphs?” When he asked this, the Buddha replied, “Nanda, they are obtained by practicing the Dhamma of a recluse.” “Venerable Sir, if you will grant me a guarantee that I shall obtain these celestial nymphs, I will practice the Dhamma of a recluse.” When he said this, the Buddha replied, “Nanda, strive on; I grant you the guarantee.”

Thus, having made the Blessed One give his guarantee in the midst of the assembly of gods, the Elder Nanda said, “Venerable Sir, please do not be long. Arise, let us go; I shall practice the Dhamma of a recluse.” The Teacher took Nanda and returned to Jetavana Monastery. The Elder Nanda then began to strive in order to practice the Dhamma of a recluse.

The Teacher then called the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, and informed him, “Sāriputta, my younger brother Nanda has made me give him a guarantee for the sake of celestial nymphs in the midst of the assembly of gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.” In this manner, he informed the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, the Elder Mahākassapa, the Elder Anuruddha, the Elder Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, and most of the eighty great disciples and the remaining monks.

The General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, approached the Elder Nanda and said, “Is it true, friend Nanda, as I have heard, that you have made the Blessed One give a guarantee because you wish to obtain celestial nymphs in the midst of the assembly of gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven?” He then shamed the Elder, making him lose his confidence, saying, “If this is so, is not your life of holiness dependent on women and dependent on defilements? For you, who practice the Dhamma of a recluse for the sake of women, what is the difference between you and a laborer who works for wages?” In this manner, all the eighty great disciples and the remaining monks shamed the Venerable Nanda.

That Elder Nanda, thinking, “Indeed, I have done what is improper,” and being moved by shame and dread of wrongdoing, put forth strenuous effort, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. He then approached the Teacher and said, “Venerable Sir, I release the Blessed One from his guarantee.” The Teacher also said, “Nanda, at the very moment you attained Arahantship, I was released from the guarantee.”
86:
63. “A hero who frequents the battlefield, renowned as powerful;
O elephant, why do you retreat after reaching the gate-tower?

64. “Quickly crush the crossbar and pull up the pillars;
Having trampled the gate-towers, enter quickly, O elephant.”

He spoke these two verses.

O noble state elephant! You are one who frequents the battlefield, trampling it. You are heroic. You are powerful. Thus, you are a renowned elephant. Having reached the gate-tower, why do you retreat?

O noble state elephant! Quickly cast down the crossbar. Pull up the gate-posts as well. Having trampled the gate-towers, enter the city quickly.

Knowing this matter, the monks in the Dhamma Hall started a discussion: “Friends, the Elder Nanda is truly amenable to instruction. With just a single instruction, he established shame and dread of wrongdoing, practiced the Dhamma of a recluse, and attained Arahantship.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, not only now is Nanda amenable to instruction; in the past also, Nanda was amenable to instruction.” He then brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of elephant trainers. When he came of age, he mastered the art of elephant training and served a king who was a rival to the King of Bārāṇasī. The Bodhisatta well-trained that king’s state elephant and made it proficient.

That king, intending to take the kingdom of Bārāṇasī, took the Bodhisatta, mounted the state elephant, and went with a great army to surround Bārāṇasī. He sent a message to the King of Bārāṇasī: “Will you give up the kingdom or give battle?” King Brahmadatta replied, “I will give battle,” and stationed his forces on the walls, gates, watchtowers, and battlements to give battle.

The rival king covered the state elephant with armor, put on armor himself, and mounted the back of the noble elephant. Holding a sharp goad, he drove the elephant toward the city, thinking, “I will break the city, bring the enemy to his end, and take the kingdom into my hands.” That state elephant, seeing people discharging hot mud, catapulted stones, and various kinds of weapons, became terrified of death and, not daring to approach, retreated.
