Then the elephant trainer approached the state elephant and said, “My dear, you are a heroic elephant, one who frequents the battlefield. In such a place, retreating is not worthy of you.” Desiring to instruct the elephant, he said:

The noble state elephant, hearing those words, turned back with just that single instruction from the Bodhisatta. He wrapped his trunk around the gate-posts and pulled them up like mushrooms. He trampled the gate-towers, cast down the crossbar, broke the city gate, entered the city, and having captured the kingdom, gave it to his king.
87:
Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, at that time, Nanda was the auspicious elephant, Ānanda was the king, and I myself was the elephant trainer." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## The bond of Saṃsāra is severed; with discipline, death is certain.

The Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Vālodaka Jātaka

## Lowly birth, loud noise

Present Story: The All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Vālodaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vālodakaṃ apparasaṃ nihīnaṃ," concerning five hundred scavengers (vighāsāda).

To elaborate: In Sāvatthī, five hundred lay followers, having entrusted their household burdens to their wives and children, went together to listen to the Buddha's Dhamma teaching. Among those lay followers, some were Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some were Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), and some were Non-returners (Anāgāmī). Not even one was a worldling (puthujjana). Even when inviting the Buddha for a meal, they would include those lay followers in the invitation.

The five hundred minor attendants of those five hundred lay followers, who provided tooth-sticks, water for washing the face, robes, perfumes, and flowers, lived as scavengers. After eating their morning meal, they would sleep, and upon waking, they would go to the Aciravatī River, where they would shout and engage in wrestling. However, those five hundred lay followers remained quiet and silent, devoted to the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti).

The Teacher, hearing the loud noise of those scavengers, asked, "Ānanda, what is that noise?" When told, "Venerable Sir, it is the noise of the scavengers," the Teacher said, "It is not only now that these scavengers shout after eating leftovers; they shouted in the past as well. And it is not only now that these lay followers sit quietly; they sat quietly in the past as well." Being requested by the Elder Ānanda, he brought forth the past story.

Past Story: In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers and, upon reaching maturity, became the king's advisor on matters of welfare and Dhamma.

At one time, the king heard that the borderlands were being harassed by bandits. He prepared five hundred Sindh horses and went with a fourfold army to pacify the borderlands. Returning to Bārāṇasī, he ordered, "The Sindh horses are exhausted; give them grape juice (muddika-pāna) that has a rich flavor." The Sindh horses drank the choice juice and went to their stables, staying in their respective places.
88:
6. Having drunk but a little, one of lowly birth becomes intoxicated by it, O Lord of Men. One of disciplined nature, born of a noble family, does not become intoxicated even after drinking the finest juice.

He spoke this verse to complete the two.

Janinda, O King who rules over men. That group of donkeys is of lowly birth. Because of that lowly birth, being fed, they drink the grape juice of little flavor and become intoxicated. But the horses, being born of a noble family and possessed of a nature to carry burdens, drink the first-taken grape juice and do not become intoxicated.

The leftovers given to those Sindh horses were small in quantity and full of dregs. The people asked the king, "What shall we do with these leftovers?"

The king said, "Knead it with water, strain it through a coarse cloth made of hemp (makaci), and give it to the donkeys that depend on the provisions of the Sindh horses."

The donkeys, having drunk the water strained from the grape dregs, became intoxicated and went about the palace courtyard braying and frolicking. The king opened a large window and, seeing them, called the Bodhisatta who was standing nearby and asked, "O Minister, do you see? These donkeys, having drunk the dregs-water, have become intoxicated and go about braying and leaping. But the Sindh horses, born of the Sindh breed, having drunk the choice juice, remain silent and quiet. They do not frolic. What is the reason?"

He then spoke the first verse:

5. Having drunk the dregs-water, of little flavor and low quality, intoxication arises in the donkeys. But having drunk this choice juice, intoxication does not arise in the Sindh horses.

O Great Minister, the donkeys, having drunk the dregs-water—the grape juice strained through a coarse hemp cloth—which is of low quality and little flavor, become intoxicated. But the Sindh horses, having drunk this choice grape juice, do not become intoxicated. What is the reason?

Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to explain the reason to King Brahmadatta, spoke.

King Brahmadatta, hearing the Bodhisatta's words, had the donkeys removed from the palace courtyard. Abiding by the Bodhisatta's advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and passed away according to his kamma.

Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Ānanda, at that time, these scavengers were the five hundred donkeys. These lay followers were the five hundred Sindh horses. Ānanda was the king. And I myself was the wise minister." Thus he identified the Jātaka.
89:
## Of low birth, noisy, yet of noble lineage, controlled in senses, and very valuable.
The Vālodaka Jātaka ends.

7. Corrupted by Giridatta, the horse Paṇḍava of King Sāma, having abandoned his former nature, follows the example of that very man.

He spoke this first verse.
By Giridatta: by the groom Giridatta. Corrupted: being spoiled. Of King Sāma: belonging to King Sāma. Paṇḍava: the state horse named Paṇḍava. Horse: the auspicious state horse. Former: previous. Nature: the habit of walking gracefully. Having abandoned: having given up. Of that very man: only of that groom Giridatta. Follows the example: he practices by imitating the limping.

## 4. Giridatta Jātaka
## Learning by Imitation

The Perfectly Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Giridatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dūsito giridattenā," concerning a monk who associated with an opponent.

This story has already been told in the Mahilāmukha Jātaka below. Specifically, the Perfectly Enlightened One said, "Monks, not only now does this monk associate with an opponent; in the past, he also associated with an opponent," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Sāma was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers and, upon reaching maturity, became a minister who advised King Sāma on matters of welfare and Dhamma. The King's auspicious state horse was named Paṇḍava. The groom for that state horse was named Giridatta. That Giridatta was lame.

The horse, seeing Giridatta walking in front of him while holding the muzzle rope, thought, "This man is training me," and by imitating him, the horse also became lame. They reported the horse's lameness to the King.

The King sent physicians. Those physicians went and, seeing no disease in the horse's body, reported to the King, "We see no disease in this horse."

The King sent the Bodhisatta, saying, "Go, friend, find out the reason for this." The Bodhisatta went and, realizing that the horse had become lame due to association with the lame groom, reported the matter to the King. To show that such a fault arises from association, he spoke the first verse:
90:
8. If a man of noble birth, well-groomed in hair and beard, should take him by the muzzle and lead him around the circle, he would quickly give up that limping and follow his example.

At that time, King Sāma asked the Bodhisatta, "What should be done for this horse now?" The Bodhisatta, intending to say that the horse would become as good as before by getting a groom with a good gait, spoke this verse to complete the two:

"O Great King. A man of noble birth: one who is suitable for the King and endowed with good conduct. Well-groomed: having hair and beard prepared in a beautiful manner. Man: a person. Him: that state horse. By the muzzle: by the muzzle rope; or... by the halter. Having taken: having held. In the circle: in the horse stable. If he should lead: if he should walk him. The horse: the state horse. Quickly: very soon. Limping: the state of being lame. Having abandoned: having given up. Of that very man: only of that graceful man. Follows the example: he will practice by imitating him."

The King had it done exactly as the Bodhisatta said. The horse returned to his natural state. The King, pleased in heart, thinking, "He even knows the desires of animals," gave great wealth and status to the Bodhisatta.

Identification of the Birth: The Master, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, Giridatta was Devadatta, the horse who associated with an opponent was this monk, the King was Ānanda, and the wise minister was I myself."

## Association with the environment leads to imitation.
The Giridatta Jātaka ends.

## 5. Anabhirati Jātaka
## The Brahmin and the Vedic Knowledge

The Perfectly Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Anabhirati Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yathodake āvile appasanne," concerning an obscure young Brahmin.

In Sāvatthī, a certain young Brahmin had reached the further shore of the three Vedas and was teaching the Vedas to many young princes and young Brahmins.
91:
...gravel, sand, and schools of fish; so too, when the mind is turbid, he does not see his own benefit or the benefit of others.

10. Just as when the water is translucent and very clear, one sees shells and snails, gravel, sand, and schools of fish; so too, when the mind is unturbid, he sees his own benefit and the benefit of others.

Thus he recited these verses.

Tāta, dear son. Udake, when the water; āvile, is turbid; appasanne, and not clear; yathā, just as one does not see; sippikasambukañca, shells and snails; sakkharañca, gravel; vālukañca, sand; macchagumbañca, and schools of fish; evaṃ-tathā, in the same way; citte, when the mind; āvile, is turbid; so puriso, that man; na passati, does not see; attadatthañca, his own benefit; paratthañca, and the benefit of others.

Tāta, dear son. Udake, when the water; acche, is clear; vippasanne, and especially bright; yathā, just as that man who searches for shells and the like sees; sippikasambukañca, shells and snails; sakkharañca, gravel; vālukañca, sand; macchagumbañca, and schools of fish; evaṃ-tathā, in the same way; cittena, when the mind; anāvilamhi, is unturbid; so puriso, that man who searches for such benefit; passati, sees; attadatthañca, his own benefit; paratthañca, and the benefit of others.

That young brahmin later entered the household life. While thinking of the welfare of his household, such as clothes, ornaments, male and female servants, fields, cattle, and wife, he came under the power of lust, hatred, and delusion, and his mind became turbid. He was unable to recite the Vedas in order. The mantras did not appear to him from here or there.

One day, taking many perfumes, flowers, and such, that brahmin went to the Jetavana monastery, worshipped the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher engaged in friendly conversation with him and asked, "Young man, do you teach the Vedas? Are your mantras proficient?" "Venerable Sir, previously my mantras were proficient. But since the time I took up the household life, my mind has become turbid. Therefore, my mantras are no longer proficient," he replied.

Then the Teacher said to that brahmin, "Young man, it is not only now that your mantras were proficient when your mind was unturbid and did not appear when turbid due to lust and the like; in the past also, your mantras were proficient when your mind was unturbid and did not appear when turbid due to lust and the like." Having said this, being requested by the brahmin, he brought forth the past story.

The Past Story of the Brahmin: In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he learned the mantras at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher. In Bārāṇasī, he taught the mantras to many princes and brahmin youths. In his presence, a certain young brahmin mastered the three Vedas. He became an assistant teacher, having no doubts even about a single word, and taught the mantras.
92:
That young man later entered the household life and, thinking of household affairs, his mind became turbid, and he was unable to recite the mantras. Then the teacher asked the young man who had come to him, "Young man, are your mantras proficient?" When he replied, "Teacher, since the time I took up the household life, my mind has become turbid, and I am unable to recite the mantras," the teacher said, "Dear son, when the mind is turbid, even proficient mantras do not appear. But when the mind is unturbid, there is nothing that does not appear." Thus he spoke:

9. Just as when the water is turbid and unclear,
One does not see shells and snails...

Identification of the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this past story and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the brahmin youth was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Jātaka? "Young man, at that time, this young man was the young man, and I myself was the world-renowned teacher." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## When the mind is clear, wisdom is gained; when confused, it will be lost.

The Anabhirati Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Dadhi-vāhana Jātaka

## The Four Powers of Weapons

The Present Story: The All-Enlightened Teacher, the instructor of the world including the devas, while staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, told this Dadhi-vāhana Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Vaṇṇagandharasūpeto", concerning a monk who associated with the opposition (enemies).

The story has been told below. Specifically, the Teacher said, "Monks, association with the unrighteous is evil and brings harm. In that case, what need is there to speak of the harm caused by association with the unrighteous among human beings? In the past, even an insentient mango tree, which had a sweet taste comparable to divine nectar, became tasteless and bitter due to its association with an unpleasant and unsweet nimb (neem) tree." Having said this, he brought the past story.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, four brahmin brothers in the Kāsī kingdom became ascetics. They built hermitages in succession in the Himālaya region and lived there. Among those four ascetics, the eldest brother passed away and became Sakka, King of the Devas.

Sakka, knowing the situation, would visit the younger brother ascetics every seven or eight days. One day, after worshipping the eldest ascetic, he sat in a suitable place and asked, "Venerable Sir, what object do you need?" The ascetic, suffering from jaundice, said, "I need fire." Hearing this, Sakka gave that elder ascetic a hatchet and an axe.
93:
An axe-hatchet is so called because, by the power of its handle, it serves as both an adze and an axe. The ascetic took this axe-hatchet and thought, 'Who will fetch wood for me?' Then Sakka, King of the Devas, said to that ascetic: 'Venerable sir, whenever you have need of wood, strike this axe-hatchet with your hand and say, "Fetch wood for me and make a fire." Say this to it.' He continued, 'Then it will fetch the wood, kindle the fire, and give it to you.' Having said this and given the axe-hatchet to the eldest ascetic, Sakka approached the middle ascetic and asked, 'Venerable sir, what do you require?'

Near that ascetic’s leaf-hut was an elephant path. Being oppressed by the elephants, the ascetic said, 'I suffer because of these elephants; make them flee.'

Sakka presented a drum to that ascetic and said, 'Venerable sir, if this side is struck, your enemies will flee; but if this side is struck, a fourfold army with hearts of loving-kindness will come and surround you.' Having said this and given the drum, he went to the youngest ascetic and asked, 'Venerable sir, what do you require?'

That young ascetic also suffered from jaundice. Therefore, he said, 'I have need of curds.' Sakka gave that young ascetic a curd-pot and said, 'Venerable sir, if you desire and pour out these curds, it will become a great river, producing a mighty flood, and will even be able to seize a kingdom for you.' Having said this, he departed.

From then on, the axe-hatchet made fire for the sake of the eldest brother ascetic. When the middle ascetic struck the side of the drum, the elephants fled. The youngest ascetic enjoyed the curds.

At that time, a certain pig, while foraging in a place where a village had formerly stood, saw a magical gem endowed with supernatural power. The pig bit the gem with its snout and, by the power of that gem, flew into the air and reached a small island in the middle of the ocean. Thinking, 'It is now proper for me to live here,' he descended and made his dwelling under a fig tree in a pleasant spot. One day, at the foot of that fig tree, the pig placed the gem in front of him and fell into a deep sleep.
94:
At that time, a certain man living in the kingdom of Kāsi was driven out of his house by his parents, who said, 'This man is of no use to us.' He reached a certain seaport village, became a laborer for mariners, and set sail. While traveling, the ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean. Floating on a plank, he reached that island. While searching for fruits large and small, he saw the pig sleeping. He approached quietly, took the gem, and by its power, flew up into the air. Sitting in the fig tree, he thought:

'This pig, it seems, lives in this place by flying through the air by the power of this gem. It is proper that I should first kill this pig, eat its flesh, and then fly away.' Having thought thus, the man broke a staff-like branch and dropped it onto the pig's head. When the pig woke and did not see the gem, its mind was agitated, and it ran here and there. The man sitting in the fig tree laughed. When the pig looked up and saw the man, it struck the fig tree with its head and died right there.

The man descended from the fig tree, kindled a fire, roasted and ate the pig's meat. Then he flew upwards and, traveling through the air over the Himalayas, saw a hermitage. He descended at the hermitage of the eldest brother ascetic and stayed for two or three days, performing various duties for the ascetic. He also saw the power of the axe-hatchet.

The man thought, 'It is proper for me to take this axe-hatchet.' After showing the power of the gem to the ascetic, he said, 'Venerable sir, take this gem and give me the axe-hatchet.' The ascetic, wishing to travel through the air, took the gem and gave him the axe-hatchet.

The man took the axe-hatchet, went a short distance, struck the axe-hatchet, and said, 'O axe-hatchet, cut off the ascetic's head and bring back the gem.' That axe-hatchet went, cut off the ascetic's head, and brought back the gem.
95:
The man hid the hatchet-axe in a concealed place and went to the middle ascetic. After staying for two or three days, having seen the power of the drum, he gave the gem and took the drum. Then, in the same manner as before, he had the middle ascetic’s head cut off. He then approached the youngest ascetic, and upon seeing the power of the curd-pot, he gave the gem and took the pot. Again, as before, he had the youngest ascetic’s head cut off. Taking the gem, the hatchet-axe, the drum, and the curd-pot, he flew into the sky. Stopping at a place not far from the city of Bārāṇasī, he sent a message to the King of Bārāṇasī by the hand of a man, asking, "Will you give up the kingdom or give battle?"

Hearing the news, the King came out of the city to capture the thief. The man struck one side of the drum, and an army of four divisions surrounded him. Realizing the King of Bārāṇasī's dominance, he poured out the curd-pot, which became a great river. The people were submerged in the river of curd and were unable to escape. He then commanded the hatchet-axe, "Go and bring the King's head." The hatchet-axe went, took the King's head, and laid it at his feet. No one else was able to lift a weapon. Surrounded by a great retinue, the man entered the city, performed the consecration, and became the King named Dadhiivāhana, ruling with righteousness and justice.

One day, while King Dadhiivāhana was playing in the great river with a net like a casket, a ripe mango fruit, an object of use for the devas from Lake Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, floated down and got caught in the net. Those lifting the net saw the mango and presented it to the King. The mango was the size of a large jar, perfectly round, and golden in color.

The King asked the forest-dwellers, "What fruit is this?" Hearing it was a mango, he consumed it and had its seed planted in his garden, watering it with milk. The mango tree grew and bore fruit in the third year. Great honor and offerings were paid to that mango tree. They watered it with milk, smeared it with perfumes and such, hung garlands, lit lamps with scented oil, and surrounded it with a cloth screen. The fruits were sweet in taste and golden in color.

When King Dadhiivāhana sent mangoes to other kings, fearing that trees would grow from the seeds, he pierced the germinating point with a poisonous thorn before sending them. When those kings ate the mangoes and planted the seeds, they failed to grow. When they asked, "What is the reason for this?" they eventually learned the cause.

Then, one king called a gardener and asked, "Can you destroy the taste of King Dadhiivāhana's mangoes and make them bitter?" When the gardener replied, "Yes, your majesty, I can," the king said, "Then go," and sent him with a thousand pieces of money.
96:
11. Endowed with color, scent, and taste, this mango was once so.
Receiving that very same honor, why is the mango now bitter-fruited?

He spoke this first verse. (Word-for-word meaning: Paṇḍita, O wise one. Ayaṃ ambo, this mango tree. Pure, in the past. Vaṇṇagandharasūpeto, was endowed with color, scent, and taste. Ahuvā, it truly was. Idāni, now. Tameva pūjaṃ, receiving only that same honor as was done in the past. Labhamāno, although receiving it. Ambo, the mango. Kena, why. Kaṭukapphalo, does it have bitter fruit?)

12. Surrounded by Neem trees, O Dadhiivāhana, your mango stands.
Root is entwined with root, and branch clings to branch.
By association with the unpleasant, the mango has bitter fruit.

He spoke this second verse to fulfill the pair. (Word-for-word meaning: Dadhiivāhana, O great King who possesses an army like curd. Te, your. Ambo, auspicious mango tree. Pucimandaparivāro, is surrounded by Neem trees. Mūlaṃ, the root of the mango tree. Mūlena, with the root of the Neem tree. Saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, is intertwined. Sākhā, the branches of the Neem tree. Sākhā, the branches of the mango tree. Nisevare, associate with/cling to. Atātasannivāsena, by association with the non-sweet Neem trees. Tena kāraṇena, for that reason. Ambo, the mango tree. Kaṭukapphalo, has bitter fruit.)

That gardener went to Bārāṇasī and had it announced to the King that a gardener had arrived. King Dadhiivāhana summoned him, and he went to the King, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. When the King asked, "Are you a gardener?" he replied, "Yes, your majesty," and described his skills. King Dadhiivāhana said, "Go and stay with our gardener."

From then on, the two men tended the garden. The newly arrived gardener made the garden delightful by making flowers bloom out of season and fruits bear out of season. King Dadhiivāhana was pleased with the new gardener, dismissed the old one, and gave the garden to him alone.

Knowing the garden was in his hands, the gardener planted Neem trees and phaggava vines around the mango tree. Gradually, the Neem trees grew. The roots of the Neem and the mango became intertwined, and the branches of the Neem and the mango became entangled. Due to the association with the unpleasant, tasteless, and non-sweet Neem trees, the sweet-fruited mango tree took on a taste like Neem leaves and became bitter. Knowing the mangoes had become bitter, the gardener fled.

King Dadhiivāhana went to the garden and, upon eating a mango, the juice that entered his mouth was like Neem juice. Unable to swallow it, he coughed and spat it out. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a minister who advised the King on matters of welfare and Dhamma. King Dadhiivāhana called the Bodhisatta and, wishing to ask the reason, said: "Wise one, this tree has not lacked its former care. Yet, its fruit has become bitter. What could be the reason?"

Then, wishing to inform King Dadhiivāhana of the cause, the Bodhisatta spoke the verses.

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, King Dadhiivāhana had all the Neem trees and phaggava vines cut down and their roots uprooted. He had the non-sweet soil removed from all around and replaced it with sweet soil. He then tended the mango tree with milk, sugar water, and scented water. Because of its association with sweet substances, the mango tree once again bore sweet fruit. King Dadhiivāhana restored the garden to the original gardener and, after living out his life, passed away according to his karma.

Identifying the Jataka: The Blessed One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, at that time, I myself was the wise minister." Thus he identified the Jataka.

## Neem and phaggava, intertwined together, ruin the essence of the sweet mango.

The Dadhiivāhana Jātaka is concluded.
97:
13. "Having climbed high upon a fork of the tree, you converse in secret. Come down and speak in a lower place; the king of beasts will also listen."

This is the first verse spoken [by the jackal].

O young geese (haṃsa)! You have climbed high upon a fork of this naturally tall tree and, having reached a secluded spot, you are holding a consultation. Come down to a lower place and speak. The king of beasts, the noble lord of animals, will also listen.

14. "When a golden one converses with a golden one, a deity with a deity, what is there for you, O jackal, who are 'excellent in four ways'? Enter your hole, O jackal."

This is the second verse spoken to complete the pair.

O jackal (jambuka)! When a golden-hued goose converses with another golden-hued goose, and a divine goose with another divine goose, what business is it of yours in that consultation—you who are 'excellent' in the four attributes of body, birth, voice, and virtue? Hey, jackal! You should enter your hole.

## 7. Catu-maṭṭha Jātaka
## The Young Geese and the Tree Deity

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Catu-maṭṭha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ucce viṭabhimāruyha," concerning an obscure old monk.

One day, while the two Chief Disciples were sitting together engaged in a discussion of questions and answers, an old monk approached them, sat down as a third person, and said, "Venerable sirs, I too will ask you a question; you also may ask me to clear your doubts."

The Elder monks, feeling disgusted with him, rose from their seats and departed. When the assembly of people who had sat down to listen to the Elders' Dhamma discourse dispersed, the monks went to the Buddha. When asked why they had come at an unusual time, they reported the matter. The Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna have departed without speaking due to disgust for this old monk; they did so in the past as well," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest region.

At that time, two young geese (haṃsa) came from Mount Cittakūṭa and perched on the tree guarded by the Bodhisatta. Even when returning from searching for food elsewhere, they would rest on that same tree before going back to Mount Cittakūṭa. As time passed, they became intimate with the Bodhisatta. Whether going or coming, they would exchange pleasantries, discuss the Dhamma, and then depart.

Then one day, while those young geese were perched on the treetop conversing with the Bodhisatta, a jackal stood beneath the tree and, wishing to join the consultation with the young geese, spoke the first verse:
98:
At that time, the young geese, feeling disgusted, rose and flew away to Mount Cittakūṭa. When the young geese had flown away, the Bodhisatta spoke to the jackal.

(The term "excellent in four ways" was spoken ironically to mock the jackal, meaning he was actually base in those four attributes.)

[Identification of the Birth Story:] Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was the old monk, the two young geese were Sāriputta and Moggallāna, and the tree deity was I myself."

## Interfering where one does not belong leads to being despised.

The Catu-maṭṭha Jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Sīhakotthu Jātaka
## The Lion-Jackal

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sīhakotthu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sīhaṅgulī sīhanakho," concerning Kokālika.

One day, when other learned monks were preaching the Dhamma, Kokālika also wished to preach. The full account should be expanded as described previously (in the Daddara Jātaka).

Hearing of that event, the Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has become known by his own voice; he was well-known in the past as well," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a lion in the Himavanta region. He lived with a female jackal and had a son by her. That son of the jackal resembled his father in his paws, claws, mane, and color, but his voice was like his mother's.

Then one day, after the rain had ceased, the lions roared and performed their lion-play. That son of the jackal, being among the true lions, also wished to roar and let out a jackal's yelp.
99:
15. With lion-like toes and lion-like claws, standing on lion-like feet,
This lion in the midst of the lion pride, alone roars differently.

He spoke this first verse:

Dear father. This lion has toes like a lion's. It has claws like a lion's. It stands only on lion-like feet. This lion, in the midst of the lion pride, alone roars differently with the sound of a jackal, which is other than the sound of a lion. Why is this?

16. Do not roar, O prince; live quietly in the forest.
They would surely know you by your voice, for your voice is not that of your father.

He spoke this second verse to complete the pair:

O prince, son of the Kesara lion king. Do not roar. Live in the forest without making a sound. By your voice, they would certainly know you to be a jackal. Truly, your voice is not like the voice of your father, the lion king.

Upon hearing the jackal's sound from the son of the she-jackal, the lions remained silent.

Hearing the sound of that son of the she-jackal, another son of the Bodhisatta, of the same breed, wishing to ask, "Father, this lion is like us in appearance and so on, but his voice is like the sound of a jackal, which is different from ours; what kind of lion is this?"

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, "Dear son, this is your brother, the son of a she-jackal; in appearance he is like me, but in voice he is like his mother."

Having said this, he called the son of the she-jackal and, wishing to admonish him, said, "Dear son, from this day forward, while living in this place, live with little sound. If you roar again, they will know your jackal nature."

Hearing this admonition from his father, the lion king, he did not dare to roar again.

Identifying the Birth: The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Kokālika, the son of the same breed was Rāhula, and the lion king was I myself."

## Because of the similarity in appearance and form, one might mistake him, but he cannot imitate the roar; observe this firmly in mind.

The Sīhakotthujātaka is finished.

## 9. Sīhacammajātaka
## The Donkey in the Lion's Skin

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Sīhacammajātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Netam sīhassa naditam," concerning Kokālika. At that time, Kokālika wished to recite the Dhamma with a melodic voice (sarabhañña). The Blessed One, hearing of this matter, brought forth the past story.
100:
17. This is not the roar of a lion, nor of a tiger, nor of a leopard.
Clad in a lion's skin, the wretched donkey brays.

He spoke this first verse:

Friends. That sound is not the roar of a lion. It is not the roar of a tiger. It is not the roar of a leopard. Clad in a lion's skin, the wretched donkey brays.

18. For a long time, the donkey might have eaten the green barley.
Clad in a lion's skin, he ruined himself just by braying.

He spoke this second verse to complete the pair:

If this donkey had not made his donkey nature known, clad in a lion's skin, he might have eaten the green barley for a very long time. But by braying, he ruined himself.

The Past Story: Monks, long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a farmer's family. When he came of age, he made his living by farming.

At that time, a certain merchant traveled about trading with a load placed upon a donkey. Wherever that merchant went, he would take the bundle off the donkey's back, clothe the donkey in a lion's skin, and let it loose in the rice and barley fields. The field-watchers, seeing it, thought it was a lion and dared not approach.

Then one day, that merchant took up residence at a village gate and, while cooking his breakfast, clothed the donkey in the lion's skin and let it loose in a barley field. The field-watchers, thinking it was a lion, dared not approach it and went home to tell the landowners.

The villagers took up weapons and, blowing conchs and beating drums, went near the field and made a great noise. The donkey, terrified of the fear of death, let out a donkey's bray. Then, knowing that creature's donkey nature, the Bodhisatta spoke the verse.

The villagers also, knowing the creature's donkey nature, beat it until its bones were broken, causing it to fall, and then took the lion's skin and went away.

Afterwards, the merchant came and, seeing the donkey fallen into ruin, spoke the second verse.

Even as the merchant was speaking thus, the donkey died right there where it lay. The merchant also abandoned the donkey and went away.

Identifying the Birth: The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the merchant was Devadatta, the donkey was Kokālika, and the wise farmer was I myself."

## Clad in a lion's skin, the donkey's true nature was met and known; one should learn and practice accordingly.

The Sīhacammajātaka is finished.
101:
## 10. Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka
## The Blessing of Virtue

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while dwelling at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Passa saddhāya sīlassa," concerning a certain faithful lay follower.

That lay follower, a faithful and devoted disciple of the Noble Ones who had confidence in the Triple Gem, was going to Jetavana Monastery one day. Reaching the banks of the Aciravatī River in the evening, he saw that the boatman had left the boat on the other side and had gone to listen to the Dhamma. Not seeing a boat at the landing place, he took up joy with the Buddha as its object and stepped into the river. His feet did not sink into the water. He walked as if on the surface of the earth.

When he reached the middle of the river, he saw waves. At that moment, his joy with the Buddha as its object became weak, and his feet began to sink. He again made his joy with the Buddha as its object firm and, walking on the surface of the water, entered Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place.

The Teacher exchanged greetings with that lay follower and asked, "Lay follower, did you arrive without much fatigue on your journey?" When the follower replied, "Venerable Sir, by taking up joy with the Buddha as its object, I found a footing on the surface of the water and came as if treading on solid ground," the Teacher said, "Lay follower, it is not only you who found a footing by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha; in the past, lay followers also found a footing by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha when their ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean." At the follower's request, the Teacher related the past story.

In the past, during the time of the Kassapa Buddha, a lay follower who was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) boarded a ship together with a certain barber. The barber's wife said, "Master, his welfare and suffering are your responsibility," and placed the barber in the hands of that lay follower.

Then, on the seventh day, that ship was wrecked in the middle of the ocean. Those two men, lying on a single plank, reached a small island. There, the barber killed birds, cooked them, and ate them, offering some to the lay follower. The lay follower said, "That is enough for me," and did not eat.

That lay follower thought, "In this place, there is no other refuge for us except the Triple Gem," and recollected the virtues of the Triple Gem. While he was thus recollecting the virtues of the Triple Gem, a Naga king born on that small island transformed his body into a great ship. A sea deity became the pilot. The ship was filled with the seven kinds of treasures. The three masts were made of sapphires (indanilamaṇi), the rigging was of gold, the ropes were of silver, and the oars and rudders were of gold.
102:
19. "Behold the fruit of faith, of virtue, and of generosity.
A Naga in the form of a ship carries the faithful lay follower.
20. Associate only with the virtuous; cultivate intimacy with the virtuous.
Through living with the virtuous, the barber goes in safety."

[Explanation:]
O friends! Behold (passa/passatha) this fruit (ayaṃ phalaṃ/idaṃ phalaṃ) of faith (saddhāya), both mundane and supramundane; of virtue (sīlassa), both mundane and supramundane; and of generosity (cāgassa), both the giving of material gifts and the abandonment of defilements. Alternatively... Behold the fruit of faith, virtue, and generosity. This Naga (ayaṃ nāgo), in the form of a ship (nāvāya vaṇṇena), carries (vahati) the lay follower (upāsakaṃ) who is endowed with faith (saddhaṃ) in the Triple Gem.

A man should associate (samāsetha) only with the wise (sabbhireva). One should cultivate intimacy (santhavaṃ) with the wise (sabbhi). Indeed, that statement is fitting. Through living with the wise (sataṃ sannivāsena), the barber (nhāpito) attains safety (sotthiṃ).

The sea deity, standing on the ship, proclaimed, "Is there anyone bound for Jambudīpa?" The lay follower said, "We will go." "If that is so, come, board the ship," said the sea deity. When the deity said this, the lay follower boarded the ship and called the barber.

The sea deity said, "It is only for you; it is not for that barber." When asked "Why?", the deity replied, "That barber has no virtue or good conduct; that is the reason. I brought the ship for your sake, not for his."

"Let it be as you say. I give him a share (patti) of the merit from my own acts of giving, the virtue I have guarded, and the meditation I have practiced," said the lay follower. The barber said, "Master, I rejoice (anumodāmi)." The deity said, "Now I will take him," and took him on board as well. He brought both men out of the ocean, went to Bārāṇasī by river, and by his own power, established wealth in both their houses. He then said, "One should associate only with the wise. If this barber had not associated with this lay follower, he would have perished in the middle of the ocean." Speaking on the benefits of associating with the wise:

Thus, the sea deity, standing in the sky, preached the Dhamma, exhorted the barber, took the Naga king, and went to his own celestial mansion.
103:
The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay devotee was established in the Fruit of Once-Returning (Sakadāgāmiphala). As for the identification of the Birth: "The lay devotee who was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) at that time has passed away; Sāriputta was the Naga King; and I myself was the Ocean Deity." Thus he identified the Birth.

## Associate only with the wise; one finds safety from the dangers that arise.

The Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Ruhaka Vagga
## 1. Ruhaka Jātaka
## The Brahmin who was shamed by his desire to look beautiful

The Story of the Present: The Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana monastery, told this Ruhaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Api ruhaka chinnāpi", concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

The story will become clear in the Indriya Jātaka of the Aṭṭhakanipāta. Specifically, the Teacher said to that monk: "Monk, this woman is one who works for your harm. In the past, she also caused you to be shamed in the midst of the assembly including the King, and made you leave your house in such a manner." Having said this, being requested by the monk, he brought forward the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: Monk, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the King's chief queen. When he came of age, upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingship and ruled righteously. He had a chaplain named Ruhaka, whose wife, a Brahmin woman, was named Purāṇī.

The King gave the Brahmin a horse adorned with horse-trappings. Ruhaka the Brahmin, mounting that horse, went to the place of service to the King. At that time, seeing Ruhaka the Brahmin going and coming while mounted on the back of the adorned horse, the people standing here and there praised only the horse, saying, "Oh, the beauty of the horse! The horse is wonderfully beautiful!"
104:
He went home, ascended the palace, and addressed his wife: "Dear, our horse is exceedingly beautiful. The people standing on both sides praise only our horse." That Brahmin woman, however, was somewhat corrupt in conduct and had a nature of transgressing with other men. Therefore, she said to Ruhaka the Brahmin: "My lord, you do not know the reason for the horse's beauty. This horse is beautiful because of the trappings adorned upon it. If you also wish to be beautiful like the horse, put on the horse-trappings, descend into the middle of the street, and go to see the King while striking your feet like a horse. The King will praise you, and the people will also praise only you."

That Brahmin, who was of a foolish nature, heard her words and, not knowing for what reason she spoke thus, thinking it to be true, did exactly as she said. Whoever saw him mocked him, saying, "The teacher is very beautiful!" The King, however, shamed him by saying, "Teacher, has your bile been disturbed? Have you become mad?" and so on.

At that time, the Brahmin was ashamed, thinking, "I have done an improper thing." Becoming angry with the Brahmin woman, thinking, "She has shamed me in the midst of the assembly including the King; I will beat her and expel her," he went home.

The Brahmin woman, who transgressed with other men, knowing that Ruhaka was coming in anger, went out through a small door beforehand and went to the King's palace, staying there for four or five days.

The King, knowing the situation, sent for the chaplain and, for the sake of reconciliation, said: "Teacher, what is called a fault in women is natural; it is proper to forgive the Brahmin woman." He spoke this first verse:

1. Even if broken, Ruhaka, the bowstring is joined again.
Be reconciled with Purāṇī; do not fall under the power of anger.

O Ruhaka! Indeed, even if a bowstring is broken, it is joined or united again. In the same way, you too should be reconciled with Purāṇī; do not fall under the power of anger.
105:
Hearing that, Ruhaka spoke this second verse:

2. While there are fibers, and while there are makers,
I will make another string; I have no need for Purāṇī.

Great King! While there are soft fibers for bow-making and men who make bowstrings, I will make another new bowstring. Enough of this old bowstring, Purāṇī; I have no use for her.

Having said this, he expelled that Brahmin woman and brought another Brahmin woman.

The Teacher, having brought forward this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). As for the identification of the Birth: "Monk, your former wife at that time was the Brahmin woman; the discontented monk was the Brahmin named Ruhaka; and the King of Vārāṇasī was I myself." Thus he identified the Birth.

## A foolish wife who shames her husband is not fit to be lived with.

The Ruhaka Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Sirikāဠကဏ္ဏိ Jātaka

This Sirikāဠကဏ္ဏိ Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Itthī siyā rūpavatī", will become clear in the Mahā-ummagga Jātaka.

The Sirikāဠကဏ္ဏိ Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Cūဠပဒုမ Jātaka
## The Royal Brothers

The Story of the Present: The Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana monastery, told this Cūဠပဒုမ Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ayameva sā ahamapi so ananyo", concerning a discontented monk.

(This story will become clear in the Ummādantī Jātaka). Specifically, when the Teacher asked the discontented monk, "Monk, is it true that you are discontented?", he replied, "It is true, Blessed One." When asked, "Who has made you discontented?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, I saw a woman in finery and, following the lead of defilements, I have become discontented in the Dispensation."
106:
Then the Blessed One said to that monk: "Monk, women are ungrateful, treacherous to their friends, and full of deceit. In the past, even when wise men gave them their own blood from the right knee to drink and even gave the gift of life, they still could not win a woman's heart." Having said this, he brought forth the story of the past.

## The Story of the Past
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the King's chief queen. On the day he was named, they gave him the name Prince Paduma. 

Later, he had six younger brothers. All seven of these men grew up in due course, married, and lived like companions of the King. 

One day, while the King was standing looking out at the royal courtyard, he saw the princes coming to pay their respects with a large retinue. Suspecting that "these princes might kill me and take the kingdom," he summoned them and said, "My sons, you may not live in this city. Go elsewhere, and after my passing, return and take the kingdom that belongs to your family."

Accepting their father's words, they wept and wailed, left their homes, took their wives, and departed from the city, thinking, "We will live wherever we may go." While traveling, they reached a wilderness. Unable to find food or drink and unable to endure their hunger, they thought, "If we remain alive, we shall find other women," and so they killed the youngest brother's wife, divided her into thirteen portions, and ate the flesh. 

The Bodhisatta set aside one of the portions he and his wife received, and the two of them ate only one portion. In this manner, for six days, they killed six women and ate their flesh. The Bodhisatta, however, set aside one portion every day, keeping six portions in total.

On the seventh day, when they said, "Let us kill the Bodhisatta's wife," the Bodhisatta gave those six portions to his brothers and said, "Eat these six portions for today; we shall see about tomorrow." After they had eaten the flesh and while they were sleeping, he took his wife and fled.

After traveling a short distance, the woman said, "My lord, I cannot go on." Then the Bodhisatta carried her on his shoulders and emerged from the wilderness at dawn. When the sun rose, she said, "My lord, I am thirsty." The Bodhisatta said, "Dear, there is no water." When she repeatedly said she was very thirsty, he pierced his right knee with a sword and said, "Dear, there is no water; drink the blood from my right knee." The woman did as the Bodhisatta said. In due course, the two of them reached a great river, drank water, bathed, ate various fruits, and having rested in a pleasant place, they built a leaf-hut at a bend in the river and lived there.

Then one day, a criminal whose hands, feet, ears, and nose had been cut off as punishment by a king was placed in a small boat and set adrift on the great river from upstream. That criminal, making a loud wailing sound, arrived at the river bend where the Bodhisatta lived. Hearing the cry of distress from that criminal, the Bodhisatta thought, "Let no being perish while I am here," went to the riverbank, rescued the criminal, brought him to the leaf-hut, and treated his wounds by washing them with astringent water and applying ointments.

The Bodhisatta's wife, however, saying "She is nursing and feeding such a person, a person without virtue, a stump without the sprouts of hands, feet, ears, and nose," went along spitting as if in disgust of that stump without the sprouts of hands, feet, ears, and nose.
107:
When the mutilated man's wounds had healed, the Bodhisatta left him and his wife at the leaf-hut and brought various fruits from the forest to support both the mutilated man and his wife.

While they were living thus, the woman's heart became attached to the mutilated man. She committed misconduct with him and, wishing to kill the Bodhisatta by a certain trick, she said: "My lord, while I was coming out of the wilderness sitting on your shoulders, I looked at a mountain and prayed, 'O Lord Mountain Deity, if I survive safely with my husband, I will make an offering to you.' That deity is now frightening me. Let us perform the offering to that mountain deity."

The Bodhisatta, unaware of her deceit, agreed, saying "Very well." He prepared the offering, had the woman carry the basket of offerings, and climbed to the top of the mountain. Then the woman said to him: "My lord, you yourself are a supreme deity even to the deity. First, I will honor you with forest flowers, perform a circumambulation, and pay homage; afterwards, I will perform the offering to the deity."

Placing the Bodhisatta facing the precipice, she honored him with flowers and performed a circumambulation. Pretending to pay homage, she stood behind him, pushed him on his back, and cast him down the precipice. With a joyful heart, thinking "I have seen the destruction of my enemy," she descended the mountain and went to the mutilated man.

As the Bodhisatta fell down the precipice, he landed on a clump of thornless leaves well-covered atop a fig tree (udumbara). He was unable to descend to the bottom of the mountain. The Bodhisatta lived there among the branches, eating the figs.

Then a great monitor lizard climbed up from the foot of the rocky mountain and ate the fruits of that fig tree. Seeing the Bodhisatta that day, the monitor lizard fled. Returning the next day, it ate figs on one side and left. After coming repeatedly, it became intimate with the Bodhisatta and asked, "For what reason did you come to this place?" When the Bodhisatta told the reason, the lizard said, "In that case, do not fear." It had the Bodhisatta sit on its back and descended. Taking him out of the forest and placing him on the main road, it said, "Go by this path," and then entered the forest.

The Bodhisatta reached a small village and, while living there, heard of his father's death. He went to Bārāṇasī and established himself in the kingship, which was his ancestral inheritance.
108:
Having become the king named Paduma, he ruled righteously without violating the ten royal virtues. In these six places—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the palace gate—he had alms-halls built, and gave alms daily, spending six hundred thousand [pieces of] wealth.

That wicked woman also carried the cripple on her back, left the forest, and went to places inhabited by people. She begged for food and gathered gruel and rice to nourish the cripple. When people asked, "How is this cripple related to you?" she replied, "I am this man's cousin, and he is my cousin. My parents gave me to him in marriage. Even though he has been sentenced to death, I carry my husband and support him by begging for alms."

People thought, "This woman serves her husband like a deity," and from then on, they were pleased and gave her plenty of gruel and rice. Other people said, "Do not wander about like this. King Paduma rules in Bārāṇasī; he gives alms that shake the whole of Jambudīpa. When King Paduma sees you, he will be pleased, and being pleased, he will give you much wealth. Go, placing your husband in this wicker basket," and they firmly made and gave her a wicker basket.

That woman of immoral conduct placed the cripple in the wicker basket, carried the basket on her head, went to Bārāṇasī, and wandered about begging at the alms-halls.

The Bodhisatta, riding on the back of a noble, decorated elephant, went to an alms-hall, gave alms with his own hands to eight or ten people, and then returned home. That woman of immoral conduct, carrying the cripple in the basket, went to the path where the Bodhisatta would come and waited on the road.

The King saw her and asked, "What woman is this?" When it was replied, "Great King, she is a woman who serves her husband like a deity," he then had her summoned. Recognizing her, he had the cripple taken out of the basket and asked, "How is this cripple related to you?" The woman said, "Great King, this man is my cousin and my childhood husband given by my parents." The people, not knowing the truth of the matter, said, "She is indeed a woman who serves her husband like a deity; it is wonderful!" and so on, praising that woman of immoral conduct.
109:
Again, the King asked, "Is this cripple truly your childhood husband given by your parents?" That wicked woman, not recognizing the King, boldly said, "Yes, Great King."

Then King Paduma said to that wicked woman, "Is this cripple the son of the King of Bārāṇasī? Are you not the wife of Prince Paduma and the daughter of such-and-such a king? Did you not drink the blood from my knee, and having a heart attached to this cripple, push me off the mountain precipice? Now, you have brought death upon your forehead and come to this place, thinking I am dead. Am I not alive?"

He then called his ministers and asked, "O ministers, when you were asked, did this woman speak in this way?" and said, "My younger brothers killed six women and ate their flesh. I, however, kept my wife from harm and took her to the riverbank. While living in a hermitage, I rescued and cared for a man whose hands, feet, ears, and nose had been cut off, who was destined for execution.

That woman, having a heart attached to that cripple, pushed me off the mountain precipice. I survived because of my own heart of loving-kindness. The woman who pushed me off the mountain is none other than this immoral woman. She is no other. The cripple whom I cared for, who was destined for execution, is none other than this cripple. He is no other." Having said this, he spoke these two verses:

5. This is she, and I am he, no other;
This is the one with severed hands, no other.
She says, 'He is my childhood husband';
Women are deserving of death; there is no truth in women.

6. Having beaten this vile wretch with a pestle,
This cruel, corpse-like adulterer;
And for this wickedly 'devoted' woman,
While she is still alive, cut off her ears and nose.

O ministers. The woman who pushed me off the mountain precipice. That woman is this very woman; no other. The man whom she pushed off the mountain precipice. That man is I myself; no other. The vile man with severed hands, feet, ears, and nose whom I cared for. That mutilated man is this very wretch; no other. This wicked woman says of this cripple, "This man is my childhood husband." She is the very woman who was my wife; no other. Women are those who have the fault of deserving death. In women, there is no truth.

This vile cripple who is harsh and cruel, who is like a corpse, and who commits adultery. Beat him with a pestle until he is crushed to pieces and punish him. And for this immoral woman who wickedly serves her husband. While she is still alive, cut off her ears and nose.
110:
The Bodhisatta, being unable to endure his anger, ordered punishment for those wicked people, yet he did not have it carried out exactly as ordered.

Indeed, having lessened his anger, he had the wicked woman bound so firmly that she could not remove the basket from her head, placed the cripple inside that basket, and had them banished from his kingdom.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher revealed the Truths and identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). As for the identification of the Jātaka: "At that time, the six brothers were the elders who are now unknown; the wife was Ciñcamāṇavikā; the cripple was Devadatta; the Iguana King was Ānanda; and King Paduma was I myself."

## Even if one has done favors for a woman, she may act as if she knows nothing and commit murder.

The Cūḷapaduma Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Maṇicora Jātaka

## The Crest-Jewel

The Present Story: While the All-Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, he told this Maṇicora Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na santi devā pavasanti nūna," concerning Devadatta who was making an effort to kill the Buddha.

At that time, the Buddha, hearing that Devadatta was making an effort to kill him, said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is making an effort to kill me; in the past too, Devadatta made an effort to kill me."
111:
"Even though he made an effort, he was unable to kill me," he said, and being requested by those monks, he related the story of the past.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder's family in a small village not far from Benares. When he reached the age of maturity, they brought a daughter of a good family from Benares for him.

That young woman had a complexion like gold and was exceedingly beautiful. She was lovely to behold, like a celestial nymph, like a flowering vine, and as graceful as a kinnarī in her prime. Her name was Sujātā.

She was perfect in her duties to her husband, as if to a deity. She was endowed with virtuous conduct. She always performed her duties toward her husband and her father-in-law and mother-in-law. The Bodhisatta loved and cherished Sujātā. Thus, the two of them lived together in harmony, with a single mind and in joy.

Then one day, Sujātā told the Bodhisatta that she wished to see her parents. The Bodhisatta said, "Very well, dear, prepare sufficient provisions for the journey." He had various delicacies cooked, loaded the food and other items onto a cart, and drove the cart, sitting in the front. Sujātā sat in the back. The couple reached the vicinity of the city, unyoked the cart, and bathed. After bathing, they ate. Having eaten, the Bodhisatta yoked the cart and sat in the front. Sujātā changed her clothes, adorned herself, and sat near the Bodhisatta.

At the time they were entering the city, the King of Benares, riding upon the back of a noble elephant, was making a ceremonial circuit of the city and arrived at that place. Sujātā got down and walked behind the cart. The King saw her, and his eyes were drawn by the perfection of her beauty. Becoming infatuated, he ordered a minister, "Go and find out whether that woman has a husband or is without one." The minister went, and learning that she had a husband, he said, "Your Majesty, she has a husband; the man sitting in the cart is her husband."
112:
7. "There are no gods; they must be away. Surely there are no world-protectors here. For those who act recklessly and without restraint, there are surely no restrainers."

This was the first verse she spoke. 

"In this world" (idha loke): In this world, gods who watch over the virtuous and restrain the wicked surely do not exist. "They must be away" (pavasanti nūna): When such matters arise, the gods who watch over the virtuous must have gone elsewhere. "World-protectors" (lokapālā): The monks and brahmins regarded as world-protectors who support the virtuous surely do not exist. "Recklessly" (sahasā): Those who act hastily and cruelly without reflection. "Without restraint" (asaññatānaṃ): Those who do not guard their body, speech, and mind. "Restrainers" (paṭisedhitāro): Gods who restrain them, saying, "Do not do such a thing; this is not allowed," surely do not exist.

The king, unable to dispel his lustful thoughts and driven by passion, planned to kill the man by a trick and take the woman. He summoned a man and said, "Go, take this crest-gem and place it in that man's cart as if it were lost there, then return." Having said this, he gave him the crest-gem and sent him off. The man agreed, took the crest-gem, placed it in the cart, and returned to report, "Great King, I have placed it."

The king then announced, "My crest-gem is lost." The people made a great commotion. The king ordered, "Close all the gates and search for the thief." The royal officials did as commanded, and the city was thrown into turmoil.

A royal official took some men and went to the Bodhisatta, saying, "Hey, stop the cart! The king's crest-gem is lost. We must search the cart." While searching, he took the crest-gem he had placed there himself, seized the Bodhisatta, and crying out, "This is the jewel-thief!" he beat him with hands and feet. He then bound his hands behind his back and brought him to the king, saying, "This man is the jewel-thief." The king ordered, "Cut off his head!"

Then the royal officials beat the Bodhisatta with whips at every crossroads and led him out of the city through the south gate. Sujātā abandoned the vehicle and followed behind, raising her arms and weeping, "My lord, because of me you have come to this suffering."

The royal officials laid the Bodhisatta on his back, intending to cut off his head. Seeing this, Sujātā reflected on the power of her virtue and thought, "In this world, there are surely no gods capable of restraining the wicked and violent men who harass the virtuous."
113:
Thus, as the virtuous Sujātā wept, the Paṇḍukambala stone throne of Sakka, King of Gods, showed signs of heat. Sakka reflected, "Who wishes to displace me from my position?" and upon investigating, he realized the cause: "The King of Bārāဏasī is committing an extremely cruel act; he is harassing the virtuous Sujātā. It is now proper for me to go." Descending from the celestial realm by his divine power, he removed the wicked king from the elephant's back and laid him on the execution block. He then lifted the Bodhisatta, adorned him with all ornaments, gave him the royal appearance, and seated him on the elephant's back.

The royal officials raised their swords to strike, and they beheaded the King of Bārāṇasī. Only after the head was severed did they realize it was the king's head.

Sakka, King of Gods, in visible form, went to the Bodhisatta, performed the royal consecration, and appointed Sujātā as the chief queen. The ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, seeing Sakka, were filled with joy, saying, "The unrighteous king is slain; now we have obtained a righteous king given by Sakka."

Sakka, standing in the air, exhorted them: "This king given by Sakka shall rule righteously from this day forth." To clearly show the faults of an unrighteous king, he said, "If a king is unrighteous, it rains out of season and does not rain in season. The three fears—famine, disease, and the sword—will surely come." Desiring to give this instruction, he spoke the second verse:

8. "For him, it rains out of season; in season, it does not rain. He falls from his heavenly place; is he not thus destroyed?"

"For him" (tassa): In the kingdom of that unrighteous king. "Out of season" (akāle): When rain falls, it falls at improper times. "In season" (kāle): In the kingdom of that unrighteous king, it does not rain at the proper times. "Falls from his heavenly place" (saggā cavati ṭhānā): The unrighteous king is deprived of the heavenly realm. Alternatively, even if an unrighteous king were ruling in heaven, he would fall from that place. "Is he not thus destroyed?" (nanu so tāvatā hato): Is that unrighteous king not ruined by this much? Or rather, he is not yet fully punished by this alone, for he will be tormented for a long time in the eight great hells and sixteen secondary hells.
114:
Thus, Sakka, having given advice to the multitude, returned to his own celestial abode. The Bodhisatta, too, ruled righteously and filled the heavenly realm.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the unrighteous king was Devadatta, Sakka was Anuruddha, Sujātā was the mother of Rāhula, but the king given by Sakka was I myself."

## Through the Good, the Deities Protect; Practice the True Dhamma

The Maṇicora Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka

## The Wise Minister

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the deities, told this Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Pabbatūpatthare ramme," concerning the King of Kosala.

It is said that a certain minister of the King of Kosala committed misconduct with a woman of the harem. When the King investigated and found it to be true, he thought, "I will inform the Teacher." He went to Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and asked, "Venerable Sir, a minister has committed misconduct with a woman of my harem. What is the proper thing to do with that minister?"

Then the Buddha asked the King, "Great King, is that minister helpful to you? And is that woman dear to you?" When the King replied, "Yes, Venerable Sir, he is very helpful and maintains the entire royal household; that woman is also dear to me," the Buddha said, "Great King, one should not destroy those who are helpful servants and beloved women. In the past, kings also heard the words of the wise and remained indifferent (forgiving)." Being requested by the King, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers. When he came of age, he became a minister who advised the King on matters of welfare and Dhamma.

At that time, a certain minister of King Brahmadatta committed misconduct with a lady of the harem. The King found it to be true and thought, "This minister is of great help to me, and this woman is also dear to me. I cannot destroy both of them. I will ask the wise minister a question. If it is something to be endured, I shall endure it; if not, I shall not." He summoned the Bodhisatta, gave him a seat, and said, "Wise one, I shall ask you a question." When the Bodhisatta replied, "Ask, Great King, I shall answer," the King, wishing to ask the question, spoke the first verse:
115:
9. In the delightful plateau at the foot of the mountain, there is a pleasant lotus pond. Knowing it was guarded by a lion, did a jackal drink from it?

This was the first verse he spoke.

Paṇḍita: wise one. Ramme: delightful. Pabbatūpatthare: on the level ground spreading at the foot of the Himālaya mountains. Sivā: endowed with cool and sweet water. Pokkharaṇī: a lotus pond. Jātā: there is. Alternatively, Pokkharaṇī: a river covered with lotuses. Jātā: there is. Taṃ: that pond (or river). Sīhena: by the lion king. Rakkhitaṃ: guarded. Jānaṃ (jānanto): knowing thus. Siṅgālo: a jackal. Apāpāyi: did he drink (is it proper to drink)?

[The King thought:] "I cannot destroy these two people. I will ask the wise minister a question. If it is to be endured, I shall endure it; if not, I shall not." Having made this resolution, he summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Wise one, I shall ask you a question." When the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, please ask, I shall answer," the King, wishing to ask the question—

The Bodhisatta, knowing for certain that a minister must have committed misconduct with a woman of the King's harem, spoke this second verse:

10. O Great King, even if beasts drink from the great river, it does not thereby cease to be a river. If she is dear to you, forgive her.

Mahārāja: Great King. Mahānadiṃ: the great river, called a lotus pond (pokkharaṇī) because it is covered with lotuses. Sāpadāni: various kinds of beasts such as birds, dogs, rabbits, cats, and deer. Pivanti ce: even if they drink. Tena: because of such drinking. Sā: that great river. Anadī: not a river. Na hoti: does not become. Sā itthī: that woman. Te: to you, Great King. Yadi piyā: if she is dear. Khamassu: please forgive her.

Thus, the Bodhisatta gave advice to the King. The King, established in the advice of the Bodhisatta, said, "Do not perform such an evil deed again," and forgave both of them. From then on, they abstained from such acts. The King also performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and, at the end of his life, filled the heavenly realm.
116:
King Kosala, having heard this Dhamma teaching, forgave both of them and became equanimous.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was I myself." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## One should be grateful, affectionate, and always patient.

The Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Valāhaka Jātaka
## The Ogresses

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Valāhaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ye na kāhanti ovādaṃ," concerning a monk who had become dissatisfied with the holy life.

When the Buddha asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?" and the monk replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha asked, "For what reason?" The monk replied, "Venerable Sir, it is because I saw an adorned woman and felt lust."

Then the Buddha said to him, "Monk, these women are called 'ogresses' (yakkhinīs) because they entice men with their forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches, as well as with their feminine wiles and charms. Once they know they have brought a man under their control, they cause the destruction of his virtue and his wealth.

This is true; in the past, ogresses also approached a caravan of merchants using feminine wiles, enticed them, and brought them under their power. Later, when they saw other men, they killed all the previous ones and ate them, filling their mouths with blood that trickled from both sides of their jaws." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, there was a city of ogresses called Sirīsavatthu. Ogresses lived there. When shipwrecked merchants arrived, these ogresses would dress and adorn themselves, take food and drink, and approach the merchants accompanied by their retinues of slave-women, carrying children on their hips.

To make the merchants believe they had reached a human settlement, they would show them people engaged in plowing and cattle-tending, as well as herds of cattle and dogs. They would go to the merchants and say, 'Drink this gruel, eat this rice, consume these delicacies.' The merchants, unaware, would consume the food and drink provided by the ogresses.
117:
Afterwards, when the merchants had eaten and drunk and were rested, the ogresses would exchange pleasantries, asking, "Sirs, where do you live? Where did you come from? Where are you going? For what business did you come here?" When the merchants replied, "We have come here because our ship was wrecked," the ogresses would say, "Good, sirs. It has been three years since our husbands went to sea; they must be dead. You are also merchants; we will be your wives (attendants at your feet)." Thus, they enticed the merchants with feminine charms, gestures, and wiles, and led them to the city of ogresses. If there were men previously captured, they would bind them with magic chains (devasaṅkhalikā) and cast them into a prison-house.

If they did not find any shipwrecked men at their own location, they would roam the seashore from Kalyāṇī on the far side to Nāgadīpa on the near side. This was the nature of those ogresses.

Then one day, five hundred shipwrecked merchants landed near their city. The ogresses went to them, enticed them, and led them to the city of ogresses. They bound the men they had previously captured with magic chains and threw them into the prison-house. The chief ogress took the chief merchant, and the remaining ogresses took the remaining merchants; thus, the five hundred ogresses took the five hundred merchants as their husbands.

During the night, when the merchants had fallen asleep, the chief ogress would get up, go to the prison-house, kill the men, eat their flesh, and return. The other ogresses did exactly as the chief ogress did. When the chief ogress returned after eating human flesh, her body was cold.

Upon investigation, the chief merchant realized she was an ogress and thought, "These five hundred women must be ogresses; we must flee." Early the next morning, he went to wash his face and informed the other merchants.

He said to the remaining merchants, "Friends, these women are ogresses, not human women. When other shipwrecked merchants arrive, they will take them as husbands and eat us. Let us flee from this place."
118:
11. Those men who will not follow the advice taught by the Buddha, they will go to destruction, like the merchants by the ogresses.
12. And those men who will follow the advice taught by the Buddha, they will go safely to the other shore, like the merchants by Valāhaka.
He preached these verses.
Monks (Bhikkhave), those men (ye narā) who will not follow (na kāhanti) the advice (ovādaṃ) taught (desitaṃ) by the Buddha (Buddhena), those men (te narā) will go to destruction (vyasanaṃ), just as the merchants (vāṇijā) enticed (palobhitā) by the ogresses (rakkhasīhi) reached great ruin (mahāviနာsaṃ). 
And those men (ye narā ca) who will follow (kāhanti) the advice (ovādaṃ) taught (desitaṃ) by the Buddha (Buddhena), those men (te narā) will reach the other shore (pāraṃ) of Saṃsāra, which is Nibbāna, in safety (sotthiṃ), just like the merchants (vāṇijā iva) who followed the words (vacanakarā) of the noble horse Valāhaka when he said, 'Come!' (āgacchatha).
Among those five hundred merchants, two hundred and fifty said, 'We cannot leave these women; you go ahead, we will not flee.' The head merchant took the merchants who followed his words and fled, fearing those ogresses.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was born as a horse. His whole body was white. He had a dark head and a mane like muñja grass. He was endowed with supernatural power and could fly through the sky. That Valāhaka horse king flew from the Himavanta to the island of Tambapaṇṇi, and there, in a marshy pond on the island of Tambapaṇṇi, he ate wild rice that grew naturally and went on.
As he went, that Valāhaka horse king spoke three times in a human voice suffused with compassion, 'Is there anyone who wishes to go to the country of Jambudīpa?' When those two hundred and fifty merchants heard the words of the Bodhisatta, they approached him, and raising their hands in salutation, they said, 'Lord, we wish to go to the country of Jambudīpa.' He said, 'If so, climb onto my back.'
Some climbed up. Among them, some held the tail. Some just stood with their hands raised in salutation. The Bodhisatta, by his own power, took all those two hundred and fifty merchants, including even those who stood with hands raised in salutation, to the country of Jambudīpa, established them in their respective places, and then went to his own dwelling place.
As for those ogresses, when other merchants arrived, they killed and ate the two hundred and fifty men who remained in that city of ogresses.
The Blessed One addressed the monks, 'Monks, just as those two hundred and fifty merchants who followed the will of the ogresses met their end, and the merchants who followed the words of the noble horse Valāhaka were established in their own places, even so, monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who do not follow the advice of the Buddhas reach great suffering in the four woeful states, such as the places where the fivefold binding and torture are performed.
But those who practice according to the Buddha's advice reach the three types of wealthy families—wealthy householders (gahapati mahāsāla), wealthy brahmins (brāhmaṇa mahāsāla), and wealthy khattiyas (khattiya mahāsāla)—as well as the six celestial realms of the sense sphere and the twenty Brahma worlds; reaching these places, they realize the great Nibbāna, the deathless, and enjoy great happiness.' Having said this, being the Fully Enlightened One, he spoke—
119:
—just like the merchants who followed his words when he said, 'Come!' Just as they crossed the ocean and went to their respective places, even so, those who follow the advice of the Buddhas go to Nibbāna, the other shore of Saṃsāra. Thus, he concluded the Dhamma teaching with the great deathless Nibbāna.
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Many others also reached the Fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, Non-returning, and Arahantship. 'At that time, the two hundred and fifty merchants who followed the words of the Valāhaka horse king were the Buddha's followers, and the Valāhaka horse king was I myself.'
## Those who indulge in sensual pleasures and are blinded by the senses meet the danger of death.
The Valāhaka Jātaka is finished.
## 7. Mittāmitta Jātaka
## Friend and Foe
The Omniscient Buddha, who teaches the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana monastery, told this Mittāmitta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Na naṃ umhayate disvā,' concerning an obscure monk.
