To elaborate: that obscure monk, thinking, 'My preceptor will not be angry if I take it,' took a piece of cloth left by his preceptor out of familiarity (vissāsa), made a sandal bag, and later asked the preceptor for permission.
Then the preceptor asked him, 'Why did you take it?' When he replied, 'I took it out of familiarity with you, thinking you would not be angry,' the preceptor said, 'What familiarity do you have with me?' and getting angry, he stood up and struck him. That action of the monk became well-known among the monks.
Then one day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, it is said that a certain young monk took a piece of cloth out of familiarity with his preceptor and made a sandal bag. Then the preceptor, saying "What familiarity do you have with me?", got angry and struck his disciple.'
The Teacher came and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, not only now has this monk been untrusting toward his co-resident; in the past too, he was untrusting.' And he brought forth the past story.
120:
Thus they started this conversation.

The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "We are gathered for such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now is this monk unfriendly with his own co-resident pupil; in the past also, he was indeed unfriendly," and he brought forth the story of the past.

## The Story of the Past
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the Kāsī country. When he reached of age, he became an ascetic, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lived in the Himavant region as the teacher of a group of ascetics.

In that group of ascetics, one ascetic did not follow the Bodhisatta's advice and raised an orphaned young elephant. Later, when that elephant reached maturity, it killed that ascetic and entered the forest. After performing the funeral rites for the ascetic's body, the group of ascetics surrounded the Bodhisatta and asked, "Venerable sir, by what means can one know the state of being a friend or the state of being an enemy?"

To those ascetics, the Bodhisatta, wishing to explain by what means one can know the state of being a friend or an enemy, spoke these verses:

13. He does not smile upon seeing him, nor does he welcome him.
He does not give him eye contact, and he acts in opposition.

14. These are the signs established in an enemy,
By which a wise man, having seen and heard, may know an enemy.

Friends, whoever is an enemy, that person, upon seeing the one he is hostile toward, does not smile, does not laugh, and does not show a joyful appearance. Even upon hearing his words, he does not welcome that person, nor does he appreciate them by saying, "Well said."

He does not give him eye contact; he does not look him in the face with eye meeting eye, but turns his eyes away. And he acts in opposition; he does not take pleasure in his bodily or verbal actions, but holds a contrary and hostile view.

By these causes such as not smiling, a wise man, having seen and heard those causes, should know, "This person is my enemy." These signs are established in an enemy.

Thus the Bodhisatta explained the causes of being a friend or an enemy, developed the sublime abodes (brahmavihāra), and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

## Identification of the Jātaka
The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the ascetic who raised the elephant was the co-resident pupil, the elephant was the preceptor, the group of ascetics was the Buddha's assembly, and I myself was the teacher of the group of ascetics."

## By observing their behavior, one knows both friend and foe.
The Mittāmitta Jātaka ends.

## 8. Rādha Jātaka
## Rādha the Parrot

**The Story of the Present**
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Rādha Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Pavāsā āgato tāta," concerning a monk who had become dissatisfied with the holy life.

When the Buddha asked that monk, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?" he replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir." When asked, "Why are you dissatisfied?" he answered, "Venerable Sir, having seen an adorned woman, I am dissatisfied through the power of defilements."

Then the Buddha said to him, "Monk, it is impossible to guard a woman. In the past, even when householders guarded them by employing doorkeepers, they were unable to do so. A woman is of no use to you; even if you obtain one, she cannot be guarded," and he then brought forth the past.

**The Story of the Past**
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the species of parrots. They named that parrot Rādha. His younger brother was named Poṭṭhapāda.

While those two brothers were still young, a hunter caught them and gave them to a certain Brahmin in Bārāṇasī. The Brahmin raised those two parrots in the position of his own sons.

However, the Brahmin's wife was unrestrained and immoral. When the Brahmin was about to leave for trade, he called the young parrots and said, "My dears, I am going away for trade. Whether at the right time or the wrong time, you must watch over the conduct of your mother, the Brahmin lady. Make sure to know whether another man comes or does not come." Having entrusted the young parrots to the Brahmin lady, he departed.

From the time the Brahmin left, that lady practiced immoral conduct. There was no limit to the men coming and going both by night and by day.

Seeing this behavior, Poṭṭhapāda asked Rādha, "Rādha, the Brahmin went away after entrusting this lady to us. This lady is performing evil deeds; shall I speak to her?" Rādha replied, "Poṭṭhapāda, do not speak." But Poṭṭhapāda did not heed Rādha's words and said, "Mother, why are you performing evil deeds?"

Desiring to kill Poṭṭhapāda, she said, "My dear Poṭṭhapāda, you are indeed my son. From this day forward, I will not do it. Come here, my dear Poṭṭhapāda," calling him as if with affection. When Poṭṭhapāda came, she seized him, saying, "You dare to admonish me! You do not know your own place!" She twisted his neck, killed him, and threw him into the space between the trivets of the hearth.

16. "Indeed, this is not a good thing to say, even if the speech is joined with truth. One would lie like Potthapāda, scorched in the hot ashes."

He spoke this verse which completes the two.

Dear father (Tāta). One who is called wise (Paṇḍitena nāma). Even such speech (Etaṃ-idisaṃ giraṃ) which is joined with truth (Saccupasaṃhitaṃ). It is not good (Na subhaṇaṃ), as it does not lead to happiness, and thus should not be spoken easily. One who speaks a truth (Saccaṃ bhaṇanto) that does not lead to liberation (Aniyyānikaṃ). Like Potthapāda (Potthapādo), scorched (Upakūthito) in the hot ashes (Mummure). Just as if one has to lie down (Sayati iva). So (Evaṃ-tathā) should one lie (Saye-tha).

The Brahmin, having come and rested from his fatigue, wishing to ask the Bodhisatta whether his wife had committed misconduct or not, spoke this first verse:

15. "I have come from a journey, dear son; I have just now arrived. Does your mother, dear son, not consort with another?"

Dear son Rādhā (Tāta Rādhā). I (Ahaṃ) have come (Āgato) from a journey (Pavāsā). I have just now (Idāni) arrived (Āgato amhi). It has not been long since I arrived (Na cirāgato). Dear son Rādhā (Tāta Rādhā). Does your mother (Te mātā) not avoid consorting (Na upasevati kaccinnu) with another man (Aññaṃ)?

Rādhā, wishing to make it known that those called wise do not speak words that do not lead to happiness, whether they be true or false:

Thus the Bodhisatta, having preached the Dhamma to the Brahmin, said, "I cannot stay in this place either," and having taken leave of the Brahmin, entered the forest.

The Master, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, Potthapāda was Ānanda, and at that time, I myself was Rādhā." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Even if it be true, if it does not increase welfare, a wise man should not speak it.

The Rādhajātaka is finished.

## 9. Gahapati Jātaka
## The Wicked Woman

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Gahapati Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ubhayāṃ me na khamati," concerning a monk who was longing for his former life.

The Teacher said, "Monks, those called women cannot be guarded; they commit evil deeds and deceive their husbands by any means," and then he brought up the past.

The Past Story: Monks, in the past, when a king named Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder's family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he took up the life of a householder. The wife of that Bodhisatta was immoral and committed misconduct with the village headman (Gāmabhojaka). The Bodhisatta, knowing that matter, went about investigating it.

At that time, during the rainy season, after the seeds had been sown, there was a famine. When the time for the grain to form ears arrived, all the villagers living in the village together took an old ox from the village headman, saying, "We will give you the grain after harvesting it two months from now," and they ate the meat.

Then one day, the village headman, watching for an opportunity to commit the theft, entered the house when the Bodhisatta had gone out. At the very moment when the two were enjoying themselves, the Bodhisatta entered through the village gate and headed towards the house. The woman, looking towards the village gate, saw the Bodhisatta and wondered, "Who is this?" Standing at the door and looking, she realized, "It is my husband," and informed the village headman.
124:
17. "Both are not acceptable to me; both do not please me. This woman who has gone down into the granary says, 'I will not give [any grain].'"

18. "I tell you this, O Village Headman, in this miserable and short life: having made an agreement for two months, you demand the price of the meat of the lean old ox before the time has arrived. That also does not please me."

These were the verses he spoke.

O Gāmapati, Village Headman. For a certain reason. Me, to me. Your actions. Do not please. For that reason. You. I. Shall tell. Our life. When it is miserable and difficult. When it is short. To us who buy beef. You who give a lean and weak old ox. You said, "The price must be paid in two months." Thus, having made a contract for a period of two months. You demand the price of the meat before that period has arrived.

That action also. I. Do not like. This wicked woman also. Having climbed into the granary. Does not see the grain. Thus she says. That action also. I. Do not like. Thus, both these actions. Are not acceptable to me. Both these actions. I do not like.

The Village Headman was terrified and trembled. Then that woman said to the Village Headman, "Do not be afraid, there is a trick. We have eaten the beef from your hand; you pretend to demand the price of the meat. I shall climb into the granary and, standing at the granary door, say there is no grain. You stand in the middle of the house and say, 'The children in our house are hungry. Give me the price of the meat.' Demand it repeatedly in this way." She then climbed into the granary and stayed at the granary door.

The Village Headman stood in the middle of the house and said, "Give me the price of the meat." That woman, staying at the granary door, said, "There is no grain; I will give it only when the harvest is gathered. Go away for now."

The Bodhisatta entered the house and, seeing the behavior of those two, realized, "This matter must be a trick devised by this vile woman." He said, "Village Headman, when we ate the meat of your old ox, we said we would pay the grain in two months from this month. Why do you demand it now, not even letting half a month pass? You did not come because you wanted to demand this meat-price; you must have come for another reason."

"I do not like your behavior. This wicked woman of vile character, who knows there is no grain in the granary, has climbed into the granary and says there is no grain. You also say, 'Give it to me.' I do not like the behavior of both of you." This was the meaning he intended.

While saying this, the Bodhisatta grabbed the Village Headman by his topknot, dragged him, and beat him in the middle of the house, saying, "Is it right for you, being a Village Headman, to offend against the property guarded and protected by another?" After reviling and beating him until he was weak, he grabbed him by the neck and threw him out of the house. He also grabbed that wicked woman by her hair, brought her down from the granary, beat her, and threatened her, saying, "If you do such a thing again, you shall see!" From then on, the Village Headman did not dare even to look at that house. That wicked woman also did not dare to transgress even in her mind again.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was longing for the lay life was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, the Village Headman was Devadatta, but the householder who inflicted the punishment was I myself."

## Women are deceptive; they cannot be guarded.
The Gahapati Jātaka is concluded.

## 10. Sādhusīla Jātaka
## Virtue
The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sādhusīla Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sarīradabyaṃ," concerning a certain Brahmin.

That Brahmin had four daughters. Four men came to ask for those four daughters. Among those four men, one was handsome and possessed a beautiful body. One was advanced in years and elderly. One was of noble birth. One was virtuous.

The Brahmin thought: "Among these four men, to whom should I give my daughters to be established in their desire? Should I give them to the one endowed with beauty? Or else, should I give them to one of the others—the one advanced in age, the one of noble birth, or the one who is virtuous?" Thus he thought.

Though he thought, he did not know. Thinking, "The Fully Enlightened One will know this matter; I will ask the Buddha and give them to the one who is suitable among those four," he had perfumes, flowers, and so on brought, went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat in a suitable place. He reported the matter from the beginning and asked, "Venerable Sir, to whom among these four men is it proper to give them?"
126:
19. Beauty, age, noble birth, and good character.
We ask you, O Brahmin, which of these should we choose?

This was the first verse spoken. 

Brahmin, teacher. My daughters are sought by four men. Among those four, one possesses physical beauty (sarīradabyaṃ), having a handsome appearance. One possesses seniority (vuḍḍhabyaṃ), being of advanced age. One possesses noble birth (sojaccaṃ), having the excellence of a good lineage. One possesses good character (sādhusīliyaṃ), being endowed with excellent virtue. Not knowing to which of these named individuals my daughters should be given, we ask only you, the Brahmin teacher. Among those four men, whom should we desire? To whom should we give these maidens?

20. There is value in the body; one should pay respect to the aged.
There is value in noble birth; but virtue is what we prefer.

This was the second verse spoken to complete the answer.

Brahmin, in a body endowed with beautiful appearance, there is indeed an advantage. To one who is advanced in age, one should indeed pay respect. In a man of noble birth, there is also an advantage; excellence of birth is also desirable. However, as for us, we prefer the one with virtue. For a virtuous person, endowed with proper conduct, even if lacking physical beauty, is worthy of honor and praise. Hearing his words, the Brahmin gave his daughters only to the virtuous man.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, the Teacher identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the Brahmin was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). "At that time, the Brahmin was this very same Brahmin, and the world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) was I myself."

Explanation of the Sādhusīla Jātaka is the tenth.
The fifth chapter, the Ruhaka Vagga, is finished.
127:
## Beauty, Age, Birth, Virtue; the last man is the best.
The Sādhusīla Jātaka ends.

## 6. Na taṃ daḷha Vagga

## 1. Bandhanāgāra Jātaka

## The Fetters of Defilement

**The Present Account**
The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Bandhanāgāra Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā," concerning a prison.

At that time, many thieves who committed housebreaking and highway robbery were captured and presented to the King of Kosala. The King had those thieves bound with wooden stocks, ropes, and iron chains.

About thirty monks living in the countryside, wishing to see the Teacher, arrived and paid their respects. While going for alms the next day, they reached the prison and saw those thieves. After returning from their alms round, in the evening, they approached the Tathāgata and asked: "Venerable Sir, today while going for alms, we saw many thieves in the prison bound with stocks and other fetters, suffering great pain. Those thieves are unable to break those bonds and escape. Is there any other bond stronger and firmer than those bonds?"

The Teacher said, "Monks, how can those be called bonds? That bond of defilement (kilesa) known as craving (taṇhā) for wealth, grain, sons, and wives—that bond is a hundred times, a thousand times stronger and firmer than those bonds of iron chains and such. Even though it is so great and difficult to break, wise men of old broke that bond of defilement, entered the Himālaya, and ordained as monks." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

**The Past Account**
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a poor householder's family. When he reached the age of maturity, his father passed away. The Bodhisatta worked for hire to support his mother.
128:
1. The wise do not say that a bond made of iron, wood, or hemp is strong. That attachment which is a longing for jeweled earrings, and for sons and wives—

2. The wise say that this bond is strong, which drags one down, is loose, yet is hard to release. Having cut even this, the wise go forth, without longing, having abandoned sensual pleasures.

These were the two stanzas he uttered.

*Ayasaṃ*: made of iron. *Yaṃ bandhanañca*: that bond known as iron shackles. *Dārujaṃ*: made of wood; that bond known as a prison. *Pabbajaṃ*: made of reeds, hemp, and so on; that bond known as a rope. *Atthi*: there is. *Taṃ bandhanaṃ*: that bond. *Daḷhaṃ*: as strong. *Dhīrā*: the wise. *Na āhu*: do not say. *Maṇikuṇḍalesu*: in ruby earrings. Alternatively, in golden earrings set with rubies. *Ye*: those who. *Sārattarattā*: being intensely lustful, are attached. *Tesaṃ*: of them. *Yo sārāgo ca*: that intense attachment. *Tesaṃ*: of them. *Puttesu dāresu*: towards sons and wives. *Yā apekkhā ca*: that bond of longing which is greed. *Atthi*: there is.

*Etaṃ bandhanaṃ*: that bond of greed. *Daḷhaṃ*: as strong. *Dhīrā*: the wise. *Āhu*: have said. *Ohārinaṃ*: which leads down to the four woeful states. *Sithilaṃ*: a loose bond, because it does not cut the outer skin, inner skin, or flesh, nor does it draw blood, nor does it make its bondage felt, and it allows one to perform tasks on land or water journeys. *Duppamuñcaṃ*: hard to untie. *Etampi*: even this bond of craving. *Dhīrā*: the wise. *Chetvāna*: having cut. *Kāmasukhaṃ*: sensual pleasure. *Anapekkhino*: being without longing. *Pahāya*: having abandoned. *Vajanti*: are able to go forth.

At that time, the Bodhisatta's mother, even though her son did not desire it, brought a young woman and gave her to him. Later, the mother passed away. Then, a child was conceived in the womb of the Bodhisatta's wife.

The Bodhisatta, unaware of the conception, said, "Sister, you must earn your living by working for hire; I shall go and ordain." The woman said, "Lord, I have conceived. When I have given birth and you have seen the child, you shall ordain." The Bodhisatta agreed. When she had given birth, he asked, "Sister, you have safely given birth; now I shall ordain." Then the woman said to the Bodhisatta, "Wait until the child is weaned," and she conceived again.

The Bodhisatta thought, "It is impossible to go by getting this woman's consent. I will flee and ordain without informing her." Having so planned, the Bodhisatta rose in the night and fled without informing his wife. At that time, the city guards seized him. The Bodhisatta said, "Sirs, I am a man who supports his mother. Please release me." Having thus secured his release from the guards, he stayed in a certain place, then departed through the main gate, entered the Himalayas, and ordained as a hermit. He produced the higher knowledges and attainments and lived enjoying the bliss of meditative absorption.

While living in the Himalayas, the Bodhisatta, desiring to utter an inspired utterance, said, "I have been able to cut the bond of defilements, known as the bond of affection for sons and wives, which is of such a nature and so difficult to cut."
129:
Thus the Bodhisatta, having uttered this solemn utterance, with his meditative absorptions intact, was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some monks became Stream-enterers, some became Once-returners, some became Non-returners, and some became Arahants. How did he identify the Jātaka? "Monks, she who was then the mother is now Mahāmāyā Devī. He who was then the father is now the Great King Suddhodana. She who was then the wife is now the mother of Rāhula. He who was then the son is now Rāhula. And the man who then renounced his wife and child and ordained was I myself." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Consider the fifteen hundred defilements as a great prison.
The Bandhanāgāra Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Keḷisīla Jātaka
## The King Fond of Play

While the All-Enlightened One, the Teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Keḷisīla Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca," concerning the Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya.

That long-lived Venerable Lakuṇḍaka Bhaddiya was famous and well-known in the Buddha's Dispensation. He had a sweet voice and was a speaker of the sweet Dhamma. He had attained the analytical insights and was a great Arahant. He was established among the eighty Great Elders. In stature, however, he was small. He was hunched. He was so small that he seemed like a young novice or as if he were made for play.
130:
One day, after paying homage to the Blessed One, as the Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya was going to the gate of the Jetavana monastery, about thirty monks from the countryside, intending to pay homage to the Ten-Powered One, entered the Jetavana. Seeing the Elder at the monastery gate and perceiving him to be a novice, they pulled the hem of his robe, grabbed his hands, touched his head, stroked his nose, and shook his ears. Having thus engaged in such playful teasing, they put away their bowls and robes, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down. After the Teacher had greeted them with sweet hospitality, they asked:

"Venerable Sir, we have heard that there is a disciple of yours named the Elder Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya, who is a sweet preacher of the Dhamma. Where is he now?"

"Monks, do you wish to see him?" the Teacher asked. "Yes, Venerable Sir," they replied. "Monks, the one you saw at the monastery gate, whom you pulled by the hem of his robe and teased—that is he," the Teacher said.

"Venerable Sir, why has such a disciple, who has made great aspirations and is endowed with merit, become so insignificant in appearance?" the monks asked. The Teacher replied, "Monks, it is because of an evil deed he committed himself." Being requested by them, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the King of Devas. At that time, King Brahmadatta could not bear to see an old, decrepit elephant, horse, or ox. Being of a playful nature, whenever he saw such an animal, he would have it chased. Seeing an old cart, he would have it broken. Seeing an old woman, he would have her summoned, pushed in the belly to make her fall, then made to stand up again to frighten her. Seeing old men, he would make them perform tumbles on the ground like acrobats. If he did not see any, and heard that there was an old person in a certain house, he would have them summoned and play with them.

People, being ashamed, sent their parents to other countries. The duty of serving one's mother and father was interrupted. The royal servants also became playful in the same way. As people died, they filled the four woeful states, and the assembly of devas diminished.

Sakka, seeing no new young devas, reflected on the cause. Knowing the reason, he thought, "I will tame him." He created the appearance of an old man, placed two pots of buttermilk on an old cart, yoked two old oxen...

3. Swans, cranes, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer—all fear the lion. There is no equality in body.

4. Even so among humans, if a youth is wise, he is indeed great there; not the fool, though he be large of body.

The Teacher spoke these verses.

Monks, in the body, there is no such thing as equality. Because of this, swans, cranes, peacocks, elephants, and deer called *pasada*—or *pasada* deer and other remaining animals—all fear the lion.

Even so among humans, if a person, though young, is wise, he is indeed great among those people. A fool, though large of body, is not called great. Therefore, do not think of Lakuṇṭaka Bhaddiya as small in wisdom just because he is small in body.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the King of Devas. At that time, King Brahmadatta could not bear to see an old, decrepit elephant, horse, or ox. Being of a playful nature, whenever he saw such an animal, he would have it chased. Seeing an old cart, he would have it broken. Seeing an old woman, he would have her summoned, pushed in the belly to make her fall, then made to stand up again to frighten her. Seeing old men, he would make them perform tumbles on the ground like acrobats. If he did not see any, and heard that there was an old person in a certain house, he would have them summoned and play with them.

People, being ashamed, sent their parents to other countries. The duty of serving one's mother and father was interrupted. The royal servants also became playful in the same way. As people died, they filled the four woeful states, and the assembly of devas diminished.

Sakka, seeing no new young devas, reflected on the cause. Knowing the reason, he thought, "I will tame him." He created the appearance of an old man, placed two pots of buttermilk on an old cart, yoked two old oxen, and on a festival day, while Brahmadatta, mounted on a decorated elephant, was circumambulating the decorated city, Sakka, dressed in rags and driving that cart, went towards the king.

Seeing the old cart, the king said, "Remove that cart!" The people said, "Great King, where? We do not see it." Sakka, by his power, showed it only to the king.

Then, as many people gathered there, he drove the cart over the king, and broke one pot of buttermilk on the king's head. As he turned back, he broke the second one. Then, from the king's head downwards, buttermilk flowed here and there. The king was distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by it.

Then, knowing the king's state of suffering, Sakka made the cart disappear, revealed his form as Sakka, and standing in the air holding a thunderbolt, he threatened him: "O evil and unrighteous king! Will you not grow old? Will old age not strike your body? Being of a playful nature, you harass the elderly. Because of you alone, people commit such deeds and fill the woeful states upon death."
132:
“People are unable to support their parents. If you do not refrain from this deed, I shall split your head with this thunderbolt weapon. From this day forward, do not do such a thing.” Having thus threatened him, he preached on the gratitude owed to parents, showed the consequences of the merit of respecting elders, and after giving his admonition, returned to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

From that time on, the king did not even allow the thought of doing such a thing to arise in his mind. The Master, having brought this story of the past, after becoming the Buddha—

Identifying the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Master, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, some of those monks became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmi), some Non-returners (Anāgāmi), and some became Arahants. How was the Jātaka identified? “Monks, that king who, because of his habit of mocking others in the past, has now become the object of mockery for others, was Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya at that time. I myself was Sakka, the King of Devas, at that time.” Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## One reaps what one sows; a matter for reflection
The Keḷisīla Jātaka is concluded.

O Hermits! May the footless being not harm me. May the two-footed being also not harm me. May the four-footed being also not harm me. May the many-footed being also not harm me. Thus, cultivate loving-kindness.

O Hermits! All beings (sattā) who are attached to the five aggregates in the cycle of existence; all breathing things (pāṇā) endowed with inhalation and exhalation; all creatures (bhūtā) that have been born or are being born; all beings in their entirety—may they see only good objects. May they not reach any kind of evil suffering. Thus, cultivate loving-kindness.

O Hermits! The Buddha is without defilements. Alternatively, the virtues of the Buddha are immeasurable. The Dhamma is without defilements. Alternatively, the virtues of the Dhamma are immeasurable. The Saṅgha is without defilements. Alternatively, the virtues of the Saṅgha are immeasurable. Thus, you should reflect upon the virtues of the Three Jewels.

O Hermits! Snakes, scorpions, centipedes, spiders, lizards, and mice—these kinds of creeping things, or those that move with their bodies, are finite (possessing defilements). May these beings that possess defilements, by the power of the Three Jewels which are immeasurable and without defilements, perform the act of protection day and night. Thus, you should aspire.

O Hermits! By me, reflecting on the virtues of the Three Jewels, protection has been made. By me, reflecting on the virtues of the Three Jewels, a safeguard has been made.

May the creatures who desire my welfare depart. Thus, you should aspire. I, such as I am, pay homage to the Blessed One who is endowed with the six glories. I, such as I am, pay homage to the seven Fully Enlightened Ones. Thus, you should perform the act of homage.

It is said that a certain snake came out from between pieces of rotten wood and bit the toe of that monk who was splitting wood at the door of the bathhouse. That monk died right there where the snake bit him. The fact of that monk's death in such a manner became well-known throughout the entire monastery.

In the Dhamma hall, the monks started a conversation: “Friends, it is said that while a monk of such-and-forth name was splitting wood at the door of the bathhouse, a snake bit him and he died right there.” The Master, having arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?” and being told, “It is this subject,” said, “Monks, if that monk had cultivated loving-kindness towards the four royal families of snakes, that snake would not have bitten him.”
134:
"The snake would not have bitten that monk; this statement is true. Ancient sages who became ascetics, even before the time of the Buddha, developed loving-kindness (mettā) towards the four families of snakes and were once freed from the dangers arising from those various snake kings." Having said this, the Buddha brought forth the past story.

### The Story of the Past
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he reached the age of maturity, he renounced sensual pleasures and entered the life of an ascetic. He attained the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and the meditative attainments (samāpatti). He created a leaf-hut at a bend of a river in the Himavant region and lived there, delighting in the bliss of meditative absorption (jhāna), surrounded by a group of ascetics.

At that time, on the banks of the Ganges, many various long-bodied animals (snakes) caused harm to the group of ascetics. For the most part, many of the ascetics met their death.
135:
The ascetics reported this matter to the Bodhisatta.

The Bodhisatta assembled all the ascetics and said, "Monks, if you were to develop loving-kindness (mettā) towards the four families of snakes, the snakes would not bite you. Therefore, from this day forward, develop loving-kindness towards the four families of snakes in this way."

Thus, the Bodhisatta composed this protection (paritta) and gave it to the group of ascetics. From that time on, the group of ascetics remained established in the Bodhisatta's instruction and developed loving-kindness. They recollected the virtues of the Buddha. While those ascetics were recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, all the snake families departed. The Bodhisatta also developed the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) and passed away to the Brahma realm.

Concluding remarks: Because of showing loving-kindness towards the four families of snake kings with two verses,
136:
### Identification of the Jātaka
Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Fully Enlightened Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the group of ascetics were the Buddha's followers, and I myself was the teacher of that group."

Alternatively, because of showing the two types of development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) by way of specific (odissaka) and non-specific (anodissaka) pervasion, this Khandha Paritta is preached here in this Dukanipāta. Thus it should be understood.

## Through the infusion of loving-kindness, all dangers are secured, and complete happiness is attained.
The Khandha Jātaka ends.

## 4. Vīraka Jātaka
## The Water-crow and the Crow

### The Story of the Present
While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Vīraka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Api vīraka passesi," concerning Devadatta's imitation of the Buddha.

To elaborate on this: When the Elders Sāriputta and Moggallāna returned, bringing back Devadatta's followers, the Buddha asked, "Sāriputta, what did Devadatta do when he saw you?" When Sāriputta replied, "Venerable Sir, he imitated the Buddha," the Buddha said, "Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has come to ruin by imitating my actions; in the past also, he came to ruin." Having said this, at the request of Elder Sāriputta, the Buddha brought forth the past story.

### The Story of the Past
Sāriputta, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a water-crow in the Himavant region and lived near a certain lake. The name of that Bodhisatta was Vīraka. At that time, there was a famine in the kingdom of Kāsi. People were unable to give food to the crows or perform offerings to the spirits (yakkhas) and nagas.
137: 7. "O Vīraka, have you seen the bird of sweet speech, resembling a peacock's neck, my husband Saviṭṭhaka?" He spoke this first verse. Vīraka, O Noble Vīraka. Mañjubhāṇakaṃ, one who has a pleasant voice. Mayūragīvasaṅkāsaṃ, having a complexion like a peacock's neck. Mayhaṃ, my. Patiṃ, husband. Saviṭṭhakaṃ, named Saviṭṭhaka. Sakuṇaṃ, bird. Tvaṃ, you. Passesi api, have you seen? 8. "The bird that moves on both water and land, always eating raw fish. Imitating him, Saviṭṭhaka died, entangled in the weeds." He spoke this verse to complete the pair. Kākī, female crow. Udakathalacarassa, of one capable of moving on both water and land. Pakkhino, the bird. Niccaṃ, always. Āmakamacchabhojino, eating raw fish that has been caught. Saviṭṭhako, Saviṭṭhaka. Tassa, of that bird capable of moving on water and land. Anukaraṃ-anukaroanto, because of imitating. Sevāle, in the weeds. Paliguṇṭhito, being entangled. Mato, has died. Crows from a famine-stricken country mostly entered the forest. In that forest, a crow named Saviṭṭhaka, who lived in the city of Bārāṇasī, brought his mate and arrived at the place where Vīraka lived, staying in a suitable spot near that pond. One day, while Saviṭṭhaka was searching for food at that pond, he saw Vīraka descending into the pond, eating fish, and then coming out to dry himself. He thought, "By relying on this water-bird, I might obtain many fish; I should serve this water-bird." Approaching Vīraka, when asked, "Friend, what do you wish for?" he replied, "Lord, I wish to serve you." Vīraka agreed, saying, "Very well," and from then on, Saviṭṭhaka served him. Vīraka would eat only as much as he needed and then catch fish to give to Saviṭṭhaka. Saviṭṭhaka also ate only as much as he needed and gave the remainder to his mate. Later, pride arose in Saviṭṭhaka. He thought: "This water-bird is black in color, and I too am black in color. In terms of eyes, beak, and claws, there is no difference between this water-bird and me. From this day forth, I have no need for the fish caught by the water-bird; I myself will catch them." Having become proud, he approached Vīraka and said, "Friend, from this day forth, I myself will descend into the pond and catch fish." Although Vīraka forbade him, saying, "Friend, you were not born in a family that descends into the water to catch fish; do not destroy yourself," Saviṭṭhaka did not heed Vīraka's words. He descended into the pond, entered the water, and dived. However, he was unable to break through the weeds to come out. He became entangled among the weeds. Only the tip of his beak was visible. Being unable to breathe, Saviṭṭhaka reached the end of his life right there in the water. At that time, Saviṭṭhaka's wife, not seeing him return, went to Vīraka to learn of the matter. Wishing to ask, "Lord, Saviṭṭhaka is not seen; where has he gone?" she spoke...
138:
Hearing those words, Viraka meant to say, "I know the place where your husband has gone"—

Hearing those words, the female crow wept and went straight to the city of Bārāṇasī.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Saviṭṭhaka was Devadatta, and Viraka was I myself."

## Incapable yet proud, you shall perish, my friend

The Viraka Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Gaṅgeyya Jātaka

## The Fish and the Turtle Competing in Beauty

The Present Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who teaches the world including the devas, told this Gaṅgeyya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sobhati maccho gaṅgeyyo," concerning two young monks.

Two young men of good family living in Sāvatthī, having ordained in the Dispensation, did not practice the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā) but went about praising and pampering their own physical appearance.

One day, a dispute arose between them based on their looks, saying, "You are not beautiful; I am beautiful." Seeing an old Elder sitting nearby, they thought, "This old monk will know whether we are beautiful or not." They approached him and asked, "Venerable Sir, who among us is the more beautiful?"

The old monk replied, "Friends, I am more beautiful than both of you." The young monks said, "This old man does not answer what we asked, but says what we did not ask," and after reviling him, they departed.

Their behavior became well-known among the community of monks. Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, it is said that an old Elder of such-and-such a name put to shame those young monks who were obsessed with their looks."

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what purpose are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such-and-such a purpose," He said, "Monks, not only now are these two young monks obsessed with praising their own looks; in the past also, they went about pampering only their own appearance." Having said this, He brought forth the past story.
139:
9. The fish of the Ganges is beautiful, and the fish of the Yamuna is beautiful. But this four-footed person, round like a banyan tree, with a neck long and curved like a chariot pole, outshines you all.

Regarding this: The Ganges fish is beautiful. Furthermore, the Yamuna fish is beautiful. This four-footed person, with a body as round as the circumference of a banyan tree, and with a neck as long and curved as a chariot pole—this man outshines all of you.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity living by the bank of the Ganges.

At that time, at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna rivers, a Ganges fish and a Yamuna fish argued over their appearance, each claiming, "I am beautiful, you are not." Seeing a tortoise on the nearby bank of the Ganges, they thought, "This tortoise will know who is beautiful and who is not." They approached him and asked, "Friend tortoise, is the Ganges fish beautiful, or is the Yamuna fish more beautiful?"

The tortoise replied, "The Ganges fish is beautiful, and the Yamuna fish is also beautiful. But I am even more beautiful than both of you." To express this meaning, he spoke the first verse:

Hearing the tortoise's words, the fish said, "O wicked tortoise, you do not answer what we asked, but speak of something else," and they spoke this verse to complete the pair:

10. He did not answer what was asked; he spoke of something else. This man who praises himself is not pleasing to us.

Regarding this: "O wicked tortoise! The tortoise who was asked did not answer the problem we posed. He spoke of something else. This man who praises himself is not pleasing to us."

Having said this, they splashed water over the tortoise and returned to their own places.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the two fish were the two young monks, the tortoise was the old monk, and I myself was the tree deity living by the bank of the Ganges who witnessed this event."

## Appearance and Praise: Disputing and Being Shamed
The Gāṅgeyya Jātaka ends.

## 6. Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka

## Three Friends
The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka concerning Devadatta, beginning with the verse "Iṅgha vaṭṭamayaṃ pāsaṃ."

To elaborate: At that time, the Buddha heard that Devadatta was making an effort to kill him. The Buddha said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is trying to kill me; he did so in the past as well," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a Kuruṅga deer living in a thicket near a lake in the forest. Near that same lake, a woodpecker lived at the top of a tree. In the lake, a tortoise lived. Thus, these three animals were friends and lived together in mutual affection.
140:
11. Come, Tortoise, bite through this leather snare with your teeth. I shall act in such a way that the hunter does not come.

Friend tortoise, I urge you. Bite through this twisted leather snare with your teeth. As for me, I shall act in such a way that the hunter will not come.

At that time, a hunter wandering in the forest saw the Bodhisatta's footprints at the water's edge and set a twisted leather snare as strong as an iron chain before leaving.

When the Bodhisatta came to drink water, he was caught in the snare during the first watch of the night and let out a cry of capture. Hearing the Bodhisatta's voice, the woodpecker came from the tree and the tortoise came from the water, and they consulted together on what should be done.

Then the woodpecker called to the tortoise, "Friend tortoise, you have teeth; bite through the snare. I will go and act so that the hunter does not come. Thus, through the efforts of both of us, our friend will regain his life." To express this meaning, he spoke the first verse:

Then the tortoise began to gnaw the leather snare. The woodpecker flew to the hunter's village and perched on a nearby tree.

The hunter set out at dawn, taking his spear. Knowing the hunter was coming out, the bird cried out, flapped its wings, and struck the hunter in the face as he exited through the front door. The hunter thought, "I have been struck by an ill-omened bird," and turned back to lie down for a while. Then he took his spear and rose again.

The woodpecker thought, "This hunter came out the front door first; now he will come out the back door," and went to perch behind the house. The hunter also thought, "When I went out the front door, I saw an ill-omened bird; now I will go out the back door." As he exited the back door, the bird cried out again and struck him in the face. The hunter thought, "Again I am struck by an ill-omened bird; it will not let me go out now." He turned back and slept until dawn, then took his spear and set out at sunrise. The bird flew swiftly and told the Bodhisatta, "The hunter is coming!"

At that moment, the tortoise had bitten through all but one strand of the leather, and his teeth were on the verge of falling out. His mouth was covered in blood. Seeing the hunter approaching with the speed of a thunderbolt, spear in hand, the Bodhisatta snapped the remaining bond and fled into the forest. The woodpecker perched at the top of a tree. The tortoise, however, because of his weakness, lay right there.
141:
12. The tortoise entered the water, the Kurunga deer entered the forest.
The woodpecker from the treetop carried his young far away.

He [the Buddha] spoke this verse which completes the two [previous verses].

Bhikkhus, monks. Tadā, at that time. Mayi, when I. Ovāde, gave the advice. Kacchapo, the tortoise. Vāriṃ, into the water. Pāvisi, entered. Kurungo, the deer named Kurunga. Vanaṃ, into the forest. Pāvisi, entered. Satapatto, the woodpecker. Dumaggamhā, from the treetop. Dūre, to a far place. Putte, his young. Apānayi, carried.

The hunter took the tortoise, put it in a bag, and hung it on a stump. When the Bodhisatta looked back and saw that the tortoise had been captured, he thought, "I will give the gift of life to my friend," and pretending to be weak, he showed himself to the hunter.

That hunter, thinking, "This Kurunga deer must be weak; I will kill it," took his spear and gave chase. The Bodhisatta, moving neither too far nor too near, lured the hunter and entered the forest. Knowing that they had gone far, he deceived him with his tracks and returned with the speed of the wind by another path. He lifted the bag with his horns, dropped it on the ground, tore it open, and brought out the tortoise. The woodpecker also descended from the tree.

The Bodhisatta, giving advice to both the bird and the tortoise, said, "I have gained my life because of you, and you have performed the duty of a friend for me. Now, the hunter will come and might catch you. Therefore, friend woodpecker, take your young and go elsewhere. Friend tortoise, you also enter the water." They did as the Bodhisatta said. The Blessed One, having become the Buddha, said:

[Conclusion of the Jātaka:] The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the hunter was Devadatta, the woodpecker was Sāriputta, the tortoise was Moggallāna, and the Kurunga deer was I myself."

## Only among each other, help one another, and you shall find happiness.

The Kurungamiga Jātaka ends.
142:
## 7. Assaka Jātaka
## The Dung Beetle

[Present Story] The Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Assaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ayamassakarājena," concerning a monk who was pining for his former wife.

To elaborate on that story: when the Buddha asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante." When asked, "Who has caused you to be dissatisfied?" he replied, "Bhante, my former wife has caused me to be dissatisfied." Then the Buddha said to that monk, "Monk, that woman has no love for you. In the past, you also reached great suffering because of her," and he brought forth the past.

[Past Story] Monk, in the past, in the city of Pāṭali in the kingdom of Kāsī, a king named Assaka reigned. King Assaka had a beloved and dear chief queen named Upari. That Upari was extremely beautiful, lovely to behold, and pleasing. She surpassed the beauty of human women but did not reach the beauty of goddesses. That Queen Upari died.

Because of Queen Upari's death, King Assaka was overwhelmed by grief and became distressed and dejected. The king placed Queen Upari's body in a coffin, filled it with oil, and had it placed under his bed. He lay there without food, weeping and lamenting.

His mother, father, remaining relatives, friends, ministers, Brahmins, householders, and others said, "Great King, do not grieve; all conditioned things are impermanent," and so on, but they were unable to make him understand. While King Assaka was thus weeping and lamenting, seven days passed.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic who had attained the five mundane psychic powers and the eight meditative attainments, living in the Himalayan region. While developing his light and looking over Jambudīpa with his divine eye, he saw King Assaka lamenting and thought, "I should be a refuge for that King Assaka." By his psychic power, he flew through the air, descended into the king's park, and sat on the auspicious stone slab like a golden statue.

At that time, a young Brahmin living in the city of Pāṭali went to the park, saw the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and sat down. The Bodhisatta engaged in conversation with that young Brahmin and asked, "Young man, is the king righteous?" "Yes, Bhante, the king is righteous. However, his queen has died. The king has placed her body in a small coffin and lies there weeping and lamenting; today is the seventh day.

Bhante, why do you not free the king from such suffering? While virtuous ones like you exist, is it proper for the king to endure such suffering?" When the young Brahmin spoke thus, the Bodhisatta said, "Young man, I do not know the king. However, if the king were to come and ask me, I would tell him the place where the queen has been reborn and make the queen speak in the king's presence."
143:
“Venerable Sir, please remain in this very place for as long as it takes for me to bring the King.” Having obtained the Bodhisatta’s promise, the young brahmin went to the King and informed him of the matter. “It is proper to go to the presence of the hermit who is endowed with the divine eye,” he said.

King Assaka, having heard that he might be able to see Queen Upari, was joyful at heart. He mounted his chariot, went to the garden, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and sat in a suitable place. “Venerable Sir, is it true what I have heard, that you know the place where the Queen has been reborn?” he asked. “It is true, Great King,” he replied. “Venerable Sir, where has she been reborn?” the King asked.

“Great King, that Queen Upari, being intoxicated by her beauty and due to her negligence, failed to perform any meritorious deeds and was reborn as a dung beetle in this very garden,” he said.

“Venerable Sir, I do not believe it,” the King said. “In that case, I shall show you that dung beetle and make her speak to you, Great King,” the Bodhisatta replied. “Very well, Venerable Sir, make her speak,” the King said. Then the Bodhisatta, by his own psychic power, willed: “Let the two dung beetles, male and female, come before the King, rolling a ball of dung.” He caused the two of them to come.

The two dung beetles came exactly as the Bodhisatta had determined. Pointing to the female dung beetle, the Bodhisatta said, “Great King, this female dung beetle is your Queen named Upari. Having abandoned you, she follows behind the male dung beetle. Look at that female dung beetle.” “Venerable Sir, I do not believe that Queen Upari would be reborn as a dung beetle,” the King said. “Great King, I shall make that female dung beetle speak,” the Bodhisatta said. “Venerable Sir, please make her speak,” the King requested.

The Bodhisatta, by his own psychic power, determined that the female dung beetle should speak and called out, “Upari!” The female dung beetle replied in human language, “What is it, Venerable Sir?” “What was your name in your past life?” he asked. “Venerable Sir, I was the chief consort of King Assaka, named Upari,” she replied.

“Do you love King Assaka now, or do you love the male dung beetle?” he asked. “Venerable Sir, that King Assaka was my husband in my previous life.

At that time, I wandered in this garden with King Assaka, enjoying sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. But now, since the time I have passed into another existence, what is that King Assaka to me? Therefore, I would now kill King Assaka and smear the feet of my husband, the male dung beetle, with the blood from his throat,” she said, and in the midst of the assembly, she spoke these verses in human language:
144:
113. “This region was once traversed by me with King Assaka, my beloved husband, according to our desires.

114. “By new happiness and suffering, the old is covered. Therefore, the beetle is dearer to me than King Assaka.”

She spoke these two verses.

“Venerable Sir. This delightful garden region is the place where I used to wander with King Assaka, my beloved husband whom I loved. 

Now, because old happiness and suffering are covered by new happiness and suffering, therefore, I love the male dung beetle much more than King Assaka.”

Upon hearing these words, King Assaka became remorseful. Standing right there, he had the corpse removed, washed his head, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, entered the city, appointed another woman as chief consort, and ruled righteously. The Bodhisatta, having admonished the King and freed him from sorrow, returned to the Himalayas.

Identification of the Jātaka: The Blessed One, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the weary monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). To identify the Jātaka: “The former wife at that time was Queen Upari; the weary monk was King Assaka; the young brahmin was Sāriputta; and the ascetic was I myself.” Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## When lustful craving is excessive, one only suffers.

The Asaka Jātaka ends.

## 8. Susumāra Jātaka
## The Monkey and the Crocodile

**The Story of the Present**
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Susumāra Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Alaṃ metehi ambehi," concerning Devadatta’s attempt to kill him.

To elaborate: At that time, the Blessed One heard that Devadatta was making efforts to kill him. He said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has attempted to kill me; he did so in the past as well, yet he was unable to cause even a tremor of fear in me." Having said this, he recounted the past story.

**The Story of the Past**
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a monkey in the Himalayan region. He possessed the strength of an elephant, was full of vigor, had a large body, and was endowed with great beauty. He lived in a forest dwelling at a bend of the Ganges.

At that time, a crocodile lived in the Ganges. The crocodile's wife, seeing the body of the Bodhisatta, developed a pregnancy craving for the Bodhisatta's heart. She said to the male crocodile, "My lord, I wish to eat the heart of that monkey king."

He replied, "Dear lady, we are water-dwellers, while he is a land-dweller. How can we possibly catch him?"

She said, "Catch him by some means or other. If I do not get it, I shall die."

"In that case, do not worry," he comforted her. "There is a way. I will let you eat his heart." He then approached the Bodhisatta while the latter was sitting on the bank of the Ganges after drinking water, and said, "O King of Monkeys, why do you wander only in this place eating sour fruits? On the other side of the Ganges, there is no end to sweet fruits like mangoes and jackfruits. Is it not proper for you to go there and eat various fruits?"

"O King of Crocodiles, the Ganges is deep and wide. How shall I go there?" the monkey king asked.

"If you wish to go, I will carry you on my back," the crocodile said. The Bodhisatta believed him and agreed, saying, "Very well."

When the crocodile said, "Then come, climb onto my back," the monkey climbed on. After carrying him a short distance, the crocodile submerged him in the water.

The Bodhisatta said, "Friend, you are drowning me in the water. What is the meaning of this?"
146:
The crocodile said, "Monkey king, I am not taking you out of kindness. My wife has a craving for your heart, and I want her to eat it. That is why I am taking you."

"Friend, it is good that you told me," the Bodhisatta replied. "If our hearts were inside our bodies, they would be crushed to pieces as we jump among the treetops."

"Where then do you keep them?" the crocodile asked.

The Bodhisatta, pointing to a nearby fig tree (udumbara) laden with clusters of ripe fruit, said, "Look, our hearts are hanging on that fig tree."

"If you give me your heart, I will not kill you," said the crocodile.

"In that case, take me there. I will give you the heart hanging on the tree," the Bodhisatta replied. The crocodile took him and went to that fig tree.

The Bodhisatta jumped from the crocodile's back, sat on the fig tree, and said, "Friend, you foolish crocodile! You thought that the hearts of these creatures are kept on treetops. You are a fool! I have deceived you. Let your fruits be yours alone. Your body is large, but you have no wisdom." To illustrate this point, he uttered these verses:

115. "Enough for me are those mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits that are on the other side of the sea; better for me is this fig tree."

116. "Great indeed is your body, but your wisdom is not proportional to it. Crocodile, you have been deceived by me; go now as you please."

(Explanation of the verses: *Susumāra* means crocodile. *Samuddassa* means of the Ganges. *Yāni* refers to the mangoes and other fruits seen by you. *Alaṃ* means I have no need for them. *Udumbara* means the fig tree is better for me. *Bondi* means body. *Tadūpikā* means wisdom that is suitable or proportional to that body is absent. *Yathāsukhaṃ gaccha* means go now as you please, for you have no way to obtain my heart.)

The crocodile, feeling miserable and dejected like one who had lost a thousand pieces of gold, went back to his own dwelling place.

**The Identification of the Jātaka**
Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, the female crocodile was Ciñcamāṇavikā, and the monkey king was I myself."

## Wisdom alone should be relied upon greatly in all matters.

End of the Susumāra Jātaka.

## 9. Kukkuṭa Jātaka

## The Hunter and the Wild Fowl

The Present Story: While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who teaches the world including the devas, told this Kukkuṭa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Diṭṭhā mayā vane rukkhā," concerning a young monk who was a co-resident (saddhivihārika) of the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.

That young monk was said to be skilled in the matter of protecting his own body. Fearing that "happiness may not come to my body," he did not use anything too cold or too hot. Fearing that "the body might be fatigued by cold or heat," he did not go outside. He did not eat rice that was too soft or undercooked, and so on. His skill in protecting his body became well-known in the midst of the Saṅgha.

The monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, it is said that a young monk of such-and-such a name is skilled in the matter of protecting his body." The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what purpose are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such-and-such a purpose," He said, "Monks, not only now is this young monk skilled in the matter of protecting his body; in the past also, he was indeed skilled." Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest region. At that time, a certain bird hunter took a decoy cock, a hair-rope snare, and a pole, and while trapping fowls in the forest, he endeavored to trap an old fowl that had fled and entered the forest.

Because of its skill regarding hair-snares, that fowl did not allow itself to be caught, but kept flying up and perching elsewhere. The hunter covered himself with branches and tender leaves and repeatedly set the pole and the snare. The fowl, wishing to put the hunter to shame, uttered human speech and said:

Having spoken thus, the fowl fled and went elsewhere. When the fowl had fled, the hunter said:

Having said this, the hunter wandered through the forest, took whatever he could get, and returned to his home.

[Jataka Connection] The Blessed One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jataka: "Monks, at that time, the hunter was Devadatta, the young monk skilled in guarding himself was the cock, and I myself was the tree deity who witnessed the event mentioned."

## Guard yourself well in all things, and danger will not approach.

The Kukkuṭa Jātaka ends.

## 10. Kandagalaka Jātaka

## The Woodpecker

[Present Story] The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Kandagalaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ambho ko nāma yaṃ rukkho," concerning the imitation of the Buddha.

To elaborate: The Buddha heard that Devadatta was imitating the Buddha and said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta met with destruction by imitating me; he also met with it in the past." Then he related the past story.

[Past Story] Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a woodpecker in the Himālaya region. His name was Khadiravaniya. He found his food in the acacia (khadira) forest. This Khadiravaniya had a friend named Kandagalaka. That Kandagalaka found his food in a forest of silk-cotton and kimsuka trees. One day, he went to Khadiravaniya. Khadiravaniya, thinking "My friend has come," took Kandagalaka into the acacia forest, struck an acacia trunk with his beak, pulled out insects from the tree, and gave them to him. Kandagalaka ate them as if they were sweet cakes given to him day after day. While eating, pride arose in him: "He was born as a woodpecker, and so was I. Why should I take food given by him? I myself in the acacia forest..."

He uttered this first verse. 
O friend Khadiravaniya, in which tree, by pecking only once, the head is split? This tree with thorns and small leaves, what is its name?

One day, that Kandagalaka went to Khadiravaniya. Khadiravaniya, thinking "My friend has come," called Kandagalaka and entered the Khadira forest. He pecked at a Khadira stump with his beak, pulled out insects from the Khadira tree, and gave them to Kandagalaka. Kandagalaka ate the insects given to him, one after another, as if they were sweet cakes.

While eating, pride arose in Kandagalaka. He thought: "This Khadiravaniya is a bird born of the woodpecker species, and I too am a bird born of the woodpecker species. What benefit is there for me in the food given by this Khadiravaniya? I will find food in the Khadira forest by myself." Having thought so, Kandagalaka said, "Friend, do not suffer for me; I myself will find food in the Khadira forest."

Then Khadiravaniya said to Kandagalaka, "Friend, you were born in a family that takes food from sapless trees in the Silk-cotton (Simbali) and Palibhaddaka forests. Those known as Khadira trees are naturally full of heartwood and are very hard. Do not desire to take food by yourself in this way."

Kandagalaka, thinking "Am I not a bird of the woodpecker species?", ignored Khadiravaniya's words, flew quickly, and struck the Khadira tree with his beak. At that very moment, Kandagalaka's beak broke. His eyes were on the verge of popping out. His head split. That Kandagalaka, unable to stay on the tree trunk, fell to the ground.

Hearing the words of Kandagalaka, Khadiravaniya—

O Kandagalaka! You, being a noble bird of such a nature, have indeed long wandered pecking in the sapless Silk-cotton and Palibhaddaka forests, among trees that are merely a collection of firewood. The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Kandagalaka was Devadatta, but Khadiravaniya was I myself."

## If one is over-conceited, one will face ruin and suffering.

The Kandagalaka Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Bīraṇatthambhavagga

## 1. Somadatta Jātaka

## The Brahmin who was afraid

While staying at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Somadatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Akāsi yoggaṃ," concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī.

To elaborate, that Lāḷudāyī was unable to complete even a single sentence when among two or three people. Being very bashful, when he intended to say one thing, he would say another. The monks sat in the Dhamma Hall discussing this matter concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī.

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit here now?" When they replied, "Venerable Sir, we are gathered to discuss this matter," the Buddha said, "Monks, Lāḷudāyī is not only bashful now; he was very bashful in the past as well," and he brought forth the story of the past.

In the past, monks, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a certain Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he studied the arts in Takkasilā. Returning home, he realized the poverty of his parents and, wishing to raise his family from a lowly state to a noble one, he took leave of his parents and went to Bārāṇasī to serve the king. The king grew fond of him.

At that time, the father of Somadatta, who made his living by plowing the field with two oxen, lost one of them. That brahmin approached the Bodhisatta and said, “Dear son, one ox is dead, and the work of plowing cannot proceed. Therefore, you ask the King for an ox.” The Bodhisatta said, “Father, it has not been long since I first saw the King. It is not yet proper for me to ask the King for an ox. You yourselves should ask.”

“Dear son, you do not know how much I suffer from shyness. It is true; I am unable to speak properly in the presence of two or three people. If I go to the King to ask for an ox, I might end up giving away this remaining ox as well before I return,” the brahmin said. The Bodhisatta said, “Father, let happen what may. I am unable to ask the King for an ox. However, I will train you.” The father replied, “If so, very well, train me.”

The Bodhisatta took his father to the cemetery named Vīraṇatthambhaka. He tied bundles of grass here and there, naming them, “This is the King, this is the Crown Prince, this is the General.” Showing them in order, he said, “Father, go to the King and say, ‘May you be victorious, Great King!’ and then recite this verse to ask for an ox.”

Thus, the brahmin practiced the verse for a full year. He then said to the Bodhisatta, “Dear son Somadatta, I have mastered the verse. Now I can speak it in anyone’s presence. Take me to the King.” The Bodhisatta said, “Very well, father,” and having him take a suitable gift, he led his father to the King.

The brahmin said, “May you be victorious, Great King!” and presented the gift. The King asked, “Somadatta, how is this brahmin related to you?” Somadatta replied, “He is my father, Great King.” The King asked, “For what purpose has he come?” At that moment, the brahmin, intending to ask for an ox...

## If one is very fearful, one tends to make mistakes; practice daily.

The Somadatta Jātaka ends.
