## 2. Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka
## The Brahmin Who Ate Leftovers
The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana monastery, told this Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Añño uparimo vaṇṇo', concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.
When the Teacher asked that monk, 'Is it true, monk, that I hear you are dissatisfied?', he replied, 'It is true, Lord.' When asked, 'Who made you dissatisfied?', he replied, 'Lord, my former wife made me dissatisfied.' Then the Teacher said, 'Monk, this woman only works for your harm; in the past, she even fed her lover's leftovers to her husband,' and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of acrobats (naṭa) who lived by wandering and begging for food. When he reached maturity, being poor and of unattractive appearance, he made his living by wandering and begging for food.
At that time, in a small village in the kingdom of Kāsi, the wife of a certain brahmin was immoral and of evil character. She committed adultery with a lover. One day, while the brahmin was away on some business, the lover watched for the moment and entered the house. After committing adultery with him, she said, 'Stay a moment, you shall go only after eating,' and she prepared a meal. Having served hot rice complete with soup and curry, she gave it to him, saying, 'You eat,' while she herself stood at the door watching for the brahmin's arrival. The Bodhisatta stood there, longing for a morsel of food at the place where the lover was eating.
At that moment, the brahmin was coming towards the house. Seeing the brahmin coming, the brahmin woman quickly entered and said, 'Get up, the brahmin is coming,' and she made the lover go down into the granary. When the brahmin had entered and sat down, she brought a wooden seat, gave him water to wash his hands, and having served hot rice on top of the cold rice that was the leftovers of the other man, she gave it to the brahmin.
The brahmin, putting his hand into the rice and seeing that it was hot on top and cold below, thought, 'This rice must be the leftovers of another person.' Having thought so, wishing to ask the brahmin woman—
154:
The brahmin woman, fearing that her deed would be revealed, remained silent even though the brahmin asked her repeatedly.
At that moment, the son of the acrobat thought, 'The man made to stay in the granary must be the lover; this brahmin must be the master of the house. The brahmin woman says nothing because she fears her deed will be made known. Now, I will reveal the deed committed by this woman and tell the brahmin about the lover being made to stay in the granary.'
Having thought so, that son of the acrobat, wishing to tell the whole story from the time the brahmin left the house—the lover's entry, the adultery, the eating of the rice, the brahmin woman's watching the road from the door, and the lover's descent into the granary—spoke this verse which completes the two:

4. I am an acrobat, sir, I have come here as a beggar.
This one who has gone down into the granary is the one you are looking for.

O venerable brahmin. I am an acrobat by birth. I have come to this place as a beggar seeking food. You are searching, thinking, 'Whose leftovers could this rice be?' This lover of the brahmin woman, who was eating this rice, has entered the granary out of fear of you. This is that very person.
'Take him by his topknot, pull him out of the granary, and discipline him so that he does not dare to commit such an evil deed again,' he said, and then departed. The brahmin also disciplined those two with threats and blows so that they would not dare to do such a thing again, and then he proceeded according to his karma.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). To identify the Jātaka: 'The former wife at that time was the brahmin woman, the dissatisfied monk was the brahmin, and I myself was the son of the acrobat.'

## Your former wife tempted you; in the past and now, she works for your harm.
The Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka is finished.
155:
## 3. Bharu Jātaka
## The King Who Took a Bribe
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Bharu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Isīnamantaraṃ katvā," concerning the King of Kosala.

To elaborate: The Blessed One and the community of monks (Saṅgha) received great gain and honor in the form of the four requisites. As a testimony to what I have said, what did He preach?

"At that time, the Blessed One was revered, honored, esteemed, worshipped, and respected; He was a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick. The community of monks was also revered... and were recipients of the requisites. However, the wandering ascetics of other sects were not revered, were not honored, were not esteemed, were not worshipped, and were not respected; those wandering ascetics were not recipients of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick."

Having thus lost their gain and honor, those sectarians met in secret day and night and consulted: "Sirs, since the time the ascetic Gotama appeared, we have lost our gain and honor. The ascetic Gotama has reached the pinnacle of gain, fame, and following. For what reason has this prosperity come to him?"

In their consultation, some of the other sectarians said: "Sirs, the ascetic Gotama lives in the best place in all of Jambudīpa, on the very head of the earth. Therefore, gain and honor arise for him." The rest said: "Sirs, that reason is valid. Let us also build a sectarian monastery in the precincts of Jetavana. In this way, we too shall have gain."

All of them reached a conclusion, saying, "So be it." They consulted further: "If we build the monastery without informing the King, the monks will prevent us. There is no one who will not break their word after receiving a bribe. Therefore, let us give a bribe to the King and take the site for the monastery." They asked their attendants, gave the King a gift of one hundred thousand, and said: "Great King, we will build a sectarian monastery in the precincts of Jetavana. If the monks come to you and say, 'We will not allow them to build it,' please do not give them an answer." Out of greed for the bribe, the King agreed, saying, "Very well."

Having won over the King, the sectarians summoned carpenters and began the work. There was a great noise. The Blessed One asked, "Ānanda, what is this loud and great noise?" Ānanda replied, "Venerable Sir, the sectarians of other sects are building a sectarian monastery in the precincts of Jetavana; that is the noise of the construction."

"Ānanda, that place is not suitable for a sectarian monastery. The sectarians desire loud noise; it is not possible to live with them," He said. He then assembled the community of monks and instructed: "Go, monks, inform the King and prevent the sectarians from building the monastery." The community of monks went and stood at the gate of the King's palace.
156:
Even though the King heard that the Saṅgha had arrived, he thought, "They must have come because of the sectarian monastery," and because he had taken the bribe, he had someone say, "The King is not in the palace." The monks returned and informed the Blessed One. Knowing that the King acted this way because of the bribe, the Blessed One sent the two Chief Disciples. Even though the King heard of the arrival of the two Chief Disciples, he had the same thing said. They too returned and informed the Blessed One.

The Blessed One thought, "Sāriputta, now the King will not be able to stay in the palace; he will have to come out." The next morning, He dressed himself, took His bowl and robe, and went to the gate of the King's palace with five hundred monks.

Hearing of this, the King descended from the palace, took the bowl, invited the Blessed One in, offered rice gruel and hard food to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat in a suitable place. Wishing to give the King a Dhamma discourse by way of another method, the Blessed One said: "Great King, in the past, kings took bribes, caused virtuous and moral people to quarrel with one another, and having lost sovereignty over their own country, they met with great destruction." At the request of the King of Kosala, He brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Great King, in the past, a king named Bharu reigned in the kingdom of Bharu. At that time, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic who was a teacher of a group, having attained the five mundane superknowledges and the eight attainments. After living for a long time in the Himalayan region, he descended from the Himalayas accompanied by five hundred ascetics to seek salt and acidic foods. In due course, he reached the city of Bharu. Having wandered for alms in that city, he went out of the city and sat at the foot of a banyan tree, rich in branches and foliage, near the North Gate. After finishing his meal, he took up residence right there at the foot of that tree.

While that group of ascetics was living there at the foot of the banyan tree, after half a month had passed, another teacher of a group with a following of five hundred arrived. Having wandered for alms in the city, he went out of the city and stayed at the South Gate, taking up residence at the foot of a similar banyan tree. Thus, both groups of ascetics lived there as long as they pleased and then returned to the Himalayas.

During the time they were gone, the banyan tree at the South Gate withered. When they returned the next time, they saw that their banyan tree was withered. After collecting alms and leaving the city, they went to the foot of the banyan tree near the North Gate, finished their meal, and took up residence at the foot of that banyan tree near the North Gate.
157:
5. Having caused a rift among the sages, King Bharu, so I have heard, was destroyed along with his kingdom and met with ruin.

6. Therefore, the wise do not praise following the path of bias (desire). One should speak words associated with truth, with a mind uncorrupted by defilements.

He preached these two verses.

Great King. In the past. King Bharu; this word. I. Have heard. That King Bharu. Sages; a rift. Having caused. With the people of the kingdom. Together. Being utterly destroyed. To ruin. Went.

Therefore. Following the path of bias (chandāgati) and so on. The wise. Do not praise. With a mind not destroyed by defilements. Associated with the truth. Words only. One should speak.

As for the other sages, they arrived later, wandered for alms in the city, went only to their own banyan tree, finished their meal, and resided there.

Those sages, thinking, "Is this your tree or our tree?", quarreled with one another depending on the tree. That quarrel became great. Some sages said, "You shall not have the place where we first resided." Some sages said, "We arrived here first at this time; you shall not have it." Thus, both groups of sages, quarreling and saying, "We alone are the owners, we alone are the owners," went to the royal palace for the sake of the foot of the tree.

The king made only the group of sages who resided there first the owners. The sages who came later thought, "We should not let ourselves be defeated by these sages now; we will make him give it to us," and looking with divine vision, they saw a chariot frame that was an accessory of a Universal Monarch. They brought it, gave it as a bribe to the king, and said, "Great King, make us the owners as well."

The king took the bribe and said, "Let both groups reside," thus making both groups the owners. The other sages then took out the wheels of that chariot frame, gave them as a bribe, and said, "Great King, make only us the owners." The king did as those sages said.

The group of sages thought, "We, who have renounced the world, abandoning both the objects of desire and the defilements of desire, have done what is improper by quarreling and giving bribes for the sake of the foot of a tree." Becoming remorseful, they fled quickly and went only to the Himavanta.

All the deities residing in the entire kingdom of Bharu gathered together and, becoming angry at King Bharu, thinking, "The king has done what is improper by causing the virtuous sages to quarrel," they caused the three-hundred-league kingdom of Bharu to be submerged in the ocean, making it a non-kingdom.

Thus, depending on one King Bharu, the inhabitants of the entire kingdom also met with destruction. The Blessed One, having brought this past story, and having become fully enlightened, said:

In that context, 'antaraṃ katvā' means creating a rift or opening through the power of bias (chandāgati). 'Bharu-rājā' means the king in the kingdom of Bharu. 'Iti me sutaṃ' means I have heard this before. 'Tasmā hi chandāgamanaṃ' means because King Bharu, having followed the path of bias, was destroyed along with his kingdom, therefore the wise do not praise following the path of bias. 'Aduṭṭhacitto' means having a mind uncorrupted by defilements. 'Bhāseyya giraṃ saccupasaṃhitaṃ' means one should speak words based only on reality, on benefit, and on reason. For those who, in that situation, spoke words associated with truth, protesting that it was improper for King Bharu to take bribes, the place where they stood is still known today as a thousand small islands in the Nāḷikera island region.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, said, "Great King, one should not be under the influence of bias; it is not proper to cause two groups of renunciants to quarrel," and he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I was the senior ascetic."

When the King had finished offering a meal to the Tathāgata and the Buddha had departed, the King sent men to destroy the monastery of the other heretics. The heretics became without a standing place.

## He who harms the virtuous, brings peril upon himself.

The Bharu Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Puṇṇanadī Jātaka
## The Chaplain and the King

Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, who is capable of disciplining the world including the devas, while residing at the Jetavana Monastery, preached this Puṇṇanadī Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Puṇṇanadīṃ yena ca peyyamāhu," concerning the Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-pāramī).

To elaborate on that: One day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks initiated a discussion concerning the wisdom of the Tathāgata: "Friends, the Fully Enlightened Buddha possesses great wisdom, wide wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, deep wisdom, and penetrating wisdom. He is endowed with wisdom in means (upāya-paññā)." Thus, they spoke concerning the wisdom of the Buddha.
160:
8. "When the King remembers me even to send crow's meat, how much more will he remember me when swans, cranes, and peacocks are brought to him? In this world, lack of mindfulness is evil; mindfulness is noble."

This verse was spoken to complete the two parts. 

When the King obtains crow's meat, he still remembers to send it to me. If swans, cranes, and peacocks were brought to him, why would he not remember to send them to me? He would certainly remember. In this world, lack of mindfulness is evil, while mindfulness is supreme.

Later, the King remembered the virtues of the Bodhisatta and thought, "It is not fitting for me to send someone to call my teacher. Instead, I will compose a verse, write it on a palm leaf, have crow's meat cooked, and wrap both the letter and the meat in a white cloth. I will seal it with the royal seal and send it. If the teacher is wise, he will read the letter, recognize the crow's meat, and come. If he is not wise, he will not come."

The King wrote this verse on a palm leaf and sent it to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta read the letter and, knowing that the King wished to see him, thought, "The King remembers me and desires my arrival; therefore, I shall go." He had his carriage prepared, went to see the King, and the King, being pleased, restored him to the position of chaplain (purohita).

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Ānanda, and the chaplain was I myself."

## The Bodhisatta, in his youth, flourished through the power of wisdom.

The Punnanadī Jātaka is concluded.

## 5. Kacchapa Jātaka
## The Swan and the Tortoise

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One who admonishes the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kacchapa Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Avadhī vata attānaṃ," concerning Kokālika.

The present story will become clear in the Mahātakkāri Jātaka. Specifically, at that time the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now has Kokālika been destroyed by his own speech; in the past also, he was destroyed by his own speech," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers. When he reached maturity, he became a minister who advised the King on matters of welfare and Dhamma. That King, however, was very talkative.
161:
When the King spoke, there was no opportunity for others to speak. The Bodhisatta, wishing to stop the King's talkativeness, went about looking for an opportunity.

At that time, a tortoise lived in a pond in the Himālaya region. Two young swans, while wandering for food, became acquainted with him. Having become close friends, one day the swans said to the tortoise, "Friend tortoise, we have a delightful dwelling place in a golden cave at the foot of Mount Cittakūṭa in the Himālayas. Come with us."

When the tortoise asked, "How can I go?", the swans replied, "We will take you, provided you can guard your mouth and not say anything to anyone." The tortoise said, "I will guard it, masters; please take me with you."

The swans agreed, made the tortoise bite the middle of a stick, and they themselves bit the two ends of the stick and flew into the sky. Seeing the tortoise being carried in this manner by the swans, some village boys cried out, "Two swans are carrying a tortoise with a stick!"

The tortoise wanted to say, "My friends are carrying me! You wicked boys, what is it to you if the swans carry me?" Because of the swift speed of the swans, by the time they reached the space above the royal palace in the city of Bārāṇasī, the tortoise let go of the stick from where he was biting it, fell from the sky, and split into two pieces. A great clamor arose: "A tortoise has fallen from the sky and split in two!"

The King, accompanied by the Bodhisatta and surrounded by a group of ministers, went to that place, saw the tortoise, and asked the Bodhisatta, "Wise one, how did this one fall?"

The Bodhisatta thought, "I have long desired to admonish the King and have been looking for a way. This tortoise must have made friends with the swans, and they must have made him bite a stick to take him to the Himālayas. Then, hearing someone's words and being unable to guard his mouth, he must have let go of the stick in an attempt to speak. Thus, falling from the sky, he must have met his end." Thinking thus, he said, "Yes, Great King, those who are talkative and speak without limit surely encounter such suffering," and he spoke these verses:

9. "The tortoise truly killed himself while uttering a word; though he held the wood well, he was killed by his own speech."

10. "Seeing this, O best of men of great energy, one should speak only skillful words and not excessively. Do you see the tortoise who has come to ruin through much speaking?"

That King Brahmadatta was indeed very talkative. When he spoke, there was no opportunity for others to speak. The Bodhisatta, wishing to restrain the King's talkativeness, had been searching for a reason.

At that time, a tortoise lived in a pond in the Himālaya region. Two young swans, while wandering for food, became acquainted with that tortoise. 

Those swans and the tortoise became firm friends. One day, they said to the tortoise, "Friend tortoise, we have a dwelling place in a golden cave on the plateau of Mount Cittakūṭa in the Himālayas. That place is delightful; come with us."

When the tortoise asked, "How can I go?", the swans said, "Friend, if you are able to guard your mouth, and if you will not say anything to anyone, we will take you and go." When the tortoise said, "Masters, I will guard it; please take me and go," the swans agreed, made the tortoise bite a stick, and they themselves bit the two ends of the stick and flew into the sky.

Village boys saw the tortoise being carried in that manner by the swans and said, "Two swans are carrying a tortoise with a stick."

The tortoise wanted to say, "My friends are carrying me; you wicked boys, what does it matter to you that the swans are carrying me?" Due to the swift speed of the swans, when they reached the area above the King's palace in the city of Bārāṇasī, he let go of the stick from his bite, fell from the sky, and split into two pieces. All at once, there was a great uproar: "The tortoise fell from the sky and split in two!"
162:
The King took the Bodhisatta and, surrounded by his ministers, went to that place. Seeing the tortoise, he asked the Bodhisatta, "Wise one, how did this tortoise fall?"

The Bodhisatta, wishing to admonish the King, had been investigating the matter for a long time. He replied, "Great King, this tortoise must have made friends with the swans. Those swans, intending to carry the tortoise to the Himavanta, had him bite a stick and flew into the sky. While they were flying, this tortoise must have heard someone's words and, because he did not guard his mouth, he wanted to say something and let go of the stick. Having let go, he fell from the sky and met his death."

Thinking thus, he said, "Great King, those who are harsh of speech and talk without limit reach such suffering."

The King, realizing "He speaks referring to me," said, "Wise one, you speak referring to us." The Bodhisatta made it clear, saying, "Great King, whether it be you or another, whoever speaks beyond measure without restraint meets such destruction." From then on, the King refrained from talking much and became a man of few words.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the tortoise was Kokālika, the two young swans were the two Chief Disciples (Sāriputta and Moggallāna), the King was Ānanda, and the wise minister was I myself."

## Guarded speech, if spoken, the speech itself kills

The Kacchapa Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Maccha Jātaka

## The Heat of the Male Fish

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the Omniscient Buddha who admonishes the world including the devas, told this Maccha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na māyamaggi tapati," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

To elaborate on that story: The Teacher asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher asked, "Who has made you dissatisfied?" The monk replied, "Bhante, my former wife has made me dissatisfied."
163:
Then the Teacher said to that monk, "Monk, this woman causes you harm. In the past, because of her, you were pierced with a spit and roasted on charcoal to be eaten, but you gained your life by relying on the wise," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the King's chaplain (purohita).

At that time, one day, fishermen hauled up a fish caught in their net and placed it on the hot sand. Intending to roast and eat the fish over charcoal, they sharpened a spit. The male fish, thinking of the female fish, lamented with these two verses:

11. "It is not this fire that burns me, nor the well-sharpened spit.
But that the female fish thinks of me: 'He has gone to another for pleasure.'

12. "The fire of passion burns me; it distresses my mind.
O fishermen, release me! Nowhere is one killed for desire."

(Gloss:) O fishermen, masters. This fire does not burn me. This well-sharpened spit also does not burn me. My mate, the female fish, will think: "That husband of mine, the male fish, has followed another female fish, delighting in the five cords of sensual pleasure." It is only that thought of the female fish that burns me.

That flame of passion, which is the attachment to the female fish, alone burns me. The mind associated with passion alone causes me distress. A being who longs for sensual pleasures is not killed at any time (by such means). O masters, fishermen, release me!

At that moment, the Bodhisatta reached the riverbank and, hearing the sound of the fish's lamentation, approached the fishermen and had the fish released.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, the former wife was the female fish, the dissatisfied monk was the male fish, and I myself was the chaplain."
164:
## Of all fires, the fire of lust is the hottest

The Maccha Jātaka is finished.

13. All the world was delighted.
Seggu, unskilled in the ways of the village.
What is this nature of yours today, maiden?
That you weep when seized in the forest.

He spoke this first verse.

Amma, mother (dear). Sabbo, all. Loko, beings. Etissā kāmasevanāya, in this indulgence of sensual pleasure. Attamano, delighted. Ahosi, was. Seggu, dear daughter Seggu. Tvaṃ pana, but you. Gāmadhammassa, in the practice of villagers. Akovidā, why are you unskilled? Tvaṃ, you. Pavane, in the forest. Mayā, by me. Santhavavasena, by the power of desiring intimacy. Gahitā, when the hand is held. Yaṃ parodasi, why do you weep? Ajja, now. Esa-eso, this nature of weeping. Tava, your. Dhammo, nature. Ko, what is it? Tvaṃ, you. Komārīnāma, are you not called a maiden?

## 7. Seggu Jātaka
## The Virtuous Maiden

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Seggu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sabbo loko," concerning a certain vegetable-seller lay disciple.

The present story is detailed in the Ekaka Nipāta. In this Duka Nipāta, the Buddha asked that lay disciple, "Lay disciple, have you come after a long time?" The lay disciple replied, "Venerable Sir, I have a daughter who always has a smiling face. I tested her and gave her to a young man of good family. Because of the wedding arrangements, I did not get the opportunity to come and see you."

Then the Buddha said, "Lay disciple, not only now is she virtuous; she was virtuous in the past as well. And you did not test her only now; you tested her in the past too." Having said this, at the request of the lay disciple, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree-deity. At that time, this very vegetable-seller, thinking "I will test my daughter," took her to the forest and, acting as if he were driven by lust, seized her by the hand.
165:
14. He who should be a refuge when touched by suffering,
That father of mine acts treacherously in the forest.
To whom shall I cry in the middle of the forest?
He who should be the protector acts with violence.

He spoke this verse which completes the two.

Tāta, father. Yo pitā, which father. Dukkha-phuṭṭhāya, when touched by suffering. Tāṇaṃ, a refuge. Bhaveyya, should be. Me, my. So pitā, that father. Vane, in the forest. Dubbhi, treachery against his own daughter. Karoti-kataṃ maññati, he thinks it is done. Sāhaṃ, that I. Vanassa, of the forest. Mazze, in the middle. Kassa, to whom. Tāṇaggahaṇatthāya, for the sake of taking refuge. Kandāmi, shall I cry? Yo pitā, which father. Tāyitā, should be the protector. So pitā, that father himself. Sahasaṃ, a violent act. Karoti, commits.

Then, to the daughter who was weeping, the father said—

Hearing those words, the maiden said, "Yes, father, I am indeed a maiden; I do not know what is called sexual intercourse," and weeping, she spoke—

That vegetable-seller lay disciple, having tested his daughter at that time, took her home, gave her to a young man, and went according to his karma.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and declared the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the vegetable-seller was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How did He identify the Jātaka? "Lay disciple, your daughter then was your daughter now. The father of the maiden then was the father of the maiden now. I myself was the tree-deity who witnessed that event." Thus He identified the Jātaka.

## A virtuous daughter, perfect in conduct, and well-disciplined

The Seggu Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka
## Mice Eat Iron, a Hawk Carries Off a Son

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Saṭhassa sāṭheyyamidaṃ," concerning a certain dishonest merchant.

To elaborate: two merchants living in Sāvatthī, one a dishonest merchant and the other a wise merchant, became friends. They filled five hundred carts with goods and traveled from the east to the west. Having traded and gained much profit, they returned to Sāvatthī. The wise merchant said to the dishonest merchant, "Friend, let us divide the goods."

The dishonest merchant thought, "This man is exhausted from sleeping uncomfortably and eating poor food for a long time. He will eat rich food at his home and die of indigestion. Then all these goods will be mine alone." Thinking thus, he delayed the time, saying, "Today the constellation is not good, the day is not good; we shall see tomorrow, we shall see the day after."
166:
At that time, the wise merchant pressured the dishonest merchant to divide [the goods]. Taking perfumes and flowers, he went to the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.

The Blessed One asked, "Lay follower, when did you arrive?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, it has been about half a month since I arrived." When asked, "Why did you delay so long before coming to the Buddha's presence?" he related the matter. The Blessed One said, "Lay follower, not only now is he dishonest; in the past, too, this merchant was dishonest." Being requested, he related the past story.

[Past Story] Lay follower, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of ministers. When he came of age, he became a judge-minister for King Brahmadatta.

At that time, there were two merchants who were friends, one living in a village and one in the city. The village merchant deposited five hundred iron plowshares with the city merchant. The city merchant sold those plowshares, took the money, and scattered mouse droppings in the place where the plowshares had been kept. Later, the village merchant came and said, "Give me my plowshares." The dishonest merchant said, "Your plowshares have been eaten by mice," and showed him the mouse droppings.

The village merchant said, "Let them be eaten; if mice have eaten them, what can be done?" Then, taking the dishonest merchant's son with him under the pretext of going to bathe, he left the boy at a friend's house, saying, "Do not let this boy go anywhere," and made him stay inside a room. After bathing, he returned to the dishonest merchant's house.
167:
The crooked merchant asked, "Where is my son?" The friend replied, "Friend, I left your son on the bank, and while I was diving into the water, a hawk came, seized your son with its talons, and flew into the sky. Although I clapped my hands and shouted, making an effort, I could not make it release him." The crooked merchant said, "You are telling a lie; there are no hawks capable of carrying off children."

"Friend, whether it is possible or not, a hawk has indeed carried off your son. What can I do?" said the other. The crooked merchant, threatening him, "Hey, you wicked thief! You kidnapper! Now I will take you to court and have you judged!" and went out. The village merchant said, "You are doing exactly what I wish," and went with him to the court.

The crooked merchant said to the Bodhisatta, "Lord, this man took my son and went to bathe. When I asked, 'Where is my son?' he said, 'A hawk carried him off.' Please judge my case."

The Bodhisatta asked the village merchant, "Friend, is it true?" The village merchant replied, "Lord, it is true. Lord, while I was taking the boy along, the fact that a hawk carried him off is indeed true." When the Bodhisatta said, "Friend, in this world, there are no hawks that can carry off children," the merchant replied:

"Lord, I too would like to ask you: if hawks cannot carry off children and fly into the sky, can mice eat iron plowshares?"

"What do you mean by this?" asked the Bodhisatta.

"Lord, I deposited five hundred iron plowshares at his house. This man said, 'Your plowshares were eaten by mice,' and showed me droppings, saying, 'These are the droppings of the mice that ate your plowshares.' Lord, if mice eat iron plowshares, then hawks will also carry off children. If they do not eat them, then hawks will not carry them off either. This man says, 'Your plowshares were eaten by mice.' Please determine whether they were eaten or not, and judge my case."

The Bodhisatta, realizing, "He must have thought, 'I will defeat the trickster by playing a counter-trick,'" said, "You have thought well," and spoke these two verses:

135. "A trick for a trickster is well-conceived here;
A cheat's own cheating is turned back on him.
If mice could indeed eat an iron plowshare,
Why would a hawk not carry off a child?

136. For a cheater, there are counter-cheaters;
For a deceiver, there is also deception.
O you who lost your son, give the plowshare to him who lost his plowshare;
Let not the one who lost his plowshare take away your son."

[Word-by-word explanation:]
Friend, you. Of the trickster, this trickery, is well-conceived. Of the crooked one, the counter-trick, is set like a trap. Plowshare, mice, if they could eat. Child, hawks, why, would they not carry off? They would certainly carry off.

Here in this world, of the crooked, there are counter-cheaters. Of the deceiver, a deceiver, there also is. O you who lost your son, to the one who lost his plowshare, the plowshare, give. The one who lost his plowshare, your, son, let him not take away.
168:
“Lord, if you give me my son, I will give you the plowshares,” said the man who lost his son. “Lord, if you give me my plowshares, I will give you the boy,” said the man who lost the plowshares. In this way, the one who lost his son received his son, and the one who lost the plowshares received his plowshares, and both of them went their ways according to their karma.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the dishonest merchant was the same dishonest merchant of today; the wise merchant was the same wise merchant of today; and I myself was the judge who decided the case.”

## If one acts deceitfully, a counterpart will appear.
The Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka is finished.

## 9. Garahita Jātaka
## Human Affairs, Monkey's Thoughts

The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana monastery, spoke this Garahita Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Hiraññaṃ me suvaṇṇaṃ me,” concerning a certain monk who was dissatisfied with the Dispensation.

This is the truth: that monk had no specific object of dissatisfaction. While he was living in a state of discontent, he was brought to the presence of the Buddha. When asked by the Buddha, “Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?” he replied, “It is true, Venerable Sir.” When asked, “For what reason?” he replied, “Venerable Sir, I am dissatisfied due to the power of defilements (kilesa).”

Then the Buddha said to that monk, “Monk, these defilements were censured by animals in the past. Why, having ordained in such a Dispensation, are you weary due to the power of defilements which are censured even by animals?” Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the monkey womb in the Himalayan region and lived there. A certain hunter caught that Bodhisatta monkey and brought him to the King.
169:
17. “Silver is mine, gold is mine,” this is the talk day and night
Of foolish humans who do not see the Noble Dhamma.

18. There are two householders in the house; one there is beardless,
With hanging breasts, braided hair, and pierced ears.
Bought with much wealth, she pierces that person with the spear of her tongue.

He spoke these verses:

Friends! Of foolish humans who do not see the Dhamma of the Noble Ones like the Buddha—or rather, the faultless ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara dhamma)—their constant talk day and night is: “This is my silver (hirañña) that has been used; this is my gold (suvaṇṇa) that is yet to be used.” This is their only talk.

In a house, there are two householders. Among those two householders, one householder has no beard or whiskers, has long hanging breasts, has hair braided in various distinct ways, and has pierced ears. Bought from parents with much wealth and brought home, that householder pierces the people, such as servants and workers, with the spear of her tongue, saying, “Hey, you useless servant, should you not be doing your work?”

[The Past Story]: Monk, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the monkey womb in the Himalayan region and lived there. A certain hunter caught that Bodhisatta monkey, brought him, and presented him to the King. While that Bodhisatta monkey lived in the King’s palace for a long time, he became accomplished in conduct.

He knew the behaviors that occur in the human world. The King, being pleased with the Bodhisatta monkey because of his conduct, summoned the hunter and ordered, “Release this monkey in the very place where he was caught.” That hunter did as ordered.

The troop of monkeys, knowing that the Bodhisatta had returned, gathered on a large rock surface for the purpose of seeing the Bodhisatta. After exchanging pleasantries with the Bodhisatta, they asked, “Friend, where have you lived for so long?” When he said, “I lived in the King’s palace in Benares,” they asked, “How were you released from living in the King’s palace?” He replied, “The King made me a play-monkey, and being pleased with my conduct, he released me.”
170:
At that time, those monkeys said to the Bodhisatta: "You will know the behavior of humans in the world of men. Please tell us; we wish to hear it." When the Bodhisatta said, "Do not ask me about the behavior of humans," the monkeys insisted, "Please tell us; we wish to hear it."

The Bodhisatta said: "Friends, as for those called humans, whether they be kings or brahmins, they only say 'mine, mine.' Because of their unstable nature, they do not know the state of impermanence (anicca). Now, listen to the ways of these very foolish humans."

Having heard those words, all the monkeys said, "Do not speak! Do not speak! We have heard what should not be heard!" and they tightly closed their ears with both hands. They condemned that place, saying, "In this place, we have heard improper words," and went elsewhere. That stone slab became known as the "Despised Stone Slab" (Garahita-piṭṭhipāsāṇa).

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jataka. At the end of the Truths, the weary monk was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). As for the identification of the Jataka: "At that time, the assembly of monkeys was the Buddha's followers, and the Monkey King was I myself."

## My house, my home, my wealth; clinging to desire, they do not realize impermanence.

The Garahita Jataka is finished.

## 10. Dhammadhaja Jataka

## The Gardener with Four Qualities

The Fully Enlightened One, the Teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Veluvana Monastery, told this Dhammadhaja Jataka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sukhaṃ jīvitarūposi," concerning Devadatta's attempt to kill him.

To elaborate: At that time, the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has made an effort to kill me; in the past also, he made an effort to kill me. Even so, he was unable to cause even a tremor of fear." Having said this, he brought forth the past.
171:
The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, a king named Yasapāṇi reigned in Bārāṇasī. His commander-in-chief was named Kāḷaka. At that time, the Bodhisatta was the chaplain (purohita) to King Yasapāṇi, named Dhammadhaja. The barber who adorned the head of King Yasapāṇi was named Chattapāṇi. The king ruled righteously.

However, the commander-in-chief of King Yasapāṇi, when making judgments, would take bribes. That commander-in-chief, who "ate the flesh of others' backs" (was corrupt), took bribes and made those who were not the owners into owners.

Then one day, a man who lost his case at the judgment hall came out crying with his arms raised. Seeing the Bodhisatta going to attend upon the king, he fell at the Bodhisatta's feet and said, "Lord, while people like you who advise the king on his welfare and the Dhamma are present, Commander Kāḷaka takes bribes and makes owners of those who are not the owners." Thus he told the Bodhisatta of his loss.

The Bodhisatta, moved by compassion, said, "Come, friend, I will judge your case," and taking the man, went to the judgment hall. When a great crowd gathered, the Bodhisatta re-judged the case and made the rightful owner the owner. The sound of the people's applause was loud.

The king heard the sound of applause and asked, "What is this sound?" When told, "Great King, the wise Dhammadhaja has rightly judged a case that was wrongly judged; this is the sound of applause at the judgment hall," the king was pleased. He summoned the Bodhisatta and asked, "Teacher, is it true I hear that you have judged a case?"

When the Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, it is true; I judged a case that was wrongly judged by Kāḷaka," the king said, "From this day forward, you alone shall judge cases. It will be a pleasure to my ears and for the welfare of the people." Although the Bodhisatta was unwilling, the king entreated him, saying, "Out of compassion for beings, please sit in judgment," and made him accept. From that day on, the Bodhisatta sat in judgment and made only the rightful owners the owners.

From then on, Kāḷaka, no longer receiving bribes and losing his gains, bore a grudge against the Bodhisatta. He slandered the Bodhisatta to the king, saying, "Great King, the wise Dhammadhaja covets your kingship," thus creating a rift in the king's mind.

The king, disbelieving, rejected it, saying, "Do not say such a thing." But Kāḷaka said again, "Great King, if you do not believe my words, look through the window when Dhammadhaja arrives. When you look, you will see how he has brought the whole city into his hands." When the king saw the crowd of litigants with Dhammadhaja and thought they were his personal following, the bond of affection was broken. He asked, "Commander, what shall we do?"
172:
When the commander submitted, "Your Majesty, it is fitting to kill that Dhammaddhaja," the king said, "Without seeing a gross fault, how shall we kill him?" The commander replied, "Your Majesty, there is a stratagem." "What kind of stratagem?" the king asked. "Your Majesty, let us assign an impossible task to Dhammaddhaja. If he is unable to perform it, we shall kill him for that fault," he submitted. The king then asked, "What is this task that Dhammaddhaja would be unable to perform?"

"Your Majesty, a garden, even when planted in excellent soil and well-tended, yields fruit only after three or four years. Your Majesty, summon Dhammaddhaja and say, 'We wish to enjoy the garden tomorrow; create a garden for me.' He will not be able to create it. When he fails, we shall kill him for that fault," the commander submitted.

The king summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Wise One, we have played in the old garden for a long time. Now we wish to play in a new garden. We shall play tomorrow; create a garden for us. If you are unable to create it, your life shall be no more."

The Bodhisatta, realizing that the king's mind had been poisoned by Kāḷaka because he did not receive a bribe, said, "Your Majesty, if I am able, you shall know it." He then went home, ate a good meal, and lay down on his bed in thought.

Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. Upon reflecting, Sakka knew the Bodhisatta's mind. He came swiftly, entered the auspicious chamber, and standing in the air, asked, "Wise One, what are you thinking about?" When asked, "Who are you?" he replied, "I am Sakka."

"Sakka, the king told me to create a garden. I am thinking about how I shall create it." When he said this, Sakka replied, "Wise One, do not worry. I will create a garden for you similar to the Nandana and Cittalatā gardens. In which place shall I create it?" When the Bodhisatta said, "Create it in such-and-such a place," Sakka created it and returned to the celestial realm.

The next day, the Bodhisatta saw the garden with his own eyes, went to the king, and submitted, "Your Majesty, the garden is finished; please enjoy it." The king went and saw the garden, which was surrounded by a wall eighteen cubits high with the color of manosilā (cinnabar), complete with gates and watchtowers, and adorned with various trees laden with flowers and fruits. He then asked Kāḷaka, "Kāḷaka, the Wise One has done as we said. What shall we do now?"

Kāḷaka said, "Your Majesty, if he is able to create a garden in a single night, why would he not be able to take the kingdom?" When he said this, the king asked, "What shall we do now?" "Your Majesty, let us make the Wise One perform another impossible task," he submitted. "What kind of task shall we make him do?" the king asked.

"Your Majesty, have him create a lotus pond made of the seven jewels," he submitted. The king agreed, summoned the Bodhisatta, and said, "Teacher, you have created the garden. Now, create a lotus pond made of the seven jewels suitable for that garden. If you are unable to create it, your life shall be no more."
173:
The Bodhisatta said, "Very well, Your Majesty, if I am able, I shall create it." Then, for the sake of the Bodhisatta, Sakka created the lotus pond. When it was created, it was a pond reaching the height of perfection, with a hundred ghats, a thousand bends, covered with five-colored lotuses, and resembling the Nandā lotus pond.

The next day, the Bodhisatta saw that pond with his own eyes and submitted to the king, "Your Majesty, I have created the lotus pond." The king saw the pond and asked Kāḷaka, "Kāḷaka, what shall we do now?"

"Your Majesty, order him to create a house suitable for the garden," he submitted. The king said, "Teacher, create a house made entirely of ivory suitable for this garden and this pond. If you do not create it, your life shall be no more."

Then, for the sake of the Bodhisatta, Sakka created the house as well. The next day, the Bodhisatta saw it with his own eyes and submitted to the king. The king saw that house too and asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?" "Your Majesty, order him to create a jewel suitable for the house," he submitted.

The king summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Wise One, create a jewel suitable for this house made of ivory; we shall walk by the light of the jewel. If you are unable to create it, your life shall be no more." Then, for the sake of the Bodhisatta, Sakka created the jewel as well.

The next day, the Bodhisatta saw the jewel with his own eyes and submitted to the king. The king saw the jewel and asked Kāḷaka, "What shall we do now?"

"Your Majesty, it seems the brahmin Dhammaddhaja has a deity who gives him whatever he desires. Now, order him to do something that even a deity cannot create," he submitted. He continued, "Your Majesty, even deities cannot create a human being who is endowed with four factors. Therefore, say to him, 'Create for me a garden-guardian endowed with four factors.'"

The king summoned the Bodhisatta and said, "Teacher, you have created for us the garden, the lotus pond, the ivory palace, and the precious jewel to provide light for that palace. Now, create for me a garden-guardian endowed with four factors to guard the garden. If you do not create him, your life shall be no more."
174:
## 19. You appear to live a life of ease, yet from the realm to the trackless wild you've come. Alone at the foot of a tree, you meditate like one who is destitute.

He spoke this first verse.

Brahmin, you have a nature of living a long life in happiness. You have come from a place filled with people to a waterless forest. Sitting alone at the foot of a tree, like a lonely person, what are you thinking about?

## 20. I appear to live a life of ease, yet from the realm to the trackless wild I've come. Alone at the foot of a tree, I meditate like one who is destitute, reflecting on the Dhamma of the Good.

Whether it be so for the Bodhisatta, he thought, "I shall know the truth." He went home, ate excellent food, and upon sleeping, he woke at the break of dawn. Sitting on his bed, he reflected: "Sakka, King of Devas, is capable of creating that matter, and he has indeed created it. However, he is not able to create a park-keeper endowed with the four factors. Since he cannot create such a one, it is better to die in the forest without a protector than to die at the hands of others."

Having reflected thus, the Bodhisatta, without informing anyone, descended from the palace, left the city by the main gate, entered the forest, and sat at the foot of a tree, contemplating the nature of being unshaken when oppressed by the eight worldly conditions of the virtuous.

Sakka, knowing this reason, became like a forest hunter and approached the Bodhisatta. "Brahmin, you are of a delicate nature, yet you seem like one who has never seen suffering. Entering this forest, what are you doing as you sit here?" Desiring to ask this, he spoke.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse which completes the two:

Reflecting on the Dhamma of the Good.

Friend, I live as one who lives a life of ease. I have come from a place filled with people to a waterless forest. Sitting alone at the foot of a tree like a lonely person, I meditate, reflecting on the Dhamma of the Good—the nature of being unshaken when oppressed by the eight worldly conditions, which is the Dhamma of the virtuous ones known as the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and their disciples.
175:
Then Sakka said to the Bodhisatta, "Brahmin, while you are reflecting on the nature of the virtuous, why are you sitting in this place?"

"Friend, the King is having a gardener brought who is endowed with four qualities. I am unable to find such a gardener. I thought, 'What should I do by dying at the hands of another? I will enter the forest and die a helpless death.' Thus thinking, I came to this forest and sat here," the Bodhisatta replied.

"Brahmin, I am Sakka, the King of Devas. I have created the garden and other things for you. However, it is not possible to create a gardener endowed with the four qualities. Your king's barber, named Chattapāṇi, who arranges the king's hair, is endowed with these four qualities. If you have need of a gardener with the four qualities, tell the king to make this barber the gardener." Having given this advice to the Bodhisatta and comforted him saying, "Do not fear," Sakka returned to his own celestial city.

The Bodhisatta went home, and after eating his breakfast, went to the palace gate. Seeing Chattapāṇi there at the palace gate, he took him by the hand and asked, "Friend Chattapāṇi, is it true that you are endowed with the four qualities?"

When Chattapāṇi asked, "Who told you that I am endowed with the four qualities?" the Bodhisatta replied, "Sakka, the King of Devas, told me." When asked for what reason Sakka told him, the Bodhisatta explained everything. Chattapāṇi then said, "It is true, I am endowed with the four qualities."

Then the Bodhisatta took Chattapāṇi by the hand, went to the King, and said, "Great King, this Chattapāṇi is endowed with the four qualities. If you desire a gardener endowed with the four qualities, please make this Chattapāṇi the gardener."

Then the King asked Chattapāṇi, "Friend, are you endowed with the four qualities?" When he replied, "Yes, Great King," the King asked, "Friend, with which four qualities are you endowed?"

"I am not envious, O King; I do not drink intoxicants; I am without worldly affection, O King; and I am established in non-anger."

"That is true, Great King; I have no envy. I have never drunk liquor. I have never felt worldly affection or anger toward others. Thus, I am endowed with these four qualities."
176:
Where fools speak, those who are not bound become bound. Where the wise speak, even those who are bound are set free.

O King, because of a woman, I caused the chaplain to be bound. He informed me of the truth; therefore, I am free from envy.

At that time, the King asked, "O Chattapāṇi, do you say that you are one who is free from envy?" When Chattapāṇi replied, "Great King, it is true that I am one who is free from envy," the King asked, "Seeing what object did you become free from envy?" Chattapāṇi replied, "Great King, please listen," and wishing to explain the reason for his lack of envy, he recited this verse:

(a) O King, because of a woman, I caused the chaplain to be bound. He informed me of the truth; therefore, I am free from envy.

[The word-for-word meaning:] Rāja: Great King. Ahaṃ: I. Pubbe: in the past. Imasmiṃ Vārāṇasinagare: in this very city of Bārāṇasī. Having been a king, itthiyā kāraṇā: because of a woman, purohitaṃ: the chaplain, bandhāpesiṃ: I caused to be bound. So: that chaplain, maṃ: to me, atthe: the truths/benefits, nivedesi: informed. Tasmā: therefore, ahaṃ: I, anusuyako: am free from envy.

According to the method found in the Bandhanamokkha Jātaka, at another time, this Chattapāṇi was a king. Having become displeased with sixty-four courtiers who were constantly at his feet, he was incited by the Queen, who wished to destroy the Bodhisatta because he would not fulfill her heart's desire, and thus he had the Bodhisatta bound.

At that time, when the Bodhisatta was bound and brought before him, the Bodhisatta revealed the Queen's actual fault. When he himself was freed, he also secured the release of all the courtiers who had been bound by the King and advised, "Great King, forgive the offenses of these sixty-four courtiers and the Queen."

Everything should be understood in detail according to the method previously mentioned. Referring to that event, he said:

[Repeats the verse: "O King, because of a woman..."]

At that time, I thought: "Even though I abandoned sixteen thousand women and supported this one woman alone out of lust, I was unable to satisfy her. To be angry at such women, who are difficult to satisfy, is like being angry at one's clothes, saying 'Why are you dirty?' when they become soiled. It is like being angry at the rice one has eaten, saying 'Why have you turned into excrement?' when it becomes waste."

"From now on, for as long as I have not reached Arahatship, let no envy arise in me based on defilements." Thus I made a resolution. From that time on, I became one free from envy. Referring to this, he said, "Therefore, I am free from envy."

Then the King asked him, "Friend Chattapāṇi, seeing what object did you become a non-drinker of intoxicants?" Explaining that reason, he spoke this verse:
177:
(b) O Great King, being intoxicated, I ate my son’s flesh. Afflicted by grief for him, I have renounced the drinking of intoxicants.

[The word-for-word meaning:] Mahārāja: Great King. Ahaṃ: I, matto: being intoxicated, puttamaṃsāni: the flesh of my son, khādayiṃ: have eaten. Ahaṃ: I, tassa: for that deceased son, sokena: by grief and longing, phuṭṭho: being oppressed, majjapānaṃ: the drinking of intoxicants, vivajjayiṃ: have renounced.

Great King, in the past, I was such a King of Bārāṇasī and was unable to live without intoxicants. I was also unable to eat a meal that did not contain meat.

On Uposatha days in the city, he had the drum beaten to proclaim, "Let there be no slaughter of animals." The cook would take meat on the thirteenth day of the fortnight and store it. However, that poorly stored meat was eaten by dogs. On the Uposatha day, the cook, unable to find meat and not daring to serve the King a meal of various excellent flavors but without meat, went to the Queen and said, "Your Majesty, today I have no meat. I do not dare to serve a meal without meat. What shall I do?"

She said, "Friend cook, the King loves and cherishes my son; he is dear to him. Upon seeing my son, the King kisses and embraces him, losing all self-awareness. I shall adorn my son and have him sit on the King's lap. While the King is delighting and playing with the prince, you shall serve the meal."

Having said this, she adorned her son with ornaments and seated him on the King's lap. While the King was playing with his son, the cook served the meal.
178:
The queen spoke thus, adorned her son with elephant-ornaments, and placed him on the king's lap. While the king was playing and rejoicing with his son, the cook served the royal meal.

The king, being intoxicated with liquor and not seeing any meat in the meal-dish, asked, "Where is the meat?" When told, "Great King, today is the Uposatha day; because of the proclamation not to kill living beings, no meat was obtained," he said, "Is meat so hard to get for me?" He then twisted the neck of his beloved son sitting on his lap, ending his life, threw him before the cook, and said, "Prepare this quickly and bring it."

The cook did as the king commanded. The king ate the meal with his son's flesh. Out of fear of the king, there was not a single person capable of crying, shedding tears, or speaking out.

After eating, the king fell into a deep sleep on his bed. Waking up at dawn when the intoxication had cleared, he said, "Bring my son to me." At that time, the queen lay weeping at his feet. When he asked, "Lady, what is it?", she replied, "Great King, yesterday you killed your son and ate your meal with your son's flesh."

The king, overwhelmed with grief, wept with tears flowing and saw the fault in drinking liquor, thinking, "This suffering has come upon me because of drinking." He made a resolution: "From this day until I reach the fruit of Arahantship, I shall not drink such destructive liquor." He took some dust, wiped his face, and made the vow. From then on, he never drank intoxicants. Referring to this, he recited the verse beginning with: "Matto ahaṃ mahārāja" (I was drunk, O Great King).
179:
Then the king asked Chatta-pāṇi, "Friend Chatta-pāṇi, what object did you see that caused you to be without affection?" Chatta-pāṇi, wishing to explain the reason, recited this verse:

(c) I was once a king named Kitavāsa, O King; my son [insulted] a Paccekabuddha.
Having broken the bowl, he passed away; because of him, I am without affection.

Rāja, Great King. Ahaṃ, I. Pubbe, in the past. Bārāṇasiyaṃyeva, in the city of Bārāṇasī itself. Kitavāso nāma, named Kitavāsa. Rājā, was a king. Tadā, at that time. Me putto, my son. Paccekabodhi-paccekabodhissa, of the Paccekabuddha. Pattaṃ, the bowl. Bhinditvā, having broken. Cavito, passed away. Tassa kāraṇā, because of that son. Ahaṃ, I. Nissneho, have no affection.

The king, hearing this reason and being oppressed by the grief concerning his son, thought: "This grief of mine arose because of a beloved object. If affection did not exist, grief would not arise." Having thought so, he made a resolution: "From now on, let no affection for any object, whether animate or inanimate, arise in me." From that time on, he had no affection. Referring to that, he recited the verse beginning with "Kitavāso nāma".

Then the king asked Chatta-pāṇi, "Friend Chatta-pāṇi, what object did you see that caused you to be without anger?" Chatta-pāṇi, wishing to explain the reason, recited this verse:

(d) Having been Araka, I developed a mind of loving-kindness for seven years.
For seven aeons I lived in the Brahma world; therefore, I am without anger.

Mahārāja, Great King. Ahaṃ, I. Arako, an ascetic named Araka. Hutvā, having been. Satta vassāni, for seven years. Mettācittaṃ, a mind associated with loving-kindness. Bhāvayiṃ, developed. Bhāvetvā, because of developing it. Satta kappe, for seven aeons of dissolution and evolution. Brahmaloke, in the Brahma world. Vasiṃ, I lived. Tasmā, therefore. Ahaṃ, I. Akkodhano, am without anger.

When Chatta-pāṇi had thus spoken of his four qualities, the king gave a signal to the assembly by blinking his eyes and nodding his head.

At that very moment, the ministers, brahmins, householders, and others rose up and cried, "Hey, you bribe-taking thief! Not receiving a bribe, you slandered the wise man and wished to kill him!" They seized General Kāḷaka by his hands and feet, dragged him down from the palace, and with whatever stone clubs they could find, they split his head, ending his life. They then took him by his feet and dragged him to the refuse heap and threw him away. From that day on, the king ruled righteously and passed away according to his karma.
180:
Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, General Kāḷaka was Devadatta, the barber Chatta-pāṇi was Sāriputta, Sakka was Anuruddha, and Dhamma-dhaja was I myself."

## Evil intended for others often strikes oneself

The Dhamma-dhaja Jātaka is concluded.

## 8. Kāsāva Vagga

## 1. Kāsāva Jātaka

## The Elephant King and the Hunter

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kāsāva Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ", concerning Devadatta.

The story originated in the city of Rājagaha. At one time, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, was residing at Veḷuvana Monastery with five hundred monks. Devadatta was also residing at Gayāsīsa, surrounded by his own suitable following of immoral people.

At that time, the residents of Rājagaha collectively organized an alms-giving. Then, a merchant who had come for trade gave a very costly, fragrant saffron-colored robe-cloth, saying, "Please let me also have a share of the merit." The citizens conducted a great alms-giving. All the items for the alms-giving were completed using the coins collected through collective will. That fragrant robe-cloth remained as a surplus.

The people gathered and consulted: "This fragrant robe-cloth is a surplus. To which venerable one shall we offer it? Shall we offer it to Venerable Sāriputta, or shall we offer it to Venerable Devadatta?"
181:
## 1. He who, not free from stain, would don the saffron robe, devoid of self-control and truth, is not worthy of the saffron robe.

## 2. But he who has purged away all stain, is well-established in virtues, endowed with self-control and truth, he indeed is worthy of the saffron robe.

He spoke these two verses.

O man, he who is not free from the 1,500 defilements, who is devoid of 'Dama' (restraint of the senses) and 'Sacca' (the ultimate truth called Nibbāna, or the fourfold truth)—alternatively, 'Dama' as restraint of the senses and 'Sacca' as the fourfold truth—such a person who dons the saffron-dyed robe does not deserve to wear it.

But he who has vomited out the 1,500 defilements, who stands well-established in the virtues of the Path and Fruition as if carrying them well, and is endowed with restraint of the senses and the ultimate truth of Nibbāna, that person indeed deserves to wear the saffron robe.

In that assembly, some said, "We will give it to Elder Sāriputta." Others said, "Elder Sāriputta will stay for two or three days and then go as he pleases. But Lord Devadatta will always reside depending on our city. In life or death, Lord Devadatta alone will be our refuge. Let us give it to Devadatta." Although it was discussed many times, those who said "Let us give it to Devadatta" were in the majority.

Then, they gave that fine, fragrant cloth to Devadatta. He had the fringe cut, the edges folded and sewn, and had it dyed to a color like a gold plate, and wore it.

At that time, about thirty monks left Rājagaha and went to Sāvatthī. Having paid homage to the Teacher and exchanged pleasantries, they reported the matter: "Venerable Sir, in this way, Devadatta wears the robe which is the banner of the Arahants, though it is unsuitable for him."

The Teacher said, "Bhikkhus, not only now has Devadatta worn the banner of the Arahants which is unsuitable for him; he wore it in the past as well," and he brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Bhikkhus, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born among the elephant herd in the Himālaya region and lived in the deep forest.

At that time, a poor man living in Bārāṇasī saw ivory workers in the ivory-workers' street making ivory bangles and such. He asked, "Sirs, if you get tusks, will you take them?" The ivory workers said, "Yes, we will."

That poor man took a weapon, put on a saffron robe, took the appearance of a Paccekabuddha, covered his head, stood in the path of the elephants, killed an elephant with the weapon, took the tusks, and made a living by selling them in Bārāṇasī.

Later, he strove to kill the very last elephant among the elephants that were the followers of the Bodhisatta.
182:
When the elephants decreased day by day, they reported to the Bodhisatta, "For what reason are the elephants decreasing?"

While investigating, the Bodhisatta thought, "A man taking the appearance of a Paccekabuddha stands near the path where the elephants go. Does that man kill them? I will investigate him." One day, putting the follower elephants in front, he himself followed behind.

That man, seeing the Bodhisatta, took his weapon and ran forward. The Bodhisatta turned and looked, thinking, "I will strike him on the ground and kill him," and extended his trunk. Seeing the robes worn by that man, he thought, "It is proper for me to pay respect to this robe which is the banner of the Arahants," and withdrew his trunk. He said, "O man, is this robe, the banner of the Arahants, not unsuitable for you? Why do you wear that robe?"

Thus the Bodhisatta told this reason to that man and threatened him, "From today onwards, do not come to this place. If you come, your life shall not exist," and made him flee.

Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "Monks, at that time, the man who killed elephants was Devadatta. At that time, I myself was the leader of the elephant herd."

## Unsuitable for oneself, the right position, is not fit to speak of or use.

The Kāsāva Jātaka ends.
183:
## 2. Cūḷanandiya Jātaka
## The Merciless Brahmin
The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Cūḷanandiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Idaṃ tadācariyavaco,' while staying at Veluvana Monastery, concerning Devadatta.
To elaborate: one day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: 'Friends, Devadatta is harsh, cruel, and violent. He incited archers against the Blessed One, rolled a boulder, and released the elephant Nālāgiri. That Devadatta has not even a shred of patience, loving-kindness, or compassion for the Tathāgata.'
The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?' When they replied, 'It is such and such,' He said, 'Monks, not only now is Devadatta harsh, cruel, and merciless; in the past also, he was indeed harsh, cruel, and merciless.' Having said this, He brought forth the past.
The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a monkey named Mahānandiya in the Himālaya region. His younger brother was named Cūḷanandiya. These two brothers, with a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys, lived in the Himālaya region, taking care of their blind mother.
These two, Cūḷanandiya and Mahānandiya, would leave their mother in a thicket and enter the forest to send sweet and choice fruits to her. However, the monkeys who carried the fruits would not give them to her. The blind mother monkey, oppressed by hunger, became mere skin and bone, and grew emaciated.
Then the Bodhisatta said to his mother, 'Mother, we send you sweet and choice fruits of various kinds. Why are you so withered?' When she replied, 'Dear son, I do not receive them,' the Bodhisatta thought: 'While I am leading the troop, my mother will perish. I will abandon the troop and attend only to my mother.'
Having thought thus, the Bodhisatta called Cūḷanandiya and said, 'Dear brother, you lead the troop; I will attend to our mother.' Cūḷanandiya replied to the Bodhisatta, 'Brother, I have no business with leading the troop; I too will attend only to our mother.'
Thus, both brothers, being of one mind, abandoned the troop, took their mother, descended from the Himālayas, and lived by a banyan tree at the edge of the forest, attending to their mother.
At that time, a young Brahmin living in Bārāṇasī, having learned all the arts in the presence of a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā, asked permission from the teacher to depart. The teacher, through the power of physiognomy (aṅgavijjā), knew his harsh, cruel, and violent nature and
184:
advised him, saying, 'Dear son, you are harsh, cruel, and violent. For such people, things do not always go well; you will meet with great ruin and great suffering. Do not be harsh; do not perform deeds that cause remorse later,' and sent him away.
The young Brahmin, having paid homage to his teacher, went to Bārāṇasī and took up the life of a householder. Being unable to make a living through other arts, he thought, 'I will live by the bow; I will make a living by doing the work of a hunter.' He left Bārāṇasī, lived in a border village, and equipped with a bow and quiver, entered the forest. He made a living by killing various animals and selling their meat.
One day, having found nothing in the forest, he was returning when he saw a banyan tree standing at the edge of an open space. Thinking, 'Perhaps there might be something here,' he headed towards the banyan tree.
At that moment, the two monkey brothers, having fed their mother with fruits and placed her in front, were sitting within the fork of the branches. Seeing the hunter coming, they hid among the branches, wondering, 'What will he do to our mother?'
That violent man came to the foot of the banyan tree and, seeing their mother monkey, who was old, weak, and blind, thought, 'What is the use of me going back empty-handed? I will shoot this monkey and take her with me.' That cruel man took up his bow to shoot the mother monkey.
Seeing this, the Bodhisatta said, 'Dear Cūḷanandiya, this man wishes to shoot our mother. I will give the gift of my life (jīvitadāna) for her. After my death, you must take care of our mother.' Having said this, he came out from among the branches and said, 'O man, do not shoot my mother. She is blind, old, and weak. I give my life for her. Do not kill her; kill me instead.' Having obtained the man's promise, he sat down near the path of the arrow.
185: 3. This is that teacher's word, which Pārāsariya spoke: "Do not commit evil, which you would later regret." 4. Whatever deeds a man does, those he sees in himself. The doer of good receives good, and the doer of evil receives evil. As the seed is sown, so is the fruit reaped. These two verses are spoken together. O young man! Do not do evil. The evil done will burn you in the future. This word which the Brahmin Pārāsariya, who reflects and contemplates, once spoke—this word is the teacher's word. Whatever deeds a man does through the doors of body, speech, and mind, when he receives their result, he sees them in himself. Just as in the world, whatever kind of seed one sows, one reaps such a fruit; likewise, the doer of good deeds experiences good results, and the doer of evil deeds experiences evil results. That merciless man, having shot the Bodhisatta down, again drew his bow to shoot the Bodhisatta's mother. Seeing this, Cūḷanandiya thought, "This man wants to shoot my mother. If my mother lives for even one day, it is truly a gain of life. I shall give the gift of life (jīvitadāna) to my mother." He came out from among the branches and said, "O man, do not shoot my mother. I shall give the gift of life to her. Shoot me instead, take both of us brothers, and grant life to our mother." Having obtained the man's promise, he stood within range of the arrow. The man shot Cūḷanandiya down as well. Then, thinking, "This old female monkey will be for the children at home," he shot the mother of the two monkey brothers down too. Carrying the three monkeys on a shoulder pole, he headed toward his home. At that time, lightning struck that wicked man's house, burning his wife and two young sons along with the house. Only the pillar where the roof-bamboo was tied remained. Then, a man at the village gate saw him and told him the news. Overcome by grief for his wife and children, the man abandoned the shoulder pole with the meat and his bow right there. Casting off his clothes, he went naked, wailing with arms raised, and entered his house. Then, the roof-beams fell on the wicked man's head and split it. The earth opened up. Flames arose from Avīci. As he was being swallowed by the earth, he remembered his teacher's advice, crying out, "Indeed, seeing this consequence, my former teacher, the Brahmin, gave me advice." Wailing thus, he entered the earth and was reborn in the Great Hell of Avīci. The Teacher (the Buddha) said, "Monks, not only now is Devadatta harsh, cruel, and merciless; in the past too, he was harsh, cruel, and merciless." Having brought this Dhamma teaching, he identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the hunter was Devadatta, the world-renowned teacher was Sāriputta, Cūḷanandiya was Ānanda, the mother was Mahāpajāpati Gotamī, and Mahānandiya was I myself." ## As the cause, so the effect; the root is surely the deed. The Cūḷanandiya Jātaka is concluded.
