## 3. Puṭabhatta Jātaka
## The Husband and the Beloved Wife

### The Present Story
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Puṭabhatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Name namantassa bhaje bhajantaṃ," concerning a certain householder.

A certain householder living in Sāvatthī was engaged in a debt transaction with another householder living in the countryside. The householder from Sāvatthī took his wife and went to the presence of that debtor. The debtor said, "I am not yet able to pay," and gave nothing. The creditor became angry and left without eating his meal.

Then, seeing that man on the road with a very hungry body, some men traveling on the road gave him a food parcel (puṭabhatta), saying, "Give some to your wife as well and eat." The man took the food parcel, but not wishing to give any to his wife, he sent her away, saying, "Sister, this place is a haunt of thieves; you go on ahead." He then ate all the food, showed her the empty parcel, and said, "Sister, they gave only bad, empty food."

Knowing that the man had eaten it all by himself, the woman became dejected. As the two of them, husband and wife, were passing by the monastery behind Jetavana, they entered Jetavana Monastery, saying, "We shall drink some water."

The Blessed One, watching for the arrival of that couple, sat in the shade of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) like a hunter waiting on a path to catch a deer. When the couple saw the Blessed One, they approached, paid homage, and sat down. The Blessed One engaged in friendly conversation with the lay disciples and asked, "Laywoman, does this husband of yours desire your welfare or not?"

"Venerable Sir, I love this man very much, but this man has no love for me. Setting aside other days, even today on the road, he received a food parcel and ate it all himself without giving any to me," she replied.

"Laywoman, you always desire his welfare and love him dearly, but this man indeed has no love for you. However, in the past, when he relied on the wise and came to know your virtues, he once handed over the lordship of all his wealth to you," the Blessed One said, and being requested by the laywoman, he brought forth the past.

### The Past Story
Laywoman, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a minister's family. When he came of age, he became a minister who advised King Brahmadatta on matters of welfare and Dhamma.

At that time, the king, suspecting his son and thinking, "I do not know if this son of mine might wrong me," banished him. The prince took his wife and left the city. He lived in a village of farmers.

Later, the prince learned of his father's death and returned to Vārāṇasī to take the kingship that was his family's inheritance. On the way, he received a food parcel given with the instruction, "Give some to your wife as well and eat," but he ate it all himself without giving any to his wife. The woman became dejected, thinking, "How harsh and cruel this man is!"
187:
That prince took the kingship in the city of Bārāṇasī and placed his wife in the position of chief queen. Thinking that this much was enough for that woman, he did not provide any other gains, honors, or respect. He did not even ask her, "How are you faring?"

The Bodhisatta thought: "This queen has been very helpful to the king and is full of love for him, but the king does not think of her even a little. I will cause him to provide her with gains, honors, and respect."

Having reached maturity, the Bodhisatta approached the queen and performed his duties. When the queen asked, "My son, what is it?", he said, in order to start a conversation, "Queen, we serve you. Is it not proper to give even a piece of cloth or a morsel of food to the elderly parents?"

"My son, I do not receive anything for my own benefit. How shall I give to you? Did I not give when I received? Now, however, the king gives me nothing. Let alone other gifts, when he was coming to take the kingdom, he obtained a rice packet on the way and ate it all by himself without giving me even a little rice," she said.

"Mother, how is it? Would you be able to say this in the presence of the king?" he asked. "I would be able, my son," she replied. "If that is so, mother, say this today when I am standing in the presence of the king and ask you. Today I will make your virtues known," the Bodhisatta said. He then went ahead and stood in the presence of the king. The queen also went and stood near the king.

Then the Bodhisatta said to the queen, "Mother, you are exceedingly harsh. Is it not proper to give even a piece of cloth or a morsel of food to the fathers?" "My son, I myself receive nothing from the king. What shall I give to you?" she replied. "Did you not receive the position of chief queen?" he asked.

"My son, when there is no honor or respect, what will the position of chief queen do? Now, what will your king give to me? On the way, he obtained a rice packet and ate it all by himself without giving any of it to me," she said. The Bodhisatta asked, "Great King, is it true as I have heard?" The king remained silent in admission.

Knowing the king's admission, the Bodhisatta said, "Mother, if that is so, from the time the king has no love or respect, what is the use of your staying here? In the world, association with the unloved is suffering. If you stay here, the king will also have association with the unloved, and there will be suffering. These beings, knowing that they are not associated with, should go elsewhere. The dwelling place of humans is wide," and he spoke these verses:
188:
5. One should bow to him who bows; one should associate with him who associates;
One should do the business of him who performs one's own business.
One should do good for him who desires one's welfare;
One should not associate with him who does not associate.

6. One should abandon him who abandons; one should not have desire for him;
One should not associate with one whose heart is gone.
Just as a bird, knowing a tree is exhausted of fruit, looks for another,
So should one look for another place, for the world is large.

He spoke these two verses.

Mother. To one who bows to oneself. One should bow in return. To one who associates with oneself. One should associate. To one who performs one's own business. The business. One should perform. Of one who does not desire one's welfare. The business. One should not perform. Even with one who does not associate together. One should not associate.

One who abandons oneself. One should abandon. Attachment to one who abandons oneself. One should not have. With one whose heart is devoid of love. One should not associate. A bird. A tree. Thinking it is exhausted of fruit. Having known. To another tree. Just as it looks for. In the same way. To another place. One should look. It is true. This dwelling place of humans. Is very wide.

"You will find a man who is full of love," he said. Hearing these words, the King of Bārāṇasī gave all sovereignty to the queen. From then on, they lived in harmony and joy.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and illustrated the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the husband and wife were established in the fruit of Stream-entry. How was the Jātaka identified? "The husband and wife of that time have now become this husband and wife. I myself was the wise minister of that time." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## He does not love, you love; just find a new one like a bird.
The Puṭabhatta Jātaka ends.

## 4. Kumbhila Jātaka
## The Monkey and the Crocodile
The Present Account: While residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kumbhila Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yassete caturo dhammā," concerning Devadatta.

7. "He who has these four qualities, O Lord of Monkeys, just as you do:
Truth, Dhamma, Fortitude, and Generosity—he overcomes his enemy."
8. "He in whom these most excellent virtues are not found:
Truth, Dhamma, Fortitude, and Generosity—he does not overcome his enemy."

*Vānarinda*, O Lord of Monkeys. *Tava*, for you, the Lord of Monkeys. *Saccaṃ*, the truth of speech (vacī-sacca). *Dhammo*, wisdom (paññā). *Dhiti*, effort or energy (vīriya). *Cāgo*, generosity or relinquishment. *Iti*, thus. *Caturo*, four. *Dhammā*, qualities. *Santi yathā*, just as they exist. *Yassa*, for whomsoever. *Ete*, these four qualities. *Santi*, if they exist. *Tvaṃ*, you. *Maṃ*, me. *Ativattati yathā*, just as you are able to overcome. *So*, that person who possesses these four qualities. *Diṭṭhaṃ*, the enemy. *Ativattati*, is able to overcome.

*Paramabhaddaka*, O most excellent crocodile. *Yassa ca*, for whomsoever. *Saccaṃ*, the truth of speech. *Dhammo*, wisdom. *Dhiti*, effort. *Cāgo*, generosity. *Iti*, thus. *Ete guṇā*, these groups of qualities. *Na vijjanti*, do not exist. *So*, that person. *Diṭṭhaṃ*, the enemy. *Nātivattati*, cannot overcome.

In this Kumbhila Jātaka, all the remaining words along with the connection of the Jātaka should be understood in the same manner as stated in the previous Kumbhila (Susumāra) Jātaka.

## Truth, Wisdom, Effort, and Generosity: These four are the causes for victory over enemies.
The Kumbhila Jātaka ends.

9. "I have a man, O King, who is busy with all my affairs.
He has committed one offense; what do you think about that?"
Thus, he spoke this first verse.

*Deva*, O Great King. *Me*, for me. *Sabbakiccesu*, in all affairs. *Byāvaṭo*, one who exerts effort. *Puriso*, a man. *Atthi*, there is. *Tassa*, for that man. *Ekā*, one. *Aparādho*, the offense of committing adultery. *Atthi*, there is. *Tattha*, because of that offense of adultery. *Kinti*, what should be done. *Tvaṃ*, you, the Great King. *Maññasi*, what do you think?

## 5. Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka
## The Minister who committed Adultery
The Present Account: While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Atthi me puriso deva," concerning the King of Kosala.

In the palace of that King of Kosala, a very helpful minister committed an offense with a woman of the harem. Although the King knew, "This man is very helpful to me," he tolerated it and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "O Great King, ancient kings also tolerated in this way," and being requested by the King of Kosala, He brought forth the past.

The Past Account: O Great King, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a certain minister in the palace of King Brahmadatta committed an offense in the harem. A servant who served that minister also committed an offense in that minister's house.
190:
That minister, being unable to tolerate the offense of that man, took the man and went to the King. Desiring to ask, "O King, this man is a servant of mine who performs all my tasks, yet he has committed an offense in my house; what is proper to do to him?" he spoke the first verse (already mentioned).

Hearing those words, the King spoke this second verse to complete the pair:

10. "We also have such a man; he is found here.
A man endowed with good qualities is hard to find; therefore, patience is what we like."

*Bho amacca*, O minister. *Amhākampi*, for us also. *Ediso*, such a. *Puriso*, a man who commits adultery. *Atthi*, there is. *Ediso*, such a man. *Idha*, right here in this place. *Vijjati*, exists. *Aṅgasampanno*, a man endowed with virtues and good qualities. *Dullabho*, is hard to find. *Tena*, therefore. *Khanti*, only patience/forbearance. *Asmākaṃ*, by us. *Ruccati*, is liked.

That minister, realizing that the King was referring to him, did not dare to commit an offense in the harem from that time onwards. The man who served that minister also realized that the matter had been reported to the King, and from that time onwards, he did not dare to commit that act.

The Connection: Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."

That minister (of the present), realizing that the King of Kosala had reported the matter to the Buddha, did not dare to commit that act from that time onwards.

## When someone is helpful, one should surely be patient with them.
The Khantivaṇṇa Jātaka ends.

## 6. Kosiya Jātaka
## The Owl and the Crows
The Present Account: While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kosiya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kāle nikkhamanā sādhu," concerning the King of Kosala. The King of Kosala set out at an improper time to suppress a border rebellion. The story is the same as the method stated below.

The Buddha, however, brought forth the past and said: "O Great King, in the past, the King of Bārāṇasī set out at an improper time and established an encampment in the park. In that..."
191: 11. Going forth at the right time is good; going forth at the wrong time is not good. For by going forth at the wrong time, even a single person [among] many people illuminates no benefit, like the owl [attacked] by a flock of crows. 12. The wise one, knowing the rules and procedures, following the weaknesses of others, having subdued all enemies, would be happy like the [wise] owl. These two verses were spoken. Great King! Only at the right time is the effort to go forth good. At the wrong time, the effort to go forth is not good. For any man, by going forth at the wrong time, cannot make any benefit shine. On the contrary, even if he is alone, many enemies will surround him when he goes forth at the wrong time and bring him to great destruction. How is this? Just as a flock of crows pecks at an owl with their beaks. Great King! Just as a wise owl that goes forth only at the right time is happy, so too a wise person who knows the traditions and procedures established by the ancient sages, and who knows the lapses of others, having brought all enemies under his control, would be endowed with happiness. The King of Kosala went forth at the wrong time to suppress a border rebellion. The story is as previously mentioned. The Blessed One brought forth the past story and preached it. The Story of the Past: Great King, in the past, the King of Bārāṇasī went forth at the wrong time and stayed in a hut made of branches in the garden. At that time, an owl entered a bamboo thicket and hid. A flock of crows came and surrounded it, thinking, "We will catch it as soon as it comes out."
192:
That owl, without waiting for sunset, attempted to fly out at an improper time. At that moment, crows surrounded that owl, struck it with their beaks, and made it fall. The King called the Bodhisatta and asked, "Why do the wise crows make the owl fall?"

The Bodhisatta, wishing to show that those who leave their dwelling place at an improper time must surely suffer such misery, and that it is not suitable to leave one's dwelling at an improper time, said:

Having heard the words of the Bodhisatta, the King returned.

Identifying the Birth: Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Blessed One identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Ānanda was the King, and I myself was the wise minister."

## Exertion at the Improper Time Leads to Ruin
The Kosiya Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Gūthapāṇa Jātaka
## The Dung-beetle and the Noble Elephant

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Gūthapāṇa Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Sūro sūrena saṅgamma," concerning a certain obscure monk.

At that time, there was a market town about three gāvutas and a half-yojana away from Jetavana Monastery. In that market town, there were many offerings of food by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and food offered during the fortnightly phases of the moon (pakkhika-bhatta). A certain foolish man named Koṇḍa lived in that village.

That fool would ask questions to the young bhikkhus and novices who came for the sake of salāka-bhatta and pakkhika-bhatta. While some bhikkhus and novices were chewing, some drinking, and some eating, he would ask them questions, and when they were unable to answer, he would put them to shame. Out of fear of that fool, those bhikkhus and novices stopped going to that village for the sake of salāka-bhatta and pakkhika-bhatta.
193:
Then one day, a certain monk went to the place where meal-tickets were distributed and asked, "Venerables, is there ticket-food (salākabhatta) or fortnightly food (pakkhikabhatta) in such-and-such a village?" The monks replied, "Friend, there is. However, in that village, there is a fool named Koṇḍa who asks questions. He abuses and reviles any monk or novice who is unable to answer. Out of fear of that fool, no monk or novice dares to go there."

When this was said, the monk replied, "Venerables, please assign the meals in that village to me. I shall tame that fool and humble his pride. From that time onwards, I will make him flee as soon as he sees you."

The monks agreed, saying, "Very well," and assigned the meals in that village to him.

That monk went to the village and put on his robes at the village gate. Seeing the monk, the fool approached him quickly like a fierce goat and said, "Monk, answer my question!" The monk replied, "Lay follower, wait until I have walked for alms in the village, taken my rice gruel, and reached the refectory."

Even when the monk had taken the gruel and reached the refectory, the fool spoke in the same manner. The monk said to him, "Wait until I have finished drinking my gruel; wait until I have swept the refectory; wait until I have brought my ticket-food." After bringing the ticket-food, he made the fool carry his alms-bowl and said, "Come, I will answer your question when the time is right." He led him outside the village, folded his robe and placed it on his shoulder, then took the bowl from the fool's hand and stood there.

There too, the fool said to the monk, "Monk, answer my question!" Then the monk said, "I will answer your question," and with a single blow, he knocked him down. He beat him as if crushing his bones, put excrement into his mouth, and threatened him, saying, "From this day forth, if you ask any monk who comes to this village a question, you shall know what follows!" and then he departed. From that time on, the fool would flee as soon as he saw monks.

Later, that monk's action became known among the Saṅgha. One day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, they say such-and-such a monk went and put excrement into the fool's mouth."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that this monk has made that fool eat excrement; he did so in the past as well," and he related the story of the past.

In the past, when the people of Aṅga and Magadha were traveling to each other's countries, they stayed one day by a pond on the boundary between the two countries. They drank liquor, ate fish and meat, and departed early in the morning after yoking their wagons. When they had gone, a dung-eating worm, drawn by the smell of the dung, came to the place where they had been drinking. Seeing the discarded liquor and being overcome by thirst, he drank it, became intoxicated, and climbed onto a pile of dung.
194:
As the worm climbed upon it, the moist dung sank slightly. The worm cried out, "The earth cannot support me!"

At that very moment, a noble elephant in rut arrived at that spot. Smelling the stench of the dung, he turned away in disgust. Seeing this, the dung-worm thought, "This elephant is fleeing out of fear of me. I should engage in battle with him." To challenge him, he spoke the first verse:

153. "A hero meeting a hero, the valiant striker,
Come, O Elephant, turn back! Why do you flee in fear?
Let the people of Aṅga and Magadha see
The prowess of both you and me."

[The meaning is:] "O Elephant! You are a hero, and I am a hero. Having met me, who am valiant in effort and capable of delivering blows, why do you go away without fighting? Surely, at least one blow should be exchanged. Therefore, come, O Elephant, turn back! Are you fleeing in fear, trembling at the thought of death? Let these people of Aṅga and Magadha, who live along this boundary, see our prowess—the valor of both of us."

The elephant listened and, hearing the worm's words, turned back and approached him. Desiring to rebuke the worm, he spoke the second verse:

154. "I will not kill you with my feet, nor with my tusks, nor with my trunk;
I shall kill you with dung; let the filthy be slain by the filthy."

[The meaning is:] "I will not kill you with my feet and so on. Instead, I will kill you with dung, which is suitable for you."

Having said, "Let the foul dung-worm be killed by foulness," the elephant dropped a large bolus of dung on the worm's head, urinated on it, and thus brought the worm's life to an end right there. Then, trumpeting like a heron, he entered the forest.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, identified the birth: "At that time, the fool was the dung-worm, the monk was the noble elephant, and I myself was the deity living in that forest grove who witnessed the event."

## Do not compete with those who are not your match; you will meet with immediate danger.

End of the Gūthapāṇa Jātaka.
195:
## 8. Kāmanīta Jātaka
## The Greedy King
The Perfectly Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kāmanīta Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Tayo giriṃ," concerning a brahmin named Kāmanīta.

The stories of the present and the past will become clear in the Kāma Jātaka of the Dvādasakanipāta.

Specifically, of those two princes, the elder prince arrived and became the King in Bārāṇasī. The younger prince became the Viceroy (Uparāja). Among those two, the King and the Viceroy, the King was insatiable in both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma), and was greedy for wealth.

At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become Sakka, the King of Gods, while surveying Jambudīpa, recognized the King's insatiability in both types of sensuality. Thinking, "I will humble this King and make him feel ashamed," he approached the King in the guise of a young brahmin and saw him.

When the King asked, "Young man, for what purpose have you come?", he replied, "Great King, I have seen three kingdoms that are secure, prosperous, and filled with many elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, wealth, gold, silver, and ornaments. Moreover, those three kingdoms can be captured with only a small force. I have come to capture those three kingdoms and give them to you, Great King."

When asked, "Young man, when shall we go?", he replied, "Tomorrow, Great King." "In that case, go for now, and return early," the King said. Sakka replied, "Very well, Great King, prepare the army quickly," and then returned to his own place in Tāvatiṃsa.
196:
155. I desire the three mountains and the land between them,
The Pañcālas, the Kurus, and the Kekakas.
I desire, O Brahmin, even more than that;
Cure me, O Brahmin, who am led by desire (Kāmanīta).

Thus, he spoke this first verse.

Brāhmaṇa: O Brahmin. Tayo giriṃ: the three cities which are like mountains because they are difficult to shake. Pañcālā: the Northern Pañcāla kingdom. Kuruyo: the Kuru kingdom. Kekake ca: the Kekaka kingdom. Iti: thus. Antarañca: and the land between the three kingdoms. Kāmayāmi: I desire. Brāhmaṇa: O Brahmin. Tatuttariṃpi: I desire even the three kingdoms that are beyond this kingship of Bārāṇasī. Brāhmaṇa: O Brahmin. Kāmanītaṃ: me, who am oppressed by objective and subjective sensuality. Sace sakkosi: if you are able to cure. Tikiccha: cure me.

The next day, the King had the drum beaten, prepared the army, and summoned the ministers, saying, "Yesterday, a young brahmin came and said he would capture and give me the sovereignty of these three cities: the city of Northern Pañcāla, the city of Indapatta, and the city of Kekaka. Let us take that young man and capture the three kingdoms; go and call him quickly." When they asked, "Great King, where was a residence provided for that young man?", the King replied, "I did not have a house provided for him." When they asked, "Were provisions and clothing given?", he said, "Those were not given either." When they asked, "In that case, where shall we find him?", he said, "Look in the city streets." After looking and not seeing him, they said, "Great King, we do not see him."

When he did not see the young man, a great sorrow arose in the King, thinking, "I have fallen away from such great wealth and power." His heart-base (hadayavatthu) became hot. His heart's blood became disordered. Dysentery (passing of blood) occurred. Physicians were unable to cure him.

Then, after three or four days had passed, Sakka, upon reflecting, knew of the King's illness and thought, "I will cure him." He came in the guise of a brahmin, stood at the door, and sent word: "A brahmin physician has come to cure the Great King."

Hearing this, the King said, "Even very great royal physicians were unable to cure me; give this physician provisions and send him away." Hearing this, Sakka said, "I have no need for clothing or provisions, nor will I take a medical fee. I will cure him; let the King see me once more." Hearing this, the King said, "In that case, let him come." Sakka entered, wished him victory, and stood in a suitable place.
197:
16. Some treat one bitten by a black snake.
The wise treat one possessed by a non-human spirit.
But no one treats one led away by desire.
For what cure is there for one who has fallen away from purity?

He spoke this stanza which completes the two [previous ones].

Great King! Some wise men perform medical treatment for a person bitten by snakes of black hue. Some wise men perform treatment for a person possessed by a demon (amanussa). No one can perform treatment for a person oppressed by desire. For what reason can they not? Because, for a person who has entered into unwholesome states (okkantasukka), how can one cure them with mantras, medicines, and the like? Therefore, no one performs medical treatment for a person oppressed by desire.

The King asked, "Will you treat me?" When [Sakka] said, "Great King, I will treat you," the King said, "If so, then treat me." [Sakka] said, "Great King, very well. Now describe the symptoms of the illness. For what reason did it occur? Did it occur depending on food or drink? Or else, did it occur depending on seeing or hearing?" The Brahmin said, "O Brahmin, my illness occurred depending on what was heard (suta)."

[Sakka] asked, "Great King, what did you hear?" The King replied, "A young man came and said he would take and give me the sovereignty over three kingdoms. I did not have him given a place to stay or provisions. That young man, being angry with me, will go to the presence of another king. If he goes thus, I shall fall from such great wealth and power. Thinking thus, this illness occurred in me. If you are indeed able to treat the illness born of my mind associated with greed, then cure it." To clarify this meaning:

Then Sakka, the King of Devas, said to that King, "Great King, you cannot be cured with roots and such; you must be cured only with the medicine of wisdom (ñāṇosadha)."

Thus the Bodhisatta, having shown this reason to the King, further said: "Great King, if you were to obtain those three kingdoms, while ruling in these four cities, would you wear four pairs of garments at the same time? Would you eat from four golden plates at the same time? Would you sleep on four noble couches at the same time? Great King, it is not proper to follow the will of craving.

That which is called craving is the root of ruin. When that craving increases, it causes sorrow to grow. It casts the person who is the locus of that craving into the eight great hells, the sixteen Ussada hells, and various other states of deprivation (apāya) excluding the hells."

In this way, the Bodhisatta, having threatened the King with the terrors of hell and so forth, preached this Dhamma. The King, having heard the Dhamma of the Bodhisatta, became free from sorrow and at that very moment attained the state of being free from disease. Sakka also gave admonition to the King, established him in the precepts, and went to the celestial realm.
198:
From that time on, the King performed meritorious deeds such as giving and went according to his kamma.

Identifying the Jātaka: The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said, "Monks, the one who was the Brahmin Kāmanīta at that time was the King, and I myself was Sakka at that time."

## Sunk in the Mire of Craving, Disease Arises, Roots Cannot Cure

The Kāmanīta Jātaka is finished.

## 9. Palāyita Jātaka

## The Fleeing King

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Palāyita Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Gajaggameghehi," concerning a fleeing wandering ascetic (paribbājaka).

That paribbājaka, for the sake of debating, traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Finding no opponent, he eventually reached the city of Sāvatthī and asked the people, "Is there anyone capable of debating with me?"

The people spoke of the Buddha's virtues: "There is the Great Gotama, the All-Knowing One, who is capable of debating even with a thousand such as you. He is the supreme among bipeds, the Lord of Dhamma, and the crusher of others' doctrines. There is no one in the whole of Jambudīpa capable of surpassing the Blessed One's doctrine. Just as waves vanish upon reaching the shore, all doctrines are crushed to pieces upon reaching the feet of the Blessed One."

The paribbājaka asked, "Where is he now?" Hearing "At Jetavana," he said, "Now I will challenge him to a debate." Surrounded by a great crowd, while going to Jetavana, he saw the gatehouse of Jetavana built by Prince Jeta at the cost of ninety million. He asked, "Is this the palace where the ascetic Gotama lives?" Hearing "This is the gatehouse," he said, "If the gatehouse is like this, what will the dwelling house be like?" When told, "The Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) is immeasurable," he fled from that very spot. The people, making a great noise, entered Jetavana. When asked by the Teacher, "Why have you come at an improper time?" they told him the news. The Teacher said, "Lay followers, not only now, but in the past too, he fled upon seeing the gatehouse of my dwelling place." Having been requested by them, he brought forth the past.
199:
"With various sounds, resounding with elephants.
Today a tumultuous noise occurs, like
lightning from a thundering rain-cloud."
This refers to the combination of these two verses.

O sirs! With elephants like clouds, trumpeting like cranes and intoxicated; with noble warriors riding horses of the Sindh breed; with infantrymen holding jeweled swords and striking firmly from side to side; with those raining down a shower of arrows as if from a thick rain-cloud; with chariot-warriors like the surging waves of the ocean; surround the city of Takkasilā from all sides. Do so quickly, in such a manner that it is completely surrounded.

O sirs! Run forward and approach. With noble elephants, make various sounds—shouting, roaring, and music. Today, let there be a tumultuous noise like thunder. Just as lightning streaks from the mouth of a thundering cloud, so you, moving about, surround the city of Takkasilā and capture the king.

Prince Jeta spent nine crores of wealth to build the gateway of the Jetavana Monastery. Upon seeing it, an ascetic asked, "Is this the dwelling of the ascetic Gotama?" When told it was only the gateway, he thought, "If the gateway is like this, what must the dwelling be like?" When told the Gandhakuṭi was incomparable, he thought, "Who can compete with such monks?" and fled from that spot.

People followed him, shouting, and entered Jetavana. When the Buddha asked why they came at an improper time, they explained the matter.

The Buddha said, "Lay followers, this ascetic did not flee only now upon seeing the gateway of my dwelling; in the past, he also fled upon seeing the gateway of my dwelling." At their request, he told the story of the past.

In the past, the Bodhisatta reigned in Takkasilā in the kingdom of Gandhāra. King Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī.

King Brahmadatta went with a large army to take Takkasilā. Standing not far from the city, he organized his troops, saying, "Send the elephants in this manner, the horses in this manner, the chariots in this manner, and the infantry in this manner. Run and strike with weapons; rain down a shower of arrows like a thick rain-cloud." He then spoke these verses:

17. "With elephants like clouds, with horses like garlands,
With chariots like waves, with a rain of arrows.
With infantry striking firmly with swords,
Takkasilā is surrounded on all sides.

18. Run forward and approach..."
200:
"...lightning streaks from the mouth of a thundering cloud; thus moving about, surround the city and take the kingdom," he said.

Thus the king, having roared and organized his army, approached the city gate. Seeing the gatehouse, he asked, "Is this the king's palace?" When told, "This is only the city gatehouse," he said, "If the city gatehouse is already like this, what must the king's palace be like?" Hearing that it was like the Vejayanta Palace, he thought, "We will not be able to fight with a king possessed of such glory and wealth." Just by seeing the gatehouse, he turned back, fled, and went quickly to Bārāṇasī.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the fleeing ascetic was the King of Bārāṇasī, and I myself was the King of Takkasilā."

## Incomparable, All-Surpassing, None Can Rival
The Palāyita Jātaka is finished.

## 10. Dutiya Palāyita Jātaka
## Two Kings in Conflict
The Buddha, the Teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Dutiya Palāyita Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Dhaja-maparimitaṃ," concerning the same fleeing ascetic.

In this story, the ascetic entered Jetavana. At that moment, the Buddha, surrounded by a great multitude, was seated on the decorated preaching throne, preaching the Dhamma like a young lion roaring on a plateau of realgar.
201:
19. Immeasurable are the banners, infinite in extent,
Difficult to overcome, like the ocean by crows.
Like a mountain by the wind, I am difficult to shake;
Today, I am such, difficult to overcome.

He spoke this first verse. 

'On the chariots, having placed peacock feathers, the raised banners (dhaja) are immeasurable and many, numbering in the hundreds. Infinite in extent (anantapāraṃ) means my army—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—is beyond the limit of counting. Difficult to overcome (duppasahaṃ) means it is impossible for enemies to endure or conquer. Like what? Like the ocean by crows (dhankehi sāgaraṃva); just as the ocean is difficult to overcome by many crows, whether by its speed or its vastness, so is this army. Like a mountain by the wind (girimiva anilena); furthermore, just as a mountain is difficult to shake by the wind, so is this army difficult to be shaken by another army. Today, I am such, difficult to overcome (duppasaho ahamajja tādiseṇa); I, who am endowed with this army, am difficult to overcome today.' He said this referring to the Bodhisatta who was standing on the watchtower.

20. Do not lament in folly, for it is not so,
You are burning, yet you find no restrainer.
You approach like a lone elephant,
Who will crush you like a reed with his foot.

He spoke this verse which completes the pair.

'Hey fool (hare bāla), do not lament (mā vilapi) your own foolishness. Truly (hi-saccaṃ), your army is not as you imagine (tādiseṇa). You are merely burning (viḍayhase) with the heat of passion, hatred, and so on. You do not find a restrainer (nisedhakaṃ) like me who can conquer and stop you. Approach (āsajjasi)! Just as a lone elephant (ekacārī gajo) crushes a reed (naḷaṃ) with its feet (pādā), so will this King of Bārāṇasī crush you (pothayissati).'

The wanderer, seeing the Buddha's body which was like that of Mahābrahmā and endowed with the ten powers, his face as beautiful as the full moon, and his forehead like a golden plate, thought, 'Who could possibly conquer such a Great Man?' and fled without entering the assembly.

The people followed the wanderer and returned to report the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, 'Lay disciples, it is not only now that he has fled upon seeing my golden-hued face; in the past too, he fled upon seeing my golden-hued face.' Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when the Bodhisatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a King of Gandhāra was reigning in the city of Takkasilā. That King of Gandhāra came with a fourfold army to take Bārāṇasī. Surrounding the city and standing near the city gate, he looked at his army and, wishing to praise his own forces, said, 'Who will be able to conquer an army of such magnitude?'
202:
'Today, I will make you flee by the same path you came.' He threatened him, saying, 'Approach! Just as a rutting elephant crushes a reed bed with its feet, so will I destroy your entire army.'

Hearing the words of the Bodhisatta who was threatening him thus, the King of Gandhāra looked up and saw the Great Forehead like a golden plate. Fearing he would be captured, he turned back and fled to his own city.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the fleeing wanderer was the King of Gandhāra, and I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī.'

## With a brave and firm posture, victory is certain.
The Second Palāyita Jātaka ends.

## 9. Upāhana Vagga
## 1. Upāhana Jātaka
## The Disciple who Competes with the Teacher

The Teacher, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Upāhana Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Yathāpi kītā', concerning Devadatta.

To elaborate: In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: 'Friends, Devadatta, having renounced his teacher, the Buddha, became an opponent and enemy of the Tathāgata and met with great destruction.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?' When they replied, 'With such a subject,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta has renounced me, his teacher, and become an opponent, meeting with great destruction; in the past too, he met with the same.' Having said this, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of elephant trainers. When he came of age, he attained mastery in the elephant craft. Then, a young man living in a village of Kāsī came and learned the craft from the Bodhisatta.
203:
'In the past too, he met with destruction,' he said, and brought forth the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of elephant trainers and, upon reaching maturity, achieved perfection in the elephant craft. Then, a young man from a village in Kāsī came and learned the craft in the presence of the Bodhisatta.

Those who are Bodhisattas, when they teach a craft, do not practice the 'teacher's fist' (withholding secrets). They teach everything without exception according to their own knowledge. Therefore, that young man learned the craft known by the Bodhisatta without remainder and said to the Bodhisatta, 'Teacher, I wish to serve the King.' The Bodhisatta said, 'Very well, my dear,' and went to inform the King.

How did he inform him? He said, 'Great King, my pupil wishes to serve Your Majesty.' The King said, 'Very well, let him serve.' 'In that case, please determine his remuneration,' the Bodhisatta requested. The King said, 'Your pupil shall not receive remuneration equal to yours. When you receive a hundred, your pupil shall receive fifty. When you receive two, your pupil shall receive one.' The Bodhisatta went home and informed his pupil of this matter. The pupil said, 'Teacher, I know the craft as well as you do. If I receive equal remuneration, I will serve. If not, I will not serve.' The Bodhisatta reported this to the King. The King said, 'If he is of equal rank to you and can demonstrate the craft as well as you, he shall receive equal pay.' The Bodhisatta informed him of this, and when the pupil said, 'Very well, I will demonstrate it,' he informed the King. The King said, 'Then demonstrate the craft tomorrow.' 'Very well, we shall demonstrate it; let the drum be beaten throughout the city.' The King had the drum beaten, announcing: 'Tomorrow, it is said, both the teacher and the pupil will demonstrate the elephant craft. Let those who wish to see gather in the palace courtyard.'

The teacher, thinking, 'My pupil does not know my skill in means (upāyakosalla),' took one elephant and, in a single night, trained it to act in reverse. He trained it so that when told 'Go,' it would back up; when told 'Back up,' it would go; when told 'Stand,' it would lie down; when told 'Lie down,' it would stand; when told 'Take,' it would drop; and when told 'Drop,' it would take. The next day, he mounted that elephant and went to the palace courtyard. The pupil also mounted a beautiful elephant. A great crowd gathered. Both demonstrated their craft equally. Then the Bodhisatta, his own...
204:
1. Just as a shoe purchased for a man,
To bring him comfort, might cause him pain.
Oppressed by heat and squeezed by the sole,
It bites the very feet of that man.

2. Even so, an ignoble person of low birth,
Who receives knowledge and learning from a teacher.
He destroys himself right there with that learning;
Such an ignoble one is called "one like a bad shoe."

This refers to the collection of these two verses.

"Mahārāja," Great King. "Sukhassa," for the sake of happiness. "Kītā," bought. "Pādesu," on the feet. "Paṭimukkā," worn. "Upāhanā," a poorly made shoe. "Purisassa," of a man. "Dukkhaṃ," suffering. "Udabbahe," would bring. "Ghammābhitattā," because of being oppressed by heat. "Talasā ca," and by the surface of the sole. "Papīḷitā," being pained. "Kītā," bought. "Pādesu," on the feet. "Paṭimukkā," worn. "Upahanā," shoes. "Tasseva purisassa," of that very man. "Pāde," the feet. "Khādare-khādantiyathā," just as they cause sores or bite.

"Evameva," in this very way. "Dukkulīno," of low birth. "Yo anariyo," which ignoble person. "Tammāka-tammākā," from the teacher who taught that craft. "Vijjañca," the craft. "Sutañca," and the learning. "Ādiya-ādiyati," learns. "Ādiya," having learned. "So," that ignoble person. "Tattha," in the presence of that teacher. "Sutena," through that learning. "Tameva," only himself. "Khādati," destroys. "So dukkulīno," that person of low birth. "Pānadūpamo," like a shoe that bites the feet. "Anariyo," an ignoble person. "Vuccati," is called. Alternatively—"Pānadūpamo," like a man with bad shoes that cut the feet. "Anariyo," an ignoble person. "Vuccati," is called.

The Bodhisatta went home and informed the student of the matter. The student said, "Teacher, I know the craft as well as you do. If I receive an equal share of provisions, I will serve; if not, I will not." The Bodhisatta informed the King of this. The King said, "If he wishes to take an equal reward, and if he is able to demonstrate a craft equal to yours, he shall receive equal provisions."

The Bodhisatta informed the student, and when the student said, "Very well, I will demonstrate," he informed the King. The King said, "In that case, demonstrate your craft tomorrow." When they agreed, the King ordered, "Let it be proclaimed by drum in the city." The King had the drum beaten, announcing: "Tomorrow, both the student and the teacher will demonstrate the elephant craft. Let those who wish to see gather at the palace courtyard."

The teacher, thinking, "My student does not know my skill in stratagems," took an elephant and in a single night taught it the reverse craft. When the Bodhisatta said "Go," the elephant was to retreat; when he said "Retreat," it was to run forward; when he said "Stand," it was to lie down; when he said "Lie down," it was to stand; when he said "Take," it was to drop; when he said "Drop," it was to take. Having trained it thus, he rode that elephant to the palace courtyard the next day. The student rode a pleasant-looking elephant. A great crowd gathered. Both teacher and student demonstrated equal craft.
205:
Then the Bodhisatta made his elephant perform the reverse craft. When that elephant was told "Go," it retreated. When told "Retreat," it ran forward. When told "Stand," it lay down. When told "Lie down," it stood up. When told "Take," it dropped it. When told "Drop," it took it.

The people said, "Hey, you malicious student! You compete with your teacher, not knowing your own measure, thinking you know the craft as well as your teacher!" and they struck him with clods of earth, sticks, and so on, causing him to meet his death right there in the middle of the arena.

The Bodhisatta dismounted from the elephant, approached the King, and said, "Great King, one learns a craft for the sake of one's own happiness. Even though one learns it for such happiness, for some, the craft they have learned brings only destruction, like a poorly made shoe."

The King was pleased and gave great wealth to the Bodhisatta.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the student was Devadatta, and I myself was the teacher."

## Challenging the Teacher, Acting in Opposition, the Foolish Meet Destruction

The Upāhana Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Vīṇāthūṇa Jātaka

## If there is a Hump, is it a Bull?

The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Vīṇāthūṇa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ekacintitoyamattho," concerning a certain young girl.

In the city of Sāvatthī, a certain merchant's daughter, seeing a lordly bull being honored in her house, asked her mother, "Mother, what is the name of this one who receives such honor?" "Dear daughter, the lordly bull is called an Usabha," she replied.

One day, while standing on the palace balcony and looking down at the middle of the road, that merchant's daughter saw a hunchback and thought, "Among cattle, the leader has a hump on his back. Among human leaders, there must also be such a hump. This man must be a 'bull-man' (purisūsabha) among humans. It is proper for me to be a handmaid at the feet of that bull-man."
206:
3. "This matter was thought of by you alone; the fool is no leader. Indeed, lady, you ought not to go with this crooked hunchback."

He spoke this first verse.

Dear daughter (Amma), this matter (attho) of such a nature was thought of (cintito) by you alone (eka). It will be so. The foolish (bālo) hunchback is not a leader (apariṇāyako). Lady (bhoti), you do not deserve (na arahesi) to unite (saṅgantuṃ) with the crooked (vāmena) hunchback (khujjena).

Having made a plan, that merchant's daughter sent a message: "The merchant's daughter wishes to go with you; go and wait at such-and-such a place." Having informed that hunchback, she took her precious belongings, descended from the palace in disguise, and fled with that hunchback. Later, that matter became known among the townspeople and the community of monks.

In the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, they say the daughter of such-and-such a merchant has fled with a hunchback." The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "Bhante, we are gathered for such a discussion," the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now has she desired a hunchback; in the past too, she desired one." Then he brought up the past.

Story of the Past: In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family in a certain market town. Having reached maturity and living as a householder, he had sons. For the sake of his son, he asked for the hand of the daughter of a Bārāṇasī merchant and fixed the day.

The merchant's daughter, seeing the honor and respect shown to a bull-king (usabha) in her own house, asked, "What is this called?" Hearing it was a "bull-king," and seeing a hunchback walking in the middle of the street, she thought, "This man must be a bull among men (purisūsabha)." Taking her precious belongings, she fled with that hunchback.
207:
4. "Thinking him a bull among men, I loved the hunchback. Now he lies curled up like a lute with broken strings."

She spoke this second verse which completes the pair.

Noble sir (Ayya), I (ahaṃ), seeing a bull (ekaṃ usabhaṃ), [noted that] on the back of the chief of cattle there is a hump (kakudhaṃ). This man also has that hump. This man must be a bull among men (purisūsabha). Thus, thinking the hunchback to be a bull among men, I loved him. Now this hunchback lies curled up (saṃkuṭito) like a lute (vīṇā) with broken strings (chinnatanti).

The Bodhisatta, intending to bring the merchant's daughter home, was traveling to Bārāṇasī with a large retinue and took that very road. Both the merchant's daughter and the hunchback had traveled the road all night.

Then, in the body of the hunchback who had not slept all night, at dawn, the wind humor was disturbed. Severe pains arose. That hunchback, reaching severe pain, lay curled up like a lute with broken strings and crooked bones. The merchant's daughter sat at the feet of that hunchback. The Bodhisatta, seeing the merchant's daughter sitting at the hunchback's feet and recognizing her, approached and, wishing to speak with her—

Then, hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the merchant's daughter—

The Bodhisatta, knowing that she had left home due to her ignorance and lack of wisdom, had her bathed, placed her in an adorned carriage, and went to his home.

Identification of the Jātaka: The Blessed One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the merchant's daughter was the same merchant's daughter, and I myself was the merchant of Bārāṇasī."

## When one considers, wisdom may be absent and mistakes occur.

The Vīṇāthūṇa Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Vikaṇṇaka Jātaka
## The Barbed Arrow

Story of the Present: The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Vikaṇṇaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kāmaṃ yahiṃ icchasi tena gaccha," concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.

To elaborate: When that monk was brought to the Dhamma Hall, the Blessed One asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," and was asked "Why?", he said, "Because of the cause of sensual pleasures."

Then the Blessed One said, "Monk, these sensual pleasures are like barbed arrows (vikaṇṇaka). Once they find a place in the heart, they pierce like a barbed arrow. A barbed arrow once brought even a crocodile to death." Then he brought up the past.

Story of the Past: In the past, when the Bodhisatta was reigning righteously in Bārāṇasī, one day he went to the park and reached the edge of a lotus pond. Those skilled in dance and song were performing.
208:
5. Go wherever you wish, indeed;
You are pierced in a vital spot by a barb-less arrow.
You are killed by the food accompanied by the sound,
Greedy as you were, following the fish.

He spoke this first verse. 

Hey crocodile! Indeed, go to whatever place you wish to flee. You are pierced in a vital spot by a barb-less arrow. You were greedy and followed the fish that came to eat the rice. Therefore, by that rice accompanied by the well-beaten drum, you are killed.

In a pond, fish and turtles, due to their attachment to the sound of music, would gather and follow the King. Seeing a multitude of fish as large as plow-poles, the King asked his ministers, "Why are these fish following me?" The ministers replied, "Your Majesty, they are serving you."

The King, pleased that the fish were serving him, established a regular food supply for them. Every day, he had an ambaṇa of rice cooked. At feeding time, some fish came, while others did not. The food went to waste. This matter was reported to the King.

The King said, "From now on, at feeding time, beat the drum. When the fish gather at the signal of the drum, give them the food." From then on, the attendants beat the drum and gave food to the gathered fish. The fish also gathered and ate at the signal of the drum.

While they were gathering and eating in this way, a crocodile came and ate the fish. The attendant in charge of feeding reported this to the King. Hearing this, the King said, "When the crocodile is eating the fish, shoot it with a barb-less arrow and catch it."

The attendant agreed, went out on a boat, and shot the crocodile that had come to eat the fish with a barb-less arrow. The arrow entered the crocodile's back. Reaching a state of great pain, the crocodile fled with the arrow.

Knowing that the crocodile had been pierced by the arrow, the attendant called out to it—
209:
6. Thus, one who falls for worldly bait,
Following the whims of the mind, is afflicted.
He is destroyed in the midst of kinsmen and friends,

That crocodile went to its home and reached the end of its life. The Teacher, showing this reason, having become fully enlightened, spoke this second verse:

Like the crocodile that followed the fish.

Monks, just as that crocodile following the fish came to destruction, so too, a person who falls for the five cords of sensual pleasure, following the whims of the mind through the power of defilements, is afflicted in the midst of kinsmen and friends.

Identification of the Jātaka: Thus, the Teacher brought this Dhamma teaching, declared the Truths, and identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How was the Jātaka identified? At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, the fish were the Buddha's followers, and the King of Bārāṇasī was I myself. Thus, the Jātaka was identified.

## Avoid defilements like the barb-less arrow, and find happiness.
The Vikannaka Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Asitābhū Jātaka
## The King Who Followed

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Asitābhū Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Tvam eva dāni makara," concerning a certain young woman.

In Sāvatthī, in the household of a supporter of the two Chief Disciples, there was a young woman who was extremely beautiful and possessed great charm. When she reached marriageable age, she went to a family of equal status. Her husband, not cherishing her in the least, lived according to his whims with another woman.

That young woman, disregarding his disrespectful behavior towards her, invited the two Chief Disciples, gave alms, and upon hearing the Dhamma, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. From then on, spending her time in the bliss of the Path and Fruit, she thought, "My husband does not want me, and I have no need for household life; I will become a nun." She informed her parents, went forth, and attained Arahantship.
210:
Having reflected, she informed her parents, ordained, and attained Arahatship. Her action became well-known among the bhikkhus. Then one day, the bhikkhus started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the daughter of such-and-such a family, seeking her own welfare, realized her husband's lack of desire for her. After listening to the Dhamma from the Chief Disciples, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Again, she asked permission from her parents, ordained, and attained the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahatta-phala). Friends, that young lady truly seeks her own welfare."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such-and-such a discussion," He said, "Bhikkhus, not only now does this daughter of a good family seek her own welfare; in the past, she also sought her own welfare." Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, having entered the life of an ascetic, produced the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and dwelt in the Himalayan region. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, seeing the abundance of followers of his son, Prince Brahmadatta, became suspicious and banished his son from the kingdom.

That Prince Brahmadatta took his queen, named Asitābhū, entered the Himalayas, and lived in a leaf-hut, subsisting on fish, meat, and various wild fruits. The prince, seeing a Kinnarī, became infatuated and, thinking "I will make this Kinnarī my wife," he ignored Queen Asitābhū and followed the tracks of that Kinnarī. 

7. "You yourself have now done this, for desire for you has departed from me.
This [desire] is now without reconnection, like ivory severed by a saw."

She spoke this verse. 

"Noble Prince (Ayyaputta), now you yourself have caused this [attainment of] bliss of jhāna for me. Now, my desire and attachment for you have departed. Like ivory (renukaṃ) severed by a saw (khara-chinnaṃ), this attachment to you has no possibility of being rejoined."

That lady's conduct became well-known among the monks. Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, this daughter of a certain family is one who seeks her own benefit. Knowing her husband's lack of desire, she heard the Dhamma from the Chief Disciples, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry, asked her parents' permission again, ordained, and reached the Fruit of Arahatship. This young woman is truly a seeker of her own benefit."

The Blessed One came and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current meeting?" When they replied, "It is this subject," He said, "Monks, not only now is this daughter of a good family a seeker of benefit; in the past, she was also a seeker of benefit," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta entered the life of a hermit, developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and lived in the Himalayan region. At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, seeing the abundance of followers of his son, Prince Brahmadatta, became suspicious and banished his son from the country.

Prince Brahmadatta took his queen named Asitābhū, entered the Himalayas, and lived in a leaf-hut, eating fish, meat, and various fruits. Prince Brahmadatta saw a Kinnarī and, with a mind full of lust, thought, "I will make this Kinnarī my wife." Ignoring Queen Asitābhū, he followed the tracks of that Kinnarī.
211:
Queen Asitābhū, seeing Prince Brahmadatta following the Kinnarī, thought: "This prince ignores me and follows a Kinnarī. What benefit is there for me with this prince?" With a mind free from attachment, she approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and asked him to teach her the preliminary exercises for kasiṇa meditation. Practicing the kasiṇa, she produced the higher knowledges and meditative attainments. Having paid homage to the Bodhisatta, she returned and stood at the door of her leaf-hut.

Prince Brahmadatta, having wandered in pursuit of the Kinnarī and failing to see even her tracks, became despondent and returned toward the leaf-hut. Queen Asitābhū, seeing Prince Brahmadatta approaching, flew up into the air and, standing in the sky which had the color of a blue sapphire, said: "Noble Prince, because of you, I have obtained this bliss of jhāna."

Having said this, while Prince Brahmadatta was still watching, she flew away to another place. Prince Brahmadatta, lamenting at the time of Princess Asitābhū's departure, spoke this second verse which completes the pair:

8. "Through excessive desire, through extreme greed, and through the intoxication of extreme greed,
Thus one falls away from one's welfare, just as I [fell away] from Asitābhū."

"Just as I have fallen away from Princess Asitābhū, so too a person who, through the power of excessive desire (atricchā)—the endless craving for various objects—and through extreme greed (atilobha), and through the intoxication of extreme greed which produces manly pride, falls away from his own welfare (attha)."

King Brahmadatta lamented with this verse. He lived alone in the forest and, upon the death of his father, he went and took the kingship.

## From bad, one must strive to get good

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, these two people were the Prince and the Princess. As for the ascetic, I myself was he."

The Asitābhū Jātaka is finished.
212:
## 5. Vacchanakha Jātaka
## The Merchant Who Invited to Sensual Pleasures
The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Vacchanakha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sukhā gharā Vacchanakha," concerning the Malla named Roja.

That Malla named Roja was said to be a lay friend of Venerable Ānanda. One day, the Malla named Roja sent a message to Venerable Ānanda, asking him to come. Venerable Ānanda, having asked permission from the Buddha, went there.

The Malla named Roja served Venerable Ānanda with food of various flavors. While sitting in a suitable place, he exchanged pleasantries with the Elder and invited him to enjoy human prosperity and the five strands of sensual pleasure, saying: "Venerable Ānanda, I possess many animate and inanimate treasures. I shall divide these treasures in half and give them to you. Come, let us both live together in the house."

Venerable Ānanda spoke of the disadvantages of the strands of sensual pleasure to the Malla named Roja, rose from his seat, and returned to the monastery. When the Buddha asked, "Ānanda, did you see the Malla named Roja?", he replied, "Yes, Bhante, I did."

When asked, "What did you say to him?", he replied, "Bhante, the Malla named Roja invited me to the household life. Then, I told the Malla named Roja about the disadvantages of both the household life and the strands of sensual pleasure." The Buddha said, "Ānanda, it is not only now that the Malla named Roja has invited monks to the household life; he did so in the past as well." Having said this, being requested by the Elder, He brought forth the past.

**The Story of the Past:** Ānanda, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a certain market town. When he came of age, he took up the ascetic life and lived for a long time in the Himalayan region. He went to Bārāṇasī to seek salt and vinegar, stayed in the royal park, and entered Bārāṇasī the following day.

At that time, a merchant of Bārāṇasī, being pleased with the Bodhisatta's deportment, invited him to his house and fed him. Having obtained a promise to stay in the park, he looked after the Bodhisatta and had him reside in the park. The ascetic and the merchant developed a mutual affection.

Then one day, the merchant of Bārāṇasī, through the power of love and intimacy for the Bodhisatta, thought: "The ascetic life is indeed painful and wearying. I will make my friend, the wandering ascetic Vacchanakha, disrobe, divide all my wealth in half and give it to him, and we shall both live together in harmony."
213:
9. "Houses are pleasant, Vacchanakha, provided with wealth and food,
Where, having eaten and drunk, one may sleep without anxiety."

He spoke this first verse.

Vacchanakha, O Venerable Vacchanakha. *Yattha*: in that house which is complete with the seven kinds of treasures and edible food. *Anussuko*: without making an effort (without anxiety). *Bhutvā ca*: having eaten. *Pivitvā ca*: having drunk. *Sayeyyātha*: come and stay/sleep. *Sahiraññā*: complete with the seven kinds of treasures such as gold. *Sabhojanā*: complete with edible food. *Gharā*: living in a house is indeed *Sukhā*: pleasant.

10. "There is no home for one who does not strive, nor for one who does not tell lies.
There is no home for one who does not take up the rod or oppress others.
Who would enter a home that is thus full of flaws and difficult to maintain?"

He spoke this second verse which completes the pair.

*Mahāseṭṭhi*, Great Merchant. *Anīhamānassa*: for one who does not constantly strive in tasks such as plowing and cattle-herding. *Gharā*: what is called a home *Na tiṭṭhati*: cannot be established. *Musā abhaṇato*: for one who does not tell lies for the sake of fields, property, gold, silver, and so on. *Gharā*: what is called a home *Na tiṭṭhati*: cannot be established. *Nādinna-daṇḍassa*: for one who does not take up punishment. *Paresaṃ*: towards others. *Anikubbato*: for one who does not oppress. *Gharā*: what is called a home *Na tiṭṭhati*: cannot be established. *Evaṃ*: in this way. *Chiddaṃ*: having holes (flaws/vulnerabilities). *Durabhisambhavaṃ*: being difficult to achieve or maintain. *Gharaṃ*: a home. *Ko*: who *Paṭipajjati*: would want to rule and live in it?

After thinking this, the merchant of Bārāṇasī, one day at the end of the meal, exchanged sweet and pleasant words with the wandering ascetic Vacchanakha and said: "Venerable Vacchanakha, the ascetic life is painful and wearying. Living in a house is pleasant. Venerable Vacchanakha, come, let us both live together in harmony, enjoying the strands of sensual pleasure." Having said this—

Then, having heard the words of the merchant of Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta said: "Great Merchant, out of ignorance and being greedy for sensual pleasures, you speak of the virtues of household life. I shall tell you the disadvantages of the household life; listen now." Having said this—

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having spoken of the faults of household life, went back to the park.
214:
Conclusion of the Jātaka: Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the birth: "At that time, the Malla King named Roja was the Treasurer of Bārāṇasī. I myself was Vacchanakha the wandering ascetic."

## Effort, Falsehood, No Punishment, Cannot Establish a Home
The Vacchanakha Jātaka is finished.

11. Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhi, dijo kumudasannibho.
Vūpasantehi pakkhehi, mandamando va jhāyati.
He recited this first verse.

Friends (Bho). This bird (ayaṃ dijo), which has wings (pakkhi), and is like the color of a white lotus (kumudasannibho). With wings (pakkhehi) that are tranquil (vūpasantehi). How good indeed (bhaddako vata)! It meditates (jhāyati) as if very gently and softly (mandamando va).

12. Nāssa sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha.
Amhe dijo na pāleti, tena pakkhi na phandati.
He recited this verse which completes the pair.

Friends (Bho). You (tumhe) do not know (na vijānātha) the virtue (sīlaṃ) of that crane (assa). Without knowing (anaññāya), you praise it (pasaṃsatha). The crane bird (dijo) does not protect (na pāleti) us (amhe). Because of that lack of protection (tena), the crane (pakkhi) remains motionless (na phandati).

## 6. Baka Jātaka
## The Hypocritical Crane

Present Story: While the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Baka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhi," concerning a certain deceitful monk.

To elaborate on this: The Teacher, seeing the monk who had been brought, said, "Monks, this monk is not deceitful only now; in the past, this monk was also deceitful," and he brought forth the past.

Past Story: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a fish in a certain lake in the Himalayan region and lived there with a large retinue.

At that time, a certain crane, thinking "I will eat the fish," stood near the lake with its head lowered and wings spread, looking at the fish as if it were very gentle, waiting for the fish to become careless.

At that moment, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by a school of fish, reached that place while seeking food. The school of fish saw the crane and—

Then, the Bodhisatta looked at the crane and—

When this was said, the school of fish churned the water and fled.
215:
Conclusion of the Jātaka: Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the birth: "At that time, the deceitful monk was the crane. I myself was the King of Fish."

## Pretending to have practice, hypocritical virtue, like the crane
The Baka Jātaka is finished.

13. Ko nu kho bhagavā hetu, ekacce idha puggale.
Atīva hadayaṃ nibbāti, cittañcāpi pasīdati.
He recited this first verse.

Blessed One (Bhagavā). In this world (idha loke), towards some (ekacce) persons (puggale). Just by seeing them (diṭṭhamatteyeva), the heart (hadayaṃ) is exceedingly (atīva) peaceful (nibbāti). The mind also (cittañcāpi) gains confidence (pasīdati). What indeed (ko nu kho) is the cause (hetu)?

## 7. Sāketa Jātaka
## Love at First Sight

Present and Past Stories: While the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Sāketa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ko nu kho bhagavā hetu," concerning a Brahmin named Sāketa.

In this Sāketa Jātaka, the past and present stories have already been told below in the Ekanipāta. When the Teacher went to the monastery, the monks, wishing to ask, "Venerable Sir, for what reason does this thing called love establish itself?"—

Then, the Teacher, wishing to show the cause of love to those monks—

14. Pubbeva sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā.
Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodake.
He spoke this verse which completes the pair.
(In this verse, the two 'vā' sounds are shortened.)

Monks (Bhikkhave). Whether it is a lotus (uppalaṃ vā) or other (sesaṃ) water-born flowers (jalajapupphaṃ vā). In the water (udake).
216:
When it arises (jāyamānaṃ). Depending on (nissāya) these two causes (imāni dve kāraṇāni): water (udakañca) and mud (pallalañca). Just as it arises (jāyati yathā), so too (evaṃ tathā). That love (taṃ pemaṃ), when it arises (jāyamānaṃ). Because of having lived together (sannivāsena vā) in a previous life (pubbe), or because of doing a favor (paccuppannahitena vā) in the present life. It arises (jāyate) due to these two causes (imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi).

Conclusion of the Jātaka: Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the birth: "Monks, these two people were the Brahmin and the Brahmin lady at that time. I myself, the Buddha who has known all things without deviation, was the son at that time."

## Lived together before, doing favors, love fits, like water and lotus
The Sāketa Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Ekapada Jātaka
## The Problem of Prosperity

Present Story: While the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Ekapada Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ingha ekapadaṃ tāta," concerning a certain householder.

There was, it is said, a certain householder living in Sāvatthī. One day, his son, sitting on his lap, asked a question concerning the door to benefit (prosperity). The householder thought, "This question is within the Buddha's range; no one else will be able to answer it." He took his son, went to Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and said, "Venerable Sir, this child, while sitting on my lap, asked a question concerning the cause of attaining benefit. I, not knowing the answer, have come here. Please explain this question, Venerable Sir."
217:
15. "Please, dear father, tell me a single word that encompasses many meanings, by which we may achieve our goals." He spoke this first verse. Tāta, father. Iṅgha, I urge you. Yena, by which single word that depends on many benefits. Atthe, benefits. Mayaṃ, we. Sādhayemase, shall achieve. Anekatthapadasitaṃ, depending on a word that shows many causes and effects. Kiñci saṅgāhikaṃ, encompassing all benefits, whether few or many. Ekapadaṃ, a single word. Brūsi-brūhi, please tell.

16. "Skillfulness is that single word, dear son, which encompasses many meanings. When combined with virtue and perfected through patience, it is sufficient to bring happiness to friends and sorrow to enemies." He spoke this second verse to complete the answer. Tāta, dear son. Dakkheyyekapadaṃ, having a single word associated with wisdom, which is the state of one skilled in producing gain. Anekatthapadasitaṃ, depending on a word that shows many causes and effects. Taṃ, that effort. Sīlena, with virtue. Saññuttaṃ, when joined. Khantiyā, with patience. Upapāditaṃ, when perfected. Mitte, friends. Sukhāpetuṃ ca, for the sake of making them happy. Amittānaṃ, enemies. Dukhāya ca, for the sake of making them suffer. Alaṃ, it is capable.

"I do not know the answer to this problem, so I have come to the Blessed One. Please, Blessed One, solve this problem," he requested.

The Blessed One said, "Lay disciple, this youth did not seek his benefit only now; in the past also, he sought his benefit and asked the wise. The wise of old also answered him. Although he asked and they answered, he does not remember because of the covering of rebirth." Having said this, the Blessed One, being requested, brought the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family. When he came of age, his father passed away, and he received the position of merchant. At that time, the merchant's young son sat on his lap and, wishing to ask for a cause based on a single word that leads to benefit, said: [Verse 15].

Then the boy's father, wishing to answer, said: [Verse 16].

Thus the Bodhisatta answered the son's question. The son also achieved his own benefit by the method told by his father and passed away according to his kamma.

Identification of the Jātaka: The Blessed One, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, both the father and the son were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, this son was the son, and I myself was the merchant of Bārāṇasī." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Effort, wisdom, practicing virtue, and patience are the causes of happiness.

The Ekapada Jātaka is finished.
218:
17. "Though I am a venomous snake, I entered the mouth of the fish trap. Friend green frog, do you approve of the fish devouring me?" He spoke this first verse. Samma haritāmātā, friend green frog. Kumināmukhaṃ, into the mouth of the fish trap. Paviṭṭhaṃ, entered. Āsīvisampi, even the venomous snake. Santaṃ, being. Maṃ, me. Macchakā, the fish. Khādanti, devour. Te-tayā, you, friend. Yaṃ, that devouring. Ruccate, do you like it?

## 9. Haritamaṇḍūka Jātaka
## The Snake and the Green Frog

The Story of the Present: The All-Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Haritamaṇḍūka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Āsīvisampi maṃ santaṃ," while staying at the Jetavana monastery, concerning King Ajātasattu.

King Mahākosala, the father of King Kosala, when giving his daughter to King Bimbisāra, gave the small village named Kāsika for the sake of his daughter's bath-powder expenses. When King Ajātasattu committed the act of parricide, that queen died not long after due to her love for the King. Even after his mother died, King Ajātasattu continued to enjoy the revenues of that Kāsika village.

King Kosala, thinking "I will not give the village which is my family property to a parricidal thief," fought a war with King Ajātasattu. Sometimes the victory belonged to the uncle, and sometimes to the nephew. Whenever King Ajātasattu won, he would enter the city with great glory, raising a banner on his chariot in delight. But whenever he lost, he would enter the city in dejection, without letting anyone know.

Then one day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, King Ajātasattu is delighted when he defeats his uncle, but becomes dejected when he is defeated."

The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such," he said, "Monks, not only now does Ajātasattu feel delight when winning and dejection when losing; in the past also, he felt delight when winning and dejection when losing." Having said this, he brought the story of the past.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a green frog.
219:
18. A man plunders only as long as it serves his purpose. But when others plunder him, he, the plundered, is plundered in return.

This verse was spoken to complete the meaning of the two points.

"Friend water-snake, as long as a man's power (issariya) prospers and prevails, he continues to plunder others. But when others become powerful and plunder him, then that man, who was a plunderer of others, is destroyed by those others who have gained power."

At that time, people set fish-traps (kummīna) in various places such as rivers and streams to catch fish. Fish entered one of the traps. Then, a water-snake entered that trap, wishing to eat the fish.

Many fish united and bit the water-snake, making its whole body red with blood. Seeing no refuge and fearing death, the water-snake escaped through the mouth of the trap and lay at the water's edge, suffering great pain.

At that moment, a green frog hopped up and sat on the top of the trap. The water-snake, finding no resolution to its plight, saw the green frog sitting there and, wishing to ask if it approved of the fish's behavior, said:

Then the green frog said to the water-snake, "Friend snake, I do approve. Why? Because you eat the fish that come to your place, and the fish bite you who have come to their place. In one's own territory and feeding ground, no one is called weak. Therefore, I approve."

When the Bodhisatta thus decided that "the plunderer meets with destruction," the school of fish, realizing the water-snake's weakness and intending to catch their enemy, came out of the trap's mouth and bit the water-snake until it died right there.

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the water-snake was King Ajātasattu, and the green frog was I, the Buddha."

## When united with the same mind, the enemy is defeated and victory is achieved.

The Haritamaṇဍūka Jātaka ends.

## 10. Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka

## The Unrighteous King

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Sabbo jano,' concerning Devadatta.
220:
When Devadatta was swallowed by the earth at the gateway of Jetavana Monastery after nine months of harboring malice against the Buddha, those living in Jetavana and throughout the entire country were delighted, saying, "Devadatta, the thorn in the side of the Buddha, has been swallowed by the earth; now the Buddha is free from his enemy."

Having heard their words through successive reports, the hosts of yakkhas, terrestrial deities, and tree deities throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa were also delighted.
