Then one day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, when Devadatta was swallowed by the earth, the people were pleased, saying that Devadatta, the enemy of the Buddha, has been swallowed by the earth."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such," He said, "Monks, not only now do people rejoice and laugh when Devadatta dies; in the past also, they rejoiced and laughed when he died," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, a king named Mahāpiṅgala ruled unrighteously and unfairly. Performing evil deeds through the power of favoritism and such, he oppressed the people with punishments, taxes, forced labor, and the extraction of coins, like sugarcane being squeezed in a press. He was harsh, cruel, and violent; he did not have even a measure of compassion for others. He was unloved and disagreeable to the women in his house, his sons and daughters, and his ministers, brahmins, and householders. He was like dust fallen in the eye, like grit in a ball of rice, or like a thorn that has pierced and entered the heel.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of King Mahāpiṅgala. After ruling for a long time, Mahāpiṅgala passed away. When he died, the inhabitants of Bārāṇasī were delighted and laughed loudly. They cremated Mahāpiṅgala with a thousand cartloads of wood and extinguished the funeral pyre with many thousands of water jars. They then consecrated the Bodhisatta as king, and being delighted that they had obtained a righteous king, they held a festival in the city, beat the drums, decorated the city with raised flags and banners, and built pavilions at every gate. Sitting in the decorated pavilions with floors adorned with scattered parched rice and flowers, they ate and drank.

The Bodhisatta also sat in the middle of a magnificent throne under a raised white umbrella in the decorated palace, enjoying great glory. Ministers, brahmins, householders, country folk, and doorkeepers stood surrounding the king.

Then, a certain doorkeeper stood not far away, sighing deeply and weeping. Seeing that doorkeeper, the Bodhisatta thought, "When my father died, everyone else is wandering about playing and celebrating the festival in delight, but you are weeping."
221:
19. "All the people were oppressed by Piṅgala;
When he died, they experienced joy.
Was the yellow-eyed one dear to you?
Why do you weep, O doorkeeper?"

He spoke this first verse.

"Bho dvārapāla, O doorkeeper! By Piṅgala, King Piṅgala, all the people were oppressed. When that King Piṅgala died, all the people experienced joy. As for you, was King Piṅgala—who is called 'Akaṇhanetta' because he had tawny eyes—dear to you? Why do you weep?"

"I fear his return.
Having gone from here, he might oppress the King of Death;
And he, being oppressed, might send him back here again."

He spoke this verse to complete the two.

"Mahārāja, Great King! King Piṅgala was not dear to me. When that King Piṅgala has gone from this life and reached the next world, he might oppress the King of Death (Maccurāja). Because of that oppression, the King of Death might send that King Piṅgala back to this place again. I fear the return of that King Piṅgala."

Others go and come. But you remain weeping. I wish to ask if you loved my father—

That doorkeeper, hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, said: "Great King, I do not weep out of sorrow, thinking 'Great Piṅgala is dead.' Relief has come to my head. This is the truth: whenever King Piṅgala descended from or ascended to the palace, he would give me eight blows on my head with his fist, as if a blacksmith were striking an anvil.

Even when that King Piṅgala goes to hell in the next world, he will likely give blows to the heads of the hell-guardians and Yama, just as he gave blows to my head. When he gives blows to the heads of those hell-wardens, they will think, 'This king oppresses us too much,' and they might send him back and release him to this very place. If he is thus released, that King Piṅgala would again give blows to my head. It is because I fear this that I weep."

20. "The yellow-eyed one was not dear to me,"

Then the Bodhisatta comforted the doorkeeper, saying: "That king has been cremated with a thousand cartloads of firewood. The burial ground of the cremated King Piṅgala has also been dug up all around.

By nature, those who have gone to the next world find a place to stay in another existence. They cannot return with that same body. Do not fear," and thus consoling the doorkeeper, he spoke this verse:
222:
181. "He was burnt with a thousand cartloads, doused with hundreds of water-pots.
That ground has been dug up; do not fear, he will not return."

He spoke this verse.

"Dovārika, O doorkeeper! That King Piṅgala has been burnt with a thousand cartloads of firewood. He has been doused with hundreds of water-pots. The ground of that cemetery has also been dug up. Do not fear. King Piṅgala will not return."

From that time on, the doorkeeper found relief. The Bodhisatta also ruled the kingdom righteously, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed away according to his kamma.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Mahāpiṅgala was Devadatta, and the son was I myself."

## An Unjust King is Hated by the Country
The Mahāpiṅgala Jātaka ends.

## 10. Siṅgāla Vagga
## 1. Sabbadāṭha Jātaka
## The Pathavījaya Mantra

*The Story of the Present:* The Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Sabbadāṭha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Siṅgālo mānatthaddho," while staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, concerning Devadatta.

Devadatta, having gained the favour of King Ajātasattu, was unable to make the gains and honour he received last for a long time. From the time the miracle was seen during the incident involving the elephant Nalāgiri, those gains and honour of Devadatta vanished. Then one day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Friends, Devadatta, having produced gains and honour, was unable to make them last for long."

The Buddha, having arrived, asked the monks: "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta caused his own gains and honour to vanish; in the past, he also caused them to vanish," and he brought forth the story of the past.
223:
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain (purohita) and had reached the further shore of the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge. That chaplain-brahmin was proficient in a spell named Pathavījayama.

The spell that can change and deceive the minds of beings is called the Pathavījayama spell. Then one day, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "I will recite that Pathavījayama spell," sat on a flat stone in an open space and performed the recitation. It is said that this Pathavījayama spell should not be heard by others who lack steadfastness. Therefore, the chaplain recited that Pathavījayama spell at such a time [in seclusion].

At that time, while the chaplain was reciting, a jackal lying in a hole heard the Pathavījayama spell and mastered it. It is said that in a previous life immediately preceding this one, that jackal had been a brahmin who was proficient in the Pathavījayama spell. Having finished the recitation, the Bodhisatta stood up and said, "Indeed, this spell is well-mastered by me." The jackal came out of the hole and said, "O Brahmin, this spell is even better mastered by me than by you," and then ran away. The Bodhisatta, thinking, "This jackal will do much evil," said, "Catch him! Catch him!" and pursued him for a short while. The jackal ran away and entered the forest.

That jackal went and bit a female jackal slightly on her body. When she asked, "Master, what is it?" he asked, "Do you know me or not?" The female jackal replied, "Master, I know you." That jackal, having recited the Pathavījayama spell, commanded hundreds of jackals and caused all four-footed animals—elephants, horses, lions, tigers, boars, deer, and so on—to surround him. Having formed this retinue, he became a king named Sabbadāṭha and made a female jackal his chief queen. A lion had to carry him on its back while standing on the backs of two elephants. On the lion's back, the jackal king named Sabbadāṭha sat together with his chief queen, the female jackal. His glory was great.

That Sabbadāṭha jackal, becoming arrogant due to his great glory, thought, "I will take the kingship of Bārāṇasī." Surrounded by the entire host of four-footed animals, he arrived at a place near Bārāṇasī. His followers spanned twelve leagues. Standing nearby, that jackal king Sabbadāṭha sent a message to the King of Bārāṇasī: "Either give up the kingdom or fight." The inhabitants of Bārāṇasī, being terrified and trembling, closed the city gates and remained inside.

The Bodhisatta approached the King and said, "Do not fear, Great King. The task of fighting the jackal named Sabbadāṭha is my responsibility. Apart from me, there is no one capable of fighting with that Sabbadāṭha." Having thus comforted the King and the citizens, the Bodhisatta thought, "I will first ask that jackal Sabbadāṭha how he intends to take the kingship." He climbed the gate-tower and asked, "Friend Sabbadāṭha, how will you take this city?"
224:
He replied, "I will make the lions roar, and by terrifying the great multitude with the sound, I will take it."

The Bodhisatta, knowing that this was his plan, descended from the tower and had a drum beaten through the city, announcing, "Let all the inhabitants of the entire twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī plug their ear-holes with bean-flour (māsa-piṭṭha)." The people, hearing the command of the drum, plugged their ear-holes with bean-flour in such a way that they could not hear the sound of others, starting from the cats and including all four-footed animals and themselves.

Then the Bodhisatta climbed the tower again and called out, "Sabbadāṭha!" When the jackal replied, "What is it, Brahmin?", the Bodhisatta asked, "How will you take this kingdom?" He replied, "I will make the lions roar, terrify the people, cause them to perish, and thus take it."

When he said this, the Bodhisatta replied, "You will not be able to make the lions roar. It is true that the noble lion-kings, endowed with excellent birth and having beautiful red paws, will not obey the command of an old jackal like you." The jackal, becoming stiff with pride, said, "Let the other lions be; I will make even this very lion on whose back I am sitting roar!" The Bodhisatta said, "If you are able, then make him roar."

Then that jackal Sabbadāṭha, who was riding upon the lion, gave a signal with his foot to the lion, saying, "Roar!" The lion, raising its face toward the elephant's temples, let out an irresistible lion's roar three times. The elephants, becoming terrified, dropped the jackal at their feet and trampled his head with their feet, crushing it to pieces. The jackal Sabbadāṭha met his end right there.

The elephants, too, hearing the lion's roar and being terrified by the fear of death, collided with one another and met their end right there. Except for the lions, all other four-footed beasts, including deer, boars, and down to rabbits and cats, met their end there. The lions fled and entered the forest. The heap of meat spanned twelve yojanas. The Bodhisatta descended from the tower, had the city gates opened, and had a drum beaten through the city, announcing, "Let everyone remove the bean-flour from their ears, and let those who want meat come and take it." The people ate the fresh meat and dried the remainder to make sun-dried meat (vallūra). It is said that the practice of making sun-dried meat (vallūra) originated at that time.
225:
1. The jackal, stiff with pride and desiring a retinue, attained a great state and became king of all clawed animals. 
2. Just so among humans, he who has a retinue becomes great there, like the jackal among the clawed animals. 
He preached these two verses. 
Monks, that jackal, having become king of all clawed animals and attained great prosperity, was stiff with pride arising from his retinue. Desiring even more retinue than he already had, he reached destruction. 
Monks, just as the jackal was great among the clawed animals, so among humans, he who is endowed with a retinue becomes great. But then, like the jackal, falling into negligence and relying on that retinue, he reaches destruction. 
The Bodhisatta descended from the tower, ordered the city gates to be opened, and told all the citizens to remove the pea-flour from their ears. He had a drum beaten in the city, announcing, "Let those who desire meat take it." 
The people ate the meat and dried the remainder to make jerked meat. It is said that the practice of making jerked meat became well-known at that time. The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: 
"At that time, Devadatta was the jackal, Sāriputta was the king, and I myself was the chaplain." 
## Due to the mastery of a mantra, the herd of beasts died and perished. 
The Sabbadāṭha Jātaka is finished. 
## 2. Sunakha Jātaka 
## The Wise Dog 
The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who admonishes the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sunakha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bālo vatāyaṃ sunakho," concerning a dog that ate rice from a trough at a rest house. 
It is said that water-carriers took that dog from the time it was born and raised it at that rest house. Later, eating rice at that rest house, it became fat. Then one day, a man living in a village arrived at the rest house, saw the dog, gave an upper cloak and a kahāpaṇa to the water-carriers, tied it with a strap, and took the dog away. While being led away, the dog did not bark; it followed behind, eating whatever food was given. 
Then the man, thinking "This dog is now fond of me," untied the strap. As soon as it was released, the dog ran back to the rest house in a single dash.
226:
The monks saw the dog and, knowing the reason for its return, raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall in the evening: "Friends, the dog at the rest house is clever at escaping bonds; as soon as it was released, it came back again." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When told, he said, "Monks, not only now is this dog clever at escaping bonds; in the past too, it was clever," and he brought forth the past story. 
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a very wealthy family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he reached maturity, he took up the life of a householder. 
At that time, a man in Vārāṇasī had a dog. That dog became fat from receiving balls of rice. Then a villager came to Vārāṇasī, saw the dog, gave the owner an upper cloak and a kahāpaṇa, took the dog, tied it with a leather strap, and while leading it by the end of the strap, entered a rest house at the edge of a forest. He tied the dog, lay down on a bench, and fell fast asleep. 
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having reached the edge of the forest for some business, saw the dog tied with the strap and spoke this first verse: 
3. "This dog is indeed a fool, who does not chew the leather strap. He could free himself from the bond and, being well-fed, go home." 
"The dog who does not chew the leather strap—this dog is truly a fool. He should free himself from the bond. Being well-fed, he should run to his own place." 
Hearing these words, the dog spoke this second verse to complete the pair: 
4. "It is fixed in my mind, and placed in my heart. I am waiting for the time, until the people fall asleep." 
"Master, the words you speak are determined in my mind. They are placed in my heart. As long as the people are asleep, I will stay. I am waiting for that time."
227:
Having said this, when the people had fallen asleep, the dog gnawed through the leather strap, and having eaten his fill, he fled and went to his masters' house.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the dog was indeed the dog, but the wise man was I myself."

## One must know the time to seek one's own safety

The Sunakha Jātaka is finished.

## 3. Guttila Jātaka

## The Master of the Lute

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, told this Guttila Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sattatantiṃ sumadhuraṃ", concerning Devadatta.

To elaborate: In the Dhamma Hall, the monks said to Devadatta, "Friend Devadatta, the Fully Enlightened One is your teacher. Depending on the Fully Enlightened One, you learned the Three Piṭakas and attained the four jhānas. It is not proper to become an enemy of one's teacher." Devadatta replied, "Friends, how can the ascetic Gotama be my teacher? I have learned the Three Piṭakas and attained the four jhānas by my own power alone." Thus, he renounced his teacher.

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Devadatta has renounced his teacher, become an enemy of the Buddha, and has come to great ruin." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now has Devadatta renounced me, his teacher, and become my enemy and come to great ruin; he did so in the past as well." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of musicians. They named him Guttila Kumāra. When he reached maturity, he attained mastery in the art of the lute and became the chief musician in all of Jambudīpa. This musician Guttila did not take a wife but supported his blind parents.
228:
At that time, merchants from Bārāṇasī went to the city of Ujjeni for trade. When a festival was proclaimed, they pooled their resources, took many flowers, perfumes, and ointments, as well as food and snacks, and gathered at the place of amusement. They said, "Bring a musician for a fee." At that time, there was a chief musician named Mūsila in Ujjeni. The merchants summoned Mūsila and had him perform his musical art.

When Mūsila played the lute, he played with the highest tuning and made it sound. To those merchants, who were accustomed to the lute-playing of Guttila, Mūsila's playing sounded like scratching a mat with a bamboo splint. Not a single person showed a sign of delight. When Mūsila saw that the merchants showed no sign of satisfaction, thinking, "I must be playing too harshly," he tuned it to the middle pitch and played with a middle tone. Even then, they remained indifferent.

Then Mūsila thought, "These people must know nothing at all." As if he himself were ignorant, he loosened the strings and played. Even then, the merchants said nothing. Then Mūsila asked the merchants, "O merchants, why are you not pleased when I play the lute?"

"Are you playing the lute? We did not even realize that this Mūsila was playing a lute," the merchants replied.

He asked, "Do you know a teacher superior to me, or are you displeased because of your own ignorance?" The merchants said, "To us, who have heard the sound of Guttila the musician's lute in Bārāṇasī, your lute-playing sounds like the noise women make to soothe children." "If that is so," Mūsila said, "take back the wages you gave me. I have no need for those wages. However, when you return to Bārāṇasī, take me with you." The merchants agreed, saying, "Very well." When it was time to depart, they took Mūsila and went to Bārāṇasī. They pointed out Guttila's dwelling place to him and went to their respective homes.

Mūsila entered the Bodhisatta's house and, seeing the Bodhisatta's ancestral lute hanging there, he took it and played it. Then the Bodhisatta's parents, being blind and unable to see him, thought, "Mice must be gnawing the lute," and made the sound "Shoo, shoo!" At that time, Mūsila put down the lute and paid respect to the Bodhisatta's parents. When asked, "Where have you come from?", he replied, "I have come from Ujjeni to learn the art from the teacher." When they said, "Very well," he asked, "Where is the teacher?" Hearing that he was away and would return today, he sat there waiting for the Bodhisatta's arrival.
229:
Musila entered the Bodhisatta's house, saw the lute hanging there, took it, and played it. At that time, the Bodhisatta's parents, being blind, did not see Musila and thought, "Mice are gnawing at the lute," and made a "shooing" sound (su-su).

Then Musila put down the lute, paid homage to the Bodhisatta's parents, and said, "Mother, Father, it is I who played the lute." When asked where he came from, he replied, "I have come from the city of Ujjeni to learn the art from the teacher." When the Bodhisatta's parents said, "Very well," he asked, "Where is the teacher?" Hearing the reply, "Dear son, he has gone elsewhere and will return soon," he stayed there. Seeing the Bodhisatta arrive, and after the Bodhisatta had performed the usual greetings, Musila informed him of the reason for his coming.

The Bodhisatta, being skilled in the science of physiognomy (Aṅgavijjā), knew Musila's wicked nature and rejected him, saying, "Go, dear son, there is no art for you." Musila then held the feet of the Bodhisatta's parents, massaged them, and after winning them over, pleaded, "Please have the teacher give me the art." When the parents repeatedly spoke to the Bodhisatta, he, unable to go against his parents' wishes, taught him the art.

Musila went to the royal palace together with the Bodhisatta. Seeing Musila, the King asked, "Teacher, who is this?" He replied, "Great King, this is my pupil." Gradually, Musila became familiar with the King. The Bodhisatta, without keeping anything back (without a "teacher's fist"), taught him the entire art according to his own knowledge and said, "Dear son, your training is complete."

Musila thought, "I have mastered the art. This city of Bārāṇasī is the foremost city in all of Jambudīpa. My teacher is old. It is fitting for me to live right here in Bārāṇasī." Having thought so, Musila said to the teacher, "Teacher, I wish to serve the King."

The teacher said, "Very well, dear son, I shall inform the King." He went and informed the King, saying, "Great King, my pupil wishes to serve Your Majesty. Please determine his remuneration." When the King said, "He shall receive half of what is given to you," the teacher informed Musila of this.

Musila said, "Teacher, if I receive a reward equal to yours, I will serve; if not, I will not." When asked why, he said, "Do I not know the entire art that you know?"

When the Bodhisatta said, "Yes, you know it," Musila replied, "If that is so, why should I be given only half the wealth when I am as skilled as the teacher?" The Bodhisatta informed the King. The King said, "Teacher, if this is the case, if he is able to demonstrate his skill equally with you, he shall receive an equal reward."

The Bodhisatta informed Musila of the King's words, and when Musila said, "Very well, I will demonstrate it," the teacher informed the King. When the King said, "Very well, let him demonstrate. On which day shall the discussion and contest take place?" the Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, let it be on the seventh day from now."
230:
5. I taught him the seven-stringed lute,
So sweet and delightful.
Now he challenges me in the arena;
Be my refuge, O Kosiya.

Thus he spoke this first verse. 
O King of Devas, Sakka. I, the teacher, taught the pupil named Musila the lute (vīṇā) which has seven strings, is named Sumadhura, and is delightful, according to my own knowledge. That Musila now calls me to the midst of the festival arena. O Sakka, born of the Kosiya clan, may you be my refuge.

The King summoned Musila and asked, "Is it true that you will hold a discussion and contest with your teacher?" When Musila replied, "It is true, Your Majesty," the King cautioned him, "A dispute with one's teacher is not proper; do not do it." Despite being forbidden, Musila said, "Enough, Great King, let the contest with my teacher take place on the seventh day. We shall know which of us is the master."

The King agreed and had the drum beaten, announcing: "On the seventh day from now, the teacher Guttila and the pupil Musila will compete with each other at the palace gate and demonstrate their art. Let the citizens assemble and witness the performance."

The Bodhisatta thought, "This Musila is young and youthful. I am old and my strength has faded. The performance of an old man is never perfect. Even if a pupil is defeated, there is no special loss; but if the pupil wins, the teacher faces great shame. It is better to enter the forest and die."

Having thought so, the Bodhisatta entered the forest, but returned out of fear of death. Then he went back again out of fear of shame. While he was thus going and coming, six days passed. The grass died [under his feet], and a path was formed.

At that moment, Sakka's throne showed signs of heat. When Sakka reflected and knew the reason, he thought, "The musician Guttila is suffering greatly in the forest out of fear of his pupil. I must be his refuge." He came swiftly, stood before the Bodhisatta, and asked, "Teacher, why have you entered the forest?" When asked, "Who are you?" he replied, "I am Sakka."

Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "O King of Devas, I have entered the forest for fear of being defeated by my pupil."

Sakka, hearing Guttila's words, said, "Teacher, do not fear. I will be your protection and your refuge," and spoke this verse which completes the two:

6. I am your refuge, friend,
I am a worshipper of teachers.
Your pupil shall not defeat you;
Teacher, you shall defeat the pupil.
231:
“Dear teacher, I shall be your refuge, support, and protection. Teacher, I shall honor you. Teacher, your pupil Musila shall not defeat you. Teacher, you shall defeat him.

Indeed, when you play the lute, cut one string and play the remaining six; your lute will still produce its natural sound. Musila will also cut a string, but then his lute will produce no sound. At that moment, he will meet with defeat. Then, recognizing his defeat, cut the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh strings, and play upon the mere frame of the lute. From the ends of the broken strings, the sound will emerge and pervade the entire city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent.”

Having said this, Sakka gave the Bodhisatta three balls and said: “When the sound of the lute pervades the whole city, throw one of these balls into the air. When you throw it, three hundred celestial nymphs will descend and dance before you. While they are dancing, throw the second ball; then another three hundred will descend and dance at the tip of your lute. After that, throw the third ball; then another three hundred will descend and dance upon the stage. I too shall come to the assembly. Go, do not be afraid.” Thus he encouraged the Bodhisatta. In the morning, the Bodhisatta went home.

The citizens built a pavilion near the palace gate and prepared a seat for the King. The King descended from the palace and sat upon a throne in the center of the decorated pavilion. Twelve thousand adorned women, along with ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, surrounded the King. All the citizens gathered. In the palace courtyard, they arranged tiers of carts and tiers of couches.

The Bodhisatta, having bathed and anointed himself, ate various foods of excellent flavor, took his lute, and sat in the place prepared for him. A great crowd surrounded him. Sakka arrived with an invisible body and stood in the air; only the Bodhisatta saw him. Musila also arrived and sat in his place. A great crowd surrounded him. From the beginning, both teacher and pupil played equally. The multitude, delighted by the playing of both, raised thousands of cheers.

Sakka, standing in the air, spoke so that only the Bodhisatta could hear: “Cut one string.” The Bodhisatta cut a string. Even though it was broken, the sound continued to issue from the broken end. It was like the music of a celestial Gandharva. Musila also cut a string, but no sound came from it. The teacher then cut the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh strings. The sound of the Bodhisatta's lute, played upon the mere frame, pervaded the city of Bārāṇasī. The people threw thousands of garments and raised thousands of cheers.
232:
The Bodhisatta threw one ball into the air. Three hundred celestial nymphs descended and danced. Likewise, when the second and third balls were thrown into the air, three hundred nymphs each time descended and danced.

At that moment, the King gave a signal to the multitude with a wink and a nod. The people rose up and threatened Musila, saying: “You strive to compete with your teacher, seeking equal gain and honor; you do not know your own measure.” They crushed him with whatever stones and clubs they could find, ending his life. They then took him by the feet and threw him onto a rubbish heap.

The King, with a delighted heart, gave much wealth to the Bodhisatta, as if causing a heavy rain to fall. The citizens likewise gave much wealth.

Sakka, having exchanged friendly greetings with the Bodhisatta, said: “Wise one, I shall send the celestial charioteer Mātali to fetch you with a chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbred horses. You should come to the celestial realm riding the noble Vejayanta chariot drawn by a thousand thoroughbreds.” Having said this, he departed.

Then, the celestial daughters asked Sakka, who had returned and was seated on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne: “Great King, where have you been?” Sakka told them the matter in detail and praised the Bodhisatta's virtue and merit. The celestial daughters said: “Great King, we also wish to see the teacher. Please invite him here to the celestial realm.”

Sakka called the celestial charioteer Mātali and said: “Friend Mātali, the celestial nymphs wish to see the musician Guttila. Go, seat the musician Guttila in the Vejayanta chariot and bring him here.” Mātali replied, “Very well,” and went to fetch the Bodhisatta.

Sakka greeted the Bodhisatta joyfully and said: “Teacher, the celestial daughters wish to hear your lute music.” The Bodhisatta replied: “Great King, we musicians live by our craft. If we receive a fee, we shall play.”

When Sakka said, “Teacher, play; I will give you a fee,” the Bodhisatta replied: “I have no need for any other fee. Let these celestial daughters speak of their own meritorious deeds; if they do so, I will play.” Then the celestial daughters said to the musician Guttila: “Teacher, we will tell you of our meritorious deeds later; please play the lute now.”
233:
Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, yā tvaṃ tiṭṭhasi devate.
Obhāsentī disā sabbā, osadhī viya tārakā.
Kena tetādiso vaṇṇo, kena te idha mijjhati.
Uppajjanti ca te bhogā, ye keci manaso piyā.
Pucchāmi taṃ devi mahānubhāve,
manussabhūtā kimakāsi puññaṃ.
Kenāsi evaṃ jalitānubhāvā,

For seven days, the Bodhisatta played the lute for the benefit of the devas. That lute-playing surpassed even the celestial music. On the seventh day, starting from the beginning, he questioned the goddesses about their past meritorious deeds.

One goddess had become an attendant of Sakka because she had offered a noble garment to a certain monk during the time of Kassapa Buddha.

The musician Guttila asked that goddess, "Goddess, what merit did you perform in your previous life to become a goddess possessed of noble garments and accompanied by a thousand nymphs?"

The manner of the musician Guttila’s questioning and the manner of the goddesses’ answering are exactly as they appear in the Vimānavatthu. Indeed, it is true; in that Vimānavatthu:

Vaṇṇo ca te sabbadisā pabhāsati.
Vatthuttamadāyikā nārī, pavarā hoti naresu nārīsu.
Evaṃ piyarūpadāyikā manāpaṃ, dibbaṃ sā labhate upecca ဌာနံ.
Tassā me passa vimānaṃ, accharā kāmavaṇṇinīhamasmi.
Accharāsahassāhaṃ, pavarā passa puññānaṃ vipākaṃ.
Tena me tādiso vaṇṇo, tena me idha mijjhati.
Uppajjanti ca me bhogā, ye keci manaso piyā.
Tenaṃhi evaṃ jalitānubhāvā, vaṇṇo ca me sabbadisā pabhāsati.

Devate, O goddess. Yā tvaṃ, you who. Osadhī tārakā viya, like the star named Osadhī. Sabbā disā, all directions. Obhāsentī, illuminating. Abhikkantena vaṇṇena, with such surpassing beauty. Tiṭṭhasi, you stand. Kena, because of what [deed]. Te vaṇṇo, is your beauty. Tādiso, of such a nature?

Kena, because of what [deed]. Te, for you. Idha, here in this celestial realm. Ijjhati, is there such prosperity? Kena, because of what [deed]. Te, for you. Ye keci bhogā ca, whatever pleasures. Manaso piyā, that are dear to the heart. Uppajjanti, do they arise?

Mahānubhāve devi, O goddess of great power. Taṃ pucchāmi, I ask you. Manussabhūtā tvaṃ, you, having been a human. Kiṃ puññaṃ, what meritorious deed. Akāsi, did you perform in the past? Kena, because of what merit. Evaṃ jalitānubhāvā, [one] with such blazing power. Asi, are you? Kena, because of what merit. Te vaṇṇo ca, does your beauty. Sabbadisā, all directions. Pabhāsati, illuminate? Iti, thus. Pucchite, when it was asked:

Bhante, venerable sir. Naresu ca nārīsu ca, among men and women. Vatthuttamadāyikā nārī, a woman who gives noble garments. Pavarā hoti, is excellent. Evaṃ, in this way. Piyarūpadāyikā, one who gives things of a pleasing nature. Sā nārī, that woman. Ṭhānaṃ upecca, having reached the celestial realm. Dibbaṃ manāpaṃ, delightful celestial things. Labhate, she obtains.

Bhante, venerable sir. Tvaṃ, you. Tā me vimānaṃ, look at this mansion of mine. Ahaṃ, I. Kāmavaṇṇinī, am possessed of a lovely complexion. Asmi, I am. Ahaṃ, I. Accharāsahassānaṃ pavarā accharā, am the foremost goddess among a thousand nymphs. Asmi, I am. Puññānaṃ vipākaṃ, the fruit of merits. Passa, behold.

Bhante, venerable sir. Tena, because of that gift of noble garments. Me vaṇṇo, my beauty. Tādiso, is of such a nature. Tena, because of that noble gift. Me, for me. Idha, here in this celestial realm. Ijjhati, there is prosperity. Tena, because of that gift of noble garments. Ye keci bhogā, whatever pleasures. Manaso piyā, that are dear to the heart. Me uppajjanti, indeed arise for me.

Tena, because of that gift of noble garments. Ahaṃ, I. Evaṃ jalitānubhāvā, [one] with such blazing power. Amhi, am. Me vaṇṇo ca, and my beauty. Sabbadisā, all directions. Pabhāsati, illuminates. Iti, thus. Vissajjati, she answered.

Another goddess gave flowers to a monk walking for alms in order to honor him. Another goddess gave scents, saying, "Please offer these five-finger marks of scent at the stupa." Another goddess gave sweet fruits of various kinds. Another goddess gave noble flavors. Another goddess offered five-finger marks of scent at the stupa of Kassapa the Buddha.

Another goddess listened to the Dhamma in the presence of monks and nuns who had come to stay at a lay house while traveling. Another goddess, while standing in the water, offered water to a monk who had finished his meal on a boat. Another goddess, while living in the midst of her home, was without anger and performed her duties toward her father-in-law and mother-in-law. Another goddess shared even from her own received portion and gave to a virtuous person. Another goddess, being a servant in another's house, was without anger and pride, and having shared from her own received portion, she became an attendant of Sakka.
234:
In this manner and other various ways, the Bodhisatta questioned all thirty-six goddesses mentioned in the Guttila-vimāna-vatthu about what specific merits they had performed to be reborn in that celestial realm. The goddesses also answered the Bodhisatta regarding their performed merits only through verses.

Having heard those words, the Bodhisatta said, "What a gain for me! What a great blessing for me! Having come here, I have heard of the celestial fortunes obtained through even small deeds. From now on, after returning to the human world, I will perform only meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna)," and he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

"Truly, my coming today is a welcome one; it is a beautiful dawn, a good rising,
Since I have seen the goddesses, the nymphs of lovely complexion.
Having heard the Dhamma from them, I shall perform much merit,
Through giving, through righteous living, through restraint, and through self-control.
I shall go to that place where, having gone, they do not sorrow."

Then, after seven days had passed, the King of Devas commanded the deity named Mātali, seated the Bodhisatta in the chariot, and sent him back to Bārāṇasī. Having reached Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta told the people about what he himself had seen in the celestial realm. From that time on, the people became diligent and mindful to perform meritorious deeds.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth (Jātaka): "At that time, Mūsila was Devadatta. Sakka was Anuruddha. The King was Ānanda. But the musician Guttila was I myself."

## When one challenges the teacher of one's craft, the public loathes and hates them.

The Guttila Jātaka ends.
235:
7. What he sees, he does not desire; what he does not see, that he desires. I think he will wander for a long time; for he will not obtain what he desires.

8. What he obtains, he is not satisfied with; what he craves, he despises once obtained. For desire has an infinite range; we pay homage to those free from desire.

He spoke these verses.

Friends, that wanderer (paribbājaka) does not desire what he sees, such as the water, as the 'Ganges'. What he does not see—that which is separate from the water and so on—that he desires as the 'Ganges'. I think this wanderer, searching for such a Ganges, will wander for a long time. Just as he searches for a Ganges separate from the water and so on, so too, searching for a self (attā) separate from form (rūpa) and so on, I think he will wander for a long time in saṃsāra. Even though he wanders for a long time, he will not obtain that kind of Ganges or self that he desires.

What he obtains, such as the water or the object of form, he is not satisfied with. Being dissatisfied with what he has obtained, whatever prosperity he craves, what is the use of it once obtained? Thus he despises it. Because desire (taṇhā) has an infinite range of objects, we pay homage to the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples who are free from desire.

## 4. Vigaticcha Jātaka
## The Fleeing Wanderer

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Vigaticcha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yam passati na tam icchati," concerning a certain fleeing wanderer.

That wanderer, having found no opponent in the whole of Jambudīpa, came to Sāvatthī and asked, "Who is able to debate with me?" Hearing that it was the Buddha, he went to Jetavana surrounded by a great crowd and asked a question while the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma in the midst of the fourfold assembly.

Then the Blessed One answered his question and asked him, "What is called 'One'?" The wanderer, unable to answer the question, stood up and fled.

The assembled crowd said, "Venerable Sir, you have refuted the wanderer with just a single word." The Blessed One said, "Lay devotees, I have not refuted this wanderer with a single word only now; I have refuted him in the past as well," and he related the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he renounced sensual pleasures, took up the life of an ascetic, and lived for a long time in the Himalayas.

Descending from the mountains, the Bodhisatta lived in a leaf-hut at a bend in the Ganges near a market town. At that time, a certain wanderer, having found no opponent in all of Jambudīpa, reached that town and asked, "Is there anyone capable of debating with me?" Hearing of the Bodhisatta's power, he went to the Bodhisatta's dwelling surrounded by many people, exchanged greetings, and sat down.

Then the Bodhisatta asked the wanderer, "Will you drink the water of the Ganges, which is imbued with color and fragrance?" The wanderer, trying to overwhelm him with debate, asked, "What is the Ganges? Is the sand the Ganges? Is the water the Ganges? Is this bank the Ganges? Is that bank the Ganges?"
236:
The Bodhisatta said, "Wanderer, if you set aside the water, the sand, this bank, and that bank, where will you find the Ganges?" The wanderer, being speechless and devoid of wisdom, stood up and fled.

When the wanderer had fled, the Bodhisatta, wishing to preach the Dhamma to the assembled crowd, spoke the verses.

[The commentary on the verses is as follows:] "What he sees" refers to the water and so on that he sees, which he does not accept as the Ganges. "What he does not see" refers to a Ganges separate from the water and so on, which he desires. "I think he will wander for a long time" means I think this wanderer will wander long searching for such a Ganges. Or, just as he searches for a Ganges separate from water, so too, searching for a self separate from form and so on, he will wander long in saṃsāra. "He will not obtain it" means even wandering for a long time, he will not find the kind of Ganges or self he desires. "What he obtains" refers to the water or form he gets, with which he is not satisfied. "He despises once obtained" means being dissatisfied with what is obtained, whatever prosperity he craves, once he gets it, he despises and looks down on it, thinking "What is the use of this?" "Desire has an infinite range" means because he despises what is obtained and desires one object after another, this desire called taṇhā has an infinite range. "We pay homage to those free from desire" means therefore we pay homage to those who are free from desire, such as the Buddhas.

Identification of the Jātaka: The Blessed One related this Dhamma teaching and identified the birth: "At that time, the wanderer was this same wanderer, and the ascetic was I myself."

## If one challenges those who are not their equal, they will be shamed.
The Vigaticcha Jātaka is finished.

## 5. Mūlapariyāya Jātaka
## The Conceited Brahmins

While staying in the Subhaga Grove near the city of Ukkaṭṭhā, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Mūlapariyāya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kālo ghasati bhūtāni," concerning the Mūlapariyāya Sutta.

At that time, five hundred brahmins who had mastered the three Vedas ordained in the Dispensation. Having learned the three Pitakas, they became intoxicated with pride, thinking, "The Fully Enlightened One knows the three Pitakas, and we also know them. This being so, what is the difference between him and us?" Thus, they did not go to attend upon the Buddha. They became hostile and went about their own way.

Then one day, when those monks came and sat in the presence of the Blessed One, he preached the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, adorned with the eight stages (bhūmi). They could not understand even a little of it. 

Then it occurred to those monks: "We used to be proud, thinking there were no wise men equal to us. Now, however, we cannot understand anything. There is no wise man equal to the Buddhas."
237:
9. Time consumes all beings, all of them together with itself.
But the being who is the consumer of time, has burnt the fire [of craving] that cooks beings.

He recited this first verse.

"O pupils, time consumes all beings along with itself. But as for the being who consumes time, that being has burnt the fire of craving—which causes beings to be cooked—with the fire of knowledge. Who is that being?"

[The monks thought,] "The virtues of the Buddha are truly marvelous." From then on, those monks had their pride discarded and became like snakes with their fangs extracted, free from arrogance.

The Blessed One, having stayed in Ukkaṭṭhā as long as he liked, went to Vesālī and preached the Gotamaka Suttanta at the shrine of the Gotamaka deity. The ten thousand world systems shook. Having heard that, those monks attained Arahatship.

At the conclusion of the Mūlapariyāya Suttanta, while the Teacher was still staying in Ukkaṭṭhā, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, how marvelous is the power of the Buddhas! Those brahmins who had gone forth and were intoxicated with the intoxication of pride were made to have their pride discarded by the Blessed One through the Mūlapariyāya discourse."

The Teacher came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past also, I made these very people—who were wandering about with their heads held high in pride—discard their pride." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. When he reached maturity, he became a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) who had reached the far shore of the Vedas, and he taught the mantras to five hundred young students.

Those five hundred students, having completed their arts, scrutinized their knowledge and thought, "We know as much as the teacher knows; there is no difference."

Becoming stiff with pride, they no longer went to the teacher's presence and did not perform their duties toward him.

One day, while the teacher was sitting at the foot of a jujube (badari) tree, those five hundred students, wishing to insult the teacher, tapped the jujube tree with their fingernails and said, "This tree is indeed hollow and worthless."
238:
10. Many are the human heads, hairy and large.
Attached to necks, but only some here have ears.

He spoke this verse to complete the two [previous ones].

'Attached to necks' (gīvāsu); 'large' (branhāni); 'hairy' (lomasāni); 'many human heads' (bahūni narasīsāni) are seen. 'Among these many heads' (ettha); 'only a certain head' (kocideva); 'has ears that understand' (kaṇṇavā).

The Bodhisatta, knowing that he was being disparaged, said to his disciples, "Disciples, I shall ask you a question." The disciples, being delighted, said, "Ask, teacher, we shall answer." The teacher, wishing to ask the question—

Upon hearing this question, not a single one among the youths was able to understand it. Then the Bodhisatta said to the youths, "O youths, do not assume that this question exists in the three Vedas. You think, 'Whatever the teacher knows, we know all of that,' and thus you treat me like a jujube tree. You shall see that I know much more than you. Go now; I give you time until the seventh day. Within this time, ponder this question."

The youths paid homage to the Bodhisatta, went to their respective dwellings, and though they pondered for seven days, they could see neither the beginning nor the end of the question. On the seventh day, they went to the teacher, paid homage, and sat down.

When asked, "O fair-faced youths, do you know the [answer to the] question?" they replied, "We do not know." Then the Bodhisatta, wishing to rebuke those youths—
239:
Having heard this, those young men, exclaiming, "Oh, how wonderful and great a teacher is!" paid homage and, with their pride humbled, attended to the Bodhisatta.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the five hundred young men were these five hundred monks, and I myself was the teacher."

## A teacher should never be emulated.

The Mūlapariyāya Jātaka is concluded.

11. Having struck, cut, and killed, an unrestrained person gives a gift. One who eats such food is smeared with sin.

He spoke this first verse. 

Ascetic, hermit. An unrestrained person, one without virtue. Having struck, having cut, and having killed, gives a gift. One who eats such food, that monk is smeared with evil.

## 6. Bālovāda Jātaka
## Blaming after feeding

The Present Account: While the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, was dwelling at the Gabled Hall in the forest near Vesālī, he told this Bālovāda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Hantvā chetvā vadhitvā ca," concerning General Sīha.

Indeed, General Sīha, having taken refuge in the Buddha and invited him, offered a meal of meat the next day. Hearing this, the Nigaṇṭhas were angry and displeased. Wishing to harass the Tathāgata, they slandered him, saying, "The ascetic Gotama knowingly eats meat specifically prepared for him."

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta is wandering about with his followers, slandering the ascetic Gotama, saying he knowingly eats meat specifically prepared for him." Hearing this, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta blames me for eating meat specifically prepared for me; he did so in the past as well." Having said this, he brought forth the past.

The Past Account: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he became an ascetic. To seek salt and vinegar, he went from the Himalayas to Bārāṇasī and entered the city for alms the next day.
240:
12. Even if one kills one's own children and wife, and an unrestrained person gives a gift; a wise person who eats it is not smeared with sin.

He spoke this verse which completes the pair.

Lay devotee, donor. An unrestrained person, one without virtue. Even if he kills his children and wife and gives a gift. A wise person, one endowed with wisdom, even if he eats that food, he is not smeared with evil.

At that time, a certain householder, wishing to harass the ascetic, invited him into his house, seated him on a prepared seat, and served him with fish and meat. At the end of the meal, he sat in a suitable place and said, "Venerable ascetic, these animals were killed specifically for you to prepare this meat. May this demerit not be ours alone, but yours as well."

The Bodhisatta, hearing those words—

Thus, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to that donor, rose from his seat, and departed.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the householder was Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and I myself was the ascetic."

## If one kills to feed, only the killer bears the guilt.

The Bālovāda Jātaka is concluded.

## 7. Pādañjali Jātaka
## The Lip-Biting Prince

The Present Account: While the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, was dwelling at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Pādañjali Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Addhā pādañjalī sabbe," concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī.

One day, the two Chief Disciples were resolving questions. The monks, hearing the resolution, praised the Elders. But Elder Lāḷudāyī, sitting in the midst of the assembly, bit his lip, thinking, "Do these [Sāriputta and Moggallāna] know as much as we do?" Seeing him, the Elders rose and departed. The assembly broke up.

The monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Elder Lāḷudāyī slandered the two Chief Disciples and bit his lip." Hearing this, the Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyī knows nothing else besides biting his lip; in the past too, he knew nothing else besides biting his lip." Having said this, he brought forth the past.
241:
13. Indeed, Pādañjali outshines all in wisdom.
For he bites his lip; surely he sees something beyond.

He spoke this first verse:
O friends! Prince Pādañjali indeed outshines everyone in wisdom. That is why he bites his lip; he must surely see some superior reason.

14. He understands neither right nor wrong, nor what is beneficial or harmful.
Apart from the twisting of his lip, he knows nothing at all.

He spoke this verse which completes the pair:
O friends! This Prince Pādañjali knows neither what is right nor what is wrong, nor what is beneficial or harmful. This Prince Pādañjali knows nothing at all, except for the biting of his lip.

Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a minister who advised the king on matters of welfare and Dhamma. The king had a son named Pādañjali, who was frivolous and of dull effort. Later, the king passed away.

The ministers performed the funeral rites and consulted on who should be consecrated as king. They said, "Let us consecrate Prince Pādañjali." But the Bodhisatta said, "This prince is frivolous and of dull effort. Let us test him and then consecrate him."

The ministers arranged a court of justice, seated the prince nearby, and while deciding cases, they decided them incorrectly. They then asked the prince, who was not yet the master, "O Prince, what do you think? Did we decide the cases well?" Prince Pādañjali merely bit his lip.

The Bodhisatta thought, "He must be a wise man; he likely realizes that the cases were decided incorrectly," and spoke the first verse.

On another day, the ministers again arranged the court, decided cases correctly, and asked, "O Great King, what do you think of the decision?" Prince Pādañjali again merely bit his lip.

Then, realizing the prince's utter foolishness, the Bodhisatta spoke the second verse.

The ministers, realizing Prince Pādañjali's foolishness, consecrated the Bodhisatta as king.

Conclusion: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Pādañjali was Lāḷudāyī, and I myself was the wise minister."

## Except for biting his lip, he knows nothing.
The Pādañjali Jātaka is finished.
242:
## 8. Kiṃsukopama Jātaka
## Four Princes and the Kiṃsuka Tree

Story of the Present: While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kiṃsukopama Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Sabbēhi kiṃsukō diṭṭhō," concerning the Kiṃsukopama Sutta.

Four monks approached the Buddha and requested meditation subjects. The Fully Enlightened One taught them meditation subjects. Taking these subjects, they went to their places for night and day meditation.

Among them, one monk attained Arahantship by contemplating the six sense bases (phassāyatana). Another attained it through the five aggregates (khandha), another through the four great elements (mahābhūta), and another through the eighteen elements (dhātu). They reported their specific attainments to the Buddha.

Then, a thought occurred to another monk: "The meditation subjects of these monks were different, yet Nibbāna is one. How did they all attain Arahantship?" He asked the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "O monk, how is your situation different from that of the four brothers who saw the Kiṃsuka tree?" Being requested by the monks, "Venerable Sir, please tell us this story," he brought forth the past.

Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he had four sons. One day, they called the charioteer and said, "Friend charioteer, we wish to see a Kiṃsuka tree. Show us a Kiṃsuka tree."

The charioteer replied, "Very well, I will show you." He did not show it to all four at once. First, he took the eldest prince in the chariot to the forest and showed him the Kiṃsuka tree when it was a bare stump. To another prince, he showed it when it had thick foliage. To another, when it was in bloom. To another, when it was bearing fruit.
243:
15. "By all the kiṃsuka was seen; why then do you doubt herein?
For in all its stages, the charioteer was not questioned."

This was the first verse spoken. 

Dear ones, you have all seen the kiṃsuka tree. Why do you have doubt regarding this tree? It is because you did not ask the charioteer about the tree in all its stages. Therefore, because you did not ask, you have doubt.

16. "Thus, those to whom the Dhammas are unknown through all knowledges,
They indeed doubt the Dhammas, just as the brothers did regarding the kiṃsuka."

He preached this verse which completes the two.

Monks, just as the four royal brothers doubted the kiṃsuka tree, so too, monks, those to whom the Dhammas—such as contact (phassa) and the sense bases (āyatana)—are unknown through all insight knowledges (vipassanā-ñāṇa), because they have not attained or penetrated the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), they indeed doubt those Dhammas such as contact and the sense bases.

Later, the four royal brothers, while living together, raised a conversation: "What is the nature of the so-called kiṃsuka tree?" Then, one prince said it was like a burnt stump. The second prince said it was like a banyan tree. The third prince said it was like a piece of meat. The fourth prince said it was like a sirīsa tree.

Thus, the princes, being dissatisfied with each other's words, went to their father and asked, "O Great King, what is the nature of the so-called kiṃsuka tree?" When the King asked, "What did you say?" they reported their respective observations to the King.

The King said, "All four of you have seen the kiṃsuka tree. However, when the kiṃsuka was shown to you, you did not ask the charioteer by way of analysis, 'What is the nature of the kiṃsuka at such a time? What is its nature at another time?' Therefore, doubt has arisen in you."

The Blessed One, having shown this reason, said, "Monks, just as those four brothers caused doubt to arise regarding the kiṃsuka tree because they did not analyze and ask, so too you have caused doubt to arise in this Dhamma."

[The Identification of the Jātaka:] The Blessed One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "Monks, at that time, I myself was the King of Bārāṇasī."

## Though the goal is the same, if the actions performed differ, one should not cast blame based on how it appears.

The Kiṃsukopama Jātaka is finished.

## 9. Sālaka Jātaka

## The Great Elder Oppresses, the Young Novice Leaves

The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sālaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ekaputtako bhavissasi," concerning an obscure elderly monk.

That elderly monk lived at Jetavana Monastery, having ordained a young boy and then mistreating him. The novice, unable to endure the mistreatment, returned to lay life. The elderly monk went and coaxed the boy, saying, "Child, your robe and your bowl shall be yours alone; even my own bowl and robe shall be yours. Come, be ordained."

Although the boy said, "I will not be ordained," he was coaxed repeatedly and thus became ordained again.
244:
He was ordained. However, from the day he was ordained, the elder mistreated him again. Unable to endure the suffering, he returned to lay life again. Even though the elder pleaded many times, the boy said, "You can neither endure me nor live without me. Go, I will not be ordained," and he remained unordained.

The monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, indeed that boy has a wise mind; knowing the Great Elder's disposition, he does not ordain."

The Blessed One, having arrived, asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," the Blessed One said, "Monks, this boy is not wise only now; in the past too, he was wise. Having seen that man's fault once, he did not associate with him again," and He brought forth the past story.

[The Past Story:] In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a householder's family. When he reached maturity, he made his living by selling grain. Another man, a snake charmer, trained a monkey, made it hold medicine, and made his living by having that monkey play with a snake.

When a festival was proclaimed in Bārāṇasī, the snake charmer, wishing to enjoy the festival, said, "Do not neglect this monkey," and left the monkey in the hands of the grain merchant. He enjoyed the festival and, on the seventh day, went to the grain merchant and asked, "Where is the monkey?"

The monkey, upon hearing its master's voice, quickly came out from the grain store.

Then, the snake charmer struck the monkey against a stone with a bamboo split, took it, went to a park, tied it in a suitable place, and fell asleep. The monkey, knowing that the snake charmer was asleep, loosened its bonds, escaped, climbed a mango tree, ate a ripe mango, and dropped the seeds onto the snake charmer's body.

The snake charmer woke up, looked up, and seeing the monkey, thought, "I will deceive him with sweet words, make him come down from the tree, and catch him." He then spoke this first verse to coax him:

17. "You shall be my only son,
And you shall be the master of our family.
Come down from the tree, Sālaka;
Let us now go home."

[The meaning is:] "Sālaka, Sālaka. You shall be the only son in our house. You shall be the master of my wealth. Come down from the mango tree. Now, let us go to our home. Come."
245:
18. "Do you not think me kind-hearted, though you beat me with a bamboo stick? We delight in the ripe mango grove; go you to your little home as you please."

He spoke this verse which completes the two. 

O snake charmer! Do you not think of me as one having a kind heart? Because you beat me with a bamboo stick, for that reason, we shall delight in the grove of ripe mangoes. You, go to your little home as you please.

When the snake charmer woke up and looked, he saw the monkey. Thinking to deceive him with sweet and pleasant words to make him descend from the mango tree so he could catch him, he tried to entice the monkey.

Having heard those words, the monkey said:

Having spoken thus, he entered the forest. The snake charmer, being displeased, went to his home.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the novice was the monkey, the Great Elder was the snake charmer, and I myself was the grain merchant."

## Even if seen once as an offender, one is not loved; not only now, but in the past life too.

The Sālaka Jātaka is finished.

## 10. Kapi Jātaka
## The Monkey in Hermit's Guise

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Kapi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ayaṃ isī upasamasamyame rato," concerning a certain hypocritical monk.

To elaborate on that story, the hypocritical nature of that monk became well-known among the monks. In the Hall of Truth, the monks initiated a discussion: "Friends, this named monk, having ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation which leads out of suffering, fulfills the practice of hypocrisy."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "With such a discussion, Venerable Sir," He said, "Monks, not only now is this monk hypocritical; in the past also, because of fire, he became a monkey and practiced hypocrisy," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsī. When he reached the age of maturity, at a time when his son was able to run about here and there, his wife died. Taking his son in his arms, he entered the Himavanta, ordained as an ascetic, made his young son a young ascetic, and lived in a leaf-roofed hermitage.
246:
19. "This hermit, delighted in peace and restraint, stands afflicted by the fear of the cold. Come, let him enter this little hut, to dispel all cold and distress."

He spoke this first verse.

Father, this hermit, who is delighted in peace—the calming of passions and such—and in restraint—the guarding of virtue—stands afflicted by the danger of cold caused by the rain and wind. Now, let this hermit enter this little hut. Let him dispel all cold and distress.

During the rainy season, when the rain fell in an unbroken stream, a monkey, oppressed by the cold, went about with teeth chattering and shivering. The Bodhisatta brought large logs of wood, lit a fire, and lay down on a couch. The Bodhisatta's young son sat massaging the Bodhisatta's feet.

That monkey, having put on and wrapped himself in the bark garments belonging to another deceased ascetic, placing a black antelope skin on his shoulder, and taking a carrying pole and water pot, arrived in the guise of an ascetic and stood at the door of the leaf-roofed hermitage, performing a hypocritical act for the sake of the fire.

The young ascetic saw him and, wishing to entreat his father, saying, "Father, a hermit stands shivering, oppressed by the cold. Call that hermit to this fire; he will warm himself," he said:

When the Bodhisatta heard his son's words, he stood up and looked; knowing the state of the monkey, he said:

20. "This is no hermit delighted in peace and restraint; this is a monkey, whose range is the branches of noble trees. He is a spoiler, a harasser, and base; if he should enter, he would spoil our hut."

He spoke this verse which completes the two.

Dear son, this creature is not a hermit delighted in peace—the calming of passions and such—and in restraint—the guarding of virtue. This creature is a monkey, who frequents the branches of noble trees. That monkey is a spoiler, and he is also a harasser.
247:
And he is base. If he should enter this hut, he would destroy the hut.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta took a firebrand, threatened the monkey, and made him flee. That monkey leaped away and fled into the forest. He never came back to that place again. The Bodhisatta developed the supernormal powers and the meditative attainments, and taught the preliminary work for the kasina to the young ascetic. That young ascetic also developed the supernormal powers and the meditative attainments. Both of them, with their meditative absorptions unimpaired, were destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, saying, "Monks, not only now, but from long ago, this person has been hypocritical," and having proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, some monks became Stream-enterers, some became Once-returners, some became Non-returners, and some became Arahats. How did He identify the Jātaka? "Monks, the monk who is now hypocritical was the monkey then, Rāhula was the son then, and I myself was the father ascetic then." Thus He identified the Jātaka.

## One with a habitual tendency shows deceptions accordingly.

The Kapi Jātaka is finished.

The Singāla Vagga, the tenth.

Its summary of titles:
Sabbadāṭhī, Sunakha, Guttila, Vigaticchā, Mūlapariyāya, Bālovāda, Pādañjali, Kiṃsukopama, Sālaka, and Kapi—these are the ten.

Then the summary of the chapters:
Daḷha Vagga, Santhava, Kalyāṇadhamma, Asadisa, Rūhaka, Daḷha Vagga (repeated), Bīraṇathambhaka, Kāsāva, Upāhana, and Singāla—there are ten chapters in the Book of the Twos.

The Commentary on the Duka Nipāta is finished.
248:
## 1. Saṅkappavagga
## 1. Saṅkapparāga Jātaka
## The Garment Slips, the Vehicle of Jhāna Falls

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Saṅkapparāga Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with 'Saṅkapparāga-dhotena,' concerning a monk who was dissatisfied with the holy life.

A certain young man of good family living in Sāvatthī, having dedicated his life to the Dispensation, ordained as a monk. One day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a woman beautifully adorned. Sensual desire (kāmarāga) arose in him, and he lived in discontent. His teachers, preceptors, and others, seeing his dissatisfaction, asked the reason. Knowing his desire to return to the lay life, they said, 'Friend, the Buddha removes the defilements of those oppressed by sensual desire and the like, reveals the Truths, and grants the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) and so forth. Come, let us take you to the Teacher.' They then took him to the Buddha.

When the Omniscient Buddha asked, 'Monks, why have you brought this monk against his will?' they informed Him of the matter. The Omniscient Buddha asked, 'Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?' When the monk replied, 'It is true, Bhante,' the Buddha asked, 'For what reason?' The monk then informed Him of the matter.

Then the Omniscient Buddha said to him, 'Monk, in the past, women have caused defilements to arise even in pure beings whose defilements were suppressed by the power of jhāna. Why would they not defile a hollow person like you? Even pure beings become defiled; even those endowed with great fame fall into disrepute. What then can be said of those who are not pure? How could the wind that can shake Mount Sineru not shake a dry, old leaf? This defilement could even disturb one who would realize the Truths while sitting at the Terrace of Enlightenment (Bodhimanda).'

'How could that defilement not oppress someone like you?' Having said this, at their request, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin Mahāsāla family with a wealth of eighty crores. When he came of age, he studied all the arts in Takkasilā, returned to Bārāṇasī, and maintained a family. After his parents passed away, he performed their funeral rites and, while looking over the gold and silver treasures, he reflected: 'This wealth is evident, but those who owned this wealth are no longer seen.'
249:
He was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and sweat poured from his body. Having lived in the world of men for a long time, he gave great alms, abandoned sensual pleasures, and left his weeping relatives. He entered the Himālaya and became an ascetic. Having built a leaf-hut in a pleasant place, he lived on forest roots and fruits. Before long, he attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lived for a long time sporting in jhāna. 

Then he thought: 'If I go to the world of men and partake of salt and acidic foods, my body will become firm, and I will also practice the deportment of walking. Those who give alms or pay respects to a monk endowed with virtue like me will fill the city of heaven.' Having thought thus—

The Bodhisatta descended from the Himālaya and, wandering by stages, reached Bārāṇasī. At sunset, looking for a place to stay, he saw the royal park and thought, 'This park is suitable for seclusion; I will stay here.' He entered the park, sat at the foot of a tree, spent the night in the bliss of jhāna, and at dawn, after attending to his bodily needs, he neatly arranged his matted hair, bark-garments, and antelope skin. Carrying his alms-bowl, with calmed senses, a peaceful mind, and perfect deportment, looking only a yoke's length ahead, he entered the city for alms, drawing the eyes of the people with his beauty and splendor. He eventually reached the gate of the King's palace.

The King, walking on the grand terrace, saw the Bodhisatta through a lattice window and was instantly impressed by his deportment. He thought, 'If there is such a thing as the Dhamma of the virtuous, it must surely exist within this ascetic.' He commanded an official, 'Go, invite that ascetic.' The official went, paid respects, took the alms-bowl, and said, 'Bhante, the King summons you.' The Bodhisatta replied, 'Great meritorious donor, the King does not know us.' The official said, 'In that case, Bhante, please stay here until I return,' and went to inform the King.

The King said, 'We have no regular ascetic teacher. Go, bring that ascetic.' He himself extended his hands through the lattice window, paid respects, and said, 'Bhante, please come this way.' The Bodhisatta gave his alms-bowl into the official's hand and ascended to the grand terrace.

Then the King, having paid respects to the Bodhisatta, seated him on the royal throne and served him with rice gruel, hard food, and soft food that he had prepared for himself. After the meal, the King asked him questions. Being greatly pleased by the answers, he paid respects and asked, 'Bhante, where do you reside? From where have you come?'
250: "Great King, we live in the Himavanta," they said when asked where they lived and where they came from. When asked for what reason they came, they replied, "Great King, during the rainy season, it is proper to obtain a permanent residence. That is why we have come." The King said, "In that case, Bhante, please stay in the royal garden. You will not lack the four requisites, and I shall attain merit that leads to the heavenly realm." Having received their consent, after his morning meal, the King went to the garden with the Bodhisatta, had a leaf-hut and a walkway built, and provided places for the night and day. He prepared the requisites of a monk and, saying, "Bhante, please live in comfort," he entrusted them to the gardener. From then on, the Bodhisatta lived in that very garden for twelve years. Then one day, the King's border region was plundered by rebels. Wishing to go and suppress it, he addressed the Queen, "Dear, you should remain in the city." When she asked, "On what account do you say this, O King?", the King replied, "On account of the virtuous ascetic, dear." The Queen said, "O King, I will not be negligent toward the noble ascetic. Taking care of the noble ascetic shall be my responsibility. You may go without any anxiety." After the King had departed, the Queen served the Bodhisatta with great respect, just as the King had instructed. As for the Bodhisatta, after the King's departure, he would come at his usual time or at a time of his choosing to the palace to have his meal. Then one day, when the Bodhisatta was very late, the Queen prepared all kinds of food, bathed, adorned herself, and laid out a small couch. While waiting for the Bodhisatta's arrival, she lay down, wearing a smooth cloth loosely. The Bodhisatta, noting the time, took his alms bowl and came through the air to the window. Hearing the sound of his bark-cloth robe, the Queen rose suddenly, and the smooth cloth slipped from her body. The Bodhisatta, seeing the unwholesome object, broke his restraint of the senses and looked with the perception of beauty. Then, his lust, which had been calmed by the power of jhāna, rose up like a cobra raising its hood when released from a basket, or like the sap of a tree when struck by a hatchet. Along with the arising of lust, the factors of jhāna disappeared. His senses became impaired. He became like a crow with clipped wings.
251: The Bodhisatta was unable to sit and eat as before; even when invited to sit, he did not. Then the Queen put all the food into the Bodhisatta's alms bowl. Although previously he would eat and then depart through the window into the air, on that day he was unable to go that way. Taking the bowl, he descended by the great staircase and went to the garden. The Queen knew that his mind was attached to her. Having gone to the garden, without eating the food, he placed the bowl under the couch and lay there for seven days, lamenting: "Such is the beauty of the Queen's hands, such is the beauty of her feet, such is her waist, such are her thighs," and so on. The food became rotten and full of blue flies. Then the King, having suppressed the border rebellion, returned. He circled the decorated city in a clockwise direction and, before going to the palace, went to the garden to see the Bodhisatta. Seeing the monastery filled with rubbish, he thought, "He must have gone elsewhere." Opening the door of the leaf-hut and entering, he saw him lying there and thought, "He must be unwell." He had the rotten food thrown away, the hut cleaned, and asked, "Bhante, what is your ailment?" "Great King, I am pierced," he said. The King thought, "My enemies, unable to find an opportunity against me, must have come and pierced this ascetic to weaken my support." He turned the body over to look for the wound, but seeing none, he asked, "Bhante, where are you pierced?" The Bodhisatta said, "Great King, no one else pierced me. I have pierced myself in my own heart." Sitting up, he spoke this verse: 1. "By the shaft of lustful thought, polished by imagination, and sharpened by thought..."
252:
Not adorned, yet auspicious, and not made by a fletcher.
2. Not released from the ear-tip, nor fletched with peacock feathers.
By that [arrow] I am pierced in the heart, which burns all limbs.
3. I do not see the wound from which blood should flow.
As far as the mind is unwholesome, I have brought suffering upon myself.

He spoke these verses.

O Great King (Mahārāja). Washed with the water of passion (saṅkapparāga-dhotena) associated with sensual thought. Sharpened on the stone of thought (vitakka-nisitena). Auspicious (bhadrena). Unadorned (nālaṅkatena). Not sharpened by fletchers (usukārākatena). Not released after being drawn to the tip of the right ear (na kaṇṇāyata-muttena). Not fletched with feathers of peacocks or vultures (nāpi morūpasevinā). Capable of burning all limbs (sabbaṅgaparidāhinā). By that defilement (tena), my (me) heart (hadaye) is pierced (viddho). I am (amhi).

O Great King. From which piercing of the arrow of defilement (yato āvedhā), blood (ruhiraṃ) should flow (assawe). I do not see (na passāmi) that wound (taṃ āvedhañca). To a great extent (yāva ativiya), the mind of passion (cittaṃ) has increased (vaḍḍhitaṃ) through improper attention (ayoniso). I (me) have myself (sayaṃ) brought (ābhataṃ) suffering (dukkhaṃ).

In this way, the Bodhisatta preached the Dhamma to the King with these verses. Having the King step outside the leaf-hut, he performed the preliminary kasina exercises, regained his lost jhāna, emerged from the leaf-hut, and while sitting in the air, he exhorted the King, saying, "O Great King, I shall go to the Himavantā." Even though it was said, "Venerable Sir, it is not proper to go to the Himavantā," he replied, "O Great King, because of living in this place, I have fallen into such corruption. Now it is not proper to live here." While the King was still pleading, he flew into the air, returned to the Himavantā, stayed there for the remainder of his life, and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who was dissatisfied with the monkhood was established in the fruit of Arahantship. Some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmi), some Non-returners (Anāgāmi), and some Arahants. As for how the Jātaka was identified: "At that time, the King of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, and I myself was the ascetic."

## Sensual Disease, Internal Affliction, Cured by the Medicine of Wisdom

The Saṅkapparāga Jātaka ends.
253:
## 2. Tilamuṭṭhi Jātaka
## Three Handfuls of Sesame, Three Strokes of the Stick

### Present Story
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha told this Tilamuṭṭhi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Ajjāpi me taṃ manasi,” concerning a certain wrathful monk.

A certain monk was reportedly wrathful and full of distress. Even when spoken to slightly, he would become angry and resentful, displaying anger, malice, and discontent. One day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, a monk named so-and-so is wrathful and full of distress. He goes about crackling like salt thrown into a stove. Having gone forth in the Buddha’s Dispensation, which is free from anger, he is unable to suppress even a little anger.”

The All-Knowing Buddha, hearing their conversation, sent a monk to summon that monk.
