He asked, “Is it true, monk, that you are wrathful?” When the monk replied, “It is true, Bhante,” the Buddha said, “Monks, not only now is he wrathful; in the past, he was also wrathful,” and he brought forth the past story.

### Past Story
Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, he had a son named Prince Brahmadatta.

Ancient kings used to send their sons to distant foreign lands to study, even if there were world-renowned teachers (disāpāmokkha) in their own city, thinking, “In this way, they will be free from pride and arrogance, they will be able to endure cold and heat, and they will know the ways of the world.”

Therefore, King Brahmadatta summoned his son, who was sixteen years old, gave him a pair of single-layered sandals, a leaf-umbrella, and a thousand pieces of money, and sent him away, saying, “Son, go to Takkasilā and learn the arts.” The Prince said, “Very well,” paid respects to his parents, and departed. In due course, he reached Takkasilā and asked for the teacher’s house. The teacher, having finished teaching the arts to his young students, was walking to and fro at the door of his house. Reaching the house, the Prince saw the teacher from where he stood; he removed his sandals, put down his umbrella, paid respects to the teacher, and stood there.

The teacher, recognizing the Prince’s exhaustion, had hospitality shown to the guest. After the Prince had eaten and rested for a while, he approached the teacher, paid respects, and stood there. When asked, “Son, where have you come from?” he replied, “From Bārāṇasī.” “Whose son are you?” “The son of the King of Bārāṇasī.” “For what purpose have you come?” “I have come to learn the arts.” When asked, “Have you brought the teacher’s fee, or do you wish to be a student who serves (dhammantevāsika)?” he replied, “I have brought the teacher’s fee.” He placed the bundle of a thousand pieces of money at the teacher’s feet, paid respects, and sat in a suitable place.
254:
The student youths (Dhamma-pupils) perform the teacher's work by day and learn their arts by night. However, the students who pay the teacher's fee live like the eldest sons in the house and only learn their arts. Therefore, that teacher of Takkasilā also taught the art to Prince Brahmadatta easily under an auspicious constellation.

While the prince was learning his arts, one day he went to bathe with the teacher. At that time, an old woman had whitened some sesame seeds, spread them out, and was sitting there guarding them. Seeing the white sesame seeds, the prince desired to eat them, took a handful, and ate them. The old woman, thinking that this youth was simply greedy, said nothing and remained silent.

On the next day, the prince did the same at that same time. That old woman said nothing to the prince. On the third day, he did the same again. Then the old woman, seeing this, cried out with her arms raised, saying, 'The world-renowned (Disāpāmokkha) teacher is letting his students rob me!'

The teacher turned back and asked, 'Mother, what is this matter?' She replied, 'Master, your pupil ate a handful of my whitened sesame seeds today, a handful yesterday, and a handful the day before. If he continues to eat like this, will he not exhaust all my property?' The teacher said, 'Mother, do not cry; I will have him pay you the price.'
255:
## 4. Even today, it is in my mind, how you, for a handful of sesame,
Having seized me by the arm, beat me with a stick.
## 5. Do you not delight in life, that you have come, O Brahmin?
Having seized me by the arm, you beat me three times.
He spoke these verses.
O Brahmin, you, because of a handful of sesame, having had me seized by the arm, with a piece of bamboo, beat me; that beating, even to this day, I remember in my mind.
O Brahmin, for what reason have you come to my presence? Because you had me seized by the arm and beat me three times, therefore, do you not indeed delight in life?
## 6. A noble person who restrains one performing an ignoble act with a stick—
That is instruction, not enmity; thus the wise know it.
He spoke this verse to complete the three.
Great King, a noble person of virtuous conduct who restrains one performing an ignoble act with punishment—that restraint is called instruction. That restraint is not enmity. Thus the wise know it.
The old woman said, "Master, I do not desire a price; just discipline this youth so that he does not do this again."
The teacher said, "Mother, if that is so, then watch," and he had two youths seize the prince by his hands and feet. Taking a piece of bamboo, he struck him three times on the back, saying, "Do not do this again." The prince became angry, his eyes turning red, and he looked at the teacher from his feet to the hair on his head. The teacher knew the state of the prince's anger.
The prince, having completed his education, kept the teacher's offense in his heart, thinking, "I will kill this teacher." When it was time to leave, he paid homage to the teacher and said, "Teacher, when I become the King of Bārāṇasī, I will send for you. At that time, please come." Having received the teacher's promise as if out of affection, he departed.
Then the prince arrived at Bārāṇasī, paid homage to his parents, and demonstrated his skills. The King, seeing his son alive and wishing to see his son's royal glory while he himself was still living, established him in the kingship.
256:
That King Brahmadatta, while enjoying the royal splendor, remembered the offense committed by the teacher and, becoming angry, sent a messenger with gifts to the teacher to summon him so that he might kill him.

The teacher, thinking that it would not be possible to make the King of Bārāṇasī understand while he was still young, did not go. When the King reached middle age, thinking, 'Now I shall be able to make him understand,' he went and stood at the palace gate, sending word, 'The teacher of Takkasilā has arrived.' The King was pleased and had the Brahmin summoned. Upon seeing the Brahmin approaching him, the King became angry, his eyes turned red, and he addressed his ministers, 'O ministers, even today, the place where the teacher struck me still hurts. Today the teacher has come with death on his forehead, thinking "I shall die." Today the teacher's life is no more.'

Hearing these words spoken as a threat of death, the teacher said:

'Great King, in such a matter, it is not proper to bear a grudge. Great King, if I had not disciplined you, thereafter you would have robbed bean cakes, sesame treats, and various fruits. By such robberies, you would have progressed to breaking into houses, robbing travelers, and raiding villages. Then, being captured with the stolen goods as a rebel against the King and presented to the King, the King would have ordered, "Go, execute the punishment fitting for this thief," and you would have faced execution. How could such royal glory as this ever have belonged to you? It is because of me, your teacher, that you enjoy this splendor.' Thus the teacher made the King understand.

The ministers in attendance, hearing the teacher's words, said, 'Great King, this splendor of yours truly belongs to the teacher.' At that moment, the King recognized the teacher's gratitude and said, 'Teacher, I give you all my splendor.' The teacher declined, saying, 'Great King, I have no desire for kingship.'
257:
The King sent for the teacher's wife and children from Takkasilā, bestowed great wealth and status upon them, appointed the teacher as the royal chaplain (purohita), and treated him as a father. Abiding by the teacher's advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and was destined for heaven.

Identification of the Jātaka: The Master, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the angry monk was established in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). Many other monks became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners. How did he identify the Jātaka? 'At that time, the King was the angry monk, and I myself was the teacher.' Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## He who disciplines the offender, recognize him as the teacher.

The Tila-muṭṭhi Jātaka is concluded.

## 3. Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka

## The Jeweled Necklace

The All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka adorned with the verse beginning with 'Mamannapānaṃ' while residing at the Aggāḷava Cetiya near the city of Āḷavī, concerning the training rule on hut-building (Kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada).

To elaborate: When the monks of Āḷavī were building huts by their own labor, they were constantly begging and making requests, saying, 'Give us a man, give us a laborer,' and so forth. Being oppressed by these requests, the people would flee upon seeing the monks.
258:
At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa went to the city of Āḷavī for alms. Upon seeing the Elder Mahākassapa, the people behaved in the same way as before. After finishing his meal and returning from his alms round, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the monks: 'Friends, formerly alms were easy to obtain in this city of Āḷavī; why are they now difficult to obtain?' Having heard the reason, and when the All-Knowing Buddha arrived at Āḷavī and was staying at the Aggāḷava Cetiya, he approached the Buddha and reported the matter.

The All-Knowing Buddha then convened the Sangha of monks and questioned the monks of Āḷavī: 'Is it true, monks, that you are building huts with materials requested by yourselves?' When they replied, 'It is true, Blessed One,' he rebuked them, saying:

'Monks, this begging is unpleasant even to the Nāga kings who live in the Nāga realm filled with the seven kinds of jewels; how much more so to humans? For those who must produce even a single kahāpaṇa or a single kyat, it is like the time of peeling a slab of stone from a rock.' (Meaning: Just as it is hard to chip stone from a rock, it is very difficult for people to earn even a single kyat or kahāpaṇa.) Having said this, he remained silent. When the monks requested him, he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy Brāhmaṇa family. When the Bodhisatta was old enough to run about, another meritorious being was born in his mother's womb.

When the two brothers reached adulthood, they were moved by the death of their parents and became ascetics. They built leaf-huts and lived by the banks of the Gaṅgā River. Of the two brothers, the elder brother's hut was upstream, and the younger brother's hut was downstream.

Then one day, a Nāga king named Maṇikaṇṭha left the Nāga realm and, wandering along the banks of the Gaṅgā in the guise of a youth, reached the younger ascetic's hermitage, paid respects, and sat down pleasantly.
259:
7. Abundant and excellent food and drink arise for me because of this jewel. I will not give it to you; you are too demanding. Nor will I come to your hermitage again.

8. Like a youth with a sword sharpened on stone in his hand, you terrify me by begging for this stone. I will not give it to you; you are too demanding. Nor will I come to your hermitage again.

He spoke these verses.

O ascetic! Because of this jewel, abundant and excellent divine food and divine drink arise for me. I will not give that jewel to you. You are one who begs excessively. I shall not come to your hermitage again.

O ascetic! Just as a youth with a sword sharpened on stone with oil in his hand threatens someone, so do you, by begging for this stone (jewel), threaten me. You are one who begs excessively. I will not give that jewel to you. I shall not come to your hermitage again.

They had become intimate, speaking words that brought mutual joy. They could not bear to be apart. The Nāga king Maṇikaṇṭha would constantly visit the younger ascetic and sit talking with him. When it was time to leave, out of affection for the ascetic, he would shed his youthful form, encircle the ascetic with his coils, embrace him, and stay for a while with his large hood spread over the ascetic's head. Then, letting go of that affection, he would uncoil himself, pay respects to the ascetic, and return to his own place.

The ascetic, out of fear of the Nāga Maṇikaṇṭha, became thin. He became unsightly, pale like a withered leaf, and his body was covered in protruding veins. One day, the younger brother went to the elder brother. The elder brother asked, 'Venerable ascetic, why are you thin, unsightly, pale like a withered leaf, and with veins standing out on your body?'

The younger brother told him the reason. When asked, 'Do you not wish for that Nāga to come?' he said he did not. When asked, 'What ornament does that Nāga king wear when he comes to you?' he replied, 'He comes wearing a precious jewel.'
260:
He spoke this third verse:

9. One should not beg from him whose love one wishes to keep;
For by excessive begging, one becomes disliked.
The Naga, when asked for his jewel by the Brahmin,
Went away and was seen no more.

"My younger brother, if one knows that a certain possession is dear to a person, one should not beg for that object. Because of excessive begging, hatred arises. The Naga king, having been asked for his jewel by the younger ascetic (the Brahmin), from that time of begging onwards, went to a place where my younger brother could not see him."

"That being so, before that Naga king comes to your presence and sits down, while he is still approaching, ask him to give you the jewel. If you beg in this way, the Naga king will depart without even encircling you with his coils. On the next day, stand at the door of the leaf-hut and ask for the jewel as he approaches. On the third day, stand by the bank of the Ganges and ask for the jewel as he emerges from the water. If you beg in this manner, that Naga will never come to your presence again."

The younger ascetic agreed, saying, "Very well," and went to his own leaf-hut. When the Naga came the next day, while he was still standing, the ascetic begged, "Give me this jewel which is your ornament." The Naga king fled without even sitting down. Then on the second day, as the Naga was approaching the door of the leaf-hut, the ascetic said, "Yesterday you did not give me the jewel-treasure; give it to me today." The Naga king fled without even entering the hut. On the third day, as the Naga stood emerging from the water, the ascetic said, "It has been three days now that I have been asking you for the jewel; give me that jewel-treasure now."

The Naga king, standing in the water, wishing to reject the ascetic—

Having spoken thus, the Naga king dived into the water, went to his own Naga realm, and never returned. Then that ascetic, because of not seeing the beautiful Naga king, became exceedingly thin and haggard. He became pale like a withered leaf, with his body covered in protruding veins.

Then the elder ascetic, wanting to know the condition of his younger brother, went to him. Seeing his younger brother so exceedingly pale, he said, "Venerable one, why have you become so exceedingly pale?" Hearing the words, "I am pale because of not seeing that beautiful Naga," and realizing, "This ascetic is unable to live without the Naga king,"—
261:
Having spoken thus to the younger brother, the elder ascetic consoled him, saying, "From today onwards, do not grieve," and returned to his own leaf-hut. Later, both brothers developed the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and attainments (samāpatti) and became destined for the Brahma world.

To conclude the Jātaka, the Teacher said, "Monks, even for Nagas living in the Naga realm full of the seven kinds of treasures, begging is unpleasant. How much more so for human beings?" Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he identified the birth story: "At that time, the younger brother was Ānanda, and the elder brother was I myself."

## Begging, borrowing, and hiring are medicines of hatred; they should be avoided from afar.

The Maṇikaṇṭha Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka
## The Sindhu Horse

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bhūtvā tiṇaparighāsaṃ," concerning the Elder Sāriputta.

To elaborate: Once, after the All-Enlightened One had spent the vassa (rainy season) in Sāvatthī and completed his wandering, he returned. The people, thinking, "We shall perform hospitality for the visitors," gave a great alms-giving to the Saṅgha with the Buddha at its head. They appointed a certain monk as the announcer (dhammaghosaka) at the monastery. That monk assigned as many monks as the people requested.

Then a certain poor old woman, having prepared a single portion of food, went to the announcer monk late in the day after he had already assigned monks to various people, and said, "Please give me one monk."

He replied, "I have already assigned all the monks. However, the Elder Sāriputta is still in the monastery. Give the alms-food to the Elder Sāriputta."

With a joyful heart, the old woman said, "Very well." She stood at the gate-tower of Jetavana, and when the Elder Sāriputta arrived, she paid homage, took the bowl from his hand, and invited him to her house to be seated.

Many faithful families heard that a certain old woman had invited the Captain of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) to her house and seated him there. Among them, King Pasenadi of Kosala, hearing of this, sent her a robe and a thousand-piece purse of money along with fine food, saying, "While serving my Lord, let her wear this robe, use these coins, and serve the Elder."

Just as the King sent gifts, so too did Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, and the great laywoman Visākhā. Other families also sent coins in amounts of one hundred or two hundred according to their means. Thus, in a single day, that old woman received one hundred thousand pieces of money.
262:
The Venerable Sāriputta drank the gruel offered by that old woman, ate the food and snacks she had prepared, gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), established the old woman in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), and returned to the monastery.
In the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion about the Elder's virtues: "Friends, the Elder Sāriputta, the Captain of the Dhamma, has released an aged housewife from poverty; he was her support. He ate the food given by her without any disgust." The Teacher (the Buddha) arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such," he said, "Monks, not only now has Sāriputta become the refuge of this woman, and not only now does he eat the food given by her without disgust; in the past also he ate it," and he brought forth the past.
The Story of the Past: Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of horse traders in Uttarāpatha. Five hundred horse traders from the Uttarāpatha region would bring horses to Bārāṇasī to sell.
One horse trader took five hundred horses and set out on the road to Bārāṇasī. Between the journey to Bārāṇasī, in a place neither too near nor too far, there was a market town. In that market town, there had formerly been a merchant of great wealth. His house was large, but the family had gradually come to ruin. Only one old woman remained, and she lived in that house.
Then that horse trader reached that market town and, saying "I will pay rent," took up residence in that old woman's house and kept the horses in a suitable place. On that very day, a thoroughbred mare (ājānīya-vaḷavā) gave birth. The horse trader stayed for two or three days to let the horses regain their strength, and then, thinking "I will see the King," he took the horses and departed.
Then the old woman said to the horse trader, "Give me the rent for staying in the house." When he said, "Very well, Mother, I shall give it," she said, "Dear son, if you are giving rent, give me this young foal as part of the payment." The horse trader did as the old woman said, gave the foal, and left. The old woman developed a motherly affection for that foal and raised it by giving it broken rice, rice crusts, and leftover grass.
Later, when the Bodhisatta was traveling with five hundred horses, he took up residence in that house. Because of the scent from the place where the Sindhu foal that ate broken rice stayed, not a single horse dared to enter the house.
263:
10. Having eaten grass remnants, having eaten rice-scum and bran,
That was your food before; why do you not eat it now?
He spoke this first verse.
*Assapotaka*, O foal. *Tvaṃ*, you. *Tiṇaparighāsaṃ*, the leftover grass. *Bhuttā*, having eaten. *Ācāmakuṇḍakaṃ*, the rice crusts and rice-bran. *Bhuttā*, having eaten. *Vaḍḍhito*, you have grown. *Etaṃ*, this food of rice-bran gruel. *Te*, your. *Bhojanaṃ*, food. *Āsi*, was. *Kasmā*, why. *Dāni-idāni*, now. *Etaṃ*, this rice-bran gruel. *Na bhuñjasi*, do you not eat?
The Bodhisatta asked, "Mother, is there a horse in this house?" "Son, there is no other horse, but I have raised a foal as my own son; he is here," she said. "Mother, where is that foal?" he asked. "He has gone to graze, son," she said. When he asked, "At what time will he return, mother?" she said, "He will return in the evening, son." The Bodhisatta, waiting for the foal's arrival, stayed while keeping his horses outside.
The Sindhava foal returned in the evening after grazing. The Bodhisatta, seeing the Sindhava foal that ate rice-bran and considering its marks, realized, "This Sindhava foal is a horse of priceless value," and thinking, "It is proper to take him after paying a price to the old woman," he waited. The Sindhava foal entered the house and stayed in his own place. At that moment, the other horses were able to enter the house.
The Bodhisatta stayed for two or three days, and after letting the horses regain their strength, as he was preparing to leave, he said, "Mother, take a price for the foal and give him to me." "Son, horse trader, what are you saying? Is there such a thing as a woman who sells her own son?" the old woman said. "Mother, what food do you feed this foal to raise him?" the Bodhisatta asked. "Son, horse trader, I feed him broken rice, rice crusts, and leftover grass, and I give him rice-bran gruel to drink," the old woman said. "Mother, if I get this foal, I will feed him fine rice. I will hang a cloth canopy over his stable and place him on a rug-covered platform," the Bodhisatta said. "Son, horse trader, if you do so, my son will enjoy happiness. Take my son and go," she said.
Then the Bodhisatta placed six thousand pieces of money at the Sindhava foal's four feet, tail, and mouth, and had the old woman dress in new clothes and stand before the Sindhava foal. The Sindhava foal opened his eyes, looked at his mother, and shed tears. The old woman also stroked the Sindhava foal's back and said, "My dear son, I have received the reward for raising you. Go now, my son," and she gave him away. The Sindhava foal followed.
264:
11. Where they do not know a person, either by birth or by conduct,
There, O Great Merchant, even rice-scum and bran are plenty.

12. But you indeed know me, what kind of noble horse I am.
Knowing my own strength, and relying on you who knows it, I will not eat your bran.

He spoke these verses.

O Great Merchant! In whatever place they do not know a person, either by birth or by conduct—meaning they do not know whether one is of noble birth or not, or whether one is possessed of good conduct or not—in that place, I eat even rice-scum and bran in abundance.

What kind of horse this is, an excellent horse—this you indeed know. I, who know my own strength, relying on you who knows my strength, will not eat your bran-gruel.

The Bodhisatta, having prepared food for the young Sindh horse the next day, thought, "Does this young Sindh horse know its own strength or not? I shall test this young Sindh horse." Thus, he poured bran-gruel into the trough and gave it. The young Sindh horse said, "I will not eat that food; I have no desire to drink the gruel." The Bodhisatta, wishing to test the young Sindh horse—

When he spoke thus, having heard those words, the young Sindh horse said:

"You did not buy me by giving six thousand pieces of silver with the intention of making me eat bran-gruel."

When the horse spoke thus, having heard those words, the Bodhisatta said, "I did this only to test you; do not be angry." He then fed the young Sindh horse with excellent food and took him to the palace courtyard. He placed five hundred horses on one side, and on the other side, he surrounded an area with exquisite screens, spread a carpet below, fastened a cloth canopy above, and placed the young Sindh horse there.

The King came and, looking at the horses, asked, "Why is this horse kept separately?" When the Bodhisatta replied, "Great King, this horse is a Sindh horse; it is an extraordinary horse among these horses," the King asked, "O horse merchant, is the Sindh horse good?" The Bodhisatta said, "Yes, Great King, it is good." When the King said he wished to see the horse's speed, the Bodhisatta harnessed the horse, mounted it, and said, "Great King, please watch." He then cleared the people away and galloped the horse in the palace courtyard.

The entire palace courtyard appeared as if it were surrounded by a continuous line of horses. Again, the Bodhisatta said, "Great King, behold the speed of the young Sindh horse," and let him go. Not a single person could see him. Again, he wrapped a red cloth around the horse's belly and let him go; they saw only the red cloth. After that, he let the Sindh horse run on the surface of the water of a garden pond within the city. As the Sindh horse ran on the surface of the water, even the tips of his hooves did not get wet. Again, as he ran over the lotus leaves, he did not cause even a single lotus leaf to sink into the water.
265:
Having thus demonstrated the horse's speed and perfection, the Bodhisatta dismounted, clapped his hands, and held out his palm. The horse came and, bringing its four feet together, stood upon the palm of his hand. Then the Great Being said to the King, "Great King, if this young horse were to show its speed in every way, the kingdom bounded by the ocean would not be enough to contain the momentum of its speed."

The King, seeing the horse's speed, gave half of the kingdom to the Great Being and, having consecrated the young Sindh horse, made him the State Mangala Horse. The King loved and cherished that Mangala horse. The honors and offerings for the Mangala horse were great. The horse's dwelling place became like the King's own decorated inner chamber. They smeared the ground with four kinds of perfumes. They hung garlands of scents and flowers. Above, a cloth canopy studded with golden stars was fastened. It was surrounded on all sides by exquisite screens. Lamps of scented oil were kept burning constantly. Even in the place where the horse passed its waste, they placed a golden vessel. He was always fed only with food fit for a king.

From the time that Mangala horse arrived, the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa came into the hands of the King of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī, established in the advice of the Bodhisatta, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and was destined for heaven.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many monks became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, and Arahants. How did he identify the birth? "The old woman then was this same old woman now; the Sindh horse was Sāriputta; the King was Ānanda; and the horse merchant was I myself." Thus he identified the birth.

## Show your wisdom before the wise; show your wealth before the wealthy.

End of the Kuṇḍakakucchisindhava Jātaka.
266:
## 5. Suka Jātaka
## The Parrot that Died of Overeating

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Suka Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Yāva so mattamaññāsī," concerning a certain monk who died of indigestion after eating excessively.

When that monk passed away, other monks gathered in the Dhamma Hall and spoke of his lack of virtue, saying, "Friends, a certain monk, not knowing the capacity of his own stomach, ate excessively and, being unable to digest it, has passed away." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?" When they replied, "It is such and such a matter," the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now has this monk died due to overeating; in the past, he also died because of excessive eating." Having said this, he remained silent. Being requested by the monks, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the parrot species in the Himavanta region and became the king of many thousands of parrots living in a part of the Himavanta bordering the ocean. He had a son. When the son reached full strength, the Bodhisatta’s eyesight became weak. It is said that parrots have great speed, and therefore, in their old age, their eyesight is the first to weaken. The Bodhisatta’s son kept his parents in the nest and supported them by bringing food. One day, having gone to the feeding ground and standing on a mountain peak, he looked out over the ocean and saw a small island. On that island, there was a golden-colored mango grove filled with sweet fruit. The next day, at feeding time, he flew up, landed in that mango grove, drank the mango juice, and returned carrying a ripe mango for his parents.

While eating that mango, the Bodhisatta recognized the flavor and asked, "Son, is this not a ripe mango from such and such an island?" When the son replied, "Yes, father," the Bodhisatta said, "Son, parrots that go to that island do not live long lives. Do not go to that island again." However, the son did not heed his words and continued to go there.

Then one day, after drinking much mango juice and carrying a ripe mango for his parents, as he was flying over the ocean, his body became exhausted due to the heavy load. Overcome by sleepiness, he continued to fly while nodding off. The ripe mango held in his beak fell. Gradually losing his way, he descended and, while flying just above the surface of the water, fell into the sea. Then a fish...
267:
...caught and ate him. When the son did not return at the usual time, the Bodhisatta knew, "He must have fallen into the ocean and died." Then, his parents, unable to obtain food, wasted away and died.

The Teacher, having brought forth this past story, being fully enlightened, spoke these verses:

13. "As long as that bird knew moderation in food, so long did he live his full span and support his mother."

14. "But when he consumed food in great excess, he sank right there; for he was one who knew no moderation."

15. "Therefore, moderation is good, being without greed for food. Those who know no moderation sink, while those who know moderation do not sink."

Monks, as long as that bird knew the measure in food, so long did he obtain a long life and was able to support his parents. But when that bird consumed an excessive amount of food—the mango juice—at that time, he sank right there in that very ocean. Indeed, this is true: he was one who knew no moderation.

Therefore, knowing the measure in food and being without greed is good. Indeed, this is the truth: those who do not know the measure in food sink. Those who know the measure do not sink.

That Bodhisatta had a son. When that son reached full strength, the Bodhisatta’s eyesight became weak. Parrots possess great speed; therefore, in their old age, their eyesight is the first to weaken. The Bodhisatta’s son kept his parents in the nest and supported them by bringing food. One day, that son went to the feeding ground and, standing on a mountain peak, looked over the ocean and saw a small island. On that island, there was a mango grove with fruit of golden hue. The next day, at feeding time, the young parrot flew and landed in that mango grove, enjoyed the flavor of the mangoes, and returned carrying a ripe mango for his parents.

While eating that mango, the Bodhisatta recognized the flavor and said, "Son, is this not a ripe mango from such and such an island?" When the son replied, "Yes, father," the Bodhisatta said, "Son, parrots that go to that island are not able to preserve their lives for long. Do not go to that island again." The young parrot did not take the Bodhisatta’s advice and continued to go.

Then one day, after drinking much mango juice and carrying a ripe mango for the sake of his parents, as he was coming over the ocean, his body became weary due to the excessive weight. Overcome by sleepiness, he continued to fly while nodding. The ripe mango held in his beak fell. Gradually, the young parrot left the path of his flight and, while coming over the surface of the water, fell into the sea and sank. Then a fish caught and ate that parrot.

When the young parrot did not arrive at the usual time, the Bodhisatta knew, "He must have fallen into the ocean and died." Then, the parents of that young parrot, unable to obtain food, their flesh and blood dried up, and they died.
268:
The Fully Enlightened One, having brought forth this past story, concluded the Jātaka:

The Fully Enlightened One brought forth this Dhamma teaching, declared the Truths, and identified the birth. At the conclusion of the Truths, many monks became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, and Arahants. As for the identification of the birth: "At that time, the parrot king's son was the monk who was immoderate in food. The parrot king, however, was I myself."

## One who eats excessively must perish.

The Suka Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Jarūdapāna Jātaka
## The Old Well

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Jarūdapāna Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Jarūdapānaṃ khaṇamānā," concerning some merchants living in Sāvatthī.

It is said that those merchants took goods in Sāvatthī, filled their carts, and when it was time to depart for trade, they invited the Tathāgata, took the refuges, established themselves in the precepts, and paid homage to the Teacher, saying, "Venerable Sir, we are going on a long journey for trade. When we have sold our goods and achieved success, we shall return safely and pay homage to you again." Having said this, they set out on their journey.

While traveling through a desert, those merchants saw an old well and thought, "There is no water in this well, and we are thirsty; let us dig this well." As they dug, they successively found lead, iron, copper, bronze, and various cat's-eye gems. They were satisfied with what they had obtained. Having filled their carts with those treasures, they returned safely to Sāvatthī.
269:
Those merchants, having stored that wealth, thought, “Since we have achieved success, we shall offer food,” and they invited the Blessed One, gave alms, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. They informed the Teacher how they had obtained the wealth.

The Teacher said, “Lay followers, because you were content with that wealth and knew moderation, you obtained both wealth and life. In the past, those who were discontent, did not know moderation, and did not listen to the words of the wise, came to the end of their lives.” Having said this, being requested by the merchants, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family in Bārāṇasī and, upon reaching maturity, became a caravan leader.

Taking goods in Bārāṇasī, he filled the wagons, took many merchants, and while traveling through that same desert, he saw that same well. There, those merchants, thinking “We shall drink water,” dug that well and successively found many treasures. Although they obtained many treasures, they were not content with them, thinking “There must be other treasures better than these here,” and they dug that well even more excessively.

Then the Bodhisatta said to those merchants, “O merchants, this greed is the root of destruction. We have obtained much wealth; be content with just this much. Do not dig excessively.” Even though they were forbidden by the Bodhisatta, they continued to dig.

That well was guarded by a Naga. Then the Naga King, who lived below, became angry as his palace was being destroyed and clods of earth and dust were falling. Except for the Bodhisatta, he struck all the others with his poisonous breath, bringing them to the end of their lives. Coming out of the Naga abode, he harnessed the wagons, filled them with all kinds of treasures, placed the Bodhisatta in a comfortable carriage, and had young Nagas drive the wagons. He led the Bodhisatta to Bārāṇasī, entered his house, stored the wealth, and then returned to his own Naga abode.

The Bodhisatta distributed that wealth, making the whole of Jambudīpa free from the need for plowing, gave alms, undertook the precepts, performed the Uposatha duties, and at the end of his life, filled the city of heaven.
270:
16. Digging an old well, merchants seeking water,
Found iron, copper, tin, and lead, O merchants;
Silver and gold, pearls and many beryls.

17. Not content with that, they dug more and more.
There, a fierce, powerful serpent killed them with its power.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and having become the Fully Enlightened Buddha, spoke these verses:

18. Therefore, dig but do not over-dig; for over-digging is evil.
By digging, wealth was gained; by over-digging, it was lost.

Lay followers, householders. *Udakatthikā*: those desiring water. *Wāṇijā*: the merchants. *Jarudapānaṃ*: the old well. *Khaṇamānā*: while digging. *Ayasaṃ*: black copper (iron). *Lohaṃ*: red copper. *Tipusīsañca*: tin and lead. *Ajjhagamuṃ*: they found. *Te ca wāṇijā*: those merchants. *Bahū*: many. *Rajatañca*: silver. *Jātarūpañca*: gold. *Muttā ca*: pearls. *Veḷuriyā ca*: beryls. *Ajjhagamuṃ*: they found.

*Te wāṇijā*: those merchants. *Tena*: with those obtained treasures. *Asantuṭṭhā*: being discontent. *Bhiyyo bhiyyo*: more and more. *Akhāṇisuṃ*: they dug. *Te*: those merchants. *Tattha*: in that well. *Āsīviso*: a swift-poisoned. *Ghoro*: a fierce-poisoned. *Tejassī*: endowed with poisonous power. *Nāgo*: the Naga. *Tejasā*: with poisonous power. *Hani*: killed.

*Tasmā*: therefore. *Khaṇe*: one should dig only what is suitable. *Nātikkhaṇe*: one should not dig excessively. *Hi-saccaṃ*: it is true. *Atikhātaṃ*: excessive digging. *Pāpakaṃ*: is evil. *Khātena ca*: by digging only what is suitable. *Dhanaṃ*: wealth. *Laddhaṃ*: is obtained. *Atikhātena*: by excessive digging. *Nāsitaṃ*: one is destroyed.

Conclusion of the Jataka: The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: “At that time, Sāriputta was the Naga King, and I myself was the caravan leader.”

## If greed for wealth is too great, destruction is certain
The Jarudapāna Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka
## Ten Questions, Ten Answers
The Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Nāyaṃ gharānaṃ kusalo”, concerning the praise of his wisdom.

To elaborate: In the Dhamma Hall, the monks sat praising the wisdom of the Teacher: “Friends, the Tathāgata has great wisdom, wide wisdom, joyful wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom. He surpasses the world including the devas with his wisdom.”

The Teacher came and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “For such a discussion,” he said, “Monks, not only now is the Tathāgata wise; in the past also the Tathāgata was wise.” Having said this, he remained silent. Being requested by those monks, he brought forth the past.

In the past, monks, when a king named Janasandha was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of King Janasandha’s chief queen. The Bodhisatta’s face was as pure as the surface of a well-polished golden mirror. He reached the height of great beauty. Therefore, on the day of naming the Bodhisatta, they gave him the name Prince Ādāsamukha.
271:
19. This [creature] is not skilled in [building] houses; this wrinkled-faced one is restless.
He would surely destroy whatever is made; such is the nature of this breed.

This was the first verse he spoke.

"O ministers! This monkey is not skilled in planning or building houses. This monkey has a restless nature. This wrinkled-faced monkey would only destroy whatever is made. This breed of monkey has the nature of destroying whatever is made."

During the seven years [of his childhood], Prince Ādāsamukha's father had him taught the three Vedas and all the worldly arts and sciences. When the prince was seven years old, his father passed away.

The ministers performed the king's funeral rites with great honor, gave offerings for the deceased (matakadāna), and on the seventh day, they assembled in the royal courtyard. They thought, "The prince is very young; it is not possible to consecrate him in kingship yet. We shall consecrate him after testing him." One day, they had the city decorated, prepared the place of judgment, set up a throne, and went to the prince's presence, saying, "Your Majesty, it is time to go to the place of judgment."

The prince said, "Very well," and went with a large retinue to sit upon the throne.

While the prince was seated, the ministers took a monkey that could walk on two legs, dressed it in the guise of an expert in site-selection (vatthuvijjācariya), and brought it to the place of judgment. They said, "Your Majesty, this man was the site-selection expert during the time of your father, the Great King. He is highly proficient in his craft and can see the merits and defects of the ground even seven cubits deep. The sites for the royal family's houses were chosen only by him. May Your Majesty favor him and appoint him to a high position."

The prince looked at the monkey from top to bottom and realized, "This creature is not human; it is a monkey." Thinking, "Monkeys know only how to destroy what has been made; they do not know how to create or plan what is not yet made," he spoke to the ministers:

When he spoke thus, the ministers said, "It shall be as Your Majesty commands," and removed the monkey. After a day or two had passed, they dressed the same monkey again and brought it to the place of judgment, saying, "Your Majesty, this person was a judge (vinicchayāmacca) during the time of your father, the Great King. He is well-versed in the law."
272:
20. This is not the hair of one with a [wise] mind; this is not a creature that can provide comfort.
I was taught by Janasandha; this [creature] understands nothing.

This was the second verse he spoke.

"O ministers! This hair is not the hair of one whose mind is endowed with wisdom. This creature is not one capable of providing relief or comfort; it is a beast. Thus was I taught by my father, King Janasandha. This monkey knows nothing of making a judgment."

21. He would not support his mother or father, nor his own brother or sister.
Such a person [as this] would not provide support; I was taught this by Dasaratha.

This was the third verse, completing the set.

"O ministers! Such a person [as this] would not support his own mother, his own father, his own brother, or his own sister. Thus was I taught by my father, the Great King Dasaratha."

[The ministers had said:] "He is highly experienced in the law; it is proper to favor him and have him perform the duties of judgment."

The prince looked at the monkey and realized, "The hair of one with a mind endowed with wisdom is not like this. This creature is a monkey without a wise mind; it is not capable of performing the duties of judgment."

Having heard these words, the ministers said, "It shall be as Your Majesty commands," and removed the monkey. Again, one day, they dressed the same monkey and brought it to the place of judgment, saying, "Your Majesty, this man was one who served his parents and showed respect to the elders of the family during your father's time. It is proper to favor him."

The prince looked at the monkey and thought, "Monkeys have fickle minds; they are not capable of performing such duties."

At that time, Prince Ādāsamukha's father was known as Janasandha because he supported the people through the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu).
273:
He is called Dasaratha because he performs with a single chariot the tasks that would require ten chariots.

Because he had heard such advice from that king, Prince Ādāsamukha spoke in this manner. The ministers said, "It shall be as the Great King commands," and after removing the monkey, they thought, "The prince is wise; he will be able to rule the kingdom." Thus, they consecrated the Bodhisatta as king and beat the drums of proclamation throughout the city, announcing, "This is the command of King Ādāsamukha."

From that time on, the Bodhisatta ruled the kingdom righteously. The fame of the Bodhisatta's wisdom spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. At that time, to demonstrate the Bodhisatta's wisdom, fourteen cases were brought forth: the ox, the son, the horse, the basket-maker, the village headman, the courtesan, the young woman, the snake, the deer, the partridge, the tree-deity, the naga, the ascetic, and the brahmin youth. Regarding these cases, the following sequential account should be understood.

When the Bodhisatta was consecrated as king, a loyal courtier of King Janasandha named Gāmaṇicanda thought: "Ruling a kingdom is suitable for those of a similar age. I am now old; I will not be able to serve a young prince. I will live by farming in the countryside." Having thought thus, Gāmaṇicanda left the city, traveled a distance of about three leagues, and settled in a small village.

1. Gāmaṇicanda did not have any oxen to perform his work. When it rained, Gāmaṇicanda borrowed two oxen from a friend, plowed all day, let them graze on grass, and then went to the owner's house to return them. At that moment, the owner of the oxen was sitting in the middle of the house eating a meal with his wife. The oxen, out of habit, entered the house. As they entered, the owner lifted his rice bowl, and the wife moved her rice bowl away. Gāmaṇicanda, watching and waiting for them to invite him to share the meal, left without formally handing over the oxen.

During the night, thieves broke into the pen and stole those very oxen. In the early morning, the owner entered the pen and, not seeing the oxen, knew they had been stolen by thieves. However, thinking, "I will make Gāmaṇicanda pay," he approached Gāmaṇicanda and said, "Friend Gāmaṇicanda, give me my oxen."

Gāmaṇicanda said, "Did the oxen not enter the house?"

The owner asked, "But did you formally hand them over to me?"

When Gāmaṇicanda replied, "I did not hand them over," the owner said, "In that case, this is the King's messenger summoning you. Come!"
274:
In those districts, if someone throws a pebble or a potsherd and says, "This is the King's messenger summoning you, come!", anyone who does not go is considered to have violated the King's command. Therefore, as soon as Gāmaṇicanda heard the words "King's messenger," he set out.

2. While Gāmaṇicanda was traveling toward the King's city with the ox-owner, they reached a town where a friend of his lived. He was extremely hungry. He said, "Friend, I am very hungry. Stay right here until I enter the village, have a meal, and return," and then he entered his friend's house. His friend was not at home. The friend's wife saw him and said, "Sir, there is no cooked food. Please wait a moment; I will cook and serve you right now." As she hurriedly climbed the ladder to the granary, she fell to the ground. At that very moment, the woman's seven-month pregnancy was miscarried. Just then, her husband arrived, saw the situation, and said to Gāmaṇicanda, "You struck my wife and caused her to miscarry. This is the King's messenger summoning you. Come!" and he took Gāmaṇicanda and set out. From then on, the two men traveled with Gāmaṇicanda between them.

3. Then, at a village gate, a horse-groom was unable to turn a horse back. The horse ran toward Gāmaṇicanda. Seeing Gāmaṇicanda, the groom said, "Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, please hit that horse with something and turn it back!" Gāmaṇicanda picked up a stone and threw it. The stone hit the horse's leg and broke it as if it were a castor-oil plant stalk. Then the groom seized Gāmaṇicanda, saying, "You have broken my horse's leg. This is the King's messenger summoning you."

4. As Gāmaṇicanda was being led away by those three men, he thought: "These people will present me to the King. I cannot even pay for the oxen, so how could I possibly pay compensation for the miscarriage? And where would I get the price for the horse? Therefore, death is better for me."

Thinking thus, as he traveled along, he saw a hill with a precipice on one side near the forest path. In the shade of that hill, a father and son, who were basket-makers, were weaving mats together. Gāmaṇicanda said, "Sirs, I wish to relieve myself. Please wait here a moment until I return." He then climbed the hill and, jumping off the side of the precipice, fell onto the back of the father basket-maker. The basket-maker died instantly. Gāmaṇicanda, however, stood up.

The basket-maker's son said, "You are the thief who killed my father. This is the King's messenger summoning you," and taking Gāmaṇicanda by the hand, he led him out of the thicket. When asked what the matter was, he said, "This man is the thief who killed my father." From that time on, the four men surrounded Gāmaṇicanda and led him away. (These are the four legal cases.)

1. Then, at a village gate, a village headman saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked, "Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?" When Gāmaṇicanda replied that he was going to see the King, the headman said, "Uncle, you will surely see the King. I wish to send a message to the King; please take it for me." When Gāmaṇicanda agreed, the headman said, "Formerly, I was naturally handsome, wealthy, and possessed a large following. I was free from disease. But now, I am poor and afflicted with jaundice. Ask the King what the reasons for this are. The King is wise; he will answer you. Then tell me the King's message again." Gāmaṇicanda agreed.
275:
2. Then, at a village gate ahead, a certain prostitute saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked, "Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?" When he replied, "I am going to see the King," she said, "The King is said to be wise; please carry a message for me. Previously, I used to receive a large fee, but now I do not even get the price of betel. No one comes to me anymore. Ask the King what the reason for this is, and tell me when you return."

3. Then, at another village gate ahead, a young woman saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked him in the same way. She said, "I am unable to live in my husband's house, nor can I live in my parents' house. Ask the King what the reason for this is, and tell me when you return."

4. Then, going forward, a snake living in an anthill near the main road saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked, "Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?" When he replied, "I am going to see the King," the snake said, "The King is said to be wise; carry a message for me. When I go out to search for food, I have a hungry and withered body, yet as I emerge from the anthill, my body fills the hole and I have to pull myself out with great difficulty. However, when I return after eating, with a full and plump body, I can enter quickly without even touching the sides of the hole. Ask the King what the reason for this is, and tell me."

5. Then, going forward, a deer saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked him in the same way. The deer said, "I am unable to eat grass in any other place; I can only eat grass at the foot of one particular tree. Ask the King what the reason for this is."
276:
6. Then, going forward, a partridge saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked him in the same way. It said, "I am able to chirp pleasantly only when sitting at the foot of a certain anthill. When sitting in other places, I cannot chirp pleasantly. Ask the King what the reason for this is."

7. Then, going forward, a tree deity saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked, "Uncle Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?" When he replied, "I am going to the King," the deity said, "The King is said to be wise. Previously, I received offerings and honor, but now I do not even receive a handful of flowers. Ask the King what the reason for this is."

8. After that, a Naga king saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked him in the same way. He said, "The King is said to be wise. Previously, the water in this pond was clear and had the color of emerald. Now it is turbid and overgrown with various kinds of water weeds. Ask the King what the reason for this is."

9. Then, going forward, ascetics living in a place near the city saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked him in the same way. They said, "The King is said to be wise. Previously, the large and small fruits in this place were sweet. Now they have become tasteless and bitter. Ask the King what the reason for this is."

10. Then, going forward, young Brahmins at a rest house near the city gate saw Gāmaṇicanda and asked, "Sir Gāmaṇicanda, where are you going?" When he replied, "I am going to the King," they said, "In that case, take our message. Previously, the Vedas we learned were clear to us. Now, the learned Vedas do not remain, like water in a broken pot; they are not clear and it is like darkness. Ask the King what the reason for this is." (These are the ten questions.)

Gāmaṇicanda took these ten messages and went to the King. The King was sitting at the place of judgment. The owner of the oxen took Gāmaṇicanda and approached the King. When the King saw Gāmaṇicanda, he recognized him and thought, "This man is a servant of my father, the King. He used to carry me. Where has he been living for all this time?" Then he said, "O Gāmaṇicanda, where have you been living for all this time? You have not been seen for a long time. For what business have you come?"

"Your Majesty, it is as you say. Since the time your father the King passed away to the heavenly realm, I went to the countryside and lived by farming. From that countryside, this man has summoned me to Your Majesty's presence as a messenger because of the matter of the oxen," he replied.

"If he had not summoned you, you would not have come. It is good that he summoned you. Now I have the opportunity to see you. Where is that man who summoned you?" the King asked. "Your Majesty, it is this man," he said. "O man, is it true that you summoned our Canda?" the King asked. "Your Majesty, it is true," he replied. "Why did you summon him?" the King asked.
277:
1. "Great King, this Canda does not give me my two oxen; therefore, I have brought him as a messenger [to court]," he submitted. The King asked, "Canda, is it true?" "Great King, I beg your pardon, please hear my words," he said, and related the whole matter.

Hearing this, the King asked the owner of the oxen, "My man, did you see the oxen entering your house?" "Great King, I did not see them," he submitted. "My man, have you not heard people calling me King Ādāsamukha? Speak the truth," the King said. "Great King, it is true that I saw them," he then admitted.

The King said, "Canda, because you did not hand over the oxen, you are liable. However, this man, despite seeing them, spoke a deliberate lie saying he did not see them. Therefore, you yourself shall act as the official; pluck out the eyes of this man and his wife, and you pay twenty-four kahāpaṇas as the price of the oxen." When this was said, they took the owner of the oxen outside.

The owner of the oxen thought, "If my eyes are plucked out, what shall I do with twenty-four kahāpaṇas?" He fell at Gāmaṇicanda's feet and said, "Master Canda, let the money for the oxen be yours alone; please take this money as well," and giving him other coins, he fled.

2. Then the second litigant submitted, "Great King, this Canda struck my wife and caused a miscarriage." The King asked, "Canda, is it true?" "Great King, please listen," Gāmaṇicanda said, and related the whole matter in detail. Then the King asked Gāmaṇicanda, "Did you strike this man's wife and cause a miscarriage?"
278:
Gāmaṇicanda submitted, "Great King, I did not cause it." The King said, "My man, are you able to prove that Canda struck her and caused the miscarriage?" "Great King, I am not able," he submitted.

"Now what will you do?" the King asked. "Great King, it is right that I should get a son," he submitted. "In that case, Canda, you take this man's wife to your house, and when she gives birth to a son, then bring him and give him to this man." That litigant also fell at Gāmaṇicanda's feet and said, "Master Canda, do not break up my home," and giving him money, he fled.

3. Then the third litigant went and submitted, "Great King, this Canda threw something at my horse's leg and broke it." The King asked, "Canda, is it true?" "Great King, please listen," Canda said, and related the matter in detail. Hearing this, the King asked the groom, "Is it true that you said, 'Hit the horse and turn it back'?" "I did not say so, Great King," he submitted. When the King asked a second time, he admitted, "Yes, I said it."

The King addressed Gāmaṇicanda, "Canda, this groom spoke a lie, saying he did not say it when he actually did. You cut out the groom's tongue, and taking a thousand kahāpaṇas from my wealth, pay the price of the horse." The groom said, "Master Canda, do not cut out my tongue," and giving Gāmaṇicanda other coins, he fled.

4. Then the son of a basket-maker submitted, "Great King, this Canda is the thief who killed my father." The King said, "Canda, is it true?" "Great King, please listen," Canda said, and related that matter also in detail. Then the King addressed the basket-maker's son and asked, "Now what will you do?" "Great King, it is right that I should get my father back," he submitted.

"Canda, it is right that this man should get his father back. However, it is not possible to bring back and give one who is dead. You take this man's mother to your house and be a father to him." The basket-maker's son said, "Master Canda, do not break up the home of my deceased father," and giving money to Gāmaṇicanda, he fled. (These are the four judgments.)

Gāmaṇicanda, having won the cases and being joyful in heart, said to the King, "Great King, some people have sent messages to you; I shall relate them to you." "Relate them, Canda," the King said. Gāmaṇicanda related each message one by one, starting from the young Brahmins' message in reverse order. The King answered them in sequence.

1. How did he answer? Hearing the first message, he said, "Formerly, in the place where those young Brahmins lived, there was a cock that knew the time to crow. Those young Brahmins would rise at the sound of that cock, take up their mantras, and while they were reciting, the dawn would rise. Therefore, whatever mantras they learned were not lost. But now, in their dwelling place, there is a cock that crows at the wrong time. It crows either too early or too late. When it crows too early, they rise and take up their mantras..."
279:
Now, in the dwelling place of those young brahmins, there is a cock that crows at the wrong time. That cock crows either too early or only when it is broad daylight.

Waking up to the sound of the cock crowing too early, the brahmins who recite the Vedas are overcome by sleepiness; they do not recite and simply go back to sleep. When they wake up to the sound of the cock crowing when it is broad daylight, they find no opportunity to recite. Therefore, it is said that the Vedas learned by the young brahmins do not become clear to them.

2. Having heard the second message: In the past, those ascetics practiced the Dhamma of recluses and were devoted to the preliminary work of kasiṇa meditation. Now, however, they have abandoned the Dhamma of recluses and are devoted to things that should not be done. They give large and small fruits grown in the grove to their supporters and live by the wrong livelihood of exchanging food for food. Therefore, the fruits are no longer sweet for those ascetics. If they become devoted to the Dhamma of recluses again as before, the fruits will become sweet for them once more. Those ascetics do not know of the King's wisdom. Tell them to practice the Dhamma of recluses.

3. Having heard the third message: Those Naga kings are quarreling with one another; therefore, the water of those Nagas is turbid. If they become harmonious again as before, the water will become clear once more.

4. Having heard the fourth message: In the past, that tree deity protected people traveling through the forest; therefore, she received various kinds of offerings. Now, however, she does not provide protection; therefore, she does not receive offerings. If she provides protection again as before, she will once more attain the highest gain. The tree deity does not know of the King's wisdom. Therefore, tell that tree deity to provide protection to the people who have reached the forest.

5. Having heard the fifth message: At the base of the termite mound where that partridge sits and chirps pleasantly, there are great treasures beneath. Dig up those treasures and take them.

6. Having heard the sixth message: Under the tree where that deer is able to eat grass, there is a large honeycomb above. That deer is infatuated with the grass smeared with honey and is unable to eat other grass. You take that honeycomb, send the first honey to me, and eat the rest yourself.
280:
7. Having heard the seventh message: In the termite mound where that snake lives, there is a large pot of gold beneath. Because that snake lives guarding that pot of gold, when it comes out, it comes out clinging to it, making its body slack out of greed. After eating, because of its love for the wealth, it enters quickly without clinging. Dig up those pots of gold and take them.

8. Having heard the eighth message: In a small village between the village of that young woman's husband and that of her parents, there is a lover. Thinking of that lover and because of her love for him, she is unable to live in her husband's house. Saying, 'I will go see my parents,' she goes and stays at the lover's house for two or three days, then stays at her parents' house for two or three days. Then, thinking of the lover again, she says, 'I will go to my husband's house,' but goes back to the lover's house instead. Inform that woman of the King's existence and tell her: 'Let her live only in her husband's house. If the King has you arrested, your life will be no more. Therefore, it is proper for you to live diligently and avoid such things.'

9. Having heard the ninth message: In the past, that courtesan, having taken a fee from one man, would not take a fee from another until she had fulfilled her service to the first. Therefore, in the past, her earnings were great. Now, however, having abandoned her own principles, she takes a fee from another man without fulfilling her service to the first. Without giving an opportunity to the first man, she gives it to the later one. Therefore, her fees are not sufficient, and no one goes to her. If she stands by her own principles, it will be just as before. Tell her to stand by her own principles.

10. Having heard the tenth message: In the past, the village headman decided cases truthfully and justly. Therefore, people loved and cherished him. Because they cherished him, people brought him many gifts. Thus, he was handsome, wealthy, and possessed of fame. Now, however, being one who takes bribes, he decides cases untruthfully. Therefore, he has become poor and destitute, and is overcome by jaundice. If he decides cases truthfully as before, it will be just as before. That village headman does not know of the King's existence. Tell the village headman to decide cases truthfully. (These are the ten answers.)

Thus, Gāmaṇicanda reported these many messages to the King. The King, with his own wisdom, explained all of them as if he were an Omniscient Buddha. He gave much wealth to Gāmaṇicanda, made the village where Gāmaṇicanda lived a royal grant, gave it to him, and sent him away.
281:
That Gāmaṇicanda left the city and delivered the messages given by the Bodhisatta to the young Brahmin, the ascetic, the Naga king, and the tree deity. He took the treasure from the dwelling place of the partridge, took honey from a tree at the deer’s grazing spot and sent it to the King, and dug up the anthill at the snake’s dwelling place to take the treasure. He delivered the messages to the young woman, the courtesan, and the village headman exactly as the King had instructed. Then, with great glory, he returned to his village, lived out the remainder of his life, and passed away according to his deeds. King Ādāsamukha also performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and, at the end of his life, went to the celestial realm.

In identifying the birth story, the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, said, "Monks, not only now is the Tathāgata possessed of great wisdom; in the past also he was wise indeed." Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, he identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many monks became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, and Arahants. How did the Fully Enlightened One identify the Jātaka? "At that time, Ānanda was Gāmaṇicanda. I myself was King Ādāsamukha." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## The Bodhisatta-to-be, the Wise One, was Great Indeed

The Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Mandhātu Jātaka

## The Great River of Craving

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mandhātu Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yāvatā candimasūriyā", concerning a monk who was dissatisfied with the Sasana.

That monk, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, saw a well-adorned woman and became dissatisfied. Then, the monks brought him to the Hall of Truth and presented him to the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, this monk is dissatisfied."

The Fully Enlightened One asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monk, when will you ever be able to fulfill your craving while living in a house? This so-called sensual craving is like the ocean, difficult to fill. Ancient kings, having exercised sovereignty as Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand minor islands, and having exercised kingship in the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika) with human retinues, and even after exercising divine kingship in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven in the dwelling place of thirty-six Sakkas, they died still unable to fulfill their sensual craving. When will you be able to fulfill this sensual craving?" Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, among the people of the first aeon, there was a king named Mahāsammata. His son was named Roja. His son was named Vararoja. His son was named Kalyāṇa. His son was named Varakalyāṇa. His son was named Uposatha. His son was named Mandhātu.
282:
That king named Mandhātu, endowed with the seven treasures and the four psychic powers, exercised sovereignty as a Universal Monarch. When King Mandhātu bent his left hand and snapped with his right hand, a rain of the seven treasures, knee-deep, fell from the sky like a divine cloud. Such a marvelous man was King Mandhātu. He spent eighty-four thousand years in youthful play. He served as viceroy for eighty-four thousand years. He exercised sovereignty as a Universal Monarch for eighty-four thousand years. His life span was an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya).

One day, being unable to fulfill his sensual craving, he showed signs of dissatisfaction. Then his ministers asked, "Great King, why are you dissatisfied?" King Mandhātu asked the ministers, "When looking at the power of my merit, what is this kingship to me? What place is truly delightful?" The ministers replied, "Great King, the celestial realm is delightful."

King Mandhātu then sprinkled the Wheel Treasure with water and, together with his retinue, went to the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājika). Then, the four great kings of the Cātumahārājika realm, holding divine flowers and perfumes and surrounded by hosts of devas, came out to welcome him. They took King Mandhātu to the Cātumahārājika realm and gave him the kingship of the devas. While King Mandhātu reigned in the Cātumahārājika realm, surrounded by his own retinue, a long period of time passed.

Even there, King Mandhātu was unable to fulfill his craving and showed signs of dissatisfaction. The four great kings of the Cātumahārājika realm asked, "Great King, why are you dissatisfied?" King Mandhātu asked the four great kings, "What place is more pleasant than this Cātumahārājika realm?" The four great kings replied, "Great King, we are but a retinue of attendants to others. The Tāvatiṃsa heaven is delightful."

King Mandhātu sprinkled the Wheel Treasure with water and, surrounded by his retinue, set out towards Tāvatiṃsa. Then Sakka, the king of devas, holding divine flowers and perfumes and surrounded by hosts of devas, came out to welcome him. Taking King Mandhātu by the hand, he said, "Come this way, Great King." While King Mandhātu was proceeding, surrounded by the hosts of devas, the Counselor Treasure (Pariṇāyaka-ratana) took the Wheel Treasure and, together with the retinue, descended to the human world and entered the city.
283:
22. As far as the sun and moon revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters,
All beings dwelling on earth are the servants of Mandhātu.
23. Even with a rain of coins, there is no satisfaction in sensual pleasures.
Sensual pleasures are of little sweetness and much suffering; thus knowing, the wise man,
24. Even in divine pleasures, he finds no delight.
The disciple of the Fully Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.

The Teacher spoke these verses.

As far as: the extent of the limit. The sun and moon revolve: they circle Mount Sineru within that limit. Illuminating the quarters: they shine and radiate in the ten directions. Shining: they are of a nature to shine by creating light. All beings dwelling on earth are the servants of Mandhātu: all beings who exist in that region are merely the servants of King Mandhātu.

Even with a rain of coins: even by causing a rain of the seven kinds of jewels to fall. There is no satisfaction in sensual pleasures: there is no such thing as satisfaction in either objective or subjective sensual pleasures. Sensual pleasures are of little sweetness: they are like a dream, having little sweetness and meager happiness. Much suffering: they contain much more suffering. Thus: in this way. The wise man, the disciple of the Fully Enlightened One: having known this.

Even in divine pleasures: even in the objects of the devas such as forms and so on. He finds no delight: that monk who practices insight, even when invited with divine pleasures, finds no delight in them, just like the Venerable Samiddhi. Delights in the destruction of craving: delights in Nibbāna. Because craving is exhausted upon reaching Nibbāna, it is called the 'destruction of craving.' Delights: he is greatly pleased. Disciple of the Fully Enlightened One: a person who is a practitioner, learned from hearing the Buddha's teaching.

Sakka brought King Mandhātu to Tāvatiṃsa, divided the celestial kingdom into two, and gave him the middle portion of the kingship. From then on, the two kings ruled. As time passed, Sakka completed his lifespan of thirty-six million years and passed away. Another Sakka arose. In this way, thirty-six Sakkas passed away. King Mandhātu, however, exercised the kingship of the devas in his human body.

As time passed, excessive sensual craving arose in King Mandhātu. He thought, "What is the use of half a kingdom? I will kill Sakka and become the sole emperor."

Although he had this thought, he was unable to kill Sakka. Craving is the root of ruin. Therefore, Mandhātu's life-force declined. Old age struck his body.
284:
A human body does not decay in the celestial realm. At that time, [Mandhātu] fell from the celestial realm and descended into the park. The park keeper informed the royal family of King Mandhātu's arrival. The King came and had a place prepared right there in the park. King Mandhātu lay down in the sleep from which one does not rise. The ministers asked, "Great King, what message shall we speak after your passing?"

He said, "After my time, you should tell the people: 'King Mandhātu, having exercised the sovereignty of a Universal Monarch over the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands, having exercised kingship among the Four Great Kings for a long time, and having exercised kingship in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for the lifespan of thirty-six Sakkas, passed away without having fulfilled his craving (taṇhā).' Tell this news to the people." Having said this, he passed away according to his kamma.

The Teacher, having become the Fully Enlightened Buddha, brought forth this past story.

[The Conclusion of the Jātaka:] The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Many other monks also reached the Fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, I myself was King Mandhātu." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Craving for sensual pleasures, even if pursued, can never be satisfied.

End of the Mandhātu Jātaka.

[259] 9. Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka

"Nayimassa vijjā..." The Teacher told this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the receipt of a thousand robes—five hundred from the hands of King Kosala's women and five hundred from the King's own hand—by the Venerable Ānanda. The story is detailed below in the Guṇa Jātaka of the Duka Nipāta.
285:
## 9. Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka
## The Ascetic and the King

The Story of the Present: While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Nayimassa vijjā," concerning the occasion when the Venerable Ānanda Thera received a thousand robes—five hundred from the hands of the five hundred queens of the King of Kosala and five hundred from the hands of the King of Kosala himself. This story is found in the Guṇa Jātaka, the seventh in the Dukanipāta (Book of Twos).

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. On the day of his naming, he was given the name Young Tirīṭavaccha. In due course, when he reached the age of maturity, he studied all the arts in the city of Takkasilā. While living as a householder, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) upon the death of his parents. He then went forth into the forest to become an ascetic and lived there, subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
286:
25. "He has no skill born of science,
He is not a kinsman, nor even a friend of yours.
Then for what reason does Tirīṭavaccha,
The bearer of the triple staff, eat the choice food?"

This was the first stanza spoken.

"Great King! This ascetic Tirīṭavaccha possesses no skill or work accomplished through science. This Tirīṭavaccha, who walks carrying a triple staff, is not your kinsman, nor is he your childhood friend. Yet, for what reason does he eat the choice food?"

While the ascetic Tirīṭavaccha was living in the forest, rebels plundered the border region of the King of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī went to the border and, upon engaging in battle, was defeated. Fearing death, he fled on the back of a noble elephant in one direction. While wandering in the forest in the morning, he entered the hermitage at a time when the ascetic Tirīṭavaccha had gone out to gather various fruits.

Recognizing it as a dwelling place of ascetics, the King dismounted from the elephant. Exhausted by the wind and heat and being thirsty, he looked for a water pot but saw none. Then, at the end of the walkway, he saw a well.

Seeing no rope or bucket to draw water, and being unable to endure his thirst, he took the girth-straps from the elephant's belly. He stationed the elephant near the well, tied the straps to the elephant's leg, and descended into the well using the straps. When the straps did not reach the water, he climbed back up, tied his upper robe to the end of the straps, and descended again. Even then, it did not reach.

Touching the water with his toes and being extremely thirsty, he thought, "If I die after quenching my thirst, it will be a good death." He then jumped into the well, drank as much as he desired, but was unable to climb back out and remained there. The elephant, being well-trained, did not go elsewhere but stayed there looking for the King.

In the evening, the Bodhisatta returned with various fruits. Seeing the elephant, he thought, "A king must have come; only an armored elephant is visible. What could be the reason?" He approached the elephant. The elephant, sensing the Bodhisatta's approach, stood aside. The Bodhisatta went to the edge of the well and, seeing the King, comforted him, saying, "Do not fear, Great King." He constructed a ladder, helped the King out, massaged his body, anointed him with oil, bathed him, gave him fruits to eat, and removed the elephant's armor.

The King rested for two or three days, obtained a promise from the Bodhisatta to visit him, and then departed. The King's army, which had been camped in a stockade near the city, saw the King coming and surrounded him. The King then entered the city.

After half a month had passed, the Bodhisatta arrived at Bārāṇasī, entered the park, and the next day went for alms, reaching the palace gate.
287:
## 26. In my misfortunes, defeated in battle,
Alone in the terrible waterless forest,
He stretched out his hand to me in my distress;
By that I was lifted up, though overwhelmed by suffering.

## 27. By his effort I have arrived here,
From the realm of Death to the world of the living.
Dear son, Tirīṭavaccha is worthy of gains;
Give him wealth and offer him sacrifice.

Thus he spoke these two verses.

Dear son (tāta), because of dangers; defeated in battle (yuddhaparājitassa); being alone without a companion (ekassa); having fallen into a well and reached distress (kicchagatassa); to me (me); this hermit, in the cruel (ghore) waterless forest (vivanasmim), having shown compassion (katvā), stretched out (pasārayī) his hand joined with effort to pull me out of the well. By that cause (tena kāraṇena), I, though surrounded by suffering (dukkhasampareto), was able to climb up (udatārim).

By the power of the act of rescue (kiccena) by that hermit Tirīṭavaccha, I have arrived again (anupatto) in this world of the living (idha jīvaloke) from the realm (visayā) of King Yama (vesāyino).
