Tirīṭavaccha is worthy of receiving (lābhārho) the gain of the four requisites. Give (detha) him the wealth (bhogaṃ) consisting of the requisites of a recluse to be used by him. And perform sacrifice (yajaṭhañca yaññaṃ); you, the ministers, and the citizens, all of you give him wealth and offer sacrifice. For the gift given to him is 'wealth' because it is to be enjoyed by him, and it is 'sacrifice' because it is a sacrificial gift from others. Therefore he said, "Give him wealth and offer him sacrifice."

When the King opened the casement window and looked out at the royal courtyard, he saw the Bodhisatta and recognized him. Descending from the palace, he paid homage and seated him on the royal throne under the well-constructed white umbrella. He offered him the food prepared for himself, and after eating himself, he invited him to the park. In the park, he had a dwelling, a walkway, and places for night and day rest prepared for the Bodhisatta. He donated all the requisites of a monk, entrusted him to the park keeper, paid homage, and departed. From that time on, the Bodhisatta ate only at the King's palace and received many gains and honors.

The ministers, who could not tolerate the Bodhisatta receiving such honors, said, "If such honors are received, what hero would not perform what task?" They approached the Crown Prince and said, "Your Majesty, our King is exceedingly fond of another hermit. What quality does the King see in that hermit? Please speak with the King."

The Crown Prince agreed and approached the King with the ministers. Hearing their words, the King called his son and asked, "My dear, do you remember my absence for two or three days after being defeated in battle in the border region?" When the son replied that he remembered, the King told him the whole story, saying, "At that time, I gained my life because of this hermit. My dear, when the one who gave me my life arrives in my presence, even if I give him the kingdom, I am still unable to repay the favor he performed."

In this way, as the King revealed the virtues of the Bodhisatta, like making the full moon appear in the sky, the virtues of the Bodhisatta became evident to everyone.
288:
Gains and honors for the Bodhisatta became very abundant. From that time on, neither the ministers, nor the sub-king, nor any other person dared to say anything to the King. The King, established in the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and filled the city of heaven. The Bodhisatta also developed the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti) and was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, saying, "Wise men of old also acted by the power of gratitude," identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the King was Ānanda, and the ascetic was I myself."

## Always Worship the Life-Saviour and Benefactor
The Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka is concluded.

## 10. Dūta Jātaka
## The Messenger of the Stomach
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Dūta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yassatthā dūramāyanti," concerning a greedy monk.

The story will become clear in the Cakkavāka Jātaka, the eighth in the Navaka Nipāta. The Fully Enlightened Buddha called that monk and said, "Monk, you are not greedy only now; you were greedy in the past as well. Because of your greed, when you were about to be beheaded with a sword, you found happiness by depending on a wise king," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as his son. When he came of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. Upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingship and became one who was pure in food. For that reason, he became known as King Bhojanasuddhika.

That King Bhojanasuddhika used to eat his meals prepared in such a way that a single bowl of rice cost a hundred thousand.
289:
30. Dadāmi te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ,
Gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena.
Dūto hi dūtassa kathaṃ na dajjaṃ.
Mayampi tasseva bhavāma dūtā.

He spoke this third verse:

"O Brahmin, I give to you a thousand red cows along with a bull. For we too are messengers of that very same stomach. Therefore, how should a messenger not give to a messenger? One should certainly give."

When he ate, he did not eat inside the house. Desiring to inspire the people who saw his meal preparations to perform meritorious deeds, he had a pavilion built at the palace gate. At mealtime, he had that pavilion decorated and sat on a royal throne made of gold under a raised white parasol, surrounded by princesses, and ate food of all flavors from a golden dish worth a hundred thousand.

At that time, a greedy man, seeing the King’s manner of eating, desired to eat that food. Unable to restrain his craving, he thought, "There is a way," and after tucking up his loincloth tightly and raising his hands, he approached the King, shouting loudly, "O sirs, I am a messenger! I am a messenger!"

At that time, in that region, they did not stop anyone who said, "I am a messenger." Therefore, the crowd split into two and gave him a path.

That man went quickly, took a handful of rice from the King's dish, and put it in his mouth. Then, a sword-bearer held his sword, thinking, "I will cut off his head." The King stopped him, saying, "Do not strike." He said, "Do not be afraid, eat," and after washing his hands, the King sat down.

At the end of the man's meal, the King had his own drinking water and betel given to him and said, "O man, you say you are a messenger. Whose messenger are you?" When asked, he replied, "Great King, I am a messenger of craving, a messenger of the stomach. Craving commanded me and sent me as a messenger, saying, 'You go!'" and he spoke these two verses:

28. Yassatthā dūramāyanti, amittampi yācituṃ.
Tassūdarassahaṃ dūto, mā me kujjha rathesabha.
29. Yassa divā ca ratto ca, vasamāyanti māṇavā.
Tassūdarassahaṃ dūto, mā me kujjha rathesabha.

"O Great King, for the sake of which stomach beings go even to distant places to beg even from an enemy—I am a messenger of that stomach. Do not be angry with me."

"O Great King, under the power of which stomach beings follow day and night—I am a messenger of that stomach. Do not be angry with me."

The King, hearing the man's words, thought, "That is true. These beings wander about as messengers of the stomach by the power of craving; craving alone governs these beings."
290:
Thinking, "This man speaks very pleasing words," and being delighted with him, the King said:

"Indeed, you have spoken a reason never heard before," and with a delighted heart, he gave that man great wealth.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmiphala). Many others also became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and so forth. He identified the Jātaka thus: "At that time, the greedy man was the greedy monk, and King Bhojanasuddhika was I myself."

## All Beings are Truly Slaves to Craving
The Dūta Jātaka is concluded.

## 2. Paduma Vagga
## 1. Paduma Jātaka
## The Lotus Stalk
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Paduma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yathā kesā ca massū ca," concerning the monks who made flower offerings at the Ānanda Bodhi tree.

The story will become clear in the Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka, the sixth in the Terasaka Nipāta. That Bodhi tree is called the "Ānanda Bodhi" because it was planted by the Venerable Ānanda Thera.

The fact that the Venerable Ānanda Thera planted the Bodhi tree near the gatehouse of Jetavana Monastery spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. Then, some monks living in the countryside, thinking, "We will make a flower offering at the Ānanda Bodhi," went to Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and the next day entered the city of Sāvatthī. They went to the lotus market but returned without getting any lotuses. They reported to the Venerable Ānanda Thera, "Venerable Sir, we went to the lotus market to get flowers for an offering, but we did not get even a single flower."
291:
1. "Just as hair and beard grow back again and again after being cut, so may your nose grow back. Being requested, give me a lotus."
This was the first verse he spoke.
Just as hair and beard grow back every time they are cut, in the same way, may your nose grow back. You, whom I have requested, please give me a lotus.

2. "Just as autumn seeds sown in a field grow, so may your nose grow back. Being requested, give me a lotus."
This was the second verse he spoke.
Just as seeds gathered in the month of Tazaungmon and sown in a field grow, in the same way, may your nose grow back. You, whom I have requested, please give me a lotus.

Venerable Ānanda said, "Friends, I shall fetch them for your sake," and went to the lotus market, took a bundle of blue lotuses, and returning, gave them to those monks. Those monks took the lotuses and offered them to the Bodhi tree.

Hearing that news, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised the topic of the Elder's virtues: "Friends, the monks from the countryside have little merit; they went to the lotus market and did not get any flowers. But Venerable Ānanda went and brought them back."

The Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now do those skilled in speech obtain flowers; in the past also, those skilled in speech obtained them," and he told a story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a merchant's son. In a certain pond within the city, lotuses were in bloom. A man with a cut nose guarded that pond.

Then one day, when a festival was proclaimed in Bārāṇasī, three merchant's sons who wished to play in the festival wearing flowers thought, "We will praise the nose-less man with falsehoods and ask for flowers." While he was gathering lotuses, they went near the pond and stood in a suitable place.

Among them, one merchant's son called out to the pond-guard—

That pond-guard was angry with that merchant's son and did not give him a lotus. Then, the second merchant's son spoke to the pond-guard—
292:
3. "Both of these are prattling, thinking 'Perhaps he will give us lotuses.' Whether they say it or not, there is no regrowing of a nose. Friend, give me lotuses; I ask you as a petitioner."
This was the third verse he spoke.
Friend, both of these men are prattling, thinking 'He will give us lotuses.' Whether they say it or not, there is no such thing as the regrowing of a severed nose. I ask for lotuses; you, whom I have requested, please give them to me.

The pond-guard was angry with those two as well and did not give them lotuses. Then, the third merchant's son spoke to the pond-guard—

Hearing those words, the pond-guard said, "These two spoke lies, but you spoke the truth. Lotuses are suitable for you." He took a large bundle of lotuses, gave them to that merchant's son, and returned to his lotus pond.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Buddha identified the birth: "At that time, I myself was the merchant's son who received the lotuses."

## Speak the truth and speak sweetly, and your desires will be fulfilled.
The Paduma Jātaka ends.

## 2. Mudupāṇi Jātaka
## Difficult to Guard
The Buddha, the Teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Mudupāṇi Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Pāṇi ce muduko assa," concerning a monk who was dissatisfied with the monkhood.

When that monk was brought to the Dhamma Hall, the Buddha asked, "Monk, is it true that you are dissatisfied?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha said, "Monk, women are by nature impossible to guard because they go according to their passions. Even the wise of old could not guard their own daughters. Even while being held by the hand by her father, a daughter once fled with a man according to her passions without her father knowing," and he told a story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen. When he came of age, he studied all the arts at Takkasilā. Upon his father's passing, he was established in the kingship and ruled righteously.
293:
The Bodhisatta, while raising both his daughter and nephew within the palace, sat with his ministers one day and said, "After my passing, my nephew shall become king, and my daughter shall be his chief queen." Later, when the nephew reached the age of maturity, the king sat with the ministers again and said, "Let us bring a princess from another kingdom for my nephew, and let us give my daughter to another royal family. In this way, our relatives will become more numerous." The ministers agreed.

Then the king had a house built for his nephew outside the palace and forbade him from entering the palace. However, the princess and the prince were in love with each other. While the prince was pondering by what means he could take the princess out, he thought, "There is a way." He gave a bribe to the nurse, and when she asked, "Young master, what is the matter?" he said, "Mother, how can we find an opportunity to get the princess outside?" The nurse replied, "I will speak with the princess and find out." He said, "Very well, mother."

The nurse went and said, "Come, dear, I will look for lice in your hair." She made the princess sit on a low stool while she herself sat on a high stool. Placing the princess's head on her lap, while searching for lice, she pricked the princess's head with her fingernails. The princess, realizing, "This nurse is not pricking with her own nails, but with the nails of the prince, my cousin," asked, "Mother, did you go to the prince?" She replied, "Yes, dear." "What message did he speak?" "Dear, he asks for a way to get you outside." The princess, thinking, "If he is wise, he will understand," composed this verse and said, "Mother, learn this verse and tell it to the prince."

4. If the hand were soft, and the elephant well-trained,
And if it were dark and raining, then indeed it might be at that time.

The nurse learned the verse, went to the prince, and when asked, "Mother, what did the princess say?" she replied, "Young master, she said nothing else but sent this verse," and she recited it. The prince, understanding its meaning, said, "Go, mother," and sent the nurse away. The meaning of the verse is: "If the hand of a single young maidservant were as soft as my hand, and if you had a well-trained elephant that would not move, and if on that day there were a very thick darkness of four factors, and if it were raining, then indeed..."
294:
"...it might be. At such a time, depending on these four conditions, the fulfillment of your heart's desire would surely come to pass."

The prince, knowing this meaning truly, prepared a beautiful young maidservant with soft hands. He gave a bribe to the royal elephant trainer, had the elephant trained to remain steady, and waited for the right time.

Then, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, immediately after the middle watch, a thick dark cloud rained. The prince, thinking, "This is the day the princess spoke of," mounted the elephant, placed the soft-handed maidservant on the elephant's back, went to the palace, and stood the elephant against the great wall at a place facing the open courtyard, near a window, while being drenched by the rain.

The king, guarding his daughter, would not allow her to sleep elsewhere, but made her sleep on a small bed near him. The princess, knowing that the prince would come that day, lay down without falling asleep and said, "Father, I wish to bathe." The king said, "Come, dear," took her by the hand, led her to the window, and saying, "Bathe, dear," lifted her up and placed her on the lotus-ledge outside the window, holding her by one hand.

While bathing, she stretched out her hand to the prince. The prince removed the ornaments from the princess's hand, put them on the maidservant's hand, lifted the maidservant, and placed her on the ledge next to the princess. The princess took the maidservant's hand and placed it in her father's hand. The king took the maidservant's hand and let go of his daughter's hand. She then removed the ornaments from her other hand, put them on the maidservant's second hand, placed that hand in her father's hand, and went away with the prince. The king, thinking "This is my daughter," after the bathing was finished, made the girl lie down in the royal chamber, closed the door, sealed it, set a guard, and went to his own bed to lie down.

When the night had turned to dawn, he opened the door, saw the girl, and asked, "What is this?" She told him how the princess had gone with the prince. The king, filled with remorse, thought, "Even when holding them by the hand, it is impossible to guard a woman; thus women are truly ungovernable," and spoke these two other verses:

5. They are never satisfied, soft-spoken, hard to fill, and like rivers. They sink into hell; knowing this, a wise man should avoid them from afar.

6. Whomever they serve, whether through mutual desire or for wealth, they quickly burn that man, just as fire burns its own place of dwelling.

These women are 'insatiable' and 'soft-spoken,' meaning they cannot be satisfied with soft words. Alternatively, they are not fit to live with men. They are soft-spoken but hard-hearted. They are 'hard to fill' and 'like rivers.' They 'sink' into hell. Knowing this, a wise man should avoid them from afar. Whomever those women serve, whether through mutual desire or for wealth, they quickly burn that man, just as fire (Jātavedo) burns its own base.

Then, when those four conditions are met, at that time, the fulfillment of your heart's desire would surely come to pass.

The prince, knowing that meaning truly, signaled a beautiful young maidservant with soft hands, gave a bribe to the royal elephant trainer, had the elephant trained not to move, and waited for the time. Then, on the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight, immediately after the middle watch, a thick dark rain fell. The prince, thinking "Today is the day the princess instructed me," mounted the elephant, placed the soft-handed maidservant on the elephant's back, went to the palace, and stood the elephant against the wall at a place facing the open courtyard, near the window, remaining there in the rain. The king, guarding his daughter, did not let her sleep elsewhere but made her sleep on a small bed near him. The princess, knowing the prince would come today, did not fall asleep but lay there and said, "Father, I wish to bathe." The king said, "Come, dear," took her hand, led her to the window, and saying "Bathe, dear," lifted her and placed her on the lotus-ledge outside the window, holding her by one hand. While bathing, she stretched her hand to the prince. The prince removed the ornaments from the princess's hand, placed them on the maidservant's hand, lifted the maidservant, and placed her on the ledge near the princess. The princess took the maidservant's hand and placed it in her father's hand. The king took the maidservant's hand and released his daughter's hand.
295:
The princess removed the ornaments from one of her hands and placed them on the second hand of that young female servant. She then left them in her father's hands and departed together with the prince.

The king, under the impression that she was his daughter, had the young girl bathed and then made her lie down in a magnificent chamber. He closed the door, secured it with a bolt, and set a guard before going to his own bed to sleep.

When dawn broke, the king opened the door and, seeing the young girl, asked, "How did this happen?" The girl then reported to the king the fact that the princess had left with the prince. The king became distressed and thought, "Even when held firmly, one cannot guard a woman; women are indeed of a nature that cannot be guarded."

Having said this, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "I myself have raised my nephew," gave his daughter to his nephew along with great wealth and appointed him to the position of heir apparent (Uparāja). Upon the death of his uncle, the nephew succeeded to the kingship.
296:
The Master, having delivered this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala). As for how the Jātaka was identified: "At that time, I myself was the king."

## Women are diverse, in every way, full of deceit
The Mudupāṇi Jātaka ends.

## 3. Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka
## The Power of Women
The Story of the Present: The All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Abhijjamāne vārīsmiṃ," concerning a certain dissatisfied monk.

To elaborate on that matter: The All-Enlightened Buddha asked the monk who had been brought to the Dhamma hall, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied in the Dispensation?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Buddha said, "Monks, women indeed defile even the pure beings of old," and at the request of the monks, he brought forth the past story.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the king, being childless, told his women, "Make a prayer for a son." They all prayed for a son.

After a long time had passed in this way, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Brahma realm and was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen. As soon as the Bodhisatta was born, he was bathed and given to nurses for breastfeeding. While being breastfed, he cried. Then he was given to another woman. Whenever he reached the hands of a woman (mātugāma), he would not remain silent.
297:
Then, they gave the Bodhisatta to an official who served at the king's feet. As soon as that official took him, he became silent.

From that time on, only men carried the Bodhisatta. When it was time for breastfeeding, they would either milk the breast and feed him, or place the breast in his mouth through a curtain. Therefore, they named the Bodhisatta Prince Anitthigandha (The Prince who has no scent of women).

Even as he grew up and moved about, the Bodhisatta could not be made to see what is called a woman. Therefore, the king had a separate sitting place and a meditation house (jhānāgāra) built for the Bodhisatta.

When the Bodhisatta reached sixteen years of age, the king thought, "I have no other son. This prince does not enjoy sensual pleasures. He will not even desire the kingship. It is indeed difficult for me to have gained such a son."

Then, a young dancing girl, who was skilled in dancing, singing, and music, and capable of bringing a man under her influence by serving him, approached the king and asked, "Great King, what are you thinking about?" The king told her the reason. She said, "Let it be so, Great King; I will seduce him and make him know the taste of sensual pleasure (kāmarasa)." The king said, "If you are able to seduce my son named Anitthigandha, he shall be the king, and you shall be the Chief Queen."

That dancing girl said, "Great King, let the seduction of your son be my responsibility; do not worry." She then approached the guards and said, "I will come at dawn and stand outside the meditation house near the prince's sleeping quarters and sing. If the prince becomes angry, tell me, and I will go away. If he listens, please tell me."
Those guards agreed, saying, "Very well."
298:
## 7. While the water was not parted, coming by your own psychic power,
Having gone to union with a woman, you sink in the great ocean.

## 8. Seducers, great deceivers, destroyers of the holy life;
Knowing them to be such, a wise man should avoid them from afar.

## 9. Whether they serve one out of desire or for wealth,
Like fire consuming its own base, they quickly consume him.

He spoke these verses.

This hermit, having come (āgamma) by psychic power (iddhiyā) without disturbing (abhijjamāne) the water (vārismiṃ), and having reached (gantvā) the state of mixing (missībhāvaṃ) with a woman (itthiyā), now sinks (saṃsīdasi) in the great ocean (mahaṇṇave).

Women are seducers (āvaṭṭanī), they have great wiles (mahāmāyā), and they destroy the holy life (brahmacariyavikopanā). They cause one to sink into the lower realms (sīdanti). Knowing (viditvāna) that fact (naṃ), a wise man (paṇḍito) should avoid (parivajjaye) those women from afar (ārakā).

Just as fire (jātavedo) burns (anudahati iva) its own place of origin (saṃṭhānaṃ), so do these women consume (anudahanti) that man (naṃ) whom (yaṃ) they serve (upasevanti) either out of lust (chandasā vā) or for wealth (dhanena vā) quickly (khippaṃ).

That dancer also stayed in that place at dawn and sang with a sweet voice, ensuring the sound of the lute did not exceed the song, nor the song the lute. The prince lay listening. The next day, he sent for her to stand nearby and sing. Again the next day, he sent for her to stand in the (meditation) hut and sing. Again the next day, he sent for her to stand close to him and sing.

In this way, gradually causing craving to arise, he indulged in the ways of worldlings. Having known the taste of sensual pleasure, he took a sword and went out to the middle of the road to chase away other men, thinking he would not give this woman to anyone else. Then the King had the prince seized and banished him from the city along with the young woman.

The two of them entered the forest and went downstream along the Ganges. Keeping the Ganges on one side and the ocean on the other, they built a hermitage and lived between the Ganges and the ocean. The young woman stayed at the hermitage and boiled roots and fruits. The Bodhisatta brought large and small fruits from the forest.

Then one day, while the Bodhisatta was away for fruits, another hermit living on a small island in the ocean came through the sky at the time of alms-round. Seeing smoke, he descended to the hermitage. Then the young woman asked the hermit to stay until the food was cooked, seduced him with feminine wiles, caused him to fall from Jhana, and made his holy life disappear. That hermit became like a crow with clipped wings.

Unable to abandon the woman, he stayed there all day. Seeing the Bodhisatta returning, he fled quickly toward the ocean. Then the Bodhisatta, thinking "This person will be my enemy," took a sword and pursued him. The hermit made a gesture as if to fly into the sky but fell into the ocean.

The Bodhisatta thought, "This hermit must have come through the sky; because of his fall from Jhana, he fell into the ocean. Now it is proper for me to be a refuge for this hermit." Standing on the shore of the ocean, he said—
299:
Hearing these words of the Bodhisatta, the ascetic, while still in the middle of the ocean, regained his lost meditative absorption (jhāna) and traveled through the air to his own dwelling place.

The Bodhisatta thought, "This ascetic, despite having such a heavy body, travels through the air like a tuft of silk-cotton. I, too, should develop jhāna and travel through the air like him." Having so reflected, the Bodhisatta went to the hermitage, took the woman back to the human world, and dismissed her, saying, "Go now." He then entered the forest, built a hermitage in a pleasant spot, ordained as an ascetic, practiced the kasina preliminaries, attained the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jataka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the monk who had become dissatisfied with the holy life was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Identifying the Jataka, he said: "At that time, I myself was Prince Anitthigandha."

## Monks and ascetics, meeting women, can fall into delusion and ruin.

The Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Mahāpanāda Jātaka

## The Story of the Past

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying on the banks of the Ganges, told this Mahāpanāda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Panādo nāma so rājā," concerning the spiritual power of the Elder Bhaddaji.

Once, while the All-Knowing Buddha was entering Sāvatthī, he set out on a journey accompanied by a large community of monks, thinking, "I will provide support to the youth Bhaddaji." Upon reaching the city of Bhaddiya, he stayed for three months in the Jātiya Grove, waiting for the youth Bhaddaji's wisdom to mature.

The youth Bhaddaji possessed great fame. He was the only son of the merchant of Bhaddiya, who possessed eighty crores of wealth. For that youth Bhaddaji, there were three palaces suitable for the three seasons. He lived in each palace for four months. After staying in one palace, he would move to another with a large retinue, surrounded by a troupe of dancers. At that moment, the entire city would be in an uproar, thinking, "We will see the youth's splendor." Between the palaces, they would set up tiers of carts and tiers of couches.

The All-Knowing Buddha, after staying for three months, informed the townspeople, "We shall depart." The townspeople invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please stay for tomorrow." On the second day, they prepared a great offering for the community of monks headed by the Buddha, built and decorated a pavilion in the center of the city, arranged seats, and announced that it was time for the meal.
300:
The Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, went to that pavilion and sat down. The people offered a great donation. Having finished his meal, the Buddha began the thanksgiving (anumodanā) with a sweet voice.

At that moment, the merchant's son Bhaddaji was moving from one palace to another. On that day, no one came to see his wealth. Only his own people surrounded him. Bhaddaji asked his people, "At other times, when I move from one palace to another, the whole city is stirred up. They set up carts upon carts and couches upon couches (to see me). But today, there is no one except my own people. What is the reason?"

"Young master, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, having resided near this city of Bhaddiya for three months, is leaving today. Having finished his meal, he is preaching the Dhamma to the great multitude. All the city dwellers are listening to his Dhamma talk."

Bhaddaji said, "In that case, come, let us also listen." Adorned with all his ornaments and accompanied by a large retinue, he approached and stood at the edge of the assembly. While listening to the Dhamma, even as he stood there, he exhausted all defilements and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

The Buddha addressed the merchant of Bhaddiya, "Great Merchant, your son, while listening to the Dhamma talk even as he was fully adorned, has become established in Arahantship. Therefore, it is proper for him today either to ordain or to attain Parinibbāna."

"Venerable Sir, I have no desire for my son's Parinibbāna. Please let him ordain. After ordaining him, please take him and come to our house tomorrow." The Buddha accepted the invitation, took the young man of good family to the monastery, had him ordained, and granted him the higher ordination (upasampadā). Bhaddaji's parents performed a great ceremony of honor for seven days. The Buddha stayed for seven days.

Taking the young man of good family, while wandering on a journey, he reached Koṭigāma. The people living in Koṭigāma gave a great donation to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. At the end of the meal, the Buddha began the thanksgiving. While the Buddha was giving the thanksgiving, the young man of good family went outside the village and sat down near the bank of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) at the foot of a tree, entering meditative absorption (jhāna), thinking, "I will rise only when the Teacher arrives." Even when the senior elders arrived, he did not rise, rising only when the Teacher arrived.

The worldling monks were angry, saying, "This Bhaddaji, as if he had ordained long ago, does not rise even when seeing the great elders arrive, though he only ordained yesterday."

The people living in Koṭigāma lashed boats together to form a raft. The Buddha, standing in the midst of the Saṅgha on the raft, asked, "Where is Bhaddaji?" "Venerable Sir, he is right here," they replied. "Bhaddaji, come, board the same boat with us," he said. The Elder Bhaddaji went and boarded the same boat with the Buddha.

Then, when they reached the middle of the Ganges, the Buddha asked the Elder Bhaddaji, "Bhaddaji, where is the palace you inhabited when you were King Mahāpanāda?" "Venerable Sir, it is submerged in this place," he replied.

The worldling monks said, "The Elder Bhaddaji is claiming the fruit of Arahantship (by speaking of his past life)." The Buddha said, "Bhaddaji, if that is so, dispel the doubts of the fellow monks."
301:
At that moment, the Elder Bhaddaji paid homage to the Buddha and, going by his psychic power, caught the pinnacle of the palace with his toe. He lifted the palace, which was twenty-five leagues in size, and soared into the sky. As the Elder Bhaddaji soared into the sky, the palace appeared to those standing below as if it were being pierced through. The Elder Bhaddaji lifted the palace from the water to a height of one league, two leagues, three leagues, up to twenty leagues.

At that time, the elder's relatives from a previous life, who had been reborn in that very palace as fish, turtles, nagas, and frogs due to their attachment to the palace, tumbled and fell back into the water as the palace was being lifted. Seeing those creatures falling into the water, the Buddha said, "Bhaddaji, your relatives are suffering." Hearing the Teacher's words, the Elder Bhaddaji released the palace. The palace settled back exactly in its original place.

On the bank of the Ganges, they prepared a seat for the Buddha. The Buddha sat on the prepared noble Buddha-seat, emitting rays of light like the young sun.

Then the monks asked the Buddha, "Venerable Sir, at what time did the Elder Bhaddaji inhabit this palace?" The Buddha said, "The Elder Bhaddaji inhabited it during the time of King Mahāpanāda," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, in the city of Mithilā in the kingdom of Videha, there was a king named Suruci. His son was also named Suruci. That Suruci's son was named Mahāpanāda. Those kings once obtained this palace. The cause for obtaining it was that in the past, a father and son built a dwelling hut for a Paccekabuddha using reeds and fig wood.

The complete story of the past in this Jātaka will become clear in the Suruci Jātaka, the sixth in the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta.
302:
10. That king named Panāda, whose sacrificial post was made of gold,
Sixteen units in width, and a thousand units in height.

11. With a thousand sections and a hundred knobs, it was adorned with banners and made of green gems;
There, the Gandharvas danced in six thousand groups of seven.

12. Thus it was then, just as you say, Bhaddaji.
I was Sakka at that time, and I was your servant.

He preached these verses.

(Of whom) - Of which king. (The sacrificial post) - The palace. (Was made of gold) - Was made of gold. (In width) - In breadth. (Sixteen units) - It was sixteen sections wide. (Upwards) - In height. (A thousand units) - It was a thousand sections high. (Was) - It existed. (That king) - That king. (Named Panāda) - Was known as Panāda.

The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this past story, after becoming the Buddha, said:

(This means that the palace was twenty-five yojanas high and eight yojanas wide.)

(A thousand sections) - The palace was a thousand sections high. (A hundred knobs) - It had a hundred storeys. (Adorned with banners) - It was full of banners. (Made of green gems) - It was encrusted with green emeralds. (There) - In that palace. (Six thousand) - Six thousand. (Gandharvas) - Dancers. (In seven groups) - In seven places. (Danced) - They danced.

(Even though they danced in this way, they were unable to make the king rejoice. Then Sakka, the King of Gods, sent a divine dancer to perform, and at that time, King Mahāpanāda rejoiced.)

(Bhaddaji) - O Bhaddaji. (As) - In the manner that. (You) - You. (Say) - Speak. (This) - That matter. (Thus) - Exactly as you say. (Then) - At that time. (Was) - It happened. (I) - I. (Then) - At that time. (Your) - Your. (Servant) - One who performed duties great and small. (Sakka) - Sakka. (Was) - I was.

At the moment this was preached, the worldling monks became free from doubt.
303:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, King Mahāpanāda was Bhaddaji, and I myself was Sakka."

## With generosity, one relies on such great power.

The Mahāpanāda Jātaka ends.

## 5. Khurappa Jātaka
## The Hero Who Dares to Die

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Khurappa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Disvā khurappe," concerning a monk who had given up his effort.

To elaborate on this: The Omniscient Buddha asked that monk, "Monk, is it true that you have given up your effort?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Venerable Sir," the Buddha said, "Monk, why have you given up your effort after ordaining in this teaching that leads out of suffering? Wise men of old made effort even in matters that do not lead out of suffering," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of forest guards. When he reached maturity, he became the chief of five hundred forest guards and lived in a village at the entrance of the forest. That forest guard would escort people through the forest for a fee.

Then one day, the son of a merchant from Bārāṇasī arrived at that village with five hundred wagons and called for him, saying, "Friend, take a thousand pieces of money and escort me through the forest." The forest guard agreed, saying, "Very well," and took the thousand pieces from the merchant's son. Having taken the fee, he dedicated his life to the merchant's son.

That forest guard then took the merchant and entered the forest. In the middle of the forest, five hundred robbers rose up. Upon seeing the robbers, all the men except the Bodhisatta lay down on their chests. The chief forest guard alone, shouting and charging, drove away all five hundred robbers and safely escorted the merchant's son across the wilderness.
304:
13. Seeing the hoof-tipped arrows shot with the speed of a bow,
And the sharp, oil-polished swords held in hand,
When that fear and death were imminent,
Why was there no trembling in you?

He spoke this first verse.

(Friend) - O friend. (Shot with the speed of a bow) - Discharged by the force of a bow. (Hoof-tipped arrows) - Arrows with heads like hooves. (Held) - Firmly grasped by the hilts. (Sharp) - Keen. (Oil-polished) - Sharpened with oil. (Swords) - Sabres. (Seeing) - Having seen. (In that fear) - In that fearful situation. (Death) - That death. (Imminent) - Appearing right before one. (Why) - For what reason. (In you) - To you. (Trembling) - Shaking of the body. (Was not) - Did not occur?

14. Seeing the hoof-tipped arrows shot with the speed of a bow,
And the sharp, oil-polished swords held in hand,
When that fear and death were imminent,
I felt a great and sublime joy.

15. Filled with joy, I overcame the enemies,
For my life had already been surrendered before.
Indeed, a hero who clings to life
Can never perform a hero's task.

He spoke these other two verses.

(Friend) - O friend. (I) - I. (Shot with the speed of a bow) - Discharged by the force of a bow. (Hoof-tipped arrows) - Arrows with heads like hooves. (Held) - Firmly grasped. (Sharp) - Keen. (Oil-polished) - Sharpened with oil. (Swords) - Sabres. (Seeing) - Having seen. (In that fear) - In that terrifying situation. (Death) - That death. (Imminent) - Appearing right before me. (Great) - Abundant. (Sublime) - Noble. (Joy) - Delight and happiness. (Felt) - I obtained.

(Filled with joy) - Having that delight and happiness. (That I) - That I. (Enemies) - The foes. (Overcame) - I conquered. (Beforehand) - Already in the past. (My) - By me. (Life) - Life. (Surrendered) - Was given up. (Was) - It happened. (Indeed) - Truly. (To life) - To life. (Clinging) - Making an attachment. (A hero) - A brave man. (Ever) - At any time. (A hero's task) - The duty of a brave man. (Can never perform) - Cannot do.

The merchant's son halted the wagons on the other side of the wilderness, provided the chief forest guard with various foods of excellent flavor, and after eating his own breakfast and sitting comfortably, he conversed with the chief forest guard. Wishing to ask, "Friend, when you were being overwhelmed by the weapons of those cruel robbers, for what reason did not even a moment of mental terror arise?"

Hearing those words, the chief forest guard—

Thus, while the rain of arrows was falling, the chief forest guard, having abandoned attachment to life, made his heroic deed known. He then sent the merchant's son on his way, returned to his own village, performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, and passed away according to his kamma.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and explained the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the explanation of the Truths, the monk who had given up his effort was established in the Fruit of Arahatship. How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, I myself was the chief forest guard." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Sacrificing life without hesitation, the brave noble one.

The Khurappa Jātaka ends.
305:
## 6. Vātaggasindhava Jātaka
## The Excessively Coy Woman

**The Story of the Present**
While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Vātaggasindhava Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Yenāsi kisiyā paṇḍu," concerning a certain householder in Sāvatthī.

In Sāvatthī, it is said that a beautiful woman saw a handsome householder and her heart became bound to him. The fire of lust (kilesa) arose within her as if her whole body were being consumed by flames. She found no physical comfort and no mental peace. She had no appetite for food and lay down merely clutching the side-frame of her bed.

Then her attendants and friends asked her, "Mother, why is your mind so agitated that you lie there clutching the bed-frame? What ailment or pain do you have?" When asked thus, she did not speak the first or second time, but when asked repeatedly, she revealed the matter.

Then the women who were her attendants and friends comforted her, saying, "Lady, do not worry; we will bring that householder to you." They went and spoke with the householder. Although he initially refused, he consented after being asked repeatedly.

Those women obtained his promise, saying, "Come on such a day at such a time," and went back to tell the woman. She prepared her private chamber, adorned herself, and sat upon the bed. When the householder arrived and sat on one side of the bed, she thought: "If I do not act with dignity and grant him the opportunity right now, my sovereignty over him will diminish. To grant the opportunity on the very day he arrives is inappropriate. Today, I will make him displeased and grant the opportunity on another day."

Then, when the householder began to flirt by taking her hand and so on, she grabbed his hand and rebuked him, saying, "Go away, go away! I have no need of you." The householder, feeling ashamed, retreated, stood up, and went back to his own home.
306:
The other women, knowing that she had refused to let him hold her hand and so on, approached her after the householder had left and asked, "You lay there rejecting food because your heart was bound to that householder. Then we pleaded with him repeatedly and brought him here; why did you not grant him the opportunity?" The woman told them the reason. The other women said, "In that case, you shall see what happens," and departed.

The householder did not return or even look back. Not getting that householder, the woman lost her appetite and came to the end of her life right there.

Knowing that she had died, the householder took many flowers, scents, and ointments, went to the Jetavana Monastery, made offerings to the Buddha, and sat in a suitable place.

The All-Knowing Buddha asked, "Lay disciple, why have you not appeared for so long?" He reported the matter. "Venerable Sir, for all this time, I was ashamed and did not come to attend upon the Buddha," he said. The Buddha said, "Lay disciple, not only now has this woman, through the power of lust, had you summoned and then made you ashamed by not granting the opportunity when you arrived; in the past also, she had her heart bound to the wise, had them summoned, and then sent them away after causing them weariness by not granting the opportunity." Having said this, at the request of the lay disciple, He brought forth the past.

**The Story of the Past**
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of Sindhu horses and became the royal auspicious horse named Vātaggasindhava. The grooms took him to bathe in the Ganges.

At that time, a female donkey named Bhaddalī saw the Sindhu horse and her heart became bound to him. Agitated by the power of lust, she would not eat grass nor drink water. She became parched and thin, until only skin and bone remained.

Then her son, a young donkey, seeing his mother parched and thin, asked, "Mother, why do you not eat grass or drink water, but lie there trembling in various places, parched and thin? What ailment do you have?" The female donkey did not speak, but when asked repeatedly, she told him the matter.

Then the son comforted the mother, saying, "Mother, do not worry; I will bring the Sindhu horse to you." When Vātaggasindhava came to bathe, the young donkey approached him and said, "Master, my mother's heart is bound to you; she is parched from lack of food and will die. Please grant her the gift of life."

"Very well, friend, I will grant it," the Sindhu horse said. "After the grooms bathe me, they will release me for a while to roam on the banks of the Ganges. You bring your mother and come to that place."
307:
16. "By what cause are you thin and pale? By what cause is food not pleasing? This husband has come; why do you run away now?"
He spoke this first verse.
"Mother. Because of having a mind attached to that Sindhu horse, you are thin and pale. Because of having a mind attached to that Sindhu horse, you do not enjoy your food. This husband, that Sindhu horse, has come. Why do you run away now?"

17. "If intimacy arises at the very beginning, the glory of women fades. Therefore, dear son, I run away."
He spoke this second verse.
"Dear son. If what is called intimacy arises at the very beginning, the glory—the wealth, happiness, and retinue—of women fades. Therefore, I make that Sindhu horse run away [or I run away from him]."

18. "She who does not desire a man born of a glorious family who has come to her, grieves for a long time, like Bhaddalī [grieving] for Vātagga."
The young donkey went and brought his mother, released her in that place, and stayed hidden in a suitable spot.
The horse-trainers also released the Vātaggasindhava horse in that place. That Vātaggasindhava horse saw the female donkey and approached her. At that time, when the Vātaggasindhava horse approached and sniffed her, the female donkey thought: "If I do not show respect and grant the Sindhu horse the opportunity the moment he arrives, my retinue, wealth, and happiness will fade. It is better to act as if I do not desire him." Thinking thus, she kicked the Sindhu horse in the lower jaw with her leg and ran away.
It was as if the Sindhu horse's teeth were broken. The Vātaggasindhava horse, feeling ashamed that he was not desired by that female donkey, fled from that place. That female donkey, becoming unhappy, fell down in that very place and lay there grieving. Then the son approached the mother and, wishing to ask—
The female donkey, hearing the son's words—
That female donkey told her son that acting in this way is the nature of women.
This third verse was spoken by the Blessed One after he had realized the Four Noble Truths:
"The woman who does not desire a man born of a noble family, endowed with wealth, who has come to her, that woman grieves for a long time, just as the female donkey named Bhaddalī grieves for the Vātaggasindhava horse."
The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the revelation of the Truths, the merchant was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). As for how the Jātaka was identified: "At that time, that woman was the female donkey. I myself was the Vātaggasindhava horse." Thus he identified the Jātaka.
## Excessive pride leads to losing a lover and can lead to death.
The Vātaggasindhava Jātaka ends.
308:
## 7. Kakkaṭaka Jātaka
## On the Crab
The All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Kakkaṭaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Siṅgī migo," concerning a certain woman.
In the city of Sāvatthī, a certain merchant took his wife and went to the countryside to collect debts. Having collected the debts, while returning, they were captured by robbers on the way. The merchant's wife was beautiful, charming, and pleasant to look at. The robber chief, out of affection for that woman, endeavored to kill the merchant.
That woman, however, was virtuous, possessed of good conduct, and devoted to her husband as a deity. She bowed at the feet of the robber chief and pleaded: "Lord Robber, if you have any affection for me, do not kill my husband. If you kill him, I will either eat poison or die by stopping my breath. I will not go with you. Do not kill my husband without cause." Thus she pleaded and had him released.
The husband and wife reached Sāvatthī safely. While passing by the edge of the monastery behind Jetavana, they thought, "We shall enter the monastery and worship the Blessed One." They went to the precinct of the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), worshipped the Blessed One, and sat in a suitable place. When the Blessed One asked the lay followers, "Where did you go?", they replied, "We went to collect debts."
When asked, "Did you return safely without illness on the way?", the merchant replied, "Venerable Sir, robbers captured us on the way. This woman pleaded with the robber chief who wanted to kill me and had me released. Because of her, I have gained my life."
The All-Knowing Buddha said, "Lay follower, it is not only now that this woman has given you your life; in the past too, she gave life to the wise." Being requested by the merchant, he brought forth the past.
In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a large lake in the Himālaya. In that lake lived a great golden crab. Because it was the dwelling place of the great golden crab, it was known as the Kuḷīra Lake. That crab was as large as a threshing floor. Elephants, out of fear of that crab, were unable to descend into that lake to feed.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of a female elephant, sired by the leader of the elephant herd who lived near that Kuḷīra Lake. Then that female elephant, thinking "I will protect the fetus," went to another mountain region, protected the fetus, and gave birth to a son. When that elephant gradually reached the age of discretion, he had a large body, was endowed with strength, reached the peak of beauty, and was like a mountain of collyrium.
309:
That elephant, having mated with a certain female elephant, thinking, "I will catch the crab," took his wife and his mother and approached the herd of elephants. Seeing his father, he said, "Father, I will catch the crab." Then his father warned him, saying, "Dear son, you will not be able to catch it; do not try to catch it." When he spoke thus repeatedly, the father said, "Then you yourself shall know."

That elephant gathered all the elephants living near the Kuḷīra Pond and went near the pond with all of them. He asked, "Does that crab catch [prey] at the time of entering the water, or at the time of feeding, or at the time of coming out?" Hearing that it catches at the time of coming out, he said, "In that case, you all descend into the Kuḷīra Pond, take as much food as you desire, and come out first. I will remain behind."

The elephants did as the Bodhisatta said. The crab, with its two claws, firmly gripped the feet of the Bodhisatta as he was coming out last, just as a blacksmith grips an iron bar with tongs. The female elephant did not abandon the Bodhisatta and stood right beside him. Though the Bodhisatta pulled, he was unable to move the crab. The crab, however, pulling the Bodhisatta, drew him toward itself. Terrified by the fear of death, he let out a cry of capture.

All the elephants, terrified by the fear of death, let out a trumpeting sound like that of cranes and fled, discharging excrement and urine. Even the female elephant, unable to withstand the fear, began to flee. Then, the Bodhisatta, making her realize his state of being caught, spoke the first verse so that she would not flee:

19. The horned beast with long eyes,
With skin of bone, water-dweller, hairless.
Overcome by him, I cry out piteously;
[Do not abandon me, who is dear as life.]
310:
20. "Noble one, I will not abandon you,
The sixty-year-old elephant king.
In this earth bounded by the four oceans,
You are most dear to me."

She spoke this verse to complete the two. [Meaning:] "Noble one, my lord. I will not abandon you, the elephant king who is weakened by the period of sixty years of age. In this earth bounded by the four oceans, you are very dear to me."

21. "Whatever crabs are in the ocean,
In the Ganges and the Yamunā,
You are the best of those water-born creatures;
Release my husband for me who is weeping."

She spoke this verse to complete the three. [Meaning:] "Noble Lord Crab, water-born one. Among whatever crabs there are in the ocean, in the Ganges, and in the Yamunā, you are the most excellent. I entreat you, release my husband for me who is weeping."

[The Bodhisatta had previously said:] "Do not abandon me, who is dear as life."

He spoke this first verse: "O female elephant, the golden crab has long eyes, skin of bone, dwells in the water, and is hairless. Overcome by that golden crab, I cry out piteously. Do not abandon me, who is dear as life."

Then the female elephant, returning and comforting the Bodhisatta, spoke [the second verse]. Then, wishing to entreat the crab, she said, "Noble one, now I will speak a little with the crab and have you released," and so she entreated the crab [with the third verse].

The crab, taking the female voice as an object of desire, and having a mind drawn by that female voice, loosened its claws from the elephant's feet. It did not realize anything, thinking, "When this elephant is released, he will do such and such." Then the elephant lifted his foot and stepped on the crab's back. At that very moment, the shells broke. The elephant let out a cry of joy.

All the elephants gathered, took the crab out, placed it on the ground outside the pond, and trampled it to fine powder. They separated the two claws from the body and left them in a suitable place.

That Kuḷīra Pond was connected to the Ganges; when the Ganges was full, it was filled with the water of the Ganges. When the water of the Ganges decreased, the water from the pond entered the Ganges. At that time, those two sharp claws also floated away into the Ganges.
311:
One claw entered the ocean, and the ten brother-kings found the other claw while playing in the water and made a drum named Āḷinga.

The Asuras took the claw that entered the ocean and made a drum named Ālambara. Later, when those Asuras were defeated in battle by Sakka, they abandoned the Ālambara drum and fled. Then Sakka had it taken for his own use. Regarding that drum, they say it thunders like the Ālambara cloud.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the husband and wife attained the Fruit of Stream-entry. As for the identification of the Jātaka: "At that time, the female elephant was this laywoman, and the elephant was I myself."

## A woman's voice causes craving in a man.
The Kakkaṭaka Jātaka ends.

## 8. Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka
## The Monkey that Destroyed the Garden

While the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was staying in the Dakkhiṇāgiri district, he told this Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yo ve sabbasametānaṃ," concerning the son of an obscure gardener.

It is said that after the rainy season retreat, the All-Knowing Buddha left Jetavana Monastery and wandered for alms in the Dakkhiṇāgiri district. At that time, a certain lay follower invited the community of monks headed by the Buddha, had them sit in his garden, and satisfied them with gruel and food. He said, "Venerable sirs, if you wish to wander through the garden, please do so with this gardener," and he commanded the gardener, "Give various fruits to the venerable sirs."

As the monks were wandering, they saw a place where trees were missing and asked, "In this place, the trees are cut off. The trees do not reach here. What is the reason?" Then the gardener explained to those monks, "Venerable sirs, a certain gardener's son, while watering the young planted trees, thought, 'I will water them according to the size of the roots,' and so he pulled them up and watered them according to the size of the roots. For that reason, the trees are missing in this place."
312:
22. "He who is considered the best among all those of equal birth—if such is his wisdom, what then of the other folk?"

He spoke this first verse.

*Sabbasametānaṃ*: among all beings born of the same kind. *Yo*: which being. *Ve*: indeed. *Seṭṭhasammato*: is considered the best. *Ahuvā*: has been. *Tassa*: of that being. *Ayaṃ paññā*: this wisdom. *Edisī*: is of such a nature. *Itarā*: other than this. *Pajā*: beings. *Kimeva*: how indeed [will their wisdom be]?

The monks went to the Buddha and reported the matter. The All-Knowing Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has this boy destroyed the garden; in the past, he also destroyed a garden," and he brought forth the story of the past.

In the past, when King Vissasena was reigning in Bārāṇasī, a festival was proclaimed. The gardener, wishing to enjoy the festival, said to the monkeys living in the garden, "This garden is of great benefit to you. I will be enjoying the festival for seven days. You must water the young trees that have been planted for these seven days." The monkeys agreed, saying, "Very well." The gardener gave the monkeys leather water-skins and pots and departed.

The monkeys said, "We shall water the young trees that have been planted." Then the leader of the monkeys said to the group, "Friends, wait a moment. Water is always difficult to obtain; it must be conserved. Pull up the young trees in the garden, determine the size of their roots, and give much water to those with long roots and little water to those with short roots." The monkeys agreed, and some pulled up the trees and went along, while others replanted them and watered them.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was a son of a certain family in Bārāṇasī. Having gone to the garden on some business, he saw the monkeys acting in that way and asked, "Who told you to do this?" When they replied, "We are doing this because the leader of the monkeys ordered it," he wished to explain the meaning, thinking, "If even the leader has so little wisdom, what must it be like for the rest of you?"

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the monkeys spoke this second verse to complete the pair:

23. "Just so, O Brahmin, you criticize us without knowing. Without seeing the root, how can one know if a tree is firmly established?"

*Brahme*: O noble one. *Tuvaṃ*: you. *Anaññāya*: without knowing. *Evameva*: just so. *Amhe*: us. *Vinandasi*: criticize. *Mūlaṃ*: the root. *Adisvāna*: without seeing. *Patiṭṭhitaṃ*: established. *Rukkhaṃ*: a tree. *Kathaṃ jaññā*: how can one know?
313:
24. I do not blame you, nor the other monkeys in the forest. Only Vissasena is blameworthy, for whose sake these tree-planters exist.

Regarding this, the Bodhisatta spoke this third verse to complete the set.

Monkeys, you who live in the forest, I do not blame you. Others here, for the sake of that King Vissasena, those like you have become tree-planters. Only that King Vissasena is blameworthy.

Having heard those words, the Bodhisatta—

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the youth who destroyed the garden was the monkey leader. I myself was the wise man."

## Only those with appropriate wisdom should be placed in the relevant positions.

The Ārāmādūsaka Jātaka is finished.

## 9. Sujāta Jātaka

## Sweet Speech

The Teacher, the All-Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sujāta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Na hi vaṇṇena sampannā," concerning Sujāta, the daughter-in-law of Anāthapiṇḍika, daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya, and younger sister of Visākhā.

That Sujāta entered Anāthapiṇḍika’s house with a great retinue. She was stubborn with pride, thinking, "I am the daughter of a great family." She was ill-tempered, fierce, and harsh. She did not perform her duties toward her parents-in-law or her husband. She went about threatening and striking the members of the household.

Then one day, the All-Enlightened One, surrounded by five hundred monks, went to the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and sat down. The great merchant, wishing to hear the Dhamma, approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down. At that moment, Sujāta was quarreling with the servants and laborers.

The All-Enlightened One, having finished preaching the Dhamma, asked, "What is that noise?" [Anāthapiṇḍika replied,] "Venerable Sir, it is a daughter-in-law of the family who is disrespectful. She has no sense of duty toward her parents-in-law or her husband. Lacking faith and devotion, she goes about quarreling day and night." "Then call her here." She came, paid homage, and stood to one side.

Then the Teacher asked her, "Sujāta, there are seven types of wives for a man. Which one of these are you?" "Venerable Sir, I do not understand the meaning of what is said in brief. Please explain it to me in detail." The Teacher said, "Then listen attentively," and spoke these verses:
314:
"She has no faith or devotion, and she goes about quarreling day and night," the Treasurer reported. "If that is so, call that daughter-in-law," the Buddha said. She came, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place.

Then the Buddha asked Sujātā, "Sujātā, there are seven types of wives a man may have. Among these seven, which wife are you?" She replied, "Glorious and Venerable Sir, I do not understand the meaning of the Dhamma spoken in brief. Please explain it to me in detail." The All-Knowing Buddha said, "If that is so, listen well and pay attention."

1. "Sujātā, a wife who has a mind corrupted by lust for other men, who has a mind to wrong her own husband, who desires his misfortune, who treats him with contempt like a slave bought with wealth, and who strives to kill him—such a wife is called a 'Slayer-like wife' (Vadhakā)."
315:
2. A wife who earns wealth through farming or trade, and yet desires to steal even a small portion of that wealth, is called a thief-like wife.

3. A wife who is not inclined to work, is lazy, gluttonous, harsh, angry, and speaks abusively, and who speaks oppressively to those who perform the work, is called a master-like wife.

4. A wife who desires her husband's welfare in every way, protects him as a mother protects her son, and guards the wealth accumulated by her husband, is called a mother-like wife.

5. A wife who respects her husband as a younger or older sister respects her brother, and follows her husband's will, is called a sister-like wife.

6. A wife who rejoices at seeing her husband as one rejoices at seeing a long-lost friend, is endowed with virtue, and serves her husband, is called a friend-like wife.

7. A wife who, even when threatened with punishment or death by her husband, does not get angry with him, remains patient, and follows her husband's will, is called a slave-like wife.

"Sujātā, there are seven types of wives for a man. Among these seven, the slayer-like wife, the thief-like wife, and the master-like wife are reborn in hell. The other four types of wives are reborn in the Nimmānarati heaven," the Buddha preached.

While the All-Knowing Buddha was thus showing these seven types of wives, Sujātā was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). When asked, "Sujātā, which of these seven types of wives are you?" she replied, "Venerable Sir, I am a slave-like wife," and she paid homage to the Buddha and asked for forgiveness.

Thus, the All-Knowing Buddha, having tamed the daughter-in-law named Sujātā with a single instruction, and having finished his meal, went to the Jetavana monastery. After the assembly of monks performed their duties, he entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī).

In the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised the praise of the Buddha's virtues: "Friends, with just a single instruction, the Buddha tamed the daughter-in-law Sujātā and established her in the fruit of Stream-entry."
316:
25. Not by appearance, though endowed with beauty, nor by a pleasant voice, nor by a lovely sight, does a harsh-spoken person become dear in this world or the next.

26. Do you not see this black, ill-favored, soot-covered cuckoo? Because of its gentle song, it is dear to many beings.

27. Therefore, one should be gentle-spoken, speaking with wisdom, not conceited. Such a one explains the meaning and the Dhamma; their speech is sweet.

He spoke these verses.

Mother, even if one is endowed with beauty, even if one has a pleasant voice, even if one has a lovely appearance, if that speech is harsh, such speech is not dear in this world or the next.

Do you not see this cuckoo, which is black, ill-favored, and soot-covered, yet is dear to many beings because of its gentle song?

Therefore, one should be gentle-spoken. One who speaks with wisdom and is not conceited explains the meaning (Attha) and the text (Dhamma); their speech is sweet.

The Blessed One arrived and asked, "Monks, what topic are you discussing as you sit here?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Sujāta has been disciplined with a single instruction; in the past, she was also disciplined with a single instruction." He then related the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the chief queen. When he came of age, he studied all the arts at Takkasilā. After his father passed away, he ascended the throne and ruled righteously.

The Bodhisatta’s mother was ill-tempered, fierce, and abusive. Although the Bodhisatta wished to give her advice, he thought it inappropriate to speak without a reason. He remained observant, looking for a metaphor to discipline her.

One day, when the king went to the garden, his mother followed him. On the way, a blue jay (kikī) screeched. Hearing that sound, the Bodhisatta’s attendants covered their ears and said, "Hey, you fierce-voiced, harsh-voiced bird, do not make that noise!"

While the Bodhisatta, surrounded by a troupe of dancers, was wandering in the garden with his mother, a cuckoo perched on a fully blossomed sāl tree and sang with a sweet voice. The people, enchanted by its sweet song, folded their hands and stood looking up with attentive ears, saying, "O gentle-voiced, pleasant-voiced, soft-voiced bird, sing again, sing again!"
317:
Then the Bodhisatta, seeing these two reasons and thinking, "Now is the time to make my mother understand," heard the sound of a cuckoo bird on the way. He noticed that people were saying, "Do not make this sound, do not make this sound," and were closing their ears. He intended to show that no one likes harsh speech. 

Thus, the Bodhisatta taught his mother with these verses and made her understand. From then on, his mother was endowed with good conduct. The Bodhisatta, having made his mother free from pride with a single instruction, went according to his kamma. 

Concluding the Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha brought this Dhamma teaching and identified the birth: "At that time, Sujātā was the mother of the King of Bārāṇasī, and I myself was the King."

## Harsh speech brings no love; sweet speech is loved by all.

The Sujāta Jātaka ends.

## 10. Ulūka Jātaka

## The Enmity between Crows and Owls

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the Omniscient One who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Ulūka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sabbhehi kira ñātīhi," concerning the quarrel between crows and owls.

At that time, crows would peck at owls during the day. From sunset onwards, the owls would cut off the heads of the crows sleeping in various places, causing them to perish. 

Then, a certain monk living in a dwelling at the edge of Jetavana Monastery had to discard many crow heads, about seven or eight measures, covered in blood, which fell from the trees during the time of sweeping. That monk informed the other monks about this matter. The monks raised the discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, at the dwelling of such-and-forth monk, this many crow heads have to be discarded every day."
318:
The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "With such a discussion," He said, "Monks, it is not only now that crows and owls have a quarrel; they also quarreled in the past." When they asked, "Venerable Sir, when did the quarrel between crows and owls begin?", the Teacher said, "It began from the time of the first world cycle," and brought the past story.

In the past, at the beginning of the world cycle, humans gathered and chose a handsome, graceful, well-behaved, and perfect man to be their king. The quadrupeds also gathered and chose a lion as their king. In the great ocean, the fish chose a fish named Ānanda as their king.

Then, the flocks of birds gathered on a flat rock in the Himālaya region and said, "Among humans, a king is known; likewise among quadrupeds and fish. But among us, there is no king. It is not proper to live without a leader. It is proper for us also to obtain a king. Find one bird who is fit to be placed in the position of king." Looking for such a bird, they liked an owl and said, "We like this one."

Then, one bird made the proclamation three times to take the consensus of all birds. After two proclamations were tolerated, at the third proclamation, a crow stood up and said, "Wait! Look at the face of this owl even at this time of coronation when he is not yet angry. What will his face be like when he is angry? If we are looked at by this owl in anger, we shall be destroyed right where we are, like salt thrown into a hot frying pan. I do not like making this owl our king." To express this meaning, he spoke the first verse:

28. By all my kinsmen, it is said, the Owl is made the lord. If permitted by my kinsmen, I would speak a single word.

[Word-for-word translation:] Sabbhehi: by all. Ñātīhi: by kinsmen. Kosiyaṃ: the owl. Issaro: the lord/king. Kato kira: is said to be made. Ñātīhi: by kinsmen. Sace anujñāto: if permitted. Ahaṃ: I. Ekavācikaṃ: a single word. Bhaṇeyya: wish to speak.

Then, the birds who wished to permit the crow said:
319:
29. Speak, friend, being permitted, only what is beneficial and righteous. For there are young birds who are wise and possess the light of wisdom.

This verse was spoken to complete the two. 

Samma: friend crow. Anujñāto: we permit you. Tvaṃ: you. Kevalaṃ: only. Atthañca: the benefit. Dhammañca: the reason/righteousness. Bhaṇa: speak. Hi saccaṃ: it is true. Daharā: though young. Paññavanto: wise. Jutindharā: possessing the light of wisdom. Pakkhī: birds. Santi: there are.

30. I do not like—blessings to you—the coronation of the Owl. Look at the face of one not angry; how will he look when he is angry?

This verse was spoken to complete the three.

Vo: to you all. Bhaddaṃ: may there be goodness. Me: I. Ulūkassa: of this owl. Abhisecanaṃ: the coronation. Na ruccati: do not like. Akkuddhassa: of the owl who is not angry. Mukhaṃ: the face. Passa: look. Kuddho: if he is angry. Kathaṃ karissati: how will he look/act?

Being thus permitted, that crow spoke thus.

Having said this, the crow flew into the sky crying, "I don't like it! I don't like it!" The owl also rose and pursued the crow. From that time on, they have held enmity toward each other. The birds then chose a Golden Goose (Suvaṇṇahaṃsa) as their king and departed.

Concluding the Jātaka, the Omniscient Buddha brought this Dhamma teaching, proclaimed the Truths, and identified the birth. At the end of the proclamation of the Truths, many monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry and so forth. How did He identify the birth? "At that time, I myself was the young Golden Goose who was consecrated as king."

## The enmity of owl and crow, learn how it began in the early world.

The Ulūka Jātaka ends.
320:
## 3. Udapāna Vagga
## 1. Udapānadūsaka Jātaka
## The Dirty Jackal
While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Udapānadūsaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Āraññikassa isino", concerning a certain jackal that defiled a well.

A certain jackal used to defile the drinking well of the Sangha of monks by voiding excrement and urine there, and then he would leave. One day, when he came near the well, the novices struck him with clods and stones, causing him distress. From that time on, he did not dare to look back at that place. The monks, learning of this, started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, it is said that since the time the novices distressed the well-defiling jackal, he has not dared to look back at that place again."

The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now has this jackal been a defiler of wells; in the past too, he was a defiler of wells," and he related the story of the past.

In the past, in the city of Bārāṇasī, this very well existed at this very Isipatana. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a family in Bārāṇasī, and upon reaching maturity, he became an ascetic and lived at Isipatana surrounded by a company of sages.

At that time, a certain jackal used to defile this very well and leave. One day, the ascetics surrounded him, caught him by a certain stratagem, and brought him before the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, wishing to speak with the jackal, recited this verse:

1. Āraññikassa isino, cirarattatapassino.
Kicchākataṃ udapānaṃ, kathaṃ samma avāhasi.

He recited this verse.

Samma, friend jackal. Āraññikassa, forest-dwelling. Isino, seeker of virtues such as morality. Cirarattaṃ, for a long time. Tapassino, the group of ascetics who practice austerities. Kicchākataṃ, made with difficulty. Udapānaṃ, the well. Kathaṃ, why. Avāhasi, did you defile it by voiding excrement and urine?

2. Esa dhammo siṅgālānam, yaṃ pitvā ohadāmase.
Pitupitāmahaṃ dhammo, na taṃ ujjhātumarahasi.

He recited this verse to complete the two.

Friend ascetic. Yaṃ, which well. Pitvā, having drunk from. Mayaṃ, we. Ohadāmase, void excrement and urine. Esa, this voiding of excrement and urine. Siṅgālānam, of jackals. Dhammo, is the nature. Pitupitāmahaṃ, of our fathers and grandfathers. Dhammo, it is the nature. Taṃ, that practice inherited from fathers and grandfathers. Ujjhātuṃ, to complain about or abandon. Na arahasi, you should not.

Hearing those words, the jackal—
321:
3. Yesaṃ vo ediso dhammo, adhammo pana kīdiso.
Mā vo dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, addasāma kudācanaṃ.

He recited this verse to complete the three.

Jackal. Yesaṃ vo, of those like you. Dhammo, the nature or practice. Ediso, is of this sort. Adhammo pana, but what then of wrongdoing? Kīdiso, what would that be like? Vo, your. Dhammaṃ vā, nature. Adhammaṃ vā, or non-nature. Mayaṃ, we. Kudācanaṃ, at any time. Mā addasāma, do not wish to see.

Then, to the jackal, the Bodhisatta—

Thus the Bodhisatta gave advice to that jackal, saying, "Do not come again," and from that time on, the jackal did not even look back again.

Identifying the Jataka: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jataka: "At that time, the well-defiling jackal was this very jackal. The leader of the group, however, was I myself."

## Such is the jackal's way: to destroy the good things it finds.

The Udapānadūsaka Jātaka ends.

## 2. Vyaggha Jātaka
## The Beast Leaves, the Forest Perishes

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Vyaggha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yena mittena saṃsaggā", concerning Kokālika.

The story of Kokālika will become clear in the Takkāriya Jātaka, the eighth in the Terasa Nipāta. Kokālika, thinking "I will bring Sāriputta and Moggallāna," went from the Kokālika country to Jetavana Monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, approached the Elders, and said, "Venerable sirs, the people living in the Kokālika country are calling for you; come, let us go." When the Elders refused, saying, "You go, friend, we are not going," Kokālika went back alone.

Then, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks started a discussion: "Friends, Kokālika is unable to live together with Sāriputta and Moggallāna, nor is he able to live without them. He cannot endure being together, nor can he endure being apart."
322:
4. Through association with which friend well-being is lost, a wise man should guard against him as he would his own eye, even before being oppressed.

5. Through association with which friend well-being increases, a wise man should behave toward him as toward himself in all matters.

These two verses were spoken.

Friend, through association with which base friend well-being—that is, the happiness of body and mind—declines, a wise man should guard against that friend even before being oppressed, just as one guards one's eye.

Friend, through association with which friend well-being—the happiness of body and mind—increases, a wise man should act with good conduct toward that friend in all matters, just as he would for himself.

The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current conversation?"
