When they replied, "It is such and such," He said, "Monks, not only now, but in the past as well, Kokālika was unable to live either with or without Sāriputta and Moggallāna," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a certain forest. Not far from his celestial abode, another tree deity lived in a great forest tree. In that forest grove, a lion and a tiger also resided.

Out of fear of that lion and tiger, no one dared to plow a field or cut a tree in that forest; there was no one even brave enough to turn back and look. However, those lion and tiger would kill and eat various kinds of prey, leaving the remains right there in the forest. Because of those rotting carcasses, the forest grove became filled with a foul stench.

Then, the other tree deity, who was foolish and did not understand the cause of things, said to the Bodhisatta one day, "Friend, because of this lion and tiger, our forest grove has become filled with an impure, foul smell. I shall drive them away."

The Bodhisatta said, "Friend, it is because of these two that our abodes are protected. If they flee, our abodes will be destroyed. When humans no longer see the tracks of the lion and tiger, they will cut down the entire forest, level it, and make fields. Do not let such a thought please you," and he spoke the first two verses.
323:
6. Come, O tigers, return! Come back to the great forest! Let not the tigerless forest be cut; let not the tigers be forestless.

This verse was spoken to complete the three.

O tigers and lions, please come! Return to the great forest. Do not let the forest, which is now without tigers, be destroyed. Let not the tigers and lions become ones without a home by being separated from their dwelling place, the forest.

He spoke thus to make the lion and tiger flee.

The Bodhisatta said, "Friend, because of these two—the lion and the tiger—our abodes are guarded. If these two flee, our abodes will be ruined. When people do not see the tracks of the lion and tiger, they will cut down the whole forest, make it a single clearing, and plow fields. Do not desire the flight of the lion and tiger."

Even though the Bodhisatta explained the reason in this way, that foolish deity did not reflect and one day showed a terrifying sight to drive the lion and tiger away. When humans did not see their tracks and realized, "The lion and tiger have gone to another forest grove," they cut down one side of the forest.

The tree deity approached the Bodhisatta deity and said, "Friend, I did not follow your words and drove them away. Now, knowing they are gone, humans are destroying the forest. What should be done?" The Bodhisatta replied, "They are now living in such-and-such a forest; go and bring them back." The deity went there, stood before them, and with joined palms, spoke the third verse.

Even though they were thus entreated by that deity, those tigers and lions rejected the plea, saying, "You go; we will not come back." The deity returned to the forest grove alone. Within a few days, the humans cut down the entire forest, made fields, and began farming.
324:
The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the foolish deity was Kokālika, the lion was Sāriputta, the tiger was Moggallāna, and the wise deity was I myself."

## The foul smell is unbearable; the entire forest abode is ruined.
The Vyaggha Jātaka ends.

## 3. Kacchapa Jātaka
## The Tortoise Hanging On
While the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, He spoke this Kacchapa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ko nu uddhitabhattovā," concerning the settling of a quarrel between two great ministers of King Kosala.

The story of the present has already been told in the Duka Nipāta.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. Upon reaching maturity, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, renounced sensual pleasures, and became an ascetic. He built a hermitage on the banks of the Ganges in the Himalayan region, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and lived enjoying the bliss of meditation.

In this Jātaka, the Bodhisatta was extremely indifferent; he was fulfilling the Perfection of Equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī).
325:
7. "Who is this, as if bringing served food, like a Brahmin with hands full? Where did you wander for alms? Which faithful one did you approach?"
This first verse was spoken.
Who is this who comes like a Brahmin with hands full, having received food from a blessing ceremony in the month of Kattika, or as if having an abundance of food served in an alms-bowl? Who is this? Where did you wander for alms? Which faithful woman did you approach?

8. "I am a foolish monkey; I touched what should not be touched. May you release me, may blessings be upon you; once freed, I shall go to the mountain."
This verse, which completes the pair, was spoken.
May blessings be upon you, venerable sir. I am a foolish monkey. I touched that which should not be touched. May you release me from this suffering. Once freed, I shall go to the mountain.

9. "Turtles are of the Kassapa clan, monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña clan. Release the Koṇḍañña, O Kassapa; a union has been made by you."
This verse, which completes the three, was spoken.
Turtles are of the Kassapa lineage. Monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña lineage. Therefore, O Kassapa, the turtle of the Kassapa lineage, release the Koṇḍañña, the monkey of the Koṇḍañña lineage, who has performed this 'union' with you.

While the Bodhisatta was staying at the gate of his dwelling, an immoral and mischievous monkey came and committed an act of inserting its private parts into his ear-holes. The Bodhisatta remained indifferent and did not forbid it.

Then one day, a turtle came up from the water and lay sunbathing with its mouth open on the bank of the Ganges. Seeing the turtle, the frivolous monkey inserted its private parts into the turtle's mouth. Then the turtle woke up and bit the monkey's private parts as if shutting them in a casket. Intense pain arose.

Unable to endure that pain, the monkey thought, "Who can release me from this suffering? To whom should I go? There is no one else but the ascetic who can free me from this misery. It is proper for me to go to the ascetic." Thus, carrying the turtle with both hands, he went to the Bodhisatta.

The Bodhisatta, wishing to joke with that immoral monkey—

Hearing those words, the immoral monkey—
326:
The Bodhisatta, out of compassion, wishing to speak with the turtle—

Hearing the Bodhisatta's words, the turtle was pleased by the reasoning and released the monkey's genitals. As soon as he was freed, the monkey paid homage to the Bodhisatta and fled. He did not even look back at that place again. The turtle also paid homage to the Bodhisatta and went to his own place. The Bodhisatta, without falling away from his jhāna, was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. How did he identify the Jātaka? "At that time, the two ministers were the monkey and the turtle; I myself was the ascetic."

## Like the one who is lustful and reckless, seeking the flower of death.
The Kacchapa Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Lola Jātaka
## The Greedy Crow's Ruin
The Story of the Present: The All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at Jetavana Monastery, told this Lola Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinī", concerning a certain frivolous monk. The All-Knowing Buddha said to the monk who was brought to the Dhamma Hall, "Monk, you are not frivolous only now; in the past too, you were frivolous. Because of your frivolity, you reached the end of your life. Depending on you, the wise ones of old were also displaced from their own dwellings." Then he brought forth the past.

The Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a cook in the kitchen of the Treasurer of Benares placed a nesting basket for pigeons for the sake of merit. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born in the pigeon family and lived in that basket.
327:
10. "Who is this crested crane, this thief who stole from the basket? Come closer, O crane; my friend the crow is fierce."
This first verse was spoken.
O crested one; O thief who steals from the basket; O one whose grandfather is the rain—what is this crane doing? O crane, my friend the crow is fierce. Come inside.

At that time, a frivolous crow, flying over the kitchen, saw various kinds of fish, meat, and delicacies and was overcome by greed. Thinking, "By depending on whom might I get an opportunity?" he saw the Bodhisatta and thought, "By depending on this pigeon, I might get an opportunity." When the Bodhisatta pigeon went to the forest to search for food, the crow followed him.

Then the Bodhisatta said to the crow, "Friend crow, we eat one kind of food, and you eat another. Why do you follow me?" The crow replied, "Sir, I like your behavior. I too wish to have food like yours and serve you. Therefore, I follow you." The Bodhisatta agreed.

The crow, as if foraging with the Bodhisatta, landed on the ground, pecked at cow-dung heaps, ate worms to fill its belly, and approached the Bodhisatta, saying, "Sir, you have been foraging for so long. Should one not know the proper measure in eating? Come, let us go quickly before it gets dark." The Bodhisatta took the crow and went to his dwelling. The cook, thinking, "Our pigeon has brought a friend," placed a basket of chaff for the crow. The crow stayed there in that manner for four or five days.

Then one day, a large amount of fish and meat was brought for the merchant. The crow, seeing that fish and meat, was overcome by greed and lay groaning from early morning. The next day, the Bodhisatta said to the crow, "Friend, come, let us go for food." The crow replied, "You go; I have a suspicion of indigestion."

"Friend, there is no such thing as indigestion for crows. Only a tiny amount of food, like a lamp-wick, stays in your belly;"
328:
11. I am not a crested crane; I am a greedy crow.
By not following your advice, see me, I have come back plucked.

He spoke this verse to complete the two parts:
I am not a crested crane (balākā sikhinī). I am a greedy (lolo) crow (vāyaso). By not following (akatvā) your word (vacanaṃ), I have been plucked (lūno). Look at me (maṃ passa) as I have returned (āgato) from the feeding ground.

12. You will fall into misfortune again, friend, for such is your conduct.
Indeed, human food is not easily enjoyed by birds.

He spoke this verse to complete the three parts:
Friend (samma), you will again (punapi) fall into such suffering (evarūpaṃ āpajjasi). It is true (hi-saccaṃ), your conduct (sīlaṃ) is such (tādisaṃ) that it is suitable for reaching such suffering. For birds (pakkhinā), human food (mānusakā bhogā) is not easily enjoyed (na hi subhuñjā honti).

"The rest of the food is digested as soon as it is swallowed; listen to my words. Do not act this way upon seeing special meat and fish," said the Bodhisatta. "What are you saying, sir? I have a disease of indigestion," the crow replied. "If that is so, then remain heedful," the Bodhisatta admonished the crow and left.

The cook prepared many varieties of fish and meat, wiped the sweat from his body, and stood at the kitchen door. The crow, thinking, "Now is the time to eat fish and meat," flew and perched above the pots where the meat was cooking.

The cook, hearing the sound of the crow and looking up, saw the crow and caught it. He took it into the kitchen, plucked all the feathers from its body except for a tuft on its head, and mixed ginger, pepper, and other spices. Saying, "You have made a mess of our master's fish and meat," he smeared the crow's entire body with the juice of ginger, pepper, and so on, and threw it into a wicker basket. The crow suffered intense pain.

The Bodhisatta, returning from his feeding ground and seeing the moaning crow, wishing to mock him—
329:
Having heard those words, the crow—
Having heard those words, the Bodhisatta—

The Bodhisatta spoke thus, and thinking, "From this day forth, it is not possible for me to live here," he flew up and went elsewhere. The crow, moaning, died right there.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the greedy monk was established in the fruit of Anāgāmi (Non-Returner). To identify the Jātaka: "At that time, the greedy crow was the greedy monk, and the pigeon was I myself."

## Greedy for food, the crow behaves wildly and finds the flower of death.
The Lola Jātaka is finished.

13. Who is this beautiful crane sitting in the crow's nest?
The crow, my friend, to whom this nest belongs, is fierce.

14. Do you not know me, friend, bird who eats millet?
By not following your advice, see me, I have come back plucked.

15. You will fall into misfortune again, friend, for such is your conduct.
Indeed, human food is not easily enjoyed by birds.

Beautiful (rucirā) refers to the white color due to being smeared with buttermilk. Beautiful, pleasant to look at, pale—this is the meaning. In the crow's nest (kākanīḷasmiṃ) means in the crow's dwelling. There is also a reading "kākaniḍḍhasmiṃ." Bird (dija) is how the crow addresses the pigeon. One who eats millet (sāmākabhojana) means one who eats grass seeds. By the mention of millet (sāmāka), all grass seeds are included here. Here too, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "It is no longer possible for me to live here from now on," flew up and went elsewhere.

## 5. Rucira Jātaka
## The Pigeon's Companion—Longing for Meat

The All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Rucira Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kāyaṃ balākā rucirā," concerning a greedy monk. The two stories (of the present and the past) are just like the previous one. However, the verses are different.

In this Jātaka as well, the Bodhisatta pigeon, thinking, "From this day forth, it is not proper for me to live here," flew up and went to another place.
330:
The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Birth Story. At the conclusion of the Truths, the frivolous monk was established in the fruit of Anāgāmi (Non-returner). To identify the Birth Story: "At that time, the frivolous crow was the frivolous monk, and I myself was the pigeon." This is how he identified the Birth Story.

## The frivolous and fickle will perish; the crow is the example

The Rucira Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Kuru-dhamma Jātaka

## Solving the Hunger Problem

The Teacher, the Omniscient One who admonishes the world together with the devas, while staying at the Jetavana Monastery, told this Kuru-dhamma Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Tava saddhañca sīlañca," concerning a monk who killed a swan.

Two friends living in Sāvatthī, having ordained and attained higher ordination, mostly went about together. One day, they went to the Aciravatī River, bathed, and stood on the sandbank basking in the sun, engaging in pleasant conversation.

At that moment, two swans were flying through the sky. Then a young monk, picking up a pebble, said, "I will hit the eye of one of those young swans." The other said, "You will not be able to." "Leave this eye aside; I will hit the eye on the other side," he said. "Even that, you will not be able to do," the other replied.

"In that case, watch," he said, and taking a sharp pebble, he threw it behind the swan. Hearing the sound of the pebble, the swan turned and looked back. Then the other monk took a round pebble and hit the eye on the far side, making it come out through the eye on the near side. The swan, crying out, tumbled and fell right at their feet.
331:
The monks standing here and there saw this and came over, saying, "Friend, having ordained in such a liberating teaching that leads out of suffering, it is improper for you to commit the taking of life." They took the monks and presented them to the Tathāgata.

The Teacher asked, "Monk, is it true that you committed the taking of life?" When he replied, "It is true, Bhante," the Teacher said, "Monk, why did you do such a thing after ordaining in such a liberating teaching? Ancient wise men, even when no Buddha had arisen, while living the defiled life in the midst of a household, felt remorse even in small matters. But you, having ordained in such a liberating teaching, do not feel even a bit of remorse. Should not a monk be restrained in body, speech, and mind?" Having said this, he brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Dhanañjaya Koravya was reigning in the city of Indapatta in the kingdom of Kuru, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of that king's Chief Queen. In due course, having reached the age of discretion, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā and was appointed to the position of sub-king by his father. Later, upon his father's passing, he attained the kingship and, without violating the ten royal virtues, lived according to the Kuru-dhamma. (The Kuru-dhamma refers to the five precepts.)

Just as the Bodhisatta kept the five precepts purely, so did his mother the Chief Queen, his younger brother the sub-king, the chaplain brahmin, the land-surveying minister, the charioteer, the merchant, the great minister who was the measurer, the gatekeeper, and the courtesan. They all kept the five precepts purely.

The king had six alms-halls built—at the four city gates, in the center of the city, and at the palace gate—and spending six hundred thousand daily, he gave alms, making the whole of Jambudīpa like a field ready for plowing. His delight and devotion in giving alms spread throughout the whole of Jambudīpa.

At that time, in the city of Dantapura in the kingdom of Kaliṅga, King Kaliṅga reigned. In his kingdom, the rain did not fall. When it did not rain, famine arose throughout the whole kingdom. Due to the failure of food, disease broke out among the people. The three fears arose: the fear of drought, the fear of famine, and the fear of disease. The people, being destitute, wandered here and there holding their children by their hands.

The inhabitants of the entire kingdom gathered together, went to Dantapura, and raised a cry at the palace gate. The king, standing by the window, heard the sound and asked, "For what reason are these people crying out?" "Great King, the three fears have arisen in the whole kingdom. The rain does not fall, the crops do not mature, and famine has occurred. People, oppressed by disease due to bad food and being destitute, wander about holding their children by their hands. Great King, make it rain!"

He asked, "What did ancient kings do when it did not rain?" "Great King, when it did not rain, ancient kings gave alms, observed virtue, undertook the Uposatha, entered a magnificent chamber, and slept on a bed of kusa grass. Then the rain would fall," they replied. The king agreed and did as they said. Even though he did so, the rain did not fall.

Then the king said to his ministers, "I have done what was required of me..."
332:
The rain did not fall. 'What shall we do?' he asked. 'Great King, in the city of Indapatta, King Dhanañjaya Koravya has an auspicious elephant named Anjanavaṇṇa. Let us bring that elephant. If we do so, the rain will fall,' they said. The King said, 'That King is endowed with great power and a vast army; he is difficult to overcome. How shall we bring his auspicious elephant?'

'Great King, there is no need for war with King Koravya. King Dhanañjaya Koravya is one who greatly delights in giving. If asked, he would even cut off his adorned head and give it; he would pluck out his eyes, full of clarity, and give them; he would even hand over his entire kingdom. Regarding an elephant, there is no need to even speak of it. If asked, he will surely give it,' the ministers said.

'Who would be able to ask for that elephant?' the King asked. 'Great King, the Brahmins are able,' the ministers replied. The King summoned eight Brahmins from the Brahmin village, honored them with gifts, and sent them to ask for the elephant.

Those Brahmins took provisions, assumed the appearance of travelers, and traveled swiftly, staying only one night at each place. Within a few days, they arrived at the city gate, ate at the alms-halls to satisfy their bodies, and asked, 'When will the King come to the alms-hall?' The people said, 'The King comes on three days of the fortnight: the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth. Tomorrow is the full-moon day (Puṇṇamī). Therefore, he will come tomorrow.'

Early the next morning, the Brahmins went and stood at the East Gate. The Bodhisatta, having bathed early, anointed his body with perfumes, and adorned himself with all ornaments, mounted his beautifully decorated elephant. Surrounded by a large retinue, he went to the alms-hall by the East Gate. He descended from the elephant, personally gave food to seven or eight people, and said, 'Continue giving in this manner.' Then he remounted the elephant and proceeded toward the South Gate.
333:
16. 'O Lord of Men, having known your faith and virtue,
We exchange [wealth] for Anjanavaṇṇa in Kaliṅga.'

They spoke this first verse. 

'O Lord of Men, King Koravya who rules over the people. We, having known your faith and your virtue, wish to exchange gold for the elephant Anjanavaṇṇa in the kingdom of Kaliṅga.' Alternatively: 'In the presence of the King of Kaliṅga, we shall praise your virtues because of the elephant Anjanavaṇṇa.'

17. 'Those who are to be supported by food and those who are not,
Whoever comes here seeking a person,
All of them must not be rejected;
This is the word of the ancient teachers.'

18. 'I give this elephant to you, O Brahmins,
Fit for a king, a royal vehicle, glorious,
Adorned and covered with a golden net...'

The Brahmins, because of the heavy guard at the East Gate, did not get an opportunity. They went to the South Gate and waited for the approaching King. Standing on high ground not far from the gate, when the King arrived, they raised their hands and shouted the cry of victory: 'May you be victorious, Great King!'

The King stopped the elephant with his diamond-studded goad, went near the Brahmins, and asked, 'O Brahmins, what do you desire?' The Brahmins, wishing to praise the virtues of the Bodhisatta, spoke the verse.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, 'O Brahmins, if you wish to sell this elephant and obtain wealth, do not worry. I shall give you the elephant just as it is, fully adorned.' Thus he reassured them and spoke these verses:
334:
78. 'I give this elephant to you, O Brahmins, fit for a king, a royal vehicle, glorious, adorned and covered with a golden net, along with its driver; go wherever you wish.'

'O Brahmins, in this world, there are those who are supported by food and those who are not. Among them, whoever goes seeking a certain person, all those who come seeking must not be rejected by that person. This is the word of the ancient teachers, the parents. This means I have been taught thus by my parents.'

'O Brahmins, because this is the word of our ancient teachers, I give this elephant to you. It is fit for a king, a royal possession, and glorious, meaning it has a large retinue. It is said that five hundred families, including elephant-keepers and elephant-doctors, live depending on this elephant. I give it to you along with them. It is adorned with various elephant ornaments and covered with a golden net. I give it along with its driver, the master elephant-keeper. Therefore, taking this elephant with its retinue and its driver, go wherever you wish.'

Thus, the Great Being, while still mounted on the elephant's back, gave the gift by word. Then he descended from the elephant's back, saying, 'If there is any part unadorned, I shall adorn it and then give it.' He walked around the elephant three times in clockwise circumambulation, and seeing no part unadorned, he placed the elephant's trunk into the hands of the Brahmins. He then poured water scented with flowers and perfumes from a golden pitcher and made the formal gift.

The Brahmins accepted the elephant with its retinue, mounted it, and went to the city of Dantapura to give it to their King. Even though the elephant had arrived, the rain still did not fall. The King asked again, 'What is the reason for this?'
335:
King Dhanañjaya Koravya practices the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, in the King's realm, rain falls every half-month and every ten days through the power of the King's virtue. Hearing that 'this animal (the elephant) has no such merit,' he had the elephant, adorned as before and with its retinue, returned to the King. He then sent brahmins and ministers, saying, 'Go and write the Kuru-dhamma that the King protects on a gold plate and bring it back.'

Those ministers and brahmins went and handed over the elephant to the King, saying, 'Great King, even though this elephant has arrived, it does not rain in our country. We hear that you, O King, protect the Kuru-dhamma. Our King also wishes to protect it; therefore, let it be written on this gold plate and brought to him. Please give us the Kuru-dhamma.'

The King replied, 'Friends, it is true that I protect this Kuru-dhamma. However, now I have a scruple regarding it; that Kuru-dhamma does not satisfy my mind. Therefore, I cannot give it to you.'

Why did that virtue not satisfy the King? It is said that every third year, in the month of Kattika, there is a festival for kings. While celebrating that festival, the kings, adorned with all ornaments and assuming the appearance of gods, stand near the yakkha named Cittarāja and shoot variegated arrows, adorned with flowers, toward the four directions.

This King Koravya, while celebrating that festival, stood near the yakkha Cittarāja by a certain pond and shot variegated arrows toward the four directions. Among those arrows, he saw three that had gone in the other directions, but he did not see the arrow shot toward the surface of the water.

The King felt a scruple, thinking, 'Could the arrow I shot have fallen on the body of a fish?' He was concerned about the breach of virtue through the act of taking life; therefore, the virtue did not satisfy him. He said, 'Friends, I have a scruple regarding the Kuru-dhamma. But my mother protects it well; receive it from her.'
336:
The ministers said, 'Great King, you had no intention to kill a living being. Without intention, there is no such thing as taking life. Please give us the Kuru-dhamma protected by yourself.'

'In that case, write it down,' he said, and had it written on the gold plate: 'One should not kill living beings. One should not take what is not given. One should not practice misconduct in sensual pleasures. One should not speak lies. One should not drink intoxicants.' Having had this written, he said, 'Even so, it does not satisfy me. Receive it from my mother.'

The messengers paid homage to the King, went to the mother, and said, 'O Queen, we hear that you protect the Kuru-dhamma. Please give it to us.' She replied, 'Friends, it is true that I protect the Kuru-dhamma. But now a scruple has arisen in me regarding it. That Kuru-dhamma does not satisfy me; therefore, I cannot give it to you.'

It is said that she had two sons: the elder was the King, and the younger was the Uparāja. Then another king sent to the Bodhisatta sandalwood essence worth a hundred thousand and a gold garland worth a thousand. He sent all of it to his mother, saying, 'I will honor my mother.' She thought, 'I neither apply sandalwood nor wear garlands; I will give them to my daughters-in-law.' Then it occurred to her, 'My elder daughter-in-law is my superior, established in the position of Chief Queen; I will give her the gold garland. But the younger daughter-in-law is poor; I will give her the sandalwood essence.'

Having given the gold garland to the King's Queen and the sandalwood essence to the Uparāja's wife, she then thought, 'I protect the Kuru-dhamma. The wealth or poverty of these women should not be my measure. It is only proper for me to perform the act of respecting the elder. I wonder if my virtue is broken because I did not do that (impartially)?' Thus a scruple arose. Then the messengers said, 'One's own property may be given according to one's pleasure. If you feel a scruple over even this much, how could you commit any other evil? Virtue is not broken by such an act. Please give us the Kuru-dhamma.' Having received it from her, they wrote it on the gold plate.

The Queen Mother said, 'Friends, even though I have given it, the Kuru-dhamma does not satisfy me. However, my daughter-in-law protects it well. Receive it from her.' When this was said, they approached the Chief Queen and requested the Kuru-dhamma as before. She also spoke in the same manner, saying, 'Now the virtue does not satisfy me; therefore, I cannot give it to you.'
337: One day, the Queen was standing by the lion-window. Seeing the Viceroy riding on the back of an elephant behind the King, who was circumambulating the city, she felt a sense of lust. She thought, 'If I could form a friendship with the Viceroy, and if he were to become King after his brother passes away, he might take me as his own.' Then, the Queen felt remorse, thinking, 'I, who observe the Kuru-dhamma, have looked upon another man with lust while having a husband. Therefore, my virtue must be broken.' Thus she spoke. Then the messengers said to the Queen, 'Lady, a mere thought does not constitute a transgression. You feel remorse for even this much; how then could you commit a real transgression? Virtue is not broken by this much. Please give us the Kuru-dhamma.' Having said this, they received the Kuru-dhamma from the Queen and recorded it on a gold plate. The Queen said, 'O friends, even though I give it, this virtue does not satisfy me. However, the Viceroy protects it well. Take it from him.' Being thus told, the messengers approached the Viceroy and requested the Kuru-dhamma in the same manner as before. Now, when the Viceroy went to attend upon the King in the evening, he would reach the royal courtyard by chariot. If he wished to dine and sleep there in the King's presence, he would leave the reins and the goad on the front of the chariot. By that sign, the people would depart and return early the next morning, waiting for the Viceroy's departure. The charioteer also, having looked after the chariot, would bring it to the palace gate early the next morning. If the Viceroy wished to leave immediately, he would leave the reins and the goad inside the chariot and go to attend upon the King. By that sign, the people would stay at the palace gate, thinking, 'He will come out now.' One day, having done this, the Viceroy entered the palace. As soon as he entered, it rained. The King, saying 'It is raining,' did not allow the Viceroy to leave. The Viceroy dined and slept there in the palace. The people, thinking 'He will come out now,' stood there all night getting wet in the rain. The next day, the Viceroy came out and saw the people standing there soaked. He felt remorse, thinking, 'I, who observe the Kuru-dhamma, have caused so many people to suffer. My virtue must be broken.' Therefore, he said to the messengers, 'It is true that I observe the Kuru-dhamma. However, I now have remorse; therefore, I cannot give it to you,' and he explained the matter. Then the messengers said to the Viceroy, 'Great King, you did not have the intention to make those people suffer. Without intention, there is no kamma. You feel remorse for even this; how could there be a transgression for you?' Having said this, they took the virtue from the Viceroy and recorded it on a gold plate. 'Even though I give it, this virtue does not satisfy me. However, the Chaplain protects it well. Take it from him.' Being thus told, the messengers went to the Chaplain and requested it.
338: One day, as the Chaplain was going to the palace to attend upon the King, he saw on the way a new, radiant chariot sent to the King of Kuru by another king. He asked, 'Whose chariot is this?' and hearing 'It is a chariot brought for the King,' he thought, 'I am old. If the King were to give me this chariot, I could travel comfortably in it.' He then went to the King's presence. When he stood there after saying 'May you be victorious, Great King,' they showed the chariot to the King. The King, seeing it, said, 'This chariot is very beautiful. Give it to the Teacher.' The Chaplain did not want it. Even though he was told repeatedly, he still did not want it. Why did he not want it? It is said he thought: 'I, who observe the Kuru-dhamma, have felt greed for another's property. My virtue must be broken.' Therefore, he did not want it. He explained this matter and said, 'O friends, I have remorse regarding the Kuru-dhamma. That practice does not satisfy me; therefore, I cannot give it.' Then the messengers said to him, 'Venerable Sir, virtue is not broken by a mere arising of greed. You feel remorse for even this much; how could you commit a transgression?' Having said this, they took the virtue from him and recorded it on a gold plate. 'Even though I give it, this virtue does not satisfy me. However, the Royal Land Surveyor protects it well. Take it from him.' Being thus told, the messengers went to the Royal Land Surveyor and requested it. One day, while the Royal Land Surveyor was measuring a field in the countryside, he tied the end of the measuring rope to a staff. He had the field owner hold one end, and he held the other end himself. The staff tied to the end of the rope held by the Surveyor happened to be over the middle of a crab's hole. He thought, 'If I plant the staff in the hole, the crab inside will perish. If I plant it beyond the hole, the King's property will be lost. If I plant it on this side of the hole, the householder's property will be lost. What should be done?' Then he thought, 'There might not be a crab in the hole. If there were, it would be apparent. I will plant the staff right in the hole.' With this thought, he dropped the staff into the hole. The crab made a 'kiri' sound. Then the Surveyor thought, 'The staff must have fallen on the crab's back. The crab will die. I observe the Kuru-dhamma; that virtue I protect must be broken.' He explained this matter and said, 'Because of this reason, I have remorse regarding the Kuru-dhamma. Therefore, I cannot give it to you.'
339:
Then the messengers said to the rope-measuring minister, "You had no intention for the crab to die. Without intention, there is no such thing as kamma. If you feel remorse even for this much, how could you ever commit a transgression?" Having said this, they took the precepts from the rope-measuring minister and recorded them on a golden plate.

Even though he gave them, he said, "This virtue does not satisfy me. However, the charioteer guards it well; go and take it from him." Being told this, the messengers went to the charioteer and made their request.

One day, that charioteer took the king to the park in a chariot. The king played in the park all day, and when he left in the evening and mounted the chariot, before reaching the city, a storm arose at sunset. Then, the charioteer, fearing the king would get wet, gave the signal with the goad to the Sindh horses. The Sindh horses galloped swiftly.

From then on, whenever those Sindh horses went to or came from the park, they would run swiftly upon reaching that spot. Why did they run swiftly? The thought occurred to the Sindh horses: "This place must be dangerous; that is why the charioteer gave us the signal with the goad then." Therefore, they would go and come swiftly.

The charioteer thought: "Whether the king got wet or not, there is no fault in that. However, I gave the signal with the goad to these well-trained Sindh horses at an inappropriate place. Because of that, these Sindh horses now become exhausted by running swiftly back and forth. I observe the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, my virtue must be broken." Having explained this matter, he said, "Because of this reason, I have remorse regarding the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, I cannot give it to you."

Then the messengers said to the charioteer, "When you gave the signal with the goad to the Sindh horses, you had no intention to make them exhausted. Without intention, there is no kamma. If you feel remorse even for this much, how could you ever commit a transgression?" Having said this, they took the precepts from the charioteer and recorded them on a golden plate.
340:
Even though he gave them, he said, "This virtue does not satisfy me. However, the Treasurer (Seṭṭhi) guards it well; go and take it from him." Being told this, the messengers went to the Treasurer and made their request.

One day, that Treasurer went to his rice field. Without careful consideration, he had a handful of rice stalks taken from the emerging heads of rice to wear as a garland, and he wore them on his head while returning home.

Then the thought occurred to the Treasurer: "I must give the king's share from this field. I have taken a handful of rice stalks from the field before the king's share has been given. I observe the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, the virtue I guard must be broken." Having explained this matter, he said, "Because of this reason, I have remorse regarding the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, I cannot give it to you."

Then the messengers said to the Treasurer, "You had no intention to steal. Without the intention to steal, there is no such thing as taking what is not given (adinnādāna). If you feel remorse even for this much, how could you ever take the property of others?" Having said this, they took the precepts from the Treasurer and recorded them on a golden plate.

Even though he gave them, he said, "This virtue does not satisfy me. However, the Grain-measuring Minister (Doṇamāpaka) guards it well; go and take it from him." Being told this, the messengers went to that minister and made their request.

One day, while sitting at the door of the granary and measuring the rice that was the king's share, that minister took grains from the unmeasured heap to use as counters. At that moment, it rained heavily. The great minister counted the counters and said, "There are this many measured grains," then gathered the counter-grains and threw them into the measured heap, and quickly went to stand in the gatehouse. Then he thought, "Did I throw the counter-grains into the measured heap or the unmeasured heap?"

Then the thought occurred to the minister: "If I threw them into the measured heap, I have increased the king's property unfairly, and the property of the householders is lost. I observe the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, my virtue must be broken." Having explained this matter, he said, "Because of this reason, I have remorse regarding the Kuru-dhamma; therefore, I cannot give it to you."

Then the messengers said to the grain-measuring minister, "You had no intention to steal. Without the intention to steal, it is impossible to designate it as taking what is not given. If you feel remorse even for this much, how could you ever take the property of others?" Having said this, they took the precepts from the grain-measuring minister and recorded them on a golden plate.
341:
“Even though I give this, the virtue does not satisfy me. The gatekeeper, however, guards it well. Take it from the gatekeeper,” he said. The messengers went to the gatekeeper and requested it.

One day, at the city gate in the evening, that gatekeeper shouted three times. At that time, a poor man went to the forest with his younger sister to gather firewood. Upon returning, he heard the gatekeeper's voice and arrived quickly with his sister. Then the gatekeeper said to that man, “Do you not know there is a king in the city? Do you not know all the city gates will be closed? You roam the forest all day, playing and delighting in sensual pleasures with your woman.”

When the woodcutter told the gatekeeper, “This woman is not my wife, but my sister,” the gatekeeper thought, “I spoke without cause. I observe the Kuru-dhamma; my virtue might be ruined.” Having heard that reason, he said, “Because of this, remorse (kukkucca) has arisen in me regarding the Kuru-dhamma. Therefore, I cannot give it to you.”

Then the messengers said to the gatekeeper, “You spoke with such a perception; there is no breach of virtue. If you feel remorse even for this much, how would you ever tell a deliberate lie?” They took the virtue from the gatekeeper and wrote it on a golden plate.

“Even though I give this, the virtue does not satisfy me. The courtesan, however, guards it well. Take it from the courtesan,” he said. The messengers went to the courtesan and requested it.

The courtesan refused in the same manner as before. Why did she refuse? It is said that Sakka, King of Devas, wishing to test her virtue, came in the guise of a youth. Saying, “I will come back,” he gave her a thousand pieces of money and went to the deva world, not returning for three years. Fearing her virtue would be breached, she did not even accept a piece of betel nut from the hand of another man for three years.

Gradually becoming poor, the courtesan thought, “It has been three years since the man who gave me a thousand pieces left. I am poor and unable to make a living. From now on, it is proper to inform the judicial ministers and take a maintenance fee.”

Having thought so, the courtesan went to the place of judgment and said, “My lords, it has been three years since the man who gave me maintenance left. I do not even know if he is dead. I am unable to make a living; what should I do, my lords?” The judicial minister said, “If he has not come for three years, what can you do? From today onwards, take maintenance.”

Having received this judgment, as she was leaving the place of judgment, a man offered her a thousand pieces of money. At the moment she stretched out her hand to take the money, Sakka revealed himself.
342:
The courtesan said, “The man who gave me a thousand pieces three years ago has arrived. Friend, I have no need for your coins,” and she withdrew her hand.

Sakka, having transformed his body, stood in the sky, shining like the young sun. A great crowd gathered from the whole city. In the midst of the people, Sakka gave an exhortation: “I gave a thousand pieces to this woman three years ago to test her. Let those who guard virtue be like this and guard it.” He filled the courtesan's house with the seven kinds of jewels and instructed her, “From today onwards, be diligent,” and then went back to the deva world.

The courtesan refused, saying, “Without having fully earned the fee I already received, I stretched out my hand to take a fee offered by another. For this reason, the virtue does not satisfy me. Therefore, I cannot give it to you.”

Then the messengers said to the courtesan, “There is no breach of virtue merely by stretching out the hand. This virtue is indeed supremely pure.” They took the virtue from her and wrote it on a golden plate.

Thus, having written the protective virtue of these eleven persons on golden plates, they went to the city of Dantapura, gave the golden plates to King Kaliṅga, and reported the matter. King Kaliṅga, established in that Kuru-dhamma, fulfilled the Five Precepts. At that moment, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kaliṅga. The three fears were appeased. The kingdom became secure and prosperous. The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving for the rest of his life, filled the city of heaven along with his followers.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the end of the Truths, some monks became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and some Arahants.

How did he identify the Jātaka? “The courtesan at that time was Uppalavaṇṇā. The gatekeeper was the Elder Puṇṇa. The surveyor was Kaccāyana. The measurer was Moggallāna.

“The treasurer was the Elder Sāriputta. The charioteer was Anuruddha. The Brahmin was the Elder Kassapa. The viceroy was the wise Nanda.

“The chief queen was the mother of Rāhula. The mother was Māyādevī. The Kuru King was the Bodhisatta. Thus you should remember the Jātaka.”

## Observe the Five Precepts, and the world will be at peace
The Kurudhamma Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Romaka Jātaka

## The Pigeon and the Ascetic

The Teacher, while staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, told this Romaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Vassāni paññāsa samādhikāni,” concerning the attempt to kill the Blessed One. The story of the present is clear.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a pigeon and lived in a mountain cave in the forest, surrounded by many other pigeons.
343:
19. For fifty years and more,
We lived in the mountain cave, O Romaka.
Formerly, the egg-born birds came to my hand,
Without suspicion, with peaceful minds.

Birds fly to another mountain cleft.
Surely they do not regard me as before.
Perhaps they have lived elsewhere for a long time,
Or perhaps these are not the same birds.

He spoke these two verses.

O Romaka, pigeon with eyes like well-polished coral. We have lived in the mountain cave for more than fifty years. Formerly, the pigeons, being free from suspicion and having peaceful minds, would come to the place reached by my hand.

O curved-necked pigeon. Now, for what purpose do these birds fly to another mountain cleft with such effort? They surely do not regard me as they did before. Perhaps these birds, having lived in another place for a long time, do not recognize me after the passing of a long period. Or else, are these not the same pigeons who lived here for so long?

A certain ascetic of obscure virtue lived in a mountain cave, supported by a border village not far from the pigeons' dwelling place. The Bodhisatta would occasionally go to the ascetic to listen to the Dhamma. After living there for a long time, that ascetic departed, and another deceitful, matted-haired ascetic (kūṭajaṭila) came to live in that cave. The Bodhisatta, surrounded by a flock of pigeons, approached him, paid respects, and after exchanging pleasantries, wandered about the hermitage, fed near the mountain cleft, and returned to his own dwelling in the evening. The deceitful ascetic lived there for over fifty years.

Then one day, the inhabitants of the border village prepared pigeon meat and offered it to him. The ascetic, bound by the craving for taste, asked, "What kind of meat is this?" Hearing it was pigeon meat, he thought: "Many pigeons come to my hermitage; it would be proper to kill them and eat their meat."

Having so planned, he brought rice, ghee, curds, milk, pepper, and other ingredients, placed them aside, and sat at the door of his leaf-hut, hiding a club under the corner of his robe, watching for the arrival of the pigeons.

The Bodhisatta arrived surrounded by the flock of pigeons and, observing the corrupt behavior of the deceitful ascetic, thought: "This corrupt ascetic is sitting in an unusual manner."
344:
In the verse, 'samādhikāni' means 'more than'. 'Romaka' is an address to the Bodhisatta pigeon, so called because his eyes and feet were the color of well-polished coral. 'Asaṅkamānā' means that while we lived in this mountain cave for over fifty years, these egg-born birds never had a single day of suspicion toward me, and with peaceful minds, they used to come to the reach of my hand.

'Te dāni' means 'they now'. 'Vakkangā' is an address to the Bodhisatta; all birds are called 'vakkanga' (curved-necked) because they curve their necks when taking flight. 'Kimatthaṃ' means 'seeing what reason?'. 'Ussukā' means 'becoming anxious'. 'Girikandaraṃ' means another mountain cleft. 'Yathā pure' means just as these birds previously regarded me with respect and affection, they surely do not do so now. He indicates: 'The ascetic who lived here before was one, I am another; I think they regard me thus.' 'Cirappavutthā atha vā na te ime'—he asks: 'Is it because they have been away for a long time and do not recognize me as the same person after a long interval? Or are these not the same birds who had peaceful minds toward us, but other visiting birds? Why do they not approach me?'

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta, standing after having retreated, spoke the third verse:

21. We know you; we are not deluded.
You are the same person, and we are the same birds.
But your mind is corrupted towards us.
Because of your livelihood, O ascetic, we are terrified of you.

O corrupt ascetic who has gone forth for the sake of a livelihood! We know you. We are not foolish or deluded. You are indeed that same ascetic from before. We are indeed those same pigeons who lived here for a long time; we are not others. But your mind is corrupted toward this flock of pigeons. Therefore, we are terrified of you.

Thinking, "Does he wish to eat the flesh of our kinsmen? I will test this ascetic," the Bodhisatta stood downwind and smelled the scent of pigeon meat from the ascetic's body. Realizing, "This ascetic wishes to kill us and eat our meat; it is not proper to go near him," he called the flock of pigeons and departed.

The ascetic, seeing that the pigeons did not come, thought: "It would be proper to speak sweet words to them, and when they approach with trust, kill them and eat their meat."

20. O curved-necked one, why do these birds now fly away?

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta retreated and stood firm.

The deceitful ascetic, realizing "These pigeons have known me," threw the club and said, "Go, pigeon! You have escaped!" Then the Bodhisatta said to the ascetic, "You have missed me first, but you will not miss the four states of misery (apāya). If you continue to live in this hermitage, I will inform the villagers that this ascetic is a thief and have you captured."
345:
"Flee quickly!" he threatened the ascetic and departed. The deceitful ascetic, unable to stay in that hermitage, went elsewhere.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and illustrated the Truths, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the deceitful ascetic was Devadatta, the former virtuous ascetic was Sāriputta, and the leader of the pigeons was I myself."

## The original nature is destroyed, as others and I know.

End of the Romaka Jātaka.

## 8. Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka

## The Wicked Monkey

While the Teacher, the fully enlightened one who disciplines the world including the devas, was staying at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Kimatthambhisandhāya," concerning a certain mischievous monkey.

In Sāvatthī, a monkey kept by a certain clansman used to go to the elephant stable, sit on the back of a virtuous elephant, and void excrement and urine. He would walk up and down on its back. The elephant, because of its virtuous nature and perfection of patience, did not get angry. One day, a fierce young elephant stood in that elephant's place. The monkey, with the notion that "This is that same elephant," climbed onto the back of the fierce elephant. Then the elephant quickly seized the monkey with its trunk, dashed him to the ground, and crushed him with its foot.

That event became well-known among the community of monks. Then one day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, it is said that a mischievous monkey, with the notion that it was the virtuous elephant, climbed on the back. Then that fierce elephant brought him to the end of his life."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your conversation as you sit here?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, not only now is this monkey mischievous; he was so since of old," and he brought forth the past.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himalaya region as a buffalo, and having reached maturity, was endowed with strength...
346:
22. "For what purpose do you endure this suffering from this fickle-minded and treacherous one, as if he were a master who grants all desires?"

23. "Kill him with your horns, and crush him with your hooves. If there is no one to restrain them, fools will only cause more trouble."

These two verses were spoken.

Mahisarāja: Great Buffalo King. Sabbakāmadadassa: Of a master who grants all desires. Dukkhaṁ: Suffering. Titikkhasī iva: As if enduring. Kimatthaṁ: For what purpose. Abhisandhāya: Aiming for. Lahucittassa: Of one with a fickle mind. Dubbhino: Of the monkey who betrays his friend. Idaṁ dukkhaṁ: This suffering. Titikkhasī: Do you endure?

Etaṁ: That monkey. Singena ca: With your horns. Nihanāhi: Kill him. Padasā ca: With your hooves. Adhiṭṭhaha: Kill him so that he dies. Paṭisedhako: A restrainer. No cassa: If there is not. Bālā: Foolish beings. Bhiyyo: Repeatedly. Pakujjheyyuṁ: Would cause harm.

24. "Thinking [others] are just like me, he will do the same to them. There they will kill him; that will be my release."

This third verse was spoken.

Rukkhadevatā: Tree deity. Ayaṁ: This monkey. Mameva: Just like me. Evaṁ-tathā: In the same way. Maññamāno: Thinking. Aññepi: Other buffaloes as well. Karissati: He will do. Tattha: In that place. Te: Those buffaloes. Naṁ: That monkey. Vadhissanti: Will kill. Sā: That killing. Me: For me. Mutti: Will be the release from suffering and the sin of taking life. Bhavissati: It will be.

"In the past also, he was just as impulsive," the Teacher said, and then he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a buffalo in the Himalayan region. When he reached maturity, he was endowed with great strength and had a massive body. While wandering through the mountain foothills, valleys, and dense forests, he saw a pleasant spot at the foot of a tree. After taking his food, he stayed at the foot of that tree during the day.

At that time, a fickle monkey came down from the tree and climbed onto the buffalo's back. He urinated and defecated there, grabbed the horns and hung from them, and played by swinging from the tail as if it were a swing. Because the Bodhisatta was endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, he took no notice of the monkey's disrespectful behavior. The monkey did this repeatedly in the same manner.

Then one day, the deity dwelling in that tree, standing in the fork of the tree, said to the buffalo king, "Why do you endure the insults of this wicked monkey? Restrain this wicked monkey." To clarify this meaning, the deity spoke the first two verses.

Hearing those words, the Bodhisatta said, "O tree deity, if I, being superior in birth, lineage, and strength, do not endure the fault of this monkey, how will my aspiration be fulfilled? This monkey, thinking others are like me, will behave disrespectfully toward them. Then, fierce buffaloes will kill him for acting this way. When he is killed by others, I shall be free from both suffering and the sin of taking life." Thus he spoke the third verse.

After two or three days had passed, the Bodhisatta went to another place. Another fierce buffalo came and stayed in that spot.
347:
The mischievous monkey, thinking "This buffalo is the same as the good buffalo," climbed onto that buffalo's back and behaved disrespectfully in the same way. Then, that buffalo shook him off, threw him to the ground, gored him in the heart with his horns, and trampled him to pieces with his feet.

The Master, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the fierce buffalo was this rogue elephant, the mischievous monkey was this monkey, but the virtuous Buffalo King was I myself."

## The wicked create their own fate quickly.

The Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka is concluded.

## 9. Satapatta Jātaka
## Mistaking an Enemy for a Friend

While the All-Knowing Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, was residing at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Satapatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Yathā māṇavako panthe," concerning the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka.

Among the Chabbaggiya monks, the two monks Mettiya and Bhumajaka resided near Rājagaha. The two monks Assaji and Punabbasuka resided near Kīṭāgiri. These two monks, Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka, resided at Jetavana Monastery near Sāvatthī. They revived legal cases (adhikaraṇa) that had been rightfully settled and caused them to arise again.

Those monks who were the seen and close friends of Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka were also supported and encouraged by them, saying, "Friends, you are not inferior to those monks in birth, lineage, virtue, or duties. Those monks are lower than you. If you give up your own view, they will become even more prominent than you." By saying such things, they did not allow them to relinquish their views. Because of this, quarrels, disputes, strife, and contentions arose.
348:
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. Then, the All-Knowing Buddha caused the monks to assemble on that account and had the monks Paṇḍuka and Lohitaka summoned. He asked them, "Monks, is it true that you revive your own legal issues (adhikaraṇa) that have already been settled, and that you do not allow other monks to give up their views?" When they replied, "It is true, Lord," the Buddha said, "Monks, your behavior is like that of the woodpecker and the young man," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a certain family in an obscure Kāsī village. When he came of age, he did not make a living through farming or trade, but instead took five hundred robbers and became their leader. He made his living by committing acts such as highway robbery and housebreaking.

At that time, a certain wealthy merchant in Vārāṇasī died after lending a thousand kahāpaṇas to a villager without having collected them back. Later, when the merchant's wife fell ill and was lying on her deathbed, she called her son and said, "My son, your father died after lending a thousand kahāpaṇas to a certain person without collecting them. If I also die, that person will not give them to you. Go while I am still alive, have him pay, and take the money."

The young man agreed, saying, "Very well," and went to that village and received the kahāpaṇas. His mother then passed away and, due to her affection for her son, was reborn as a jackal (siṅgālī) by way of spontaneous birth (opapātika) on the path where her son would return.

At that time, the robber chief was staying on that road with his followers, plundering travelers. When the son reached the entrance of the forest, the jackal mother repeatedly crossed his path to stop him, saying, "My son, do not enter the forest. Robbers are stationed here; they will kill you and take your kahāpaṇas."

Not knowing the reason, the young man thought, "This wretched jackal is crossing my path," and he picked up clods of earth and a stick, threw them at his mother to drive her away, and entered the forest.

Then, a woodpecker (satapatta) bird cried out, "This man has a thousand kahāpaṇas in his hand! Kill this man and take those kahāpaṇas!" and flew towards the robbers.
349:
The young man, not knowing the reason for the bird's action, thought, "This is an auspicious bird; now I shall have safety," and raising his hands in reverence, he said, "Cry out, master! Cry out, master!"

The Bodhisatta, who understood the cries of all animals, saw the actions of those two and thought: "This jackal must be this man's mother. Therefore, out of fear that he will be killed and his kahāpaṇas taken, she stops him. But this woodpecker must be an enemy; therefore, he informs us to kill him and take the kahāpaṇas. This man, however, not knowing the truth, threatened and drove away his mother who wished for his welfare, yet he raises his hands in reverence to the woodpecker who wishes for his harm, thinking, 'He wishes for my welfare.' Oh, how foolish this man is!"

Indeed, this is true. For even for such Great Beings as Bodhisattas, the taking of others' property occurs by the power of an unfavorable rebirth; some also say it occurs due to the fault of the constellations (nakkhatta-dosa).

The young man continued and reached the boundary of the robbers. The Bodhisatta had him captured and asked, "Where do you live?" "I live in Vārāṇasī," he replied. "Where did you go?" "There were a thousand kahāpaṇas to be received in a certain village; I went there." "Did you receive them?" "Yes, I received them." "Who sent you?" "Master, my father is dead and my mother is ill. Thinking that if she died I would not receive them, she sent me."

"Do you know your mother's current state?" "I do not know, master." "As soon as you left, your mother passed away and, due to her love for her son, became a jackal. Fearing the danger of your death, she crossed your path and tried to stop you, but you threatened her and drove her away. The woodpecker bird, however, is your enemy. He told us to kill you and take the kahāpaṇas. In your foolishness, you thought your well-wishing mother was your enemy, and the ill-wishing woodpecker was your friend. That bird has no virtue toward you, but your mother is of great virtue. Take your kahāpaṇas and go," and he released him.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, as the Fully Enlightened One, uttered these verses:

25. Just as the young man on the path,
Thought the forest-dwelling jackal,
Who was announcing his welfare,
To be one who wished him harm;
And thought the woodpecker,
Who wished him harm, to be a well-wisher.

26. Even so, there is a certain person here,
Who is of such a nature;
When spoken to with words of benefit,
He takes them in the wrong way.

27. But those who praise him,
Or flatter him out of fear,
Those he considers as friends,
Just as the young man did the woodpecker.

(Commentary on the verses:)
*Panthe*: on the path. *Māṇavako*: the young man. *Vanagocariṃ*: dwelling in the forest. *Atthakāmaṃ*: desiring his welfare. *Pavedentiṃ*: announcing the benefit. *Siṅgāliṃ*: the jackal. *Anatthakāmāti*: as one desiring harm. *Maññati yathā*: just as he thought. *Anatthakāmaṃ*: desiring harm. *Satapattaṃ*: the woodpecker. *Atthakāmoti*: as one desiring welfare. *Maññati yathā*: just as he thought.

*Evameva*: in this very way. *Idha*: in this world. *Ekacco*: a certain. *Tādiso*: of such a nature. *Puggalo*: person. *Hoti*: there is. *Tādiso*: such a person. *Hitehi*: with things of benefit. *Vacanaṃ*: words of advice. *Vutto*: when spoken to. *Vāmato*: wrongly (from the left/bad side). *Paṭiggaṇhāti*: takes it.

*Ye ca kho*: and those persons who. *Naṃ*: that person. *Pasaṃsanti*: praise. *Bhayā*: by showing fear. *Ukkaṃsayanti vā*: or uplift/flatter. *So*: that person. *Taṃ hi*: only that person. *Māṇavo*: the young man. *Satapattaṃ*: the woodpecker. *Mittaṃ*: as a friend. *Maññate iva*: just as he thought. *Maññati*: he considers.
350:
The Satapatta bird is indeed your enemy. This Satapatta bird told us, 'Kill the youth and take the coins.' Due to your own foolishness, you thought your mother, who desires your welfare, was one who desires your harm, and you thought the Satapatta bird, who desires your harm, was one who desires your welfare. Therefore, there is no gratitude owed to you. Your mother's kindness is great. In consideration of that mother's kindness, take these thousand coins and go," he said, releasing him.

The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, after becoming Buddha—

The Identification of the Birth: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "At that time, I myself was the leader of the thieves."

## If one knows the friend and the enemy by their cause, one will be happy.

The Satapatta Jātaka is finished.

## 10. Puṭadūsaka Jātaka

## The Monkey who Destroys the Packets

The Present Story: The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Puṭadūsaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Addhā hi nūna migarājā," concerning a certain boy who destroys leaf-packets.

In Sāvatthī, a certain minister invited the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, and while giving alms in a garden, he said, "Venerable sirs, if you wish to wander in the garden before the meal, please do so."
351:
28. "Addhā hi nūna migarājā, puṭakammassa kovido.
Tathā hi puṭaṃ dūseti, aññaṃ nūna karissati."

He spoke this first verse:

"Migarājā, O King of Beasts (Monkey). Addhā hi, certainly. Puṭakammassa, in the art of making leaf-packets. Kovido nūna, you are indeed skilled. Tathā hi, for that reason. Puṭaṃ, the packet. Dūseti, you destroy. Aññaṃ, another pleasant packet. Karissati nūna, will you surely make?"

29. "Na me mātā vā pitā vā, puṭakammassa kovido.
Kataṃ kataṃ kho dūsema, evaṃ dhammamidaṃ kulaṃ."

He spoke this second verse:

"Ambho purisa, O man. Me, my. Mātā vā, mother. Pitā vā, or father. Puṭakammassa, in the art of making leaf-packets. Na kovido, are not skilled. Mayaṃ, we. Kataṃ kataṃ kho, whatever leaf-packet is made. Dūsema, we only destroy. Idaṃ kulaṃ, this race of monkeys. Evaṃ dhammaṃ, has such a nature of destroying."

30. "Yesaṃ vo ediso dhammo, adhammo pana kīdiso.
Mā vo dhammaṃ vā adhammaṃ vā, addasāma kudācanaṃ."

He spoke this third verse:

"Migarājā, O King of Beasts. Yesaṃ vo, of you all. Dhammo, the nature (virtue). Ediso, is such as this. Adhammo pana, then what would your vice (non-virtue) be like? Vo, your. Dhammaṃ vā, nature. Adhammaṃ vā, or vice. Kudācanaṃ, ever. Mā addasāma, we do not wish to see."

The monks wandered in the garden.

At that moment, the gardener climbed a tree full of leaves, plucked large leaves, and thinking, "This will be for flowers, this will be for fruits," he made packets and dropped them at the foot of the tree. The gardener's son destroyed every packet as it was dropped.

The monks reported this matter to the Buddha. The Omniscient Buddha said, "Monks, not only now has this boy destroyed packets; in the past also, he was a destroyer of packets," and he brought forth the past story.

Many monkeys lived in that garden. The gardener dropped leaf-packets in this same manner. A senior monkey destroyed every leaf-packet as it was dropped. The Bodhisatta called that senior monkey and said, "You destroy the leaf-packets dropped by the gardener; I suppose you want to make another more beautiful one," and said:

Hearing those words, the monkey said:

Upon hearing those words, the Bodhisatta:

Having said this, he rebuked the troop of monkeys and departed.

The Identification of the Birth: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, declared the Truths and identified the birth: "At that time, the boy who destroyed the packets was the senior monkey. The wise man, however, was I myself."

The Puṭadūsaka Jātaka is finished.

The Third Chapter, Udapāna Vagga.
352:
## The nature of monkeys is to destroy whatever they see.

The Puṭadūsaka Jātaka is finished.

## 4. Abbhantara Vagga

## 1. Abbhantara Jātaka

## The Parrot Messenger

The Present Story: The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Abbhantara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Abbhantaro nāma dumo," concerning the gift of mango juice by the Elder Sāriputta to the Elder Nun Bimbādevī.

When the Omniscient Buddha, having turned the Wheel of Dhamma, was residing in the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgāra) in Vesālī, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, taking five hundred Sakyan princesses, went and requested ordination, and received both the initial and higher ordination. Later, those five hundred nuns, having heard the Nandakovāda Sutta, attained Arahatship.

While the Omniscient Buddha was residing near Sāvatthī, Queen Bimbādevī, the mother of Rāhula, thought, "My husband has ordained and attained omniscience. My son has also ordained and lives near him. What shall I do staying in the house? I too will ordain, go to Sāvatthī, and live constantly seeing the Buddha and my son." She went to the nunnery, ordained, and went to Sāvatthī with her teachers and preceptors. Seeing the Buddha and her beloved son, she lived in a certain nunnery. The novice Rāhula would come and see his mother.

Then one day, the Elder Nun suffered from wind in the stomach. When her son came to see her, she was unable to come out to see him. Others came and told him of her illness. The novice Rāhula went to his mother and asked, "What do you need to get?" "Dear son, when I lived in the house, my wind ailment was cured by drinking mango juice mixed with sugar and syrup. Now we live by wandering for alms. Where shall we get such mango juice mixed with sugar and syrup?" The novice said, "If I can get it, I will bring it," and departed.
353:
The preceptor of the Venerable Rāhula was the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma. His teacher was the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. His junior uncle was the Elder Ānanda. His father was the Fully Enlightened Buddha. Such was his great fortune. Despite this, he did not go to anyone else but went to his preceptor, paid homage, and stood with a dejected expression.

Then the Elder Sāriputta asked him, "Rāhula, why do you stand there looking dejected?"

"Venerable Sir, my mother, the Theri, is suffering from a wind-ailment in her stomach," he replied.

When asked, "What would be suitable for her?" the Venerable Rāhula answered, "It is said that she would find relief with mango juice mixed with sugar-candy."

The Elder Sāriputta said, "Rāhula, let it be so, you shall have it. Do not worry."

The next day, the Elder Sāriputta took the Venerable Rāhula and entered the city of Sāvatthī. He had the novice sit in the refectory and went to the palace gate. King Kosala saw the Elder Sāriputta and invited him to sit. At that very moment, a gardener brought a bundle of sweet, ripe mangoes. The King peeled the mangoes, added sugar-candy, crushed them himself, filled the Elder's bowl, and offered it.

The Elder Sāriputta left the palace, went to the refectory, and gave it to the novice Rāhula, saying, "Take this and give it to your mother."

The novice took the mango juice and gave it to his mother. As soon as the Theri consumed it, her wind-ailment subsided.

The King also sent a man, saying, "The Elder sat here but did not consume the mango juice. Go and find out to whom he gave it." The man followed the Elder Sāriputta, learned what happened, returned, and told the King.

The King thought: "If the Fully Enlightened One had lived the household life, he would have been a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). The novice Rāhula would have been the Jewel of the Heir Apparent, and the Theri Yasodharā would have been the Jewel of a Woman. The sovereignty over the entire universe would have belonged to them. We would have been their servants. Now that they have gone forth and live depending on us, it is not right for us to be negligent towards the Fully Enlightened One and his family." From then on, King Kosala had mango juice regularly offered to the Theri.

The fact that the Elder Sāriputta offered mango juice to the Theri Bimbādevī became known among the community of monks. One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, it is said that the Elder Sāriputta satisfied the Theri Bimbādevī with mango juice."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they told him, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta has satisfied Rāhula's mother with mango juice; he did so in the past as well." Having said this, he brought forth the past story.
354:
1. There is a tree named Abbhantara, whose fruit is divine.
A woman with a pregnancy craving, having eaten it, gives birth to a Universal Monarch.
2. You too, O auspicious one, are the Chief Queen, and dear to your husband.
The King will bring for you this Abbhantara fruit.
He spoke these two verses.

"Auspicious Queen (bhadde), of which mango tree (yassa), this fruit (idaṃ phalaṃ) is fit for the use of gods (dibyaṃ). Having eaten it (bhutvā), a woman with a pregnancy craving (dohalinī nārī) gives birth to (vijāyati) a Universal Monarch (cakkavattiṃ). That tree (so dumo) is named Abbhantara (abbhantara nāma)."

"Auspicious Queen, you too (tvampi) are the Chief Queen (mahesī asi). To your husband (patino), the King of Vārāṇasī, you are also (sā cāpi) dear (piyā asi). Therefore (tasmā), for you (te), the King (rājā) will bring (āharissati) this Abbhantara mango fruit (idaṃ abbhantara phalaṃ)."

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a village of Kāsī. When he reached maturity, he studied all the arts in Takkasilā, established a household, and after his parents passed away, he renounced the world as an ascetic. He attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti) in the Himalayan region. Surrounded by a group of ascetics, he became their teacher. After a long time, he descended from the foot of the mountains to seek salt and vinegar. While wandering, he reached Vārāṇasī and took up residence in the royal park.

At that time, due to the power of the ascetics' virtue, Sakka's throne trembled. Upon reflecting, Sakka realized the cause and thought: "I will strive to make these ascetics lose their dwelling. Then, being harassed and losing their place, they will wander and fail to achieve one-pointedness of mind. In this way, I shall be at ease."

While considering what means to use, he saw this plan: "At the end of the middle watch of the night, I will enter the royal chamber of the Chief Queen, stand in the air, and say, 'Auspicious one, if you eat an internal (Abbhantara) ripe mango, you will obtain a son, and he will become a Universal Monarch.' The Queen will tell the King, and the King, hearing her words, will send someone to the park for a ripe mango. Then I will make the mangoes disappear. They will report the absence of mangoes in the King's park. When asked, 'Who is eating them?' they will say, 'The ascetics are eating them.' Hearing this, the King will have the ascetics beaten and driven away. Thus they will be harassed." He saw this strategy.

Having seen this, Sakka entered the royal chamber at the end of the middle watch, stood in the air, made his identity as the King of Gods known, and wishing to converse with the Queen—

Thus Sakka spoke these two verses to the Queen and exhorted her: "Do not be negligent; do not delay. Tell the King tomorrow." Then he returned to his own abode.
355:
The next day, the queen feigned illness, gave a signal to her attendants, and lay down.

The king, seated on his lion throne under the raised white parasol, was watching the dancers when he noticed the queen's absence and asked, "Where is the queen?" The attendants replied, "Great King, the queen is unwell."

The king went to the queen, sat by the bedside, and stroking her back, asked, "Dear queen, what ailment do you have?" She replied, "Great King, I have no other ailment, but a pregnancy craving has arisen in me." He asked, "What do you desire, dear?" She replied, "Great King, where is the mango called Abbhantara?" The king said, "Queen, I do not know what the Abbhantara mango is." The queen replied, "If I do not obtain the fruit of that Abbhantara mango, I shall die."

"If that is so, I shall have it brought; do not worry," the king comforted the queen. He then rose, went to his royal throne, summoned his ministers, and asked, "A pregnancy craving for the Abbhantara mango has arisen in the queen; what should be done?" The ministers replied, "Great King, a mango situated between two other mango trees is called an Abbhantara mango. Send someone to the garden and have them bring a fruit from a mango tree situated between two others and give it to the queen."

The king said, "Very well," and sent them to the garden, saying, "Bring such a mango." Sakka, by his divine power, made the mangoes in the garden appear as if they had been eaten and then made them disappear. The people who went for the mangoes searched the entire garden but, finding not even a single mango, went back and reported the absence of mangoes in the garden to the king.

"Who ate the mangoes?" the king asked. They replied, "Great King, the ascetics ate them." The king said, "Beat the ascetics and drive them out of the garden." The people agreed. Sakka's heart's desire was fulfilled. The queen continued to lie down for the sake of the mango.

The king, seeing no solution, gathered his ministers and Brahmins and said, "Find out the existence of the Abbhantara mango."

The Brahmins replied, "Great King, the Abbhantara mango, which is for the use of the deities, is located inside the Golden Cave in the Himavanta; thus we have heard through tradition." The king asked, "Who will be able to bring the mango from there?" They replied, "Great King, it is not possible for a human being to go there; it is appropriate to send a young parrot."
356:
At that time, there was a young parrot in the royal household who was large in body, about the size of a chariot wheel hub. He was full of strength, wise, and skilled in means. The king had the parrot brought and said, "Dear young parrot, I have been very helpful to you. You live in a golden cage, eat honey-parched grain from a golden dish, and drink sugar-water. You, too, should accomplish a task for us."

He asked, "What is it, Great King?" The king said, "Dear, a pregnancy craving for the Abbhantara mango has arisen in the queen. That Abbhantara mango is located between the Golden Mountains in the Himavanta and is for the use of the deities. It is not possible for a human being to go there; you should go and bring the mango fruit from there." He replied, "Very well, Great King, I shall bring it."

Then the king fed the parrot honey-parched grain from a golden dish, gave him sugar-water to drink, anointed the gaps between his feathers with oil refined a hundred times, and holding him with both hands, stood at the lion-window and released him into the sky.

The young parrot, showing respect to the king, flew into the sky, passed the human realm, and went to the parrots living in the first mountain range of the Himavanta. He asked, "Where is the mango called Abbhantara? Tell me its location." They replied, "We do not know; the parrots in the second mountain range will know."

Hearing their words, he flew from that first mountain range and went to the second mountain range. Likewise, he went to the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth mountain ranges. There too, the parrots living in the sixth range said, "We do not know; the parrots in the seventh mountain range will know."

He went to that seventh mountain range and asked, "Where is the mango tree called Abbhantara?" They replied, "It is in the Golden Mountain range at such-and-such a place."

When he said, "I have come for the sake of that Abbhantara mango; take me there and give me the fruit from that tree," the assembly of parrots said, "Friend, the Abbhantara mango is for the use of King Vessavaṇa; it is impossible to approach. The entire tree is covered from its roots with seven layers of iron nets."
357:
3. Striving for the sake of the master, whatever state he attains;
