The hero who sacrifices himself, I shall be one who attains that.

He spoke this verse which completes the three.

'Bhatturatthe' means in the affairs of parents or master. 'Parakkanto' means one who strives. 'Attapariccāgī' means one who sacrifices himself. 'Sūro' means a hero. 'Yaṃ ṭhānaṃ' means whatever cause of happiness. 'Adhigacchati' means he attains. 'Taṃ ṭhānaṃ' means that cause of happiness. 'Ahaṃ' means I also. 'Labhamāno bhavāmi' means I shall attain.

'A thousand Kumbhaṇḍa demons guard it; for any creature seen by those Kumbhaṇḍa demons, there is no such thing as life; it is a place like the fire that burns the world, a place like the Avīci hell. Do not desire to go to that place,' they said. If the parrot said, 'If you will not follow, then tell me the way to that place,' the parrots said, 'Then go by such and such a way.'

That parrot, by the power of what those parrots told him, marked the way well and went to that place. Not showing himself during the day, at the time when the demons fell asleep immediately after the middle watch, he went to the Abbhantara mango tree and began to climb gently through a space between the roots. The iron net made a sound like 'kiri'.

The demons woke up, saw the young parrot, and saying, 'This is a mango thief,' they caught him and planned his punishment.

One demon said, 'I will put him in my mouth and swallow him.' Another demon said, 'I will knead him with my hands, crush him, and scatter him.' Another said, 'I will split him in two, roast him on the embers, and eat him.'

The parrot, hearing the demons' plan of punishment, was not terrified and called out to those demons, 'O demons, whose men are you?' They said, 'We are the men of the Great King Vessavaṇa.' 'O demons, you are the men of one king; I too am the man of a king. The King of Bārāṇasī sent me for the sake of the Abbhantara mango fruit. I have come here having given my life to my king. He who sacrifices his life for the sake of his parents and master is reborn in the deva world. Therefore, I too, passing away from this animal birth, shall be reborn in the deva world,' he said, intending to say—
358:
In this way, the parrot preached the Dhamma to those demons with this verse. Having heard the parrot's Dhamma talk, the demons were pleased in heart and said, 'This one is righteous; it is not proper to kill him. Let us release him.' Having released the young parrot, they said, 'O young parrot, you are free; go in safety from our hands.'

'O demons, do not make my coming in vain; give me one mango fruit,' the parrot said. 'Young parrot, it is no burden for us to give you one mango fruit. However, although it is no burden, the mangoes on this tree are kept numbered. If one fruit is not found, our lives will be no more. For if Vessavaṇa becomes angry and looks but once, a thousand Kumbhaṇḍas will be broken and scattered like sesame seeds put in a hot frying pan. Therefore, we dare not give it to you. But we will tell you the place where it can be obtained,' they said.

'Let anyone give it; I only need the fruit. Tell me the place where it can be obtained,' he said. 'Between these golden mountains, an ascetic named Jotirasa lives in a leaf-hut called Kañcanapatti, performing fire sacrifices. He is the teacher of Vessavaṇa. Vessavaṇa constantly sends four mango fruits to him. Go to that ascetic,' they said.

The parrot accepted, saying 'Very well,' went to the ascetic, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Then the ascetic asked him, 'Where have you come from?' 'I have come from the King of Bārāṇasī,' he replied. 'For what purpose have you come?'

'Noble ascetic, our King's Queen has a pregnancy craving for the Abbhantara mango. Therefore, I have come to obtain the Abbhantara mango. The demons, however, did not give me the mango themselves but sent me to you,' he explained. 'In that case, you shall receive it,' the ascetic said.

Then the King Vessavaṇa sent four mango fruits to the ascetic. The noble ascetic ate two of those four mangoes. He gave one mango fruit to the young parrot to eat. When the young parrot had eaten that fruit, the ascetic put one mango fruit in a net, hung it around the young parrot's neck, and released him, saying, 'Now, go.'
359:
The young parrot brought that mango and gave it to the Queen. The Queen ate the mango and her pregnancy craving was appeased; however, because of eating that mango, she did not conceive a son. 

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the All-Enlightened Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Queen was the mother of Rāhula, the parrot was Ānanda, Sāriputta was the ascetic Jotirasa who gave the ripe mango, and the ascetic living in the garden was I myself."

## Not for self-interest, but due to circumstances, the gift from a deity, or a dream seen; none of these are truly certain.

The Abbhantara Jātaka ends.

## 2. Seyya Jātaka

## Benefit from Adversity

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Seyya Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Seyyaṃso seyya-so hoti," concerning a certain minister of the King of Kosala.

That minister was of great service to the King and accomplished all his affairs. Thinking, "This man is of great service to me," the King bestowed great wealth and status upon him. Others, unable to endure his success, slandered him to the King and caused a rift. The King, believing their words and without investigating the fault, had the virtuous and innocent minister bound in iron chains and cast into prison.

While living alone in prison, relying on his perfection of virtue, the minister attained one-pointedness of mind. Contemplating the formations (saṅkhāras) with a concentrated mind, he attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Later, the King, realizing the minister's innocence, had the chains removed and bestowed upon him wealth and status even greater than before.

Intending to pay homage to the Teacher, the minister took many flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, went to the monastery, honored and prostrated before the Blessed One, and sat in a suitable place. The All-Enlightened Buddha, engaging in friendly conversation with him, said, "We have heard that misfortune has befallen you." The minister replied, "Yes, Bhante, it did occur; however, I turned that misfortune into a benefit. While sitting in prison, I attained the Fruit of Stream-entry."

The All-Enlightened Buddha said, "Lay follower, it is not only you who has brought benefit out of misfortune; the wise of old also brought benefit out of their own misfortune." Having said this, at the minister's request, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen. When he came of age, he learned all the arts in Takkasilā. After his father's passing, he was established in the kingship and ruled in accordance with the ten royal virtues, giving alms, observing the five precepts, and performing the Uposatha duties.
360:
At that time, one of the Bodhisatta King's ministers committed an offense in the inner palace. The attendants and other ministers, becoming aware of it, reported to the King, "A certain minister has committed an offense in the inner palace." The King investigated and, knowing it to be true, summoned him and expelled him, saying, "From this day forth, do not serve me." That minister went and served a neighboring king.

The entire story is just as told below in the Mahāsīlava Jātaka (Jā. 1.1.51).

In this Jātaka as well, that neighboring king investigated three times and, believing the words of the minister, arrived at the border of the kingdom with a large retinue, intending to seize the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. Seven hundred great warriors of the King of Vārāṇasī, hearing of this, said, "Great King, it is said that a certain king is coming to destroy the country and seize Vārāṇasī. Let us go and capture him right here." The King replied, "I have no need for a kingdom obtained by harming others. Do not do anything."

The rebel king arrived and surrounded the city. The ministers approached the King and said, "Great King, do not be so patient. We will capture him." The King said, "Nothing is to be done. Open the city gates." Having said this, he sat upon the royal throne on the great upper floor, surrounded by his group of ministers.

The rebel king entered the city, striking people at the four gates, ascended the palace, captured the King who was surrounded by seven hundred ministers, had him bound in chains, and cast into prison.

While sitting in prison, the King of Vārāṇasī radiated loving-kindness toward the rebel king and developed the absorption of loving-kindness (metta-jhāna). By the power of the King of Vārāṇasī's loving-kindness, a burning sensation arose in the rebel king's body. His entire body felt as if it were being burned by a pair of torches. Oppressed by great suffering, he asked, "What could be the cause of this?" They replied, "You have cast a virtuous king into prison; therefore, this suffering has arisen."

The rebel king went and asked for the Bodhisatta's forgiveness, saying, "Let your kingdom be yours alone." He restored the kingship to the Bodhisatta and said, "From this day forth, let your enemies be my responsibility." He then carried out the King's command upon the corrupt minister and returned to his own city.

The Bodhisatta, sitting upon the throne with the white parasol raised in the decorated great palace, wishing to converse with his ministers, spoke these first two verses:
361:
6. Having said this, the Great King Kaṃsa, the conqueror of Vārāṇasī, laid down his bow and arrow and entered into self-restraint.

He spoke this third verse. 

'Vārāṇasīggaho' means the one who took possession of the city of Vārāṇasī. 'Kaṃsa' is his name. 'Mahārājā' means the Great King. 'Idaṃ' refers to these words of the verse. 'Vatvā' means having said. 'Dhanuñca' and 'kaṇḍañca' mean the bow and the arrow. 'Nikkhippa' means having laid down. 'Saṃyamaṃ' means the state of an ascetic. 'Ajjhupāgami' means he entered into.

4. He who associates with the superior becomes superior, having a portion of the noble wholesome Dhamma. By making a bond with one, I released a hundred from execution.

5. Therefore, by making a bond of loving-kindness with the whole world as one, one would go to heaven or the Brahma realm after passing away. Listen to this, O people of Kāsi.

He spoke these two verses.

'Kāsiyā' refers to the ministers of the Kāsi kingdom. 'Seyyaṃso' means one who has a portion of the noble wholesome Dhamma. 'Yo' means whoever. 'Seyyaṃ' means the noble wholesome Dhamma or a noble person. 'Upasevati' means associates with. 'So' means that person. 'Seyyaso hoti' means becomes more excellent. 'Ekena' means with one robber king. 'Sandhiṃ katvāna' means having made a bond. 'Sataṃ vajjhe' means the hundred ministers who were to be executed. 'Amocayiṃ' means I have set free.

'Tasmā' means therefore. 'Sabbena lokena' means with the entire world. 'Ekato' means as one. 'Sandhiṃ katvāna' means having made a bond. 'Pecca' means in the next life. 'Saggaṃ' means the heavenly realm or Brahma realm. 'Nigaccheyya' means one should go. 'Idaṃ' means these words. 'Kāsiyā' means you who are inhabitants of the Kāsi kingdom. 'Suṇātha' means listen.

Thus the Great Being, having praised the virtues of the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) to the multitude, renounced the white parasol in the city of Vārāṇasī, which was twelve yojanas in extent, and entered the Himālaya to lead the life of an ascetic. The Blessed One, having become the Fully Enlightened Buddha, said:

After becoming an ascetic, he developed meditative absorption (jhāna) and, with his jhāna intact, was reborn in the Brahma realm.
362:
Identification of the Birth Story: The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the robber king was Ānanda, and the King of Vārāṇasī was I myself."

## When facing danger, dwell in loving-kindness; the heat of enmity will be destroyed.

The Seyya Jātaka is concluded.

## 3. Vaḍḍhakīsūkara Jātaka

## The Great Boar General

The Teacher, the Fully Enlightened One who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Vaḍḍhakīsūkara Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Varaṃ varaṃ tvaṃ," while residing at Jetavana Monastery, concerning the Elder named Dhanuggahatissa.

King Mahākosala, the father of King Pasenadi of Kosala, when giving his daughter named Videhā to King Bimbisāra, gave the village of Kāsi, which yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand, as money for her bath powder. When King Ajātasattu killed his father, Queen Videhā also died, overcome by grief. Thereafter, King Pasenadi of Kosala thought: "Ajātasattu has killed his father. My sister also died from grief when her husband passed away. I will not give the village of Kāsi to a parricide robber." Thus, he did not give it to Ajātasattu.

Because of that village, war broke out between the two kings from time to time. Ajātasattu was young and capable, while Pasenadi was old. King Pasenadi was constantly defeated. His men were also mostly defeated.

Then King Pasenadi asked his ministers, "We are constantly defeated; what should we do?" They replied, "O Great King, the venerable ones are wise in counsel. It would be proper to listen to the conversation of the monks at Jetavana Monastery." The King then ordered his spies, "In that case, listen to the conversation of the monks at that time." From then on, the spies did as the King commanded.

At that time, two elderly elders, Elder Datta and Elder Dhanuggahatissa, lived in a leaf-hut at the edge of the monastery. Among those two, Elder Dhanuggahatissa, having slept during the first and middle watches, woke up in the last watch, tended the embers, and sat warming himself by the fire. He said, "Venerable Datta, what is the use of sleeping? Get up and sit."
363:
When Elder Datta stood up and sat down, he said to Elder Dhanuggahatissa, 'Venerable Datta, your big-bellied King of Kosala only knows how to make a pot-sized amount of rice go bad; he knows nothing of military strategy and only knows how to flee in defeat.' Elder Datta asked, 'What then should be done?' At that moment, the spies stood listening to the conversation of the two elders.

Elder Dhanuggahatissa then spoke of military strategy: 'Venerable sir, there are three types of battle arrays: the Lotus Array (Padumavyūha), the Wheel Array (Cakkavyūha), and the Wagon Array (Sakaṭavyūha). If one wishes to capture Ajātasattu, one should station men on both walls of such-and-such a mountain valley, show a weak force in front, and once it is known that he has entered the mountain pass, block the entrance. Then, by shouting from both mountain walls and attacking from the front and rear, he can be captured like a fish caught in a net or a young quail held in a fist.' The spies reported this news to the King.

Upon hearing these words, the King had the drums of war beaten, set out, and arranged the Wagon Array. He captured King Ajātasattu alive, gave his daughter Vajirakumārī to his nephew, and gave the village of Kāsi to her as 'bath-powder money' before sending them off.

This matter became well-known among the Saṅgha. Then one day, the monks raised the topic in the Dhamma Hall: 'Friends, it is said that the King of Kosala conquered King Ajātasattu through the strategy of Elder Dhanuggahatissa.' The Buddha arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?' When they replied, 'For such a discussion,' He said, 'Monks, not only now is Dhanuggahatissa skilled in military strategy; in the past also, he was indeed skilled in military strategy,' and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in the forest. At that time, a certain carpenter from a carpenter's village near Bārāṇasī went to the forest for timber, saw a piglet that had fallen into a pit, took it home, and raised it. 

When the piglet grew up, it had a large body, curved tusks, and was well-behaved. Because it was raised by the carpenter, it became known as the Carpenter's Pig (Vaḍḍhakisūkara). When the carpenter was hewing wood, the pig would turn the wood with its snout. It would fetch and carry the billhook, axe, and mallet with its mouth, and hold the end of the measuring line.

Later, the carpenter, fearing that someone might eat the pig, took it and released it in the forest. The pig entered the forest and, while looking for a safe and pleasant place, saw a large mountain gorge in a valley.
364:
That mountain gorge was filled with many pigs living in comfort. When those pigs saw the Carpenter's Pig, they approached him. The Carpenter's Pig said to them, 'I have been traveling while looking for you; indeed, I have found you. This place is delightful; I shall live right here.' They replied, 'It is true that this place is delightful, but even though it is so, there is danger here.'

He said, 'When I saw you, I thought to myself that there is no flesh or blood on the bodies of these pigs living in a place so full of food. What danger do you have here?' They replied, 'A certain tiger comes early in the morning and takes away every pig it sees.' He asked, 'Does that tiger come and take them regularly, or only occasionally?' They said, 'It takes them regularly.'

He asked, 'How many of those tigers are there?' They replied, 'There is only one.' He asked, 'Are so many of you unable to fight against a single tiger?' They said, 'We are not able.' He said, 'I shall catch that tiger. You must follow my words. Where does that tiger live?' They said, 'It lives on this mountain.'

That Carpenter's Pig, having the pigs forage during the night, arranged the strategy for battle. He said, 'Battle is of three kinds: by way of the Lotus Array, the Wheel Array, and the Wagon Array,' and he arranged it by way of the Lotus Array.

That pig knew the strategic lay of the land. Therefore, thinking, 'It is proper to arrange the battle in this place,' he placed the piglets and their parents in the center. Surrounding the piglets and parents, he placed the sows.

Surrounding the sows, he placed the young pigs. Surrounding the young pigs, he placed the old pigs. Surrounding the old pigs, he placed the long-tusked pigs. Surrounding those pigs, he placed the strong pigs capable of fighting, in groups of ten, twenty, or thirty in various positions. In front of his own position, he had a circular pit dug. Behind it, he had a pit dug that was well-formed, gradually sloping, and resembling a cave.
365:
7. You used to roam this region in the past, slaying the best of the best among the pigs. Now you flee alone and brood; O Tiger, is your strength gone today?
This is the first verse he spoke.
O Tiger! In the past, you roamed this place, oppressing the pigs and killing the very best of them. Now, you have fled alone and are moping. O Tiger, do you have no strength today?

8. In the past, these pigs, oppressed by fear and seeking shelter, would flee in all directions. Now they dwell together in assembly; where they stand, they are difficult for me to overcome today.
This is the second verse, completing the pair.
These pigs, in the past, upon seeing me, were oppressed by fear and would flee in all directions, seeking a place to hide. Now, they dwell together in one place, and where they stand, I cannot overcome them today.

While that pig named Vaḍḍhakisūkara was organizing about sixty or seventy fighting pigs, telling them not to be afraid, dawn broke.

The tiger arose, and knowing it was time, went and stood on the mountain slope in front of the pigs. He opened his eyes and looked at them. The pig named Vaḍḍhakisūkara gave a signal to the other pigs, saying, "Look back at him!" and they did so. The tiger looked up and listened; the pigs did the same. The tiger urinated; the pigs did the same. Whatever the tiger did, the pigs did likewise.

The tiger thought, "In the past, when I looked at the pigs, they could not even run away. Today, they do not flee but have become my opponents. Whatever I do, they do the same. There must be a leader among those pigs standing on that high ground. If I go today, victory is not apparent to me." Thinking thus, the tiger turned back and went to his own dwelling.

There was a wicked ascetic who used to eat the meat brought by the tiger. Seeing the tiger returning empty-handed, and wishing to speak with him, he spoke the first verse.

Hearing this, the tiger spoke the second verse:
366:
Then, the wicked ascetic, wishing to incite the tiger, said, "Do not be afraid. Go! When you roar and spring, all the pigs will be terrified and will scatter and flee." Encouraged by the wicked ascetic, the tiger became brave, went back, and stood on the mountain.

The pig named Vaḍḍhakisūkara stood between two pits. The pigs said, "Master, the great thief has returned!" He replied, "Do not be afraid, I shall catch him now." The tiger roared and pounced upon Vaḍḍhakisūkara. As the tiger pounced, the pig turned and quickly retreated into the straight-dug pit. The tiger, unable to check his momentum, flew over and fell into the very narrow mouth of the crosswise-dug pit, which was shaped like a winnowing basket, and he remained there as if with his paws folded.

The pig emerged from the pit and, with the speed of a thunderbolt, struck the tiger between the thighs with his tusks, ripping him open up to the kidneys. He tore out the five choice pieces of flesh with his tusks, whirled them over the tiger's head, and cried, "Take your enemy!" then he tossed the tiger out of the pit.

The pigs who arrived first got the tiger's meat. Those who arrived later went around sniffing the snouts of those who had eaten, asking, "What does tiger meat taste like?"

The pigs were not yet satisfied with just the tiger's death. Vaḍḍhakisūkara, seeing their demeanor, asked, "Why are you not yet satisfied?" They replied, "Master, what is the use of killing just one tiger? There is still the wicked ascetic who is capable of commanding another tiger." "Who is he?" he asked. "A certain immoral ascetic," they replied.

"I have killed even the tiger; how much easier is it to kill that ascetic?" he said. "Come, let us catch him!" and he set out with the herd of pigs.
367:
9. Homage be to the assembled community!
Having seen it myself, I speak of this wonderful friendship.
Where tusked beasts conquered a tiger;
Through unity, those with the strength of tusks are freed.

He uttered this verse which completes the three.

'Samāgatānaṃ' means those who are united. 'Saṅghānaṃ' means to the groups of pigs. 'Namo' means homage. 'Atthu' means let there be. 'Abbhutaṃ' means a wonder that has never happened before. 'Sakhyaṃ' means the state of friendship. 'Sayaṃ' means myself. 'Disvā' means having seen. 'Ahaṃ' means I. 'Vadāmi' means speak. 'Dāṭhino' means those who have tusks. 'Yattha' means in such a manner. 'Migā' means although they are pigs. 'Byagghaṃ' means the tiger. 'Jiniṃsu' means they conquered. 'Dāṭhabalesu' means among the pigs who have the strength of tusks. 'Sāmaggiyā' means through unity. 'Te' means those pigs. 'Muccare' means they are freed from the danger of death.

The wicked ascetic, wondering if the pigs had caught the tiger after a long time, went to meet them. Seeing those pigs coming, he took his requisites and fled. As the pigs pursued him, he abandoned his requisites and quickly climbed a fig tree (Udumbara).

The pigs said, "Master, the ascetic has now fled and climbed a tree." He asked, "What kind of tree did he climb?" They replied, "He climbed a fig tree." That Carpenter Pig (Vaḍḍhakīsūkara) then organized them: "Let the sows bring water, let the young pigs dig the earth, let the long-tusked pigs cut the roots, and let the remaining pigs surround and stand guard." When those pigs did as they were commanded, he himself struck the straight, thick root of the fig tree as if with an axe, felling the fig tree with a single blow.

The surrounding pigs threw the wicked ascetic to the ground, tore him into pieces, and ate him down to the bone. Then, they seated the pig named Vaḍḍhakīsūkara on the trunk of the fig tree, fetched water in the wicked ascetic's conch shell, and consecrated him as king. They also made a certain young sow his chief queen.

From that time until today, it is said that kings are seated on a fig-wood throne (udumbara-bhaddapīṭha) and consecrated with three conch shells.

The deity dwelling in that forest grove, seeing that miracle, appeared in the fork of a tree facing the pigs and—

Identifying the Jātaka: The All-Knowing Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the monk Dhanuggaha-Tissa was the pig named Vaḍḍhakīsūkara, and I myself was the tree deity."

## Through the power of unity, many pigs conquered the tiger and the ascetic, and received consecration.

The Vaḍḍhakīsūkara Jātaka ends.
368:
## 4. Siri Jātaka
## Glory

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Siri Jātaka adorned with the verse beginning with "Yaṃ ussukā saṅgharanti," concerning a certain Brahmin who stole glory.

The present story of this Siri Jātaka is detailed below in the Khadirāṅgāra Jātaka.

In the present time, however, a deity of wrong view who lived in the fourth gate-tower of Anāthapiṇḍika's house, as an act of penance, brought fifty-four crores of gold and filled the granaries, becoming friends with the merchant. Then the merchant took the deity to the Teacher. The All-Knowing Buddha preached the Dhamma to the deity. After hearing the Dhamma, the deity became a Sotāpanna.

From that time on, Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant's wealth was restored as before. Then, a certain Brahmin living in Sāvatthī, who was an expert in the signs of glory (Siri), thought: "Anāthapiṇḍika was once poor but has become wealthy again. What if I go to his house as if I wish to see him, and steal the glory from his house?"

With this thought, the Brahmin went to Anāthapiṇḍika's house. Having been welcomed and honored by the merchant, and after engaging in pleasant conversation, when asked for what purpose he had come, he looked around to see where the glory resided.

The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had a cock that was entirely white, like a polished conch shell, kept in a golden cage. Glory resided in the comb of that cock. The Brahmin, looking around and realizing that glory resided in the cock's comb, said: "Great Merchant, I teach the Vedas to five hundred young students. We and those students are troubled by a cock that crows at the wrong time. This cock of yours, I hear, crows at the right time. I have come for this cock; please give it to me." "Take it, Brahmin, I give it to you." At the very moment he said, "I give it," the glory left the cock's comb and settled in a gem-stone (maṇikkhandha) placed at the head of the bed.

The Brahmin, realizing that the glory had settled in the gem, asked for the gem as well. At the very moment he said, "I give the gem too," the glory left the gem and settled in a protective staff (ārakkhayaṭṭhi) placed at the head of the bed. The Brahmin, realizing that the glory had settled in the staff, asked for that as well. At the very moment he said, "Take it and go," the glory left the staff and settled on the head of the merchant's chief queen, named Puṇṇalakkhaṇā Devi.
369:
The Brahmin who sought to steal the glory (Siri), realizing that it had become established on the head of the Queen, thought: 'The Queen is a possession that cannot be given away. It is not possible to ask for her.' He then said, 'Great Merchant, I came to your house thinking, "I will steal your glory and depart." However, the glory was established in the comb of the cock. When that cock was given to me, it moved from the comb and became established in the Mani gem. When the Mani gem was given, it moved to the protective staff. When the staff was given, it departed from there and became established on the head of Queen Puññalakkhaṇā. This possession is one that cannot be given away; therefore, I cannot take this either. I cannot steal your glory. Let your property remain yours alone.' Having said this, he rose from his seat and departed.

Anāthapiṇḍika the merchant, thinking, 'I will report this matter to the Blessed One,' went to the monastery, paid homage to the Buddha, and sitting in a suitable place, reported everything to the Tathāgata.

The All-Knowing Buddha, hearing his words, said, 'Householder, it is not only now that glory goes elsewhere. In the past also, glory produced by those of little merit went to the feet of those with great merit.' Having said this, at the merchant's request, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in the kingdom of Kāsi. When he came of age, he studied the arts in Takkasilā. While living as a householder, he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) upon the death of his parents and went into the forest. He became an ascetic in the Himavanta region and attained the five higher powers (abhiññā) and the eight meditative attainments (samāpatti). After a long time, he went to the countryside to seek salt and acidic foods and stayed in the royal park of the King of Bārāṇasī. The next day, while going for alms, he reached the door of an elephant trainer's house. The elephant trainer, being pleased with the Bodhisatta's calm demeanor, offered him alms, invited him to stay in the park, and looked after him regularly.

At that time, a certain woodcutter, while bringing wood from the forest, was unable to reach the city gate in time. At night, he lay down to sleep at a shrine, placing his bundle of wood as a pillow. Many cocks that had been released at the shrine were sleeping in a tree nearby. Among them, the cock sleeping on the upper branch, while relieving itself at dawn, let its droppings fall on the body of the cock sleeping below. When asked, 'Who dropped excrement on my body?' the upper cock replied, 'I did.' When asked, 'Why did you do it?' he replied, 'I did it without thinking,' and then did it again. 

Then both of them became angry with each other and quarreled, saying, 'What is your power? What is your power?' Then the cock sleeping below said, 'Whoever kills me and eats my meat roasted over charcoal will receive a thousand kahāpaṇas this very morning.' The cock sleeping above said, 'Friend, do not boast so much. Whoever eats my thick fleshy meat will become King.'
370:
'If a man eats my outer meat, he will attain the position of Commander-in-chief; if a woman, she will attain the position of Chief Queen. If a layman eats the meat near my bones, he will attain the position of Treasurer; if a monk, he will become the King's advisor.'

The woodcutter, hearing the words of those cocks, thought, 'If I become King, I have no need for a thousand coins.' He climbed up quietly, caught the cock sleeping above, killed it, and put it in his waist-cloth. Thinking, 'I shall become King,' he entered the city through the open gate, plucked the cock's feathers, cleaned its belly, and gave it to his wife, saying, 'Prepare this cock meat well.' His wife prepared the meat and rice and served it to her husband, saying, 'Eat, my lord.'

The husband said, 'Dear wife, this meat has great power. By eating this cock meat, I shall become King and you shall become the Chief Queen. Let us take the rice and meat, go to the Gaṅgā, bathe, and then eat.' They placed the food basket on the bank and descended into the water to bathe. At that moment, a wave stirred by the wind came and swept away the food basket.

An elephant trainer, a high official who was bathing his elephant downstream, saw the food floating in the river. He had it picked up and opened, and asked, 'What is in here?' They replied, 'My lord, it is rice and cock meat.' He had the basket closed and sealed, and sent it to his wife with the message, 'Do not open this rice until I arrive.'

As for the woodcutter, he fled with a belly swollen from the sand and water that had entered his mouth.

At that time, an ascetic with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), who was the teacher of that elephant trainer, thought, 'My supporter does not leave his position as an elephant trainer; when will he attain prosperity?' While investigating with his divine eye, he saw that man, understood the situation, and went ahead to sit in the elephant trainer's house.

The elephant trainer arrived, paid homage to the ascetic, and sitting in a suitable place, had the food basket brought and said, 'Serve the ascetic with the meat and rice.' The ascetic took the rice, but when the meat was offered, he did not take it, saying, 'I will divide this meat.' When told, 'Please divide it, venerable sir,' he separated the thick fleshy meat and other parts into individual portions. He gave the thick fleshy meat to the elephant trainer, the outer meat to the trainer's wife, and he himself ate the meat near the bones.
371:
That ascetic, having finished his meal and about to depart, said, "On the third day from today, you will become king; do not be negligent," and then he left.

On the third day, a neighboring king arrived and surrounded the city of Bārāṇasī. The King of Bārāṇasī ordered the elephant trainer to take on the appearance of the king, mount the elephant, and fight. He himself took on an inconspicuous appearance and directed the army. While doing so, he was struck by a swift arrow and died instantly. Realizing the king's death, the elephant trainer brought out many kahāpaṇas and had the drums beaten, announcing, "Let those who desire wealth fight at the front." In a moment, the army brought the neighboring king to his end.

The ministers performed the funeral rites for the king and consulted, "Whom shall we make king?" They decided, "While our king was alive, he gave his appearance to the elephant trainer. The elephant trainer himself fought and took the kingdom. We shall give the kingship to him alone." Thus, they consecrated him as king and made his wife the chief queen. The Bodhisatta was the king's advisor.

The Omniscient Buddha, having brought forth this past story and having become fully enlightened, recited these two verses:

100. That which the diligent collect, the luckless ones' great wealth; the skilled and the unskilled alike, the meritorious one enjoys it.

101. For one who has performed merit everywhere, surpassing other living beings; many enjoyments arise, even in places that are not their source.

Whether they are skilled or unskilled, those without merit strive and collect much wealth. The meritorious person enjoys that wealth. A person with merit enjoys the fruits of their merit, even without doing any work.

Surpassing other living beings means exceeding those who have not performed merit. Many enjoyments, both animate and inanimate—such as jewels in places that are not mines, gold in places that are not gold mines, and elephants in places that are not elephant habitats—arise for the one who has performed merit. In this context, the story of the Great King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī Abhaya regarding the arising of pearls and gems in non-source areas should be told.

The Omniscient Buddha, having preached these verses, said, "Householder, for these beings, there is no other refuge like merit. For those with merit, jewels arise even in places that are not their source."

"This is a treasure that gives all desires to gods and humans; whatever they wish for, all that is obtained by this.

Beauty of complexion, beauty of voice, beauty of form, beauty of appearance, sovereignty, and a retinue; all that is obtained by this."
372:
102. A cock, gems, a staff, and women of auspicious marks; these arise for a person who is without evil and has performed merit.

For the Treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika, who was without evil and had performed merit, the cock, the gems, the staff, and the woman named Puññalakkhaṇā Devī arose.

Local kingship, empire, the pleasant happiness of a Cakkavatti king, even celestial kingship among the gods; all that is obtained by this. Human prosperity, delight in the deva world, and the attainment of Nibbāna; all that is obtained by this.

Depending on the accomplishment of friendship, for one applying themselves wisely, the mastery of knowledge, liberation, and power; all that is obtained by this.

Analytical insights, liberations, the perfection of a disciple, the enlightenment of a Paccekabuddha, and the stage of Buddhahood; all that is obtained by this.

Thus, this is of great benefit, namely the accomplishment of merit; therefore, the steadfast and wise praise the state of having performed merit.

Having preached this discourse, the Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the ascetic advisor was I, the Fully Enlightened Buddha."

## Whatever the meritless perform, the glory of it all goes to the meritorious without exception.

End of the Siri Jātaka.
373:
## 5. Maṇisūkara Jātaka
## The Gem Cave
While the Teacher, the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, was staying at Jetavana Monastery, he told this Maṇisūkara Jātaka, beginning with the verse "Dariyā sattavassāni," concerning the death of Sundarī. At that time, the Blessed One was highly honored and revered.

The present story is found in the Udāna. Here is a summary of it:

When great gain and honor, like the mighty flood of the five great rivers, arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, the sectarians of other religions lost their gain and honor. Becoming lusterless like fireflies at sunrise, they gathered together and deliberated: "Since the appearance of the ascetic Gotama, we have lost our gain and honor; no one even knows of our existence. With whom can we unite to bring disrepute to the ascetic Gotama and make his gain and honor disappear?" Then it occurred to those sectarians: "By uniting with Sundarī, we shall be able to do it."

One day, those sectarians remained silent when Sundarī entered their park and stood there after paying respects. Although she spoke repeatedly, she received no reply and asked, "Noble sirs, has someone harassed you?" They said, "Sister, do you not see the ascetic Gotama wandering about, having oppressed us and deprived us of our gain and honor?"

Sundarī said, "What should I do in this matter?" The sectarians replied, "Sister, you are beautiful and possessed of great charm. Cast disrepute upon the ascetic Gotama, make the people believe your words, and cause his gain and honor to perish." Sundarī agreed, saying "Very well," paid her respects, and departed.

From then on, taking flowers, perfumes, ointments, camphor, and pungent fruits, she would go towards Jetavana Monastery in the evening when the people were entering the city after hearing the Teacher's Dhamma. When asked, "Where are you going?" she would say, "To the presence of the ascetic Gotama; I stay with him in the same Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī)." After sleeping in another sectarian park, she would come down to the road to Jetavana early in the morning and head towards the city. When asked, "Sundarī, where have you come from?" she would say, "I have come after staying with the ascetic Gotama in the same Perfumed Chamber and delighting him with sensual pleasure."

After a few days had passed, the sectarians gave money to some rogues and said, "Go, kill Sundarī and throw her body amidst the flower refuse near the ascetic Gotama's Perfumed Chamber."
374:
The rogues did as the sectarians said.

Then the sectarians made a great clamor, saying "We do not see Sundarī," and informed the King. When asked, "Where do you have suspicion?" they said, "In these days she has been staying at Jetavana Monastery; we do not know what has happened to her there." Being permitted by the King, who said "Then go and search for her," they took their attendants, went to Jetavana, and while searching, found her amidst the flower refuse. They placed her on a litter, brought her into the city, and informed the King: "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama, wishing to conceal the evil deed committed by their teacher, killed Sundarī and threw her amidst the flower refuse."

The King said, "Then go and wander through the city." Those sectarians cried out in the streets of the city, "Look at the deed of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics!" and so on, and then returned to the palace gate. The King had Sundarī's body placed on a platform in the charnel ground and guarded.

Except for the Noble Disciples, most of the inhabitants of Sāvatthī wandered about inside and outside the city, reviling and abusing the monks, saying "Look at the deed of the Sakyaputtiya ascetics!" and such.

The monks reported that matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, "Monks, in that case, you too should rebuke those people thus:

'The speaker of untruth goes to hell, as does he who, having done a deed, says "I did not do it." Both of them, being men of base actions, become equal in the hereafter.'

Speak these words to them."

The King sent men to find out if Sundarī had been killed by others. At that time, those rogues were drinking liquor with the money they had received and were quarreling with one another. One rogue said, "You killed Sundarī with a single blow and threw her amidst the flower refuse, and now you drink liquor with the money you received. What kind of men are you?"

The King's men seized those rogues and presented them to the King. Then the King asked them, "Did you kill Sundarī?"
375:
The King summoned the heretics and had Sundarī placed on a litter. He ordered them, "Go and wander through the city, announcing: 'This Sundarī was killed by us, who desired to cast blame upon the Ascetic Gotama. There is no fault in the Ascetic Gotama, nor in the disciples of Gotama; the fault lies only with us.'" The heretics did as the King commanded.

At that time, the foolish multitude believed them. The heretics were also harassed by the punishment for murder. From that time onwards, even greater gain and honor (lābhasakkāra) arose for the Buddhas.

Then one day, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, the heretics acted with the intention, 'We will bring defilement to the Buddhas,' yet they themselves have become defiled. For the Buddhas, however, great gain and honor have arisen."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your present discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such," He said, "Monks, it is impossible to bring defilement to the Buddhas. Attempting to make the Buddhas defiled is like attempting to defile a precious gem. In the past, even when beings strove, saying 'We will defile the Jōtirasa gem,' they were unable to do so." Having said this, and being requested by the monks, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a certain village. When he came of age, he saw the peril in sensual pleasures, renounced the world, and went to the Himalayan region. Crossing three mountain ranges, he became an ascetic and lived in a leaf-hut.

Near that hermitage, there was a crystal cave. In that crystal cave lived about thirty pigs. Near the crystal cave, a lion used to roam. The reflection of that lion appeared in the crystal. Seeing the lion's reflection, the pigs were terrified and frightened, and they became thin, with little flesh and blood.

Those pigs thought, "This reflection appears because of the clarity of this crystal. Let us make this crystal defiled and dull." They went to a nearby pond, rolled in the mud, came back, and rubbed against the crystal. As the crystal was rubbed by the pigs' bristles, it became even more clear and brilliant.
376:
15. This gem is lapis lazuli (veḷuriya), flawless, pure, and beautiful.
Its glory cannot be destroyed; go away, O pigs!

He spoke this verse which fulfilled the three points:
O pigs, this gem is lapis lazuli. It is not coarse; it is free from impurities; it is beautiful. It is not possible to destroy the radiance of this gem. You all, go away!

The pigs, unable to see the reason, thought, "We will ask the ascetic the means by which we can defile the crystal." They approached the Bodhisatta, and standing in a suitable place, they spoke these verses:

13. For seven years we have lived in this cave, being thirty in number.
"We shall destroy the light of the gem," such was our counsel.

14. However much we rub the gem with mud, the gem becomes even brighter.
Now we ask you this: what do you think of our task here?

O Ascetic, for seven years, we thirty have lived in this crystal cave. "We shall destroy the radiance of the gem," such was our deliberation.

However much mud we use to rub the gem, the gem becomes exceedingly radiant. Now, we ask you, the ascetic, about this matter. In this situation, what do you think of our effort?

Then, wishing to inform those pigs, the Bodhisatta spoke:

Hearing the words of the Bodhisatta, those pigs went away just as the Bodhisatta had said. The Bodhisatta developed meditative absorption (jhāna) and was destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the ascetic."

## Evil intended for others returns to oneself; truly, the danger strikes back.
The Maṇisūkara Jātaka is finished.

## 6. Sālūka Jātaka
## The Side-Dish

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Sālūka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Mā sālūkassa pihayi," concerning a monk tempted by a fat maiden.

This present story will become clear in the Cūḷanārada Jātaka, the fourth story of the Terasa Nipāta.

The Teacher summoned that monk and asked, "Is it true, monk, that you are dissatisfied?" When the monk replied, "It is true, Blessed One," He asked, "Who has made you dissatisfied?" The monk replied, "A fat maiden, Blessed One." The Teacher said, "Monk, this woman works for your harm. In the past, too, you became the side-dish (uttaribhaṅga) for the company that came at the time of her marriage." Having said this, and being requested by the monks, He brought forth the past.
377:
Story of the Past: Long ago, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as an ox named Mahālohita. His younger brother was an ox named Cūḷalohita. Both oxen performed work for a certain family.

That family had a daughter who had reached marriageable age. A young man from another family asked for her hand in marriage. At that time, the family raised a pig named Sālūka on rice porridge, intending to use him as a special side dish (uttaribhanga) when the daughter was married into the other family. That Sālūka used to sleep under the bed.

Then one day, the ox named Cūḷalohita said, "Elder brother, we perform the work for this family, and this family lives depending on us. Despite this, these people give us only grass and straw. But they raise this pig with rice porridge and let him sleep under the bed. What on earth will he do for them?"

Mahālohita the ox replied, "Younger brother Cūḷalohita, do not envy the pig Sālūka's rice porridge. These people are raising him to make his flesh fat, intending to make Sālūka a side dish on the day of that girl's wedding. After two or three days have passed, you will see Sālūka being pulled out from under the bed, slaughtered, cut into pieces, and made into food for the guests." To convey this meaning, he uttered these two verses:

106. Do not envy Sālūka; he eats the food of distress.
Contentedly eat your chaff; this is the sign of long life.

107. Now that man, the groom's party, has arrived,
As a guest who has come to join the household.
Then you will see Sālūka lying there,
With his snout like a pestle.

"Tāta," younger brother Cūḷalohita. "Tvaṃ," you. "Sālūkassa," the pig Sālūka's. "Bhojanaṃ," food. "Mā pihayi," do not love or desire. "Sālūko," Sālūka. "Āturannāni," eats the food of those about to die. "Tvaṃ," you. "Appossukko," being without anxiety. "Bhusaṃ," the chaff mixed with grass and straw. "Khāda," eat. "Etaṃ," this matter. "Dīghāyulakkhaṇaṃ," is the cause and sign of long life.

"Idāni," now. "So," that man who is to be married. "Idha," to this house. "Yuttasevako," who has come to join and associate. "Atithī," being a guest. "Āgantvā-āgato," has come. "Bhavissati," will be. "Atha," at that time. "Musaluttaraṃ," having an upper lip like a pestle. "Sālūkaṃ," Sālūka. "Sayantaṃ," lying down to be slaughtered. "Dakkhasi," you will see.
378:
108. Having seen the slaughtered pig,
Lying with its snout like a pestle,
The old oxen thought,
"Our chaff is indeed better."

He preached this verse which completes the three.

"Vikantaṃ," crying out in distress. "Musaluttaraṃ," having an upper lip like a pestle. "Sukaraṃ," the pig. "Sayantaṃ," lying down to be slaughtered. "Disvā," having seen. "Jaraggavā," the old oxen. "Amhākaṃ," our. "Bhusaṃ iva-eva," only the chaff mixed with grass and straw. "Varaṃ," is noble. "Vicintesuṃ," they thought.

Two or three days after that was said, when the wedding took place, they slaughtered Sālūka and made him into a side dish. Seeing that destruction of Sālūka, those two oxen thought, "Only our food of grass and straw is good and noble." The Omniscient Buddha, having attained Enlightenment, uttered this third verse to show the meaning.

Identification of the Jātaka: The Omniscient Buddha, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did he identify the Jātaka? "The girl at that time has now become the fat girl (Thullakumārikā). The pig Sālūka at that time has now become the dissatisfied monk. The ox Cūḷalohita at that time has now become Ānanda. I myself was the ox Mahālohita at that time." Thus he identified the Jātaka.

## Feeding well is for this purpose; investigate and examine with wisdom.

The Sālūka Jātaka is finished.

## 7. Lābhagaraha Jātaka
## To Obtain Gains

Story of the Present: The Omniscient Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Lābhagaraha Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Nānummatto," concerning a co-resident disciple of the Venerable Sāriputta.

The co-resident disciple of Venerable Sāriputta approached the Elder, paid homage, and while sitting there, asked, "Venerable Sir, please tell me the practice that is the cause for the arising of gains. By doing what does one obtain gains such as robes?"

Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to that monk, "Friend, gains and honor arise for a monk who is endowed with four factors. One must destroy shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) within oneself, abandon the state of a monk, and though not mad, act as if mad. One must speak slanderous words (pisuṇavācā). One must be like a dancer. One must have scattered and nonsensical speech. This practice is the practice that is the cause for the arising of gains." That monk, disparaging that practice, stood up and left.

Venerable Sāriputta approached the Buddha, paid homage, and reported that matter.
379:
19. "One who is not mad but acts like a madman, not a slanderer but slanders, not a dancer but acts like one, not a gossip but acts like one—such a person gains wealth among fools. This is my instruction to you."

This first verse was spoken.

Tāta: My dear. Nānummatto: One who is not mad but behaves like a madman. Nāpisuṇo: One who is not a slanderer but practices the habit of slandering. Nānaṭo: One who is not a dancer but behaves like a dancer. Nākutūhalo: One who is not a gossip but behaves like those who speak distractedly. Satto: A being. Mūḷhesu: From those who are foolish and deluded. Or, from the midst of the foolish and deluded. Lābhaṁ: Gain. Labhate: Obtains. Esā: This. Te: To you. Dinnā: Given. Anusāsanī: Is the instruction.

The Omniscient Buddha said, "This monk has not only now criticized the conduct that leads to gain; he criticized it in the past as well." At the request of the Elder Sāriputta, he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. When he reached the age of sixteen, he mastered the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge, becoming a world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) and teaching five hundred young students.

Among those students, there was one who was endowed with virtue and good conduct.
380:
20. "Fie on that fame and wealth, O Brahmin, which is obtained through one's own downfall or through unrighteous conduct."

21. "Even if one wanders homeless with an alms bowl, that life is better than seeking wealth through unrighteousness."

These verses were spoken.

Brāhmaṇa: O Brahmin. Vinipātena vā: By destroying oneself. Adhammacaraṇena vā: Or by practicing unrighteousness. Yā vutti: Whatever acquisition of wealth. Hoti: There is. Taṁ yasalābhañca: That acquisition of fame. Taṁ dhanalābhañca: And that acquisition of wealth. Dhiratthu: I loathe it.

Adhammena: Through unrighteousness. Yā ca esanā: Whatever seeking of wealth there is. Atthi: There is. Tato: Rather than that unrighteous seeking of wealth. Anagāro: Being homeless. Pattaṁ: An alms bowl. Ādāya: Taking. Paribbaje api ce: If one were to go for alms. Esāva jīvikā: This way of life. Seyyo: Is noble.

One day, that student approached the teacher and asked about the practice that leads to gain, saying, "By what means do beings obtain gain?" The teacher replied, "My dear, beings obtain gain through four means," and spoke the verse.

Upon hearing the teacher's words, the student, wishing to criticize such gain, spoke these verses.

This student, speaking of the benefits of monkhood, renounced the world to become an ascetic. Seeking alms righteously, he developed higher spiritual powers (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and eventually passed away to the Brahma realm.
381:
*Yā cādhammena esanā*: whatever seeking of livelihood through unrighteousness there is; compared to that, this practice of wandering for alms with a bowl in the houses of others is indeed better; he shows it is a hundred times, a thousand times more excellent.

Thus, the student, having praised the virtues of renunciation, went forth and became an ascetic. Seeking alms righteously, he produced the higher knowledges and attainments, and became one destined for the Brahma realm.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the student who criticized gain was this monk; the teacher, however, was I myself."

## Madness, dancing, showing wonders, and slandering—these methods are truly the causes of much gain.

The Lābhagaraha Jātaka is finished.

## 8. Macchuddāna Jātaka
## The Benefit of Sharing Merit

The Teacher, while staying at Jetavana, told this Macchuddāna Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Agghanti macchā," concerning a certain dishonest merchant. The present story has already been told below.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of householders. When he reached maturity, he established his wealth. The Bodhisatta also had a younger brother. Later, their father passed away.
382:
22. The fish are worth more than a thousand;
There is no one who would believe this.
For me, it was seven māsakas;
I would buy that string of fish again.

He spoke this first verse.

The fish are worth a thousand coins plus seven māsakas. When asked by others, the fishermen say this. There is no one who would believe this statement. In this flock of fish, for me, the price was seven māsakas. I too would buy that string of fish.

One day, two brothers went to a certain village to trade their father's wealth. Having obtained a thousand coins, they were returning and, having moored their boat at a river landing, they ate their meal. The Bodhisatta gave the remnants of his meal to the fish in the Ganges and shared the merit of his gift with the river deity. The river deity, rejoicing in the sharing of merit, increased in divine glory and retinue. Reflecting on the increase of her own glory, she knew the cause.

The Bodhisatta spread his upper robe on the sand and fell fast asleep. The Bodhisatta's younger brother, however, was of a thievish nature. Because he wished to take the money for himself without giving it to the Bodhisatta, he made a bundle of gravel similar to the money bundle. He placed the two bundles together. When they reached the middle of the Ganges by boat, the younger brother, intending to throw the gravel bundle into the water by shaking the boat, accidentally threw the bundle of a thousand coins into the water. He then cried out, "Brother, the bundle of a thousand coins has fallen into the water! What shall we do?"

"What can we do if it has fallen into the water? Do not worry," said the Bodhisatta. The river deity thought: "This man shared the merit of his gifts with me and increased my divine glory. I will protect his property." By her power, she had a large fish swallow that bundle and she herself took charge of its protection.

The thievish brother went home thinking, "I have deceived my brother." But when he opened the bundle and saw the gravel, his heart withered with grief, and he lay down hugging the frame of his bed.

At that time, fishermen cast their net to catch fish. That fish, by the power of the deity, entered the net. The fishermen took it and entered the city to sell it. People, seeing the large fish, asked the price. The fishermen said, "Give us a thousand coins and seven māsakas and take it." The people ridiculed them, saying, "We have never even seen a fish worth a thousand." The fishermen then took the fish to the door of the Bodhisatta's house and said, "Take this fish." "What is its price?" he asked. "Give us seven māsakas and take it," they replied. "How is it that you offer it to others for one price and to me for another?" "To others, we offer it for a thousand and seven māsakas, but for you, give seven māsakas and take it."

He gave them the seven māsakas and sent the fish to his wife. While she was splitting the belly of the fish, she saw the bundle of a thousand coins and informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta looked at it, saw his own seal, and knowing it was his own property, thought: "Now these fishermen, when offering this fish to others, asked for a thousand and seven māsakas. But upon reaching us, because it was our property, they took only seven māsakas and gave it. It is impossible to make anyone believe this without them knowing the underlying reason."
383:
23. "Having given food to the fish, you dedicated the merit to me. Remembering that merit, I have guarded the honor you showed me."

(Word-for-word meaning:) To the fish (macchānaṃ), food (bhojanaṃ), having given (datvā). To me (mama), the share of the gift (dakkhiṇaṃ), you dedicated (adisi). By you (tayā), performed (kataṃ), the dedication of the share of the gift (dakkhiṇaṃ), that honor (taṃ apacitiṃ), I who remember (sarantiyā), your (tava), wealth (dhanaṃ), have guarded (rakkhitaṃ).

24. "For one with a corrupt mind, there is no prosperity, nor do the deities honor him. He who cheats his brother of his paternal inheritance is a doer of evil deeds."

She spoke this verse which completes the set of three. (Word-for-word meaning:) A doer of evil deeds (dukkaṭakammakārī), who (yo), cheats (avañcayi), his brother (bhātaraṃ), of the paternal (petti-kaṃ), inheritance (sāpateyyaṃ). For one with a corrupt mind (paduṭṭhacittassa), prosperity (phāti), does not occur (na hoti). That person (taṃ), the deities also (devatā cāpi), do not honor (na pūjayanti).

At that time, fishermen cast their nets to catch fish. By the power of the deity, that [specific] fish entered the net. The fishermen took the fish and entered the city to sell it. People saw the large fish and asked the price. The fishermen said, "Take it for one thousand kahāpaṇas and seven māshakas." The people mocked them, saying, "We have never seen a fish worth a thousand kahāpaṇas."

The fishermen took the fish to the door of the Bodhisatta's house and said, "Buy this fish." He asked, "How much is the price?" They said, "Take it for seven māshakas." He asked, "For how much did you offer it to others?" They replied, "We offered it to others for one thousand kahāpaṇas and seven māshakas." "But for you," the fishermen said, "take it for only seven māshakas."

The Bodhisatta gave the fishermen seven māshakas and sent the fish to his wife. When the Bodhisatta's wife cut open the belly of the fish, she saw a bundle of a thousand kahāpaṇas and informed the Bodhisatta.

Seeing the bundle of coins and recognizing his own seal, the Bodhisatta knew it was his property. He thought, "Just now, these fishermen were offering this fish to others for a thousand kahāpaṇas and seven māshakas. But upon reaching us, because the thousand kahāpaṇas are our own property, they took only seven māshakas and gave it to us. It would be impossible to make someone who does not know the reason believe this."

Having thought thus, he pondered, "By what means did I obtain these coins?" At that moment, the river deity, standing in the sky in a visible form, declared, "I am the deity of the Ganges. You gave the leftover food to the fish and shared the merit of your gift with me. Therefore, I have guarded your property." To demonstrate this, she spoke this verse: [Verse 23].

After saying this, the deity told the Bodhisatta all about the deceitful act committed by his younger brother, saying, "This man is now lying down with a withered heart. For one with a corrupt mind, there is no such thing as prosperity. I brought this wealth and gave it to you so that your property would not be lost. Do not give this wealth to your thieving younger brother; you alone should take it." To convey this, she spoke the third verse: [Verse 24].
384:
Thus, the deity, unwilling to give the money to the thief who had betrayed his friend, spoke in this manner. However, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "It is not right to act thus," sent five hundred kahāpaṇas to the younger brother as well.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, concluded the Jātaka. At the end of the revelation of the Truths, the merchant was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. As for the conclusion of the Jātaka: "The cheating merchant of that time was the younger brother, and I myself was the elder brother."

## Those who act with deceit and trickery are hated by both humans and deities.

The Macchuddāna Jātaka is concluded.

## 9. Nānāchanda Jātaka

## The Boons

The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the deities, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Nānāchanda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Nānāchandā mahārāja," concerning the attainment of the eight boons by the Venerable Ānanda.

The present story will become clear in the Juṇha Jātaka, the second in the Ekādasa Nipāta.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the King’s chief queen. Upon reaching maturity, he learned all the arts in Takkasilā and, after his father’s passing, attained the kingship. There was a former purohita of his father who had been removed from his position. That purohita, having become poor, lived in an old house.

Then one day, the Bodhisatta, in disguise, wandered about the city to inspect it. Thieves who had already committed their crimes were drinking liquor in a tavern. As they were going to their homes carrying pots of liquor, they saw him in the middle of the street. They said, "Hey, who are you?" and beat him, took his upper garment, made him carry the pot, and went along threatening him.

At that moment, the brahmin [purohita] came out and, standing in the middle of the street, looked at the stars. Realizing that the King had fallen into the hands of enemies, he called his wife. She said, "What is it, my lord?" and quickly came to him. Then he said to her, "Lady, our King has fallen into the power of enemies." She replied, "My lord, what is the King’s business to you? The brahmins who receive wealth from the King will know of it."
385:
25. Various are our desires, O Great King, though we live in one house.
I desire a choice village, and the brahmin lady a hundred cows.

The King, hearing the brahmin’s voice, followed for a short distance and said to the drunkards, "Masters, I am a poor man. Take my upper garment and release me." When he spoke repeatedly, they released him out of pity. The King, noting the brahmin’s residence, returned.

Then the brahmin, the former purohita, said, "Lady, our King is released from the hands of the enemy." The King, hearing that too, noted the house and ascended to the palace.

When the night had brightened, the King summoned the brahmins and asked, "Teachers, did you observe the stars during the night?" They replied, "Yes, O King." "Was it good?" the King asked. "It was good, O King," they said. "Was there no danger?" "There was none, O King."

The King said, "Summon the brahmin from such-and-such a house," and had the former purohita called. He asked, "Teacher, how were the stars last night? Did you observe them?" "Yes, O King," he replied. "Was there any danger?" "Yes, Great King. This very night, you fell into the power of enemies and were released in a mere moment."

The King said, "One who is called an expert in the stars should be like this." He had the remaining brahmins driven out of the city and said, "Brahmin, I am pleased with you. Accept a boon." The brahmin replied, "Great King, I will consult with my wife and children and then accept it." "Go, consult them and return," said the King.

The brahmin went and called his wife, son, daughter-in-law, and slave girl, and asked, "The King is giving me a boon. What shall we take?" The wife said, "Bring me a hundred cows." The son, named Chatta Māṇava, said, "Bring me a chariot yoked with four Sindh horses the color of white water-lilies." The daughter-in-law said, "Bring me all kinds of ornaments, starting with ruby earrings." The slave girl, named Puṇṇā, said, "Bring me a mortar, a pestle, and a winnowing fan." The brahmin, however, wished to take a choice village.

The brahmin went to the King, and when asked, "Brahmin, have you consulted your wife and children?" he replied, "Yes, Great King, I have. They have various desires," and spoke:

26. The son desires a chariot with noble horses, and the young woman ruby earrings.
And this wretched Puṇṇikā [the slave girl] yearns for a mortar.
386:
27. "A choice village for the Brahmin, a hundred cows for the Brahmin’s wife,
A chariot with thoroughbreds for the son, and jeweled earrings for the maiden.
And for that low-born Puṇṇikā, give her a mortar and pestle."

He spoke this verse.

Brāhmaṇassa: to the Brahmin. Gāmavaraṃ: a choice village. Brāhmaṇiyā: to the Brahmin’s wife. Gavaṃ sataṃ: a hundred cows. Puttassa: to the son. Ājaññarathaṃ: a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. Kaññāya: to the daughter-in-law. Maṇikuṇḍalaṃ: jeweled earrings. Jammiṃ yañcetaṃ puṇṇikaṃ: to that low-born maidservant named Puṇṇikā. Udukkhalaṃ: a mortar along with a winnowing tray and pestle. Paṭipādetha: please give.

He spoke these two verses:

"Great King, we who have various desires live in the same house. I desire a choice village. The Brahmin’s wife desires a hundred cows.

The son desires a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. The daughter-in-law desires jeweled earrings. And there is that low-born maidservant named Puṇṇikā; she desires a mortar along with a winnowing tray and pestle."

The King, wishing to command, "Give to everyone according to their respective desires," said:

Thus the King gave the Brahmin the wealth he yearned for and much other glory, and saying, "From this day forward, take interest in our affairs," he kept the Brahmin in his presence.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the Brahmin was Ānanda, and the King was I myself."

## Desires are truly never the same
The Nānāchanda Jātaka ends.

## 10. Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka
## Testing Virtue
The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇam," concerning a certain Brahmin who tested his own virtue.

Both the present story and...
387:
28. "Virtue is indeed good; virtue is supreme in the world.
Look at the fierce poisonous snake; because of virtue, one is not harmed."

29. "I will undertake that virtue, which is praised by the world and is peaceful.
One who practices the conduct of the Noble Ones is called 'one of virtue'."

30. "The virtuous person is dear to kinsmen and shines among friends.
With the breakup of the body, the virtuous person is reborn in a happy destination."

He spoke these verses.

Loke: in the world. Sīlaṃ eva: virtue alone. Kalyāṇam kira: is indeed good. Sīlaṃ: virtue. Anuttaraṃ kira: is indeed supreme. Passa: look. Ghoraviso nāgo: a snake with fierce poison. Sīlavāti: because of virtue. Na haññati: is not harmed.

Yena: because of which virtue. Ariyavuttisamācāro: one who practices the conduct of the Noble Ones. Loke: in the world. Sīlavā: as a virtuous person. Vuccati: is called. Sivaṃ: as being peaceful and free from danger. Anumataṃ: accepted by the wise. Taṃ sīlaṃ: that virtue. So ahaṃ: I, that person. Samādissaṃ: shall undertake.

Sīlavā: the virtuous person. Ñātīnañca: by kinsmen also. Piyo: is loved. Hoti: becomes. Sīlavā: the virtuous person. Mittesu ca: among friends also. Virocati: shines. Kāyassa bhedā paraṃ: after the breakup of the body. Sugatiṃ: in a happy destination. Upapajjati: is reborn.

The past story was already told in the Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka of the Ekanipāta below.

In this Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka, the specific details are:

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, his chaplain, wishing to test his own virtue, took one kahāpaṇa coin each day for two days from a goldsmith's tray. Then, on the third day, they seized him as a thief and took him before the King.

On the way, the chaplain saw a snake charmer making a snake play. Then the King asked him, "Why did you do such a thing?" The chaplain replied that he did it because he wanted to test his own virtue, and said:

Thus the Bodhisatta, illustrating the merits of virtue with three verses, preached the Dhamma to the King, saying, "Great King, in my house there is much wealth—inherited from my parents, earned by myself, and given by you; its end is not known. I took the coins from the goldsmith's tray only because I wished to test my virtue.

Now I have realized the inferiority of birth, lineage, and family in this world, and the supremacy of virtue alone. I shall go forth as a monk; please grant me permission to go forth." Having obtained permission, even though the King pleaded with him repeatedly, he departed and entered the Himavanta. There he became an ascetic, attained the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti), and became destined for the Brahma realm.
388:
Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, the All-Knowing One, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was the Brahmin chaplain who tested his virtue."

## Lineage is not noble; only virtue is noble
The Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka ends.

## 5. Kumbha Vagga
## 1. Surāghaṭa Jātaka
## The Foolish One
The Teacher, the All-Knowing One who disciplines the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Surāghaṭa Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Sabbakāmadadaṃ kumbhaṃ," concerning a nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer.

That nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer squandered forty crores of gold, which was the wealth of his parents, by drinking liquor, and then went to the Treasurer. The Treasurer gave him a thousand coins, saying, "Engage in trade." Having squandered that too, he went again. Again, he gave him five hundred coins. Having squandered those too, he gave the nephew, who came again, two large cloths. Having squandered those too, when he came again, the Treasurer had him seized by the neck and cast out. That nephew, being without refuge, died leaning against someone else's wall. They dragged him out and threw him away outside.

Anāthapiṇḍika the Treasurer went to the monastery and informed the All-Knowing Buddha of all that had happened to his nephew. The All-Knowing Buddha said, "Treasurer, how could you satisfy him? In the past, even when I gave him a pot that granted all desires, I could not satisfy him." Being requested by the Treasurer, He brought forth the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a treasurer's family and attained the position of treasurer after his father passed away. That treasurer had forty crores of buried treasure in his house. He also had an only son. That Bodhisatta, after performing meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna), died and became Sakka.
389:
1. Having obtained a jar, a pot that grants all desires, the drunkard prospers as long as he protects it.

2. When, drunk and arrogant, he breaks the jar through negligence, then naked and clothed in rags, the fool later suffers.

3. Even so, one who, having obtained wealth, consumes it negligently, that unwise one later grieves, like the drunkard who broke the pot.

Having preached these three verses, the Teacher identified the birth-story.

'Duttako' means the drunkard. 'Sabbakāmadadaṃ' means that which gives everything desired. 'Kumbhaṃ' refers to the jar called 'kuṭa'. 'Yāva' means for as long as. 'Naṃ' refers to that jar. 'Anupāleti' means he protects. 'Tāva' means for that long. 'So' refers to that drunkard. 'Sukhaṃ eti' means he attains happiness.

'So' refers to that drunkard. 'Yadā' means when. 'Matto ca' means he is intoxicated. 'Ditto ca' means he is reckless and wild. 'Tadā' means then. 'Pamādā' means through negligence. 'Kumbhaṃ' means the jar. 'Abbhidā' means he breaks it. 'Pacchā' means after breaking the jar. 'Bālo' means the foolish drunkard. 'Naggo ca' means sometimes being naked. 'Pottho ca' means sometimes wearing soiled rags. 'Vihaññati' means he suffers distress.

'Duttako' means the drunkard. 'Kumbhaṃ' means the jar. 'Bhitvā' means having broken. 'Pacchā' means afterwards. 'Tappati iva' means as if suffering. 'Evameva' means in this very way. 'Yo dummedho' means that foolish person. 'Dhanaṃ' means wealth. 'Laddhā' means having obtained. 'Pamatto' means being negligent. 'Paribhuñjati' means he consumes. 'So dummedho' means that foolish person. 'Pacchā' means afterwards. 'Tappati' means he grieves.

The son of the Bodhisatta blocked the road, had a pavilion built, and sat there surrounded by a great crowd, intending to drink. That merchant's son gave a thousand pieces of wealth to each of those who performed acrobatics, running, dancing, and singing. He became addicted to women, liquor, and meat. Asking, "Where is the singing? Where is the dancing? Where is the music?", he wandered about in search of festivals. Being negligent, he soon squandered forty crores of wealth, along with household goods and utensils. He became a destitute pauper, wandering about wearing soiled rags.

Sakka, while reflecting, realized his son's destitute state and, out of love for his son, came to him. Giving him a jar that grants all desires, he advised: "Dear son, protect this jar so that it does not break. As long as you have this, there will be no limit to your wealth. Be heedful." Having said this, he returned to the deva realm.

From then on, the son went about drinking. One day, while intoxicated, he tossed the jar into the air and tried to catch it, but he missed once. The jar fell to the ground and broke. From the moment the jar broke, he became poor again. Wearing soiled rags and carrying a begging bowl, he begged for food and eventually died leaning against someone else's wall.

The Perfectly Enlightened One, having brought this past story, identified the birth-story:

How did he identify the birth-story? At that time, the nephew of Anāthapiṇḍika was the drunkard who broke the jar. I myself was Sakka, the King of Devas, at that time. Thus he identified the birth-story.
390:
## The Drunkard's Ruin, Even Sakka Cannot Save Him

The Surāghaṭa Jātaka is finished.

## 2. Supatta Jātaka
## The General of the Crows

Regarding the present story: The Perfectly Enlightened One, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Jetavana monastery, told this Supatta Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Bārāṇasyaṃ mahārāja," concerning the rice mixed with fresh ghee and red-carp broth given by the Elder Sāriputta to the Elder Nun Bimbādevī.

The story is similar to the Abbhantara Jātaka mentioned below. At that time also, a wind-ailment arose in the stomach of the Elder Nun Bimbādevī. The Venerable Rāhula informed the Elder Sāriputta. The Elder Sāriputta had the Venerable Rāhula sit in the refectory, went to the palace of the King of Kosala, and brought back rice mixed with fresh ghee and red-carp broth for the Venerable Rāhula. The Venerable Rāhula brought it and gave it to his mother, the Elder Nun. As soon as the Elder Nun Bimbādevī ate it, the wind-ailment was relieved. The King sent his men to investigate and, from then on, offered such food to the Elder Nun Bimbādevī.

One day, the monks in the Dhamma Hall raised a discussion: "Friends, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) has satisfied the Elder Nun with such food." The Perfectly Enlightened One came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, not only now has Sāriputta given the desired food to Rāhula's mother; he did so in the past as well." Having said this, he brought the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the womb of a crow. When he reached maturity, he became the Crow King named Supatta, the leader of eighty thousand crows. The Chief Queen of the Crow King Supatta was named Suphassā. His General was named Sumukha. That Crow King lived near Bārāṇasī, surrounded by eighty thousand crows.

One day, while that Crow King was searching for food with his Queen Suphassā, they flew over the kitchen of the King of Bārāṇasī. The cook was standing there, having opened the pots slightly to let out the steam from the King's various fish and meat dishes and various side dishes.
391:
Queen Crow Suphassā, smelling the scent of fish and meat, desired to eat the King's food. She said nothing that day, but on the second day, when told, "Come, dear, let us go search for food," she replied, "You go; I have a certain craving." When asked, "Dear, what kind of craving is it?" she said, "I wish to eat the food of the King of Bārāṇasī. Since it may not be possible for the Great King to obtain that food, I shall give up my life." The Bodhisatta sat reflecting.

General Sumukha came and asked, "Great King, why are you troubled in mind?" The King informed him of the matter. The Crow General said, "Do not worry, Great King," and after comforting the Crow King and Queen, he said, "Stay here today; I will bring the food," and departed.
