The Crow General assembled the crows, explained the situation, and said, "Come, let us bring the food." Accompanied by the crows, he entered Bārāṇasī, stationed groups of crows near the kitchen for protection in various places, and he himself, along with eight crow warriors, sat on the kitchen roof, watching for the time when the King's food would be carried out.

He told those crows, "When the King's food is being carried, I will cause the dishes to fall. When the dishes fall, my life will be no more. Four of you take a beakful of rice, and four of you take a beakful of fish and meat, and feed Queen Suphassā and the Crow King. If asked, 'Where is the general?' say, 'He will come later.'"

Then the cook, having prepared the King's special dishes, carried them on a yoke and set out for the palace. When the cook reached the palace courtyard, the Crow General gave the signal to the crows, flew down, perched on the cook's chest, struck him with his claws, and biting the tip of the cook's nose with his beak—which was like the tip of a spear—he covered the cook's face with both wings.

The King, walking to and fro on the terrace of the magnificent palace, looked through a window and saw the crow's action. He called out to the cook, "O cook, drop the dishes and catch only the crow!" The cook dropped the dishes and caught the crow firmly. The King then said, "Bring him here."
392:
At that moment, the crows came, ate their fill, and took the remainder according to the general's instructions. Afterward, the rest of the crows came and ate what was left. Those eight crows went and fed the Crow King and his queen. Queen Crow Suphassā's craving was satisfied.

The cook brought the Crow General before the King. Then the King questioned him, "Crow, you have no shame before me, you have cut the cook's nose, broken the food dishes, and did not even protect your own life. Why did you do such a thing?"

The crow replied, "Great King, our Crow King lives near the city of Bārāṇasī. I am his general. That Crow King's queen, named Suphassā, desired to eat your royal food. The Crow King informed me of the queen's craving. I have come here having sacrificed my life in the presence of the Crow King. Now I have sent the food for the queen. My heart's desire is fulfilled. For this reason, I have done such a deed." To explain this, he spoke these verses:

4. "In Bārāṇasī, Great King, lives the Crow King,
Supatta, who is surrounded by eighty thousand crows.

5. His wife, Suphassā, has a craving; she wishes to eat
The choice royal food cooked in the King's kitchen.

6. I am sent as a messenger by them; I have come here for the King.
I have shown honor to my master; I have caused a wound on the nose."

Great King, in the city of Bārāṇasī, the Crow King named Supatta lives constantly surrounded by eighty thousand crows.

His wife, named Suphassā, has a craving. She wishes to eat the royal food, of various kinds and great value, cooked in the King's kitchen.

I am a messenger who acts for the benefit of that Crow King and Queen. I am also the one sent by the Crow King. Therefore, I have come here. I perform this act of honor and respect for my master, the Crow King. I have caused a wound on the cook's nose.

"Now, Great King, whatever punishment you wish to inflict, do so," he said. Hearing the general's words, the King thought, "We humans, even though we give great wealth, are unable to make others love us. Even though we give villages and so on, we do not find anyone who would give their life for us. This one, though a crow, sacrifices his life for the Crow King."
393:
“He is truly a virtuous person, possessing a sweet voice and being a preacher of the Dhamma.” Having gained faith in his virtues, the King honored the general with a white umbrella.

The Crow General, in turn, honored the King with the white umbrella he had received and spoke of the virtues of the Bodhisatta. The King then had the Bodhisatta summoned, and after listening to the Dhamma, he provided food to both the Crow General and the Crow King in the same manner as his own meals. To the remaining crows, he provided one ambaṇa of cooked rice daily. He himself remained established in the Bodhisatta's admonition, granted amnesty to all beings, and observed the five precepts. The admonition of Supatta, the Crow King, lasted for seven hundred years.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the King was Ānanda, the general named Sumukha was Sāriputta, the Crow Queen named Suphassā was the mother of Rāhula, and the Crow King Supatta was I myself.”

## Through life-risking effort in service, the way to success shall be found.
The Supatta Jātaka is concluded.

## 3. Kāyanibbinda Jātaka
## The Loathsome Body

While residing at Jetavana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, spoke this Kāyanibbinda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Phuṭṭhassa me,” concerning a certain man.

In the city of Sāvatthī, a certain man was afflicted by jaundice (paṇḍuroga). He was given up by the physicians, and even his wife was unable to care for him. He thought, “If I am cured of this disease, I will become a monk.” Within two or three days, he obtained suitable medicine, recovered from the illness, went to Jetavana Monastery, and requested ordination from the All-Knowing Buddha. Having received the novice ordination and the higher ordination in the presence of the Teacher, he attained Arahantship before long.

Then one day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, such and such a person, having suffered from jaundice and thinking he would ordain if he recovered, did indeed ordain and has now attained Arahantship.”
394:
“Having thought, ‘I will ordain when I recover from this disease,’ he ordained and attained Arahantship.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “For such a discussion,” He said, “Monks, it is not only now that this person has ordained and worked for his own benefit after recovering from illness; in the past, the wise also ordained and worked for their own benefit after recovering from illness in this same way.” Having said this, He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family. While living and accumulating wealth, he was afflicted by jaundice. The physicians were unable to cure him, and his wife and children were distressed. The Bodhisatta thought, “If I recover from this disease, I will become a monk.” Having obtained some suitable medicine, he recovered, entered the Himalayas, became an ascetic, and attained the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and meditative attainments (samāpatti). While dwelling in the bliss of Jhāna, he desired to utter an inspired utterance, thinking, “For so long a time, I have never before attained such bliss as this Jhāna bliss,” and spoke these three verses:

7. “Afflicted by a certain malady, suffering greatly from disease and being oppressed,
This body of mine quickly withers, like a delicate flower cast upon hot sand in the sun.

8. That which is unlovely is regarded as lovely; that which is impure is considered pure.
To one who does not see its true nature, this form, filled with various kinds of filth, appears attractive.

9. Woe to this ailing, putrid body, loathsome, impure, and subject to disease,
Wherein heedless beings are deeply infatuated and lose the path to a happy rebirth.”

(Word-by-word explanation): *Aññatarena*: by one of the ninety-eight diseases, namely jaundice. *Byādhinā*: by that which oppresses. *Rogena*: by the disease, so called because of its nature to cause pain. *Baḷhaṃ*: severely. *Phuṭṭhassa*: being afflicted. *Dukhitassa*: of one who is suffering. *Ruppato*: of me who is being oppressed. *Idaṃ kaḷevaraṃ*: this carcass of mine. *Khiddaṃ*: quickly. *Parisussati*: withers, *yathā*: just like *pupphaṃ*: a delicate flower *kataṃ*: cast *paṃsuni*: on the sand *ātape*: in the heat of the sun.

*Kaḷevaraṃ*: the putrid carcass. *Ajaññaṃ*: is not desirable. *Jaññasaṅkhātaṃ*: is designated as desirable by the foolish. *Asuciṃ*: being foul and loathsome. *Sucisammataṃ*: is considered pure by the foolish. *Nānākuṇapaparipūraṃ*: it is full of various impurities. *Apassato*: to the foolish worldling who does not see. *Jaññarūpaṃ*: it appears to have a desirable nature.

*Yattha*: in which putrid carcass. *Pajā*: beings. *Pamattā*: being heedless. *Adhimucchitā*: being excessively infatuated. *Hāpenti*: lose. *Maggaṃ*: the cause. *Sugatūpapattiyā*: of rebirth in a happy realm. *Dhiraṭṭhu*: how loathsome is *imaṃ pūtikāyaṃ*: this putrid body, *āturaṃ*: which is ailing, *jegucchiyaṃ*: which is disgusting, *asuciṃ*: which is impure, *byādhidhammaṃ*: and which is subject to disease.
395:
In this way, the Bodhisatta, reflecting upon the various ways in which the body is impure and constantly ailing, became weary of it. He cultivated the four Brahma-vihāras (sublime states) for the rest of his life and was reborn in the Brahma world.

The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and proclaimed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, many worldlings reached the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth. As for the identification of the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the ascetic.”

## Reflect upon illness and disease, and strive for your own true welfare.
The Kāyanibbinda Jātaka is concluded.

## 4. Jambukhādaka Jātaka
## The Crow and the Jackal

While residing at Veḷuvana Monastery, the All-Knowing Buddha, who disciplines the world including the devas, spoke this Jambukhādaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with “Koyaṃ bindussaro vaggū,” concerning Devadatta and Kokālika.

At that time, when Devadatta’s gains and honor had declined, Kokālika would visit the families of supporters and say, “Supporters, the Elder named Devadatta was born in the lineage of King Okkāka, the succession of Mahāsammata. He was raised in an unmixed warrior (Khattiya) lineage. He is a bearer of the Tipitaka, an attainer of Jhāna, possesses a sweet voice, and is a preacher of the Dhamma. Give to the Elder and support him,” thus speaking in praise of Devadatta.

Devadatta also would say, “The Elder Kokālika came forth from a high-born Brahmin family to ordain. He is very learned (bahussuta) and is a preacher of the Dhamma. Give to the Elder Kokālika and support him,” thus speaking in praise of Kokālika. In this way, Devadatta and Kokālika went about speaking each other’s praises and eating in the houses of supporters.
396:
11. "Only a noble person knows how to praise a noble person. O friend jackal, with a body like a young tiger, eat; I give to you."

This verse was spoken to complete the pair.

'Kula-putto va' means only a noble person. 'Kula-puttaṃ' means a noble person. 'Pasaṃsituṃ' means to praise. 'Jānāti' means knows. 'Byagghacchāpasari-vaṇṇa' means having a body like a young tiger. 'Samma' means friend jackal. 'Te' means to you. 'Ahaṃ' means I. 'Dadāmi' means give. 'Tvaṃ' means you. 'Bhuñja' means eat.

Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a conversation: "Friends, Devadatta and Kokālika go about eating by speaking false praise of each other."

The Blessed One came and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered now?" When they replied, "For such and such a discussion," He said, "Monks, not only now do Devadatta and Kokālika eat by speaking false praise of each other; in the past, they also ate in this way," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a tree deity in an obscure Jambu grove.

In that grove, a crow perched on a Jambu branch was eating ripe Jambu fruits. Then a jackal came, and looking up, he saw the crow and thought, "If I speak false praise of this crow, I shall eat the Jambu fruits." Desiring to speak of the crow's virtues, he spoke this verse:

10. "Who is this with a round and sweet voice, the best among those with voices? Perched on the Jambu branch, he warbles like a young peacock."

'Ayaṃ' means this bird. 'Bindussaro' means having a round voice. 'Vaggu' means having a sweet voice. 'Saravantānaṃ' means among birds endowed with voice. 'Uttamo' means supreme. 'Accuto' means without falling. 'Jambu-sākhāya' means on the Jambu branch. 'Moracchāpo va' means like a young peacock. 'Kūjati' means warbles. 'Ko' means what bird?

Then the crow, wishing to praise the jackal in return:

Having said this, he shook the Jambu branch and made the fruits fall. Then the deity dwelling in that Jambu tree, seeing the jackal and the crow eating Jambu fruits by speaking false praise...
397:
12. "Indeed, after a long time, I see liars gathered together—the vomit-eater and the corpse-eater, praising each other."

This third verse was spoken.

'Musāvādī' means those who are in the habit of speaking lies. 'Samāgate' means those who have met. 'Vantādañca' means the crow who eats what is vomited. 'Kuṇapādañca' means the jackal who eats corpses. 'Aññamaññaṃ' means each other. 'Pasaṃsake' means those who praise. 'Cirassaṃ' means after a long time. 'Vata' means indeed. 'Passāmi' means I see.

Having spoken this verse, the deity showed a terrifying form and drove the jackal and the crow away from the Jambu tree.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching to an end, the Buddha identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the crow was Kokālika, and the tree deity was I myself."

## Lack of virtue, flattery, and the influence on everyone

The Jambukhādaka Jātaka ends.

13. "Your shoulders are like those of a bull; your majesty is like that of a lion. O King of Beasts, homage to you! May we also get a little something?"

This verse was spoken.

'Migarāja' means King of Beasts. 'Te' means your. 'Khandho' means shoulder. 'Usabhassa khandho iva' means like the shoulder of a bull. 'Hoti' means is. 'Te' means your. 'Vijambhitaṃ' means the majesty of the body. 'Sīhassa vijambhitaṃ iva' means like the majesty of a lion. 'Hoti' means is. 'Te' means to you. 'Namo' means homage. 'Atthu' means let there be. 'Api kiñci' means even a little leftover meat. 'Mayaṃ' means we. 'Labhāmase' means wish to get.

14. "Only a noble person knows how to praise a noble person. O crow, with a neck like a peacock's, come here!"

This verse was spoken.

'Kula-putto va' means only a noble person. 'Kula-puttaṃ' means a noble person. 'Pasaṃsituṃ' means to praise. 'Pajānāti' means knows. 'Mayūragīva-saṅkāsa' means having a color like a peacock's neck. 'Vāyasa' means crow. 'Tvaṃ' means you. 'Ito' means from this place. 'Pariyāhi' means come.

## 5. Anta Jātaka

## Praising the virtue-less

While staying at the Jetavana monastery, the Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, told this Anta Jātaka, adorned with the verse starting with "Usabhassēva tē khandho," concerning those same Devadatta and Kokālika. The present story is just like the previous one.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a deity of a castor-oil tree on the outskirts of a certain village.

At that time, a dead ox in a certain village was dragged out and discarded in the castor-oil grove at the village gate. A jackal came and ate the meat of that old ox.
398:
135. Among beasts, the jackal is the lowest; among birds, the crow. Among trees, the castor-oil tree is the lowest; these three low ones have come together.

Among beasts (migānaṃ), the jackal (siṅgālo) is the lowest (anto). Among birds (pakkhiṇāṃ pana), the crow (vāyaso) is the lowest (anto). Among trees (rukkhānaṃ), the castor-oil tree (eraṇḍo) is the lowest (anto). These three (tayo) low ones (antā) have come together (samāgatā).

A certain crow arrived and perched on a castor-oil tree. Upon seeing the jackal, he thought he might get meat by speaking false praise to the jackal.

Hearing those words, the jackal—

Seeing the behavior of the crow and the jackal, the tree deity spoke the third verse:

Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, the All-Enlightened One, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, the crow was Kokālika, but I myself was the tree deity who guarded the castor-oil tree."

## Boasting of non-existent virtues, speaking as one pleases, truly everyone hates.

The Anta Jātaka is concluded.

## 6. Samudda Jātaka

## Using the ocean water sparingly

While residing at the Jetavana Monastery, the All-Enlightened Teacher, who disciplines the world including the devas, told this Samudda Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Ko nāyaṃ," concerning the Elder Upananda.

The Elder Upananda was gluttonous and very greedy. He could not be satisfied even with requisites that filled carts. During the time of entering the rains retreat, he would enter the retreat at two or three monasteries. He would leave a pair of sandals at one monastery, a walking staff at another, and a water pot at another. He himself resided at one monastery. Going to a village monastery and seeing monks with excellent requisites, he would preach the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma (the Noble Lineage). He would make those monks take up robes made of discarded rags (paṃsukūla) and then take their robes for himself. He would make them take clay bowls and then take their pleasant bowls and vessels. Filling a cart with these, he would return to the Jetavana Monastery.

Then one day, the monks started a conversation in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, Upananda of the Sakyan clan is gluttonous and very greedy. He preaches the practice to other monks and then returns with a cart filled with the monks' requisites."

The All-Enlightened Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?" When they replied, "For such a discussion," he said, "Monks, what Upananda did by preaching the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma to others is improper. First, one should be of few desires oneself, and only then should one preach the Ariyavaṃsa to others."
399:
"One should first establish oneself in what is proper; then one may instruct others. A wise man should not suffer [defilement]." (Dhammapada 158)

Having preached this verse from the Dhammapada and rebuked Upananda, the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now is Upananda greedy; in the past, he also thought that the water of the great ocean should be guarded," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a sea deity. At that time, a crow living near the sea, while flying over the ocean, went about forbidding the schools of fish and flocks of birds, saying, "Drink the ocean water in measure; drink it while guarding it."

Seeing that crow, the sea deity spoke the first verse:

16. Who is this that runs all around the salty water, forbidding the fish and sea monsters, and wearying himself among the waves?

Who is this bird (ayaṃ) that runs (paridhāvati) all around (samantā) the salty water (loṇatoyasmiṃ)? He forbids (vāreti) the fish (macche ca) and the sea monsters (makare ca), and wearies himself (vihanyati) among the waves (ūmīsu ca). Who indeed is he (ko nu)?

Hearing those words, the crow living near the sea spoke the second verse:

17. I am the bird known in all directions as the 'Endless Drinker,' the insatiable one. I wish to drink the ocean, the lord of rivers, the repository of jewels.

I (ahaṃ) am the bird (sakuṇo) known in all directions (disāsuto) as the insatiable one (atitto). I am the 'Endless Drinker' (anantapāyī) who drinks the boundless ocean water. I (ahaṃ) wish (icchāmi) to drink (pātuṃ) the ocean (samuddaṃ), the lord of rivers (saritaṃ patiṃ), the repository of excellent jewels (sāgaraṃ).

18. This great ocean ebbs and flows. Even if the whole world were to drink from it, the end of what is drunk would not be known. Indeed, the ocean is undrinkable.

This great ocean (so ayaṃ mahodadhi) both ebbs (hāyati ceva) and flows (pūrate ca). Even if the whole world (sakala-loko) were to drink (sace piveyya) its water (naṃ), even then (tathāpi), the end (anto) of the water drunk (pītaṃ) from this ocean (ito) would not be known (na nāyati). Indeed, the ocean (sāgaro) is undrinkable (apeyyo kira); no one is able to drink it to exhaustion.
400:
Hearing these words, the deity of the ocean—

Having said this, the deity displayed a terrifying form and drove away the crow that lived near the ocean.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, Upananda was the ocean crow, and I myself was the deity of the ocean."

## To Admonish Others, One Must First Practice Oneself

The Samudda Jātaka is finished.

19. "O bird flying high, traveler of the sky with wings as your vehicle,
Tell my wife with thighs like banana stems that she will have to wait a long time.

20. She does not know of this stake that has been set up, like a sword or a spear.
That fierce woman will be angry; it is that which burns me, not this stake.

21. There is a lotus-like ornament, a gold ring worth five suvaṇṇas,
And a pair of soft Kāsi cloths; let my dear wife, who desires wealth, take them and be satisfied."

He spoke these verses.

(Gloss:) Ucce: in the high sky. Ḍemāna: flying. Vihaṅgama: traveler of the sky. Pattayāna: having wings as a vehicle. Sakuṇa: O crow. Tvaṃ: you. Vāmūruṃ: to my wife whose thighs are like banana stems. Vajjāsi kho: please tell. Sā: that wife of mine. Ciraṃ kho: for a long time. Karissati: will think and wait.

Oḍḍitaṃ: set up to impale. Asiṃ ca: like a sword. Sattiṃ ca: like a spear. Idaṃ kho: this very stake. Sā: that wife. Na jānāti: does not know. Sā: that woman. Aticirāyatīti: thinking 'it is taking too long'. Mayi: towards me. Caṇḍī: being of a fierce nature. Kodhaṃ: anger. Kāhati: will feel. Taṃ: that woman's anger. Maṃ: me. Tapati: causes to burn with anxiety. Idaṃ: this stake. No tapati: does not cause me to burn.

Uppalasannāho: the lotus-like ornament. Nikkhañca: the gold ring purchased with five suvaṇṇas. Kāsikañca muduṃ vatthañca: the pair of soft cloths made in the Kāsi kingdom. Ettakaṃ: this much wealth. Ussīsake: at the head of the bed. Ohitaṃ: has been placed. Taṃ: that collection of wealth. Dhanikā: desiring wealth. Esa piyā: that dear wife. Gahetvā: having taken. Tappetu: let her be satisfied.

## 7. Kāmavilāpa Jātaka
## The Heat of Desire

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who admonishes the world including the devas, told this Kāmavilāpa Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Ucce sakuṇa ḍemāna," concerning a monk tempted by his former wife.

The story of the present is told in the Puppharatta Jātaka. The story of the past will become clear in the Indriya Jātaka, the seventh in the Aṭṭhakanipāta.

In the past story, that man was impaled on a stake while still alive.
401:
That man, remaining on that stake, saw a crow coming through the sky and, disregarding his intense pain, called out to it to send a message to his dear wife—

In this way, that man, lamenting and crying, died and was reborn in hell.

Having brought this Dhamma teaching and revealed the Truths, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied monk was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). How did He identify the Jātaka? "The wife then was the wife now, and I myself was the deity who saw the event." Thus He identified the Jātaka.

## Burned by the Heat of Desire, That Person is Greatly Exhausted

The Kāmavilāpa Jātaka is finished.
402:
## 8. Udumbara Jātaka
## The Monkey who Stole a Place

While staying at Jetavana Monastery, the Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who admonishes the world including the devas, told this Udumbara Jātaka, adorned with verses beginning with "Udumbarā cime pakkā," concerning an obscure monk.

That monk built a monastery in a small border village and lived there. The monastery was pleasant, situated at the foot of a rock slab. The area to be swept was small. Water was convenient. The alms village was neither too far nor too near. The people, being fond of him, offered alms food.

At that time, another monk, while wandering on a journey, arrived at that monastery. The resident monk performed the duties of a host for the visiting monk and, the next day, took him along to the village for alms. The people offered excellent alms food and invited them for the next day. That visiting monk, after eating for two or three days, thought, "By some means, I will trick this resident monk, drive him out, and take this monastery for myself."

Then, he asked the resident monk who had come to attend to the senior monk, "Friend, why do you not go to pay respects to the Buddha?" The resident monk replied, "Venerable sir, there is no one to look after this monastery; therefore, I have not been able to go and pay respects to the Buddha." The visitor said, "I will look after it for as long as it takes for you to go to the Buddha and return." The resident monk agreed, saying, "Very well, venerable sir," and after telling the people, "Do not neglect the elder until I return," he departed.

From then on, the visiting monk slandered the resident monk to the people, saying, "This and that are the faults of that resident monk." The other monk, having paid respects to the Buddha, returned. Then, the visiting monk did not give him a place to stay in the monastery.

That resident monk stayed in another place and went into the village for alms the next day. The people did not even show him common courtesy. That resident monk, becoming dejected, went back to Jetavana Monastery and reported the matter to the monks.

Those monks started a discussion in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, it is said that such-and-such a monk drove such-and-such a monk out of his monastery and is living there himself." The All-Knowing Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what subject are you gathered here discussing now?" When they replied, "With such-and-such a subject," He said, "Monks, not only now has that monk driven this monk from his place; in the past too, he did the same," and He brought forth the past story.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in the forest. There, during the rainy season, it rained for seven weeks. Then, a small red-faced monkey, who lived in a dry rock cave, was at the entrance of the cave in a place that was not wet—
403:
22. "Ripe are these figs (udumbara), banyans (nigrodha), and wood-apples (kapitthana). Come out and eat; why do you die of hunger?"
He spoke this first stanza.
O young monkey! These figs, these banyans, and these wood-apples are ripe. Come, come out and eat. Why do you wish to die of hunger?

23. "Thus he becomes satisfied, who respects the elders; just as I am satisfied today, having eaten ripe tree-fruits."
He spoke this second stanza.
Today, having eaten ripe fruits, I am satisfied. Likewise, whoever respects an elder becomes satisfied.

24. "That a forest-born monkey should trick a forest-born monkey—a young monkey might believe it, but not a worn-out, aged monkey."
He spoke this third stanza.
A forest-born monkey might trick another forest-born monkey; a young monkey might believe such words. But an old, aged monkey would certainly not believe it.

"In the past, you were also driven out from your place," he said, and told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a tree deity in a forest. In that forest, during the rainy season, it rained for seven consecutive days. At that time, a red-faced young monkey stayed in a dry cave. One day, he sat comfortably at the entrance of the cave where it was dry.

At that time, a large black-faced monkey, drenched by the rain and suffering from the cold, was wandering about. Seeing the young monkey sitting there, he thought, "I will drive him out by a trick and live there myself." He made his belly hang down to appear full and stood before the young monkey.

That young monkey, hearing the words of the large monkey and believing him, desired to eat the fruits. He went out and wandered here and there, but finding no fruit, he returned. Seeing the large monkey inside the cave, he stood before him to trick him back.

Upon hearing those words, the large monkey said:
"Friend young monkey, the large and small fruits in the Himālaya have fallen, drenched by the rain. This place is no longer yours. Go away."
That young monkey had to leave that place.
404:
The Omniscient Buddha, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, identified the birth: "The resident monk of today was the young monkey then; the visiting monk of today was the large black-faced monkey then; and I, the Buddha, was the tree deity then."

## Tricked by Old Habits and Deception
The Udumbara Jātaka ends.

## 9. Komāraputta Jātaka
## Association
The Omniscient Buddha, the teacher of the world including the devas, while staying at the Pubbārāma monastery, told this Komāraputta Jātaka, adorned with the stanza beginning with "Pure tuvaṃ," concerning some playful monks.

While the Omniscient Buddha was staying in the upper palace, those monks sat in the lower palace, talking about things seen and heard, engaging in quarreling and mockery. The Omniscient Buddha called the Elder Mahāmoggallāna and said, "Go and frighten those monks."

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna flew up into the air and struck the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe, shaking the palace down to its water-level foundations. Those monks, terrified by the fear of death, went out and stood outside.

The playful nature of those monks became well-known among the other monks. One day, in the Dhamma Hall, the monks raised a discussion: "Friends, some monks, having ordained in such a liberating teaching, live with playful habits and do not practice meditation on the insight of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā)."

The Omniscient Buddha arrived and asked, "Monks, what is the subject of your current discussion?" When they replied, "It is such and such a subject," he said, "Monks, not only now are they playful; in the past too, they were of a playful nature," and he told the story of the past.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a Brahmin family in a small village. They named him Komāraputta. Later, that Komāraputta renounced the world to become an ascetic and lived in the Himālaya region.
405:
25. "Formerly you played in this hermitage in the presence of the virtuous ones.
In this hermitage, you played by leaping about.
O monkey, perform your monkey-tricks;
We do not delight in your [new] virtue."

This was the first verse spoken.

O monkey! You, as in the past, play by leaping about in the presence of us who are playful. Perform your monkey-like facial distortions in the hermitage. O monkey! We do not now delight in that habit of yours which was practiced in the past. You also do not make us delight. Why is that?

26. "I have heard of the supreme purity,
Of the learned Komāraputta.
Do not think of me now as I was before.
I live devoted to meditation, friend."

This was the second verse spoken to complete the set.

Friend! I have indeed heard of the supreme purity of meditation of the ascetic Komāraputta, who is very learned. Now, do not think of me as I was in the past. Now, having found a good teacher, I live striving in meditation.

At that time, other ascetics who were playful by nature built a hermitage in the Himalaya region and lived there. Being playful, they had no preliminary practice for the kasiṇa (meditation objects). They spent their time bringing large and small fruits from the forest, laughing and playing in various ways.

In the presence of those ascetics, there was a monkey. That monkey was also very playful. He would perform various tricks for the ascetics, such as making facial distortions.

After living there for a long time, the ascetics went to human settlements to seek salt and vinegar. From the time they left, the Bodhisatta went to that place and resided there. Just as the monkey had played with those ascetics, he also played with the Bodhisatta.

The Bodhisatta snapped his fingers and gave an admonition to the monkey, saying, "One who lives in the presence of well-trained monks should be endowed with good conduct, well-restrained in body and so forth, and should strive in meditation." From that time on, the monkey became virtuous and endowed with good conduct. The Bodhisatta then went elsewhere from that place.

Then, those ascetics, having consumed salt and vinegar, returned to that place.
406:
In this context, 'mayhaṃ' is used in the sense of the instrumental case. 'Visuddhi' means the purity of meditation. 'Bahussutassa' means one who is learned because of hearing and penetrating many preliminary kasiṇa practices and the eight attainments. Addressing one of the ascetics as 'tuvaṃ', the monkey explains, "Do not recognize me now as I was before; I am not like I was previously, for I have found a teacher."

Having heard this, the ascetics spoke the third verse:

27. "Even if one sows seed on a rock,
And the rain falls, it will not grow.
You have only heard of that supreme purity;
You are far from the ground of meditation, O monkey."

This was the third verse spoken to complete the set.

O monkey! Even if one were to sow the five kinds of seeds on a stone slab, and even if the rain were to fall properly, they would not grow because it is not a fertile field. In the same way, you have only heard of the supreme purity of meditation. But because you are of animal birth, you stand far from the ground of meditation. It is not possible for you to produce meditation. Thus, they censured the monkey.

The Teacher, having brought this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the playful ascetics were these monks, but Komāraputta was I myself."

## Associate with the virtuous, and one's conduct will become good.
The Komāraputta Jātaka ends.

## 10. Vaka Jātaka
## Keeping the Precepts even without a Full Stomach

The Teacher, the All-Knowing Buddha, who admonishes the world including the devas, while residing at Jetavana Monastery, told this Vaka Jātaka, adorned with the verse beginning with "Parapāṇarodhā jīvanto," concerning an old rug.

The present story appears in detail in the Vinaya. In this Jātaka, it should be understood in brief as follows:

When the Venerable Upasena had two years of standing, he approached the Teacher with a co-resident pupil of one year. When he was censured by the All-Knowing Buddha, he paid homage and departed. He then developed insight and attained Arahantship. Endowed with virtues such as fewness of desires, he undertook the thirteen dhutaṅga (ascetic practices) and made his followers also observers of the thirteen dhutaṅga. While the Blessed One was in solitary retreat for three months, Upasena approached the Teacher with his followers. Having first received censure on account of his followers, he then received praise for not following an unrighteous agreement. The All-Knowing Buddha then granted permission, saying, "From this day forth, let the monks who carry out the dhutaṅga practices come and see me whenever they wish." Upasena then went out and informed the monks of this matter.
407:
28. Living by obstructing the lives of others, feeding on flesh and blood, the wolf undertook a vow and entered upon the Uposatha.

29. Sakka, knowing his vow, approached in the form of a goat. Having lost his penance, the blood-drinker reached out and broke his penance.

30. Even so, some here are weak in their undertaking; they make themselves light, like the wolf because of the goat.

He [the Buddha] spoke these verses.

*Parapāṇarodhā*, in the kind that delights in taking the lives of others. *Jīvanto*, living. *Maṃsalohitabhojano*, eating flesh and blood. *Vako*, the wolf. *Vataṃ*, virtue. *Samādāya*, having undertaken. *Uposathaṃ*, the Uposatha. *Upapajji*, observes.

*Sakkō*, Sakka. *Tassa*, of that wolf. *Vataṃ*, the practice. *Aññāya*, because of knowing. *Ajarūpena*, in the form of a goat. *Upāgami*, approached. *Vītatapo*, being one whose Uposatha is gone. *Vako*, the wolf. *Taṃ*, towards that goat. *Ajjhappatto*, approached. *Lohitapo*, the blood-drinking wolf. *Tapaṃ*, the Uposatha. *Bhañji yathā*, just as he destroyed.

*Evameva*, in this very same way. *Idha*, in this Dispensation. *Ekacce*, some people. *Samādānamhi*, in the merit they have undertaken. *Dubbalā*, being weak. *Ajakāraṇā*, because of the goat. *Vakovā*, like the wolf. *Attānaṃ*, themselves. *Lahuṃ*, light (frivolous). *Karonti*, they make.

From that time on, the monks, having taken up ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), approached to pay homage to the Fully Enlightened One. When the Fully Enlightened One emerged from his solitary seclusion, they discarded the refuse-heap rags (paṃsukūla) in various places and took only their own bowls and robes.

While the Fully Enlightened One was wandering through the lodgings with many monks, he saw the discarded refuse-heap rags in various places. Upon inquiring and hearing the reason, he said, "Monks, the undertaking of ascetic practices by these monks is not long-lasting; it is like the wolf's observance of the Uposatha," and he brought forth the past story.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, the king of gods. At that time, a wolf lived on a flat rock on the bank of the Ganges. Then, the floodwaters of the Ganges came and surrounded that rock. The wolf climbed up and lay on the flat rock. There was no food for him, nor was there a path to go for food. The water continued to rise.
408:
That wolf thought, "I have no food, and there is no path to go for food. For me, who is idle, it is better to observe the Uposatha than just to lie here." Having thought so, he resolved upon the Uposatha in his mind, undertook the precepts, and lay down.

Then Sakka, the king of gods, while reflecting, knew of that wolf's weak undertaking of virtue. Thinking, "I will harass this wolf," he came in the form of a goat and stood near the wolf, showing himself. The wolf, seeing the goat, thought, "I will attend to the Uposatha on another day," and getting up, he sprang to catch the goat. The goat sprang here and there and did not allow himself to be caught. The wolf, being unable to catch the goat, returned and thought, "My Uposatha is not yet broken," and lay down again as before.

Sakka, standing in the air in his own form as Sakka, rebuked and censured the wolf, saying, "What is the use of undertaking the Uposatha for one like you with such weak intention? Not knowing that I am Sakka, you merely wished to eat goat's meat," and then he returned to the celestial realm.

The Fully Enlightened One, having brought forth this past story, and having become the Buddha—

The Connection: The Fully Enlightened One, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, I myself was Sakka."

## When livelihood is difficult, keeping virtue is just like the wolf.

The Vaka Jātaka is finished.

The fifth chapter, the Kumbha Vagga, is finished.

The summary of it:
Vara-Kumbha, Supatta, Siri-vhayana, Suci-sammata, Bindusara, Usabha, Saritampati, Caṇḍī, Jarā-kapi, and the tenth with the Vaka.

Then the summary of the chapters:
Saṅkappa, Paduma, the third is Udapāna, Abbhantara, Ghaṭabheda; thus the Tika Nipāta is adorned.

The commentary on the Tika Nipāta is finished.

(The second part is finished.)
